In this lesson, we will explore fundamental concepts such as lines, angles, triangles, and circles to understand how they interact within a plane. We will then move on to calculating area and volume, which are essential for solving real-world problems involving land measurement and container capacity. Mastering these rules requires understanding the underlying logic rather than just memorizing formulas.

Lines & Angles

A line is a straight one-dimensional figure having no thickness that extends infinitely in both directions, while a ray starts at a point and goes on forever in one direction. An angle is formed when two rays share a common endpoint, known as the vertex. The most critical rule here is that angles on a straight line always add up to 180 degrees because a straight line represents a half-circle. Furthermore, angles around a single point sum to 360 degrees. In competitive exams, you will frequently encounter questions asking you to find an unknown angle given two others on a straight line or within a triangle.

Triangles

A triangle is a polygon with three edges and three vertices, making it the simplest possible polygon. The sum of all interior angles in any triangle is always 180 degrees; this is true because if you draw a line parallel to the base through the top vertex, the interior angles match up perfectly with the alternate interior angles on the straight line above. A right-angled triangle contains one angle that measures exactly 90 degrees. The Pythagorean theorem states that in a right-angled triangle, the square of the hypotenuse (the side opposite the right angle) is equal to the sum of the squares of the other two sides. This rule exists because the relationship between the legs and the hypotenuse is constant for all right triangles.

Circles

A circle is a set of points in a plane that are all at an equal distance from a fixed point called the center. The distance from the center to any point on the circle is called the radius, and the diameter is exactly twice the radius. A fundamental property is that the circumference (the perimeter) of a circle is calculated by multiplying the diameter by pi (π). The area of a circle is found by squaring the radius and multiplying it by pi. In exams, questions often involve finding the radius when given the area or vice versa, requiring you to rearrange the formula.

Area

Area measures the amount of two-dimensional space enclosed within a shape. For rectangles, the area is simply length multiplied by width because you are counting how many unit squares fit inside. For triangles, the formula is half the base times the height; this factor of one-half exists because a triangle is essentially exactly half of a rectangle with the same base and height. For circles, we use the radius squared multiplied by pi. When calculating the area of composite shapes, you must break them down into these basic forms, calculate each area separately, and then add or subtract them as needed.

Volume

Volume measures the amount of three-dimensional space an object occupies. For a cuboid (a box), volume is length times width times height. For a cylinder, which has a circular base, the volume is the area of that circle multiplied by the height. The logic is consistent: you are stacking layers of the base shape on top of each other until you reach the height. Surface area calculations for 3D shapes involve finding the area of every face and adding them together. For a cylinder, this includes the two circular bases and the rectangular side that wraps around.

Technique: The Pythagorean Shortcut
Question: A right-angled triangle has a base of 6 cm and a height of 8 cm. Find the length of the hypotenuse.
Solution:
We identify this as a classic Pythagorean theorem application where a = 6 and b = 8.
The formula is c2 = a2 + b2.
Substitute the values: c2 = 62 + 82.
Calculate squares: c2 = 36 + 64.
Add them: c2 = 100.
Take the square root of both sides: c = √(100).
Therefore, c = 10 cm. This is a very common integer triplet in exams.
Technique: Area of Composite Shapes
Question: A shape consists of a rectangle with length 10 cm and width 4 cm, topped by a semicircle with a diameter equal to the width (4 cm). Find the total area.
Solution:
First, calculate the area of the rectangle: Area = Length × Width.
10 × 4 = 40 sq cm.
Next, handle the semicircle. The diameter is 4 cm, so the radius is 2 cm.
The area of a full circle is π r2. Using π ≈ 3.14, Area = 3.14 × 22 = 12.56 sq cm.
Since it is a semicircle, divide by 2: 12.56 / 2 = 6.28 sq cm.
Total Area = Rectangle Area + Semicircle Area.
40 + 6.28 = 46.28 sq cm.

Common Traps

  • Mixing up Radius and Diameter: Students often plug the diameter into the circle area formula (π r2) instead of halving it first to get the radius. This doubles the error significantly.
  • Forgetting the 1/2 for Triangles: A frequent mistake is calculating triangle area as base times height without dividing by two, treating it like a rectangle.
  • Confusing Surface Area with Volume: In volume questions, students sometimes add the areas of the faces instead of multiplying them to find the space inside. Remember: Area is 2D (flat), Volume is 3D (space).
  • Ignoring Units: If length is in centimeters and width is in meters, you cannot multiply them directly without converting to the same unit first.

Memory Tricks

  • The "Half" Rule: Whenever you see a triangle or a semicircle, immediately think of dividing by 2. Triangles are half-rectangles; semicircles are half-circles.
  • Circle Formula Mnemonic: Remember "Pi R Squared". The shape is round like a plate (π), the distance from center to edge is radius (r), and you count the squares in that circle (r2).
  • Volume Logic: Think of volume as "Area of Base × Height". Whether it is a cube, cylinder, or prism, this logic holds true. Imagine pouring water into a container; the amount depends on how wide the bottom is and how deep you fill it.
  • Right Triangle Check: If you see a right angle symbol in a diagram, immediately think Pythagoras (a2 + b2 = c2). It is the most likely formula to apply.
Exam-Day Strategy
When facing a complex geometry problem, first draw or visualize the shape clearly. Identify every known value (sides, angles) and mark them on your scratchpad. Decide if you need to find an area, volume, or length. If you are stuck, look for hidden right angles or parallel lines that create equal alternate angles. Always write down the formula before substituting numbers to ensure you use the correct variables. Finally, check your final answer: does a negative length make sense? Is the unit consistent?
maths/statistics:
Welcome to the Statistics and Probability module, where we transform raw numbers into meaningful insights and predict future outcomes based on chance. In this lesson, you will master the four pillars of data analysis: Mean, Median, Mode, and Variance, alongside the fundamental rules of probability. By the end of this session, you will be able to calculate central tendencies, understand data spread, and solve complex probability problems with confidence.

Mean

The mean is often called the average, but it is specifically defined as the sum of all values divided by the total count of those values. This formula works because it distributes the total value equally among every data point, creating a balance point for the dataset. Examiners typically ask you to calculate the mean from a list of numbers or find an unknown variable when the mean is given.

To calculate the mean, add up every single number in your set and then divide that total by how many numbers there are. If one value changes, the mean shifts immediately because it depends on the sum of all parts. This makes the mean sensitive to extreme values, or outliers, which can pull the average higher or lower than the typical data point.

Median

The median is the middle number in a dataset that has been arranged from smallest to largest, representing the exact center of the distribution. Unlike the mean, the median does not change if you add an extremely large or small number to the list, making it robust against outliers. The examiner usually provides a list of numbers and asks for the median, often testing your ability to handle sets with an odd count versus an even count.

If your dataset has an odd number of items, the median is simply the single number sitting exactly in the middle of the sorted list. If your dataset has an even number of items, there are two numbers in the middle, so you must find their average to get the median. Always remember to sort the data first; without sorting, identifying the middle position is impossible.

Mode

The mode is the value that appears most frequently within a specific dataset, indicating the most common occurrence in your group of numbers. A dataset can have one mode, multiple modes if several values share the highest frequency, or no mode at all if every number appears exactly once. Examiners love to trick students by presenting datasets with two modes, known as bimodal distributions, or asking you to identify that a mode does not exist.

To find the mode, count how many times each unique number appears in your list and select the one with the highest count. If two numbers appear the same amount of times and that count is higher than any other, the dataset has two modes. It is crucial to distinguish between a set with no repeating numbers, which has no mode, and a set where all numbers repeat equally.

Variance

Variance measures how spread out the data points are from the mean, providing a numerical value for the dispersion of your dataset. It is calculated by finding the difference between each data point and the mean, squaring those differences to avoid negative values canceling out positives, averaging them, and taking the square root for standard deviation. The examiner often asks for the variance or standard deviation to determine if a dataset is tightly clustered or widely scattered.

The process begins by calculating the mean, then subtracting the mean from each individual data point to find the deviation. Square each of these deviations to ensure they are positive, sum them up, and divide by the number of items for population variance or by one less than the count for sample variance. Taking the square root of this result gives you the standard deviation, which is in the same units as your original data.

Probability Basics

Probability is a measure of how likely an event is to occur, expressed as a number between zero and one where zero means impossible and one means certain. The fundamental rule states that probability equals the number of favorable outcomes divided by the total number of possible outcomes in the sample space. Examiners frequently test your understanding of independent events versus dependent events and ask you to calculate probabilities for multiple steps.

For a single event, count all the ways the specific outcome can happen and divide that by the total number of distinct possibilities available. If two events are independent, meaning the first does not affect the second, you multiply their individual probabilities together to find the combined probability. If events are mutually exclusive, meaning they cannot happen at the same time, you add their probabilities together.

Calculating Mean and Median from a List
Find the mean and median of the following set of test scores: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25.
To find the mean, sum the values: 5 + 10 + 15 + 20 + 25 equals 75. Divide this sum by the count of 5 numbers to get a mean of 15. To find the median, look at the list; it is already sorted from smallest to largest. Since there are 5 numbers (an odd count), the middle number is the third one, which is 15. In this specific case, the mean and median are identical because the data is perfectly symmetric.
Dealing with Outliers in Mean vs Median
Compare the mean and median of two sets. Set A: 10, 20, 30. Set B: 10, 20, 100.
For Set A, the sum is 60 divided by 3, giving a mean of 20. The middle number in the sorted list is also 20. For Set B, the sum is 130 divided by 3, giving a mean of approximately 43.3. However, the median for Set B is still 20 because it is the middle number regardless of the extreme value 100. This demonstrates that the mean is heavily influenced by the outlier 100, while the median remains stable at 20.

Common Traps

  • Forgetting to sort data: Students often try to find the median without arranging numbers in order, leading to incorrect identification of the middle value.
  • Miscounting the divisor for variance: Using 'n' instead of 'n-1' when calculating sample variance is a frequent error that lowers the final result artificially.
  • Ignoring negative deviations in variance: Failing to square the differences before averaging them causes positive and negative numbers to cancel out, resulting in a false zero variance.
  • Multiplying dependent events incorrectly: Assuming independence when one event changes the conditions for the next, such as drawing cards without replacement.

Memory Tricks

  • The "Balance Scale" for Mean: Imagine a seesaw; the mean is the fulcrum where the total weight balances perfectly. If you add a heavy weight (outlier), the fulcrum must move toward it.
  • The "Middle Seat" for Median: Visualize students sitting in a row. The median is simply the student sitting in the exact middle seat, regardless of how tall or short they are.
  • The "Most Popular" for Mode: Think of a popularity contest; the mode is the candidate who receives the most votes, even if they do not win by a landslide.
  • The "Spread Checker" for Variance: Variance tells you how far the students are standing from the center line. If everyone stands right next to the center, variance is low. If they scatter everywhere, variance is high.
Exam-Day Strategy
When facing a statistics question on exam day, always write down the mean first if you need to find the variance or standard deviation. This saves time and prevents calculation errors later. For probability questions, draw a tree diagram mentally or on scratch paper to visualize independent versus dependent steps. If asked for the median, take one second to sort your numbers; it is faster than recalculating an average that might be skewed by outliers. Finally, read the question carefully to see if it asks for sample variance (divide by n-1) or population variance (divide by n), as this single detail determines your final answer.
quant/basic-maths:
Basic Mathematics for CLAT

CLAT quantitative techniques basic mathematics covers number systems, LCM & HCF, simplification, surds & indices, logarithms, averages, and elementary algebra — all at Class 10 level. Speed and accuracy matter more than advanced concepts.

  • Number system:
    • Digits: 0–9; face value vs place value.
    • Types: natural, whole, integers, rational, irrational, real numbers.
    • Even/odd, prime/composite, co-prime numbers.
    • Divisibility rules: 2 (last digit even), 3 (sum of digits), 4 (last two digits), 5 (ends 0/5), 6 (2 & 3), 9 (sum of digits), 10 (ends 0), 11 (alternate sum difference).
  • LCM & HCF:
    • HCF (GCD): highest common factor — prime factorization or division method.
    • LCM: lowest common multiple — prime factorization.
    • Product of two numbers = HCF × LCM.
    • LCM of fractions = LCM of numerators / HCF of denominators; HCF of fractions = HCF of numerators / LCM of denominators.
    • Word problems: bells tolling together, largest tile size, etc.
  • Simplification (BODMAS): Brackets → Orders (powers/roots) → Division/Multiplication (left to right) → Addition/Subtraction (left to right).
  • Surds & Indices:
    • a^m × a^n = a^(m+n); a^m / a^n = a^(m−n); (a^m)^n = a^(mn); (ab)^n = a^n b^n; a^0 = 1; a^−n = 1/a^n.
    • √a × √b = √(ab); √(a/b) = √a/√b; rationalize denominator.
    • Surds: √2 ≈ 1.414, √3 ≈ 1.732, √5 ≈ 2.236.
  • Logarithms: log_a(m×n) = log_a m + log_a n; log_a(m/n) = log_a m − log_a n; log_a(m^n) = n log_a m; log_a a = 1; log_a 1 = 0; change of base: log_a b = log b / log a.
  • Averages: Mean = sum/count; weighted mean; combined average; average speed = total distance/total time (not average of speeds).
Technique: LCM & HCF word problem
Three bells toll at intervals of 6, 8, 12 minutes. When toll together again?
Answer: LCM(6,8,12) = 24 minutes — they toll together again after 24 minutes.
Technique: Indices
Simplify: (2^3 × 2^4) / 2^2.
Answer: 2^(3+4−2) = 2^5 = 32.
Technique: Average speed
Car travels 60 km at 30 km/h and 60 km at 60 km/h. Average speed?
Answer: Total distance 120 km; total time = 2 + 1 = 3 h; average = 120/3 = 40 km/h (NOT 45).

Common Traps

  • Average speed ≠ average of two speeds — always total distance ÷ total time.
  • BODMAS: division and multiplication have equal precedence — go left to right.
  • Logarithm of sum ≠ sum of logarithms: log(m+n) ≠ log m + log n.
  • LCM vs HCF confusion: LCM ≥ each number; HCF ≤ each number.
  • Square root of a² = |a|, not always a.

Memory Tricks

  • Product rule: Product of two numbers = HCF × LCM.
  • Indices: Multiply → add powers; Divide → subtract powers; Power of power → multiply powers.
  • Logs: log of product = sum; log of quotient = difference; log of power = power × log.
  • Average speed: total distance ÷ total time.
CLAT Basic Maths exam strategy
Apply BODMAS strictly. Cancel common factors before multiplying. Approximate roots/decimals when options are far apart. Read units carefully. Flag calculation-heavy questions and return if time permits.
quant/numerical-ability:
Numerical Ability for CLAT

CLAT quantitative techniques numerical ability covers percentages, profit-loss, discounts, simple & compound interest, ratios & proportions, averages, time-work, speed-distance-time, mixtures, and number systems. Questions are elementary (Class 10 level) but require speed and accuracy.

  • Percentages: x% of y = (x/100)×y; increase by r% → multiply by (1+r/100); decrease by r% → multiply by (1−r/100); successive changes multiply factors.
  • Profit & Loss: Profit% = (profit/CP)×100; Loss% = (loss/CP)×100; SP = CP ± profit/loss; Discount% = (discount/MP)×100; SP = MP − discount.
  • Simple Interest: SI = (P×R×T)/100; Amount = P + SI.
  • Compound Interest: Amount = P(1+R/100)^T; CI = Amount − P.
  • Ratio & Proportion: a:b = a/b; if a:b = m:n and b:c = p:q → a:b:c = m·p : n·p : n·q (make middle term equal). Direct/inverse proportion.
  • Averages: Average = sum/count; weighted average accounts for different weights.
  • Time & Work: Work = Rate × Time; if A does work in n days, 1 day's work = 1/n; combined rate = sum of individual rates; wages divided in ratio of work done.
  • Time & Distance: Distance = Speed × Time; Speed = Distance/Time; Time = Distance/Speed; relative speed: same direction = difference; opposite direction = sum; boats: downstream = b+s, upstream = b−s.
  • Mixtures & Alligation: Cheaper quantity / Dearer quantity = (Dearer price − Mean price) / (Mean price − Cheaper price) — 'cross' method.
  • Number system: Divisibility rules, LCM & HCF, remainder, factors, digits.
Technique: Profit & Loss
CP = ₹200, SP = ₹250. Profit%?
Answer: Profit = 50; Profit% = (50/200)×100 = 25%.
Technique: Alligation
Tea at ₹60/kg and ₹90/kg mixed to get ₹75/kg. Ratio?
Answer: (90−75):(75−60) = 15:15 = 1:1.
Technique: Time & Work
A completes work in 10 days, B in 15 days. Together in how many days?
Answer: Rates: 1/10 + 1/15 = (3+2)/30 = 5/30 = 1/6 per day → 6 days.

Common Traps

  • Computing profit% on SP instead of CP — always denominator is CP for profit/loss%.
  • Simple vs compound interest — CI compounds, SI doesn't.
  • Relative speed: add for opposite directions, subtract for same direction.
  • Boats: downstream = b+s, upstream = b−s — don't swap.
  • Average speed ≠ average of speeds — total distance/total time.

Memory Tricks

  • P&L: Profit% on CP; Loss% on CP.
  • Alligation: 'Cheaper above, Dearer below' — cross subtract: (D−M):(M−C).
  • Relative speed: Towards each other = add; same direction = subtract.
  • Boats: Downstream = with stream = faster; upstream = against = slower.
CLAT Quant exam strategy
Approximate first — options are usually widely spaced. Use fractions instead of decimals (1/8 = 12.5%). Read units carefully. Mark and move on if a calculation looks lengthy — come back if time permits.
reasoning/analogy-series:
Analogy and Series questions are the backbone of the Logical Reasoning section in competitive exams like CLAT. These problems test your ability to identify underlying relationships between words or numbers and detect hidden patterns within sequences. Mastering these skills requires a shift from rote memorization to active pattern recognition, allowing you to solve complex puzzles under time pressure.

Analogy: Understanding Relationships

An Analogy is a question type that asks you to identify the relationship between two given terms and apply that same logic to a pair of unknown terms. The core principle here is consistency; if "A is to B as C is to D," the logical connection must be identical in both halves.

The most common relationships tested include synonyms, antonyms, part-to-whole, cause-and-effect, and functional associations. For instance, a "Heart" is to "Body" as a "Wheel" is to "Car." This follows a part-to-whole pattern. Conversely, "Hot" is to "Cold" as "Day" is to "Night," which follows an antonym or opposite relationship.

Examiners typically present these in the format A : B :: C : D. Your task is to find the missing term (D) when A, B, and C are provided, or to identify the pair that does not fit the established group. The key to solving these quickly is to categorize the relationship immediately upon reading the first pair.

Series Completion: Decoding Patterns

A Number Series presents a sequence of digits where you must determine the rule governing the progression and find the missing number or the next term in the list. The fundamental rule is that every series follows a mathematical operation, such as addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, or a combination thereof.

The most basic pattern is an arithmetic progression where a constant value is added or subtracted at each step. For example, in the sequence 2, 5, 8, 11, the rule is "+3." More complex series involve alternating operations, such as adding 2 and then multiplying by 2. Another frequent pattern involves square numbers (1, 4, 9, 16) or cube numbers (1, 8, 27), where the position of the number in the sequence dictates its value.

Letter Series follow similar logic but use alphabetical positions. The alphabet is treated as a continuous line from A to Z. Patterns often involve skipping letters (e.g., every second letter: B, D, F) or moving backward and forward based on a specific count. Sometimes, the pattern involves reversing the alphabet order (Z to A), which requires knowing that A=1 and Z=26.

Odd One Out: Finding the Discrepancy

The Odd One Out question presents a set of four items where three share a common characteristic or follow a specific rule, while one item deviates from this norm. The goal is to identify that single outlier based on logic, category, or mathematical property.

This section tests your ability to group information effectively. You must look for the "common thread" among three items. For example, if you are given {Apple, Banana, Carrot, Grape}, the odd one out is Carrot because it is a root vegetable while the others are fruits. In number sets, the outlier might be the only even number in a group of odd numbers, or the only prime number.

Examiners often use this to test lateral thinking. The rule might not be obvious immediately; you may need to look at the shape of the letters, the sound they make, or the mathematical properties of the numbers. Always check for multiple possibilities before committing to an answer, but ensure your chosen outlier is the one that breaks the strongest logical link.

Technique: The Relationship Matrix
Question: "Book" : "Library" :: ? : "Museum"
Solution:
First, analyze the relationship between "Book" and "Library." A library is a place where books are stored. This is a "Place of Storage" relationship.
Next, apply this rule to the second pair. We need an item that is stored in a Museum.
The missing term must be an object found inside a museum. Common options might be "Painting," "Sculpture," or "Artifact."
If the options were: A) Car, B) Painting, C) Shoe, D) Chair.
"Car" is stored in a garage. "Shoe" is stored in a closet. "Chair" is furniture for sitting.
Therefore, "Painting" is the correct answer because it fits the "Place of Storage" pattern perfectly.
Technique: The Difference Method
Question: Find the missing number in the series: 10, 16, 24, 34, ?
Solution:
Step 1: Calculate the difference between consecutive numbers.
16 - 10 = +6
24 - 16 = +8
34 - 24 = +10

Step 2: Observe the pattern in the differences. The differences are increasing by 2 each time (6, 8, 10).
Step 3: Apply the next difference to the last known number.
Next difference should be +12.
Calculation: 34 + 12 = 46.
The missing number is 46.

Common Traps

  • Assuming a simple pattern: Students often jump to the conclusion that a series is just adding or subtracting a constant. If the differences change, you must look for second-order patterns (like the difference of differences).
  • Ignoring letter positions: In letter series, students sometimes treat letters as isolated symbols rather than numbers on a scale (A=1, B=2). This leads to errors in alternating forward-backward movements.
  • Misidentifying the Odd One Out category: A common mistake is focusing on surface-level attributes like color or shape when the rule is actually mathematical. For example, in {4, 9, 16, 20}, one might think 20 is odd because it doesn't look like a square number, but the rule is strictly "perfect squares."
  • Overthinking analogies: Sometimes students try to find complex scientific relationships when a simple synonym or antonym relationship is intended. Stick to the most direct logical link first.

Memory Tricks

  • The "Skip Count" Mnemonic: For series like A, C, E, G (every second letter), remember the phrase "Every Other." If you skip two letters (A, D, G), think of the song "Skip Skip Skip."
  • Square Number Visualization: Memorize squares up to 12. Visualize a grid: 3x3 is 9 dots, 4x4 is 16 dots. This helps instantly in series involving 1, 4, 9, 16, 25.
  • The "Three-Of-Four" Rule for Odd One Out: Never look for the odd one out until you have identified a common trait shared by at least three items. If no group of three shares a clear trait, re-evaluate your initial assumptions about the category.
  • Analogy Keywords: When solving analogies, associate specific keywords with relationship types: "Place" (Library, School), "Opposite" (Hot/Cold), "Tool" (Hammer/Nail), "Part" (Wheel/Car).
Exam-Day Strategy
Strategy for the Exam Hall:
Do not spend more than two minutes on any single analogy or series question. If you cannot spot a pattern quickly, mark it and move on to save time for easier questions.
For Odd One Out, scan the options first; sometimes the answer is obvious if you look at the choices rather than just the stem.
Always double-check your arithmetic in number series before bubbling your answer. A simple addition error can cost you marks even if your logic was perfect.
reasoning/arguments:
Arguments & Assumptions for CLAT

Logical Reasoning arguments questions present a short argument (premises + conclusion) and ask you to identify assumptions, strengtheners, weakeners, conclusions, or flaws. Answers must be based only on the argument given.

  • Argument structure:
    • Premise: A statement offered as support/reason (because, since, as, given that).
    • Conclusion: The claim the premises support (therefore, thus, hence, so, consequently, it follows that).
    • Assumption: An unstated premise that MUST be true for the conclusion to hold — the missing link.
  • Question types:
    • Assumption: 'The argument assumes that...' / 'Which is assumed?' — find the necessary condition.
    • Strengthen: 'Which most strengthens the argument?' — adds support.
    • Weaken: 'Which most weakens the argument?' — attacks the assumption/logic.
    • Conclusion: 'Which can be concluded?' — must follow from premises alone (not go beyond).
    • Flaw: 'The argument is vulnerable to criticism because...' — logical error.
    • Parallel reasoning: 'Which argument is most similar?' — same logical structure.
  • Assumption test (negation test): Negate the option. If the negated statement destroys the argument, it's a necessary assumption.
  • Strengthen vs weaken: Strengthener makes conclusion more likely; weakener makes it less likely — without changing the premises.
  • Conclusion must be supported: A valid conclusion is entailed by premises — not merely plausible, not outside knowledge.
  • Common flaws: Correlation≠causation, sampling bias, false dichotomy, ad hominem, circular reasoning, equivocation, confusing necessary/sufficient conditions.
Technique: Assumption via negation
Argument: 'The new traffic law will reduce accidents because it imposes heavy fines on speeding.' Assumption?
Answer: 'Heavy fines deter speeding.' Negation: 'Heavy fines do NOT deter speeding' — if true, the argument collapses (heavy fines won't reduce speeding, so won't reduce accidents). Hence it's a necessary assumption.
Technique: Correlation ≠ Causation
Argument: 'Cities with more ice-cream sales have more drowning deaths, so ice-cream causes drowning.' Flaw?
Answer: Correlation does not imply causation — both rise in summer (hot weather), a third factor explains both. Ice-cream doesn't cause drowning.
Technique: Strengthen
Argument: 'Abolishing exams will reduce student stress because exams cause stress.' Strengthener?
Answer: Evidence that exams are the main cause of student stress, or that abolishing similar assessments reduced stress elsewhere — supports the causal claim.

Common Traps

  • Bringing outside knowledge instead of using only the argument.
  • Choosing a statement that is merely plausible rather than necessarily entailed (for conclusions).
  • Choosing a strengthener/weakener that addresses a side issue, not the core assumption.
  • Confusing necessary assumption (must be true) with sufficient assumption (if true, guarantees conclusion).
  • Treating 'some' as 'all' or vice versa.

Memory Tricks

  • Assumption = Negation test: If negating kills the argument, it's assumed.
  • Conclusion = Must be true: If premises true, conclusion must follow — not just likely.
  • Strengthen/Weaken: Target the assumption/link between premises and conclusion.
  • Correlation ≠ Causation: Two things happening together doesn't mean one causes the other.
CLAT Logical Reasoning strategy
Read the argument, identify premise and conclusion, then evaluate each option against the argument's logic — not your outside knowledge. For assumption questions, apply the negation test to the two best options.
reasoning/inferences:
Inferences & Syllogisms for CLAT

CLAT Logical Reasoning inference questions ask what must follow from given statements. Syllogisms are deductive arguments with two premises and a conclusion. Answers must follow strictly from given statements — no outside knowledge.

  • Inference rules:
    • A valid inference must be true in ALL cases where premises are true.
    • 'Some A are B' does NOT mean 'All A are B' or 'All B are A'.
    • 'All A are B' does NOT mean 'All B are A' (conversion error).
    • Negative premises → negative/no conclusion (two negative premises = no conclusion).
    • Two particular premises ('some') → no definite conclusion.
    • The middle term must be distributed at least once.
    • No term can be distributed in the conclusion if not distributed in premises.
  • Venn diagram method: Draw circles for each term; shade/exclude areas per premises; check if conclusion holds in ALL possible diagrams. If conclusion holds in every valid diagram — valid; if false in any — invalid.
  • Syllogism forms (A/E/I/O):
    • A: All A are B (universal affirmative)
    • E: No A are B (universal negative)
    • I: Some A are B (particular affirmative)
    • O: Some A are not B (particular negative)
  • Valid moods (examples): AAA-1 (Barbara: All M are P, All S are M → All S are P); AII-1 (Darii: All M are P, Some S are M → Some S are P); EAE-1 (Celarent: No M are P, All S are M → No S are P); AOO-2 (Baroco: All P are M, Some S are not M → Some S are not P).
  • Immediate inferences: Conversion (All A are B → Some B are A; No A are B → No B are A; Some A are B → Some B are A; Some A are not B → no valid converse); Obviation (All A are B → No A are non-B; Some A are B → Some A are not non-B; etc.); Contraposition (All A are B → All non-B are non-A; No A are B → No B are A).
  • Complementary pairs: If one of a pair must be true and the other false: All A are B / Some A are not B; No A are B / Some A are B. If the first is false, second true and vice versa (in either-or conclusions).
Technique: Venn diagram for syllogism
Statements: All dogs are mammals. Some mammals are pets. Conclusion: Some dogs are pets. Valid?
Answer: Invalid. Draw dogs inside mammals; pets overlapping mammals somewhere — pets may be entirely outside the dog circle. 'Some dogs are pets' is not guaranteed (drawn diagram where pets circle doesn't touch dog circle is valid). So conclusion does not follow.
Technique: Either-or (complementary)
Statements: All students are hardworking. Some students are not rich. Conclusions: (1) All hardworking are rich. (2) Some hardworking are not rich.
Answer: Conclusion (2) follows (some students who are hardworking are not rich). Conclusion (1) doesn't follow. In complementary pairs, check whether one must be true — here (2) is supported.
Technique: Conversion trap
Statement: All teachers are educated. Can we conclude 'All educated are teachers'?
Answer: No — universal affirmative (All A are B) converts only to 'Some B are A' (Some educated are teachers), not 'All B are A'.

Common Traps

  • Converting 'All A are B' to 'All B are A' — invalid.
  • Assuming 'Some A are B' means 'Some A are not B' — both can be true simultaneously.
  • Drawing conclusion from two particular premises — invalid.
  • Using outside knowledge ('All birds fly' → penguins counterexample).
  • Treating 'Some' as 'many/most' — in logic, 'some' means 'at least one' (could be all).

Memory Tricks

  • Distribution: Subject distributed in universal (All/No), predicate distributed in negative (No/...not).
  • Middle term: Must be distributed at least once, else fallacy of undistributed middle.
  • Two negatives = no conclusion; two particulars = no conclusion.
  • Complementary pairs: All/Some-not and No/Some.
CLAT inference strategy
For syllogisms, draw Venn diagrams — test whether the conclusion holds in ALL valid diagrams. For inference questions, ask 'Does this HAVE to be true?' — probable isn't enough. Eliminate options that go beyond given statements.
english/synonyms-antonyms:
Why Synonyms and Antonyms Are Tested

A synonym is a word with the same or nearly the same meaning; an antonym is a word with the opposite meaning. SSC CGL, CHSL, MTS, banking, CDS, NDA and CLAT papers ask them directly, and reading comprehension, cloze and fillers test them indirectly. The examiner rarely asks for a rare word in isolation: the trap is a familiar word used in an unfamiliar sense, or two options that are close but differ in tone, intensity or collocation.

Build vocabulary in pairs, not single words. Learn abundant / scarce, benevolent / malevolent, candid / evasive and frugal / extravagant together. A pair fixes both the meaning and the direction of the contrast, which is exactly what a multiple-choice question rewards.

High-Frequency Synonym Pairs

  • Abandon — forsake, desert, relinquish; antonym: retain, keep.
  • Abbreviate — shorten, condense, abridge; antonym: expand, lengthen.
  • Abundant — plentiful, ample, copious; antonym: scarce, meagre.
  • Acute — sharp, severe, intense; antonym: mild, blunt.
  • Adamant — firm, unyielding, obstinate; antonym: flexible, yielding.
  • Alleviate — relieve, ease, mitigate; antonym: aggravate, worsen.
  • Amalgamate — merge, combine, unite; antonym: separate, divide.
  • Ambiguous — unclear, vague, equivocal; antonym: clear, explicit.
  • Amicable — friendly, cordial, harmonious; antonym: hostile, antagonistic.
  • Arduous — difficult, strenuous, laborious; antonym: easy, effortless.
  • Audacious — bold, daring, reckless; antonym: timid, cautious.
  • Benevolent — kind, generous, charitable; antonym: malevolent, cruel.
  • Blatant — obvious, glaring, shameless; antonym: subtle, concealed.
  • Candid — frank, honest, forthright; antonym: evasive, insincere.
  • Coerce — force, compel, pressure; antonym: persuade, coax.
  • Concise — brief, succinct, terse; antonym: verbose, rambling.
  • Deteriorate — worsen, decline, degenerate; antonym: improve, recover.
  • Diligent — hardworking, industrious, assiduous; antonym: lazy, negligent.
  • Eminent — distinguished, renowned, prominent; antonym: obscure, unknown.
  • Exacerbate — worsen, intensify, aggravate; antonym: soothe, alleviate.
  • Frugal — thrifty, economical, sparing; antonym: extravagant, wasteful.
  • Gregarious — sociable, outgoing, convivial; antonym: reclusive, solitary.
  • Hostile — unfriendly, antagonistic, adverse; antonym: friendly, favourable.
  • Impartial — unbiased, neutral, fair; antonym: biased, partisan.
  • Indifferent — unconcerned, apathetic, detached; antonym: concerned, interested.
  • Lucid — clear, coherent, intelligible; antonym: obscure, confused.
  • Meticulous — careful, precise, scrupulous; antonym: careless, sloppy.
  • Mitigate — reduce, lessen, moderate; antonym: intensify, aggravate.
  • Obstinate — stubborn, headstrong, inflexible; antonym: flexible, compliant.
  • Placid — calm, serene, tranquil; antonym: turbulent, agitated.
  • Pragmatic — practical, realistic, sensible; antonym: idealistic, impractical.
  • Prudent — wise, cautious, judicious; antonym: reckless, imprudent.
  • Reluctant — unwilling, hesitant, averse; antonym: eager, willing.
  • Resilient — adaptable, tough, buoyant; antonym: fragile, brittle.
  • Scrutinise — examine, inspect, investigate; antonym: ignore, overlook.
  • Tenacious — persistent, determined, dogged; antonym: irresolute, weak.
  • Transient — temporary, fleeting, ephemeral; antonym: permanent, lasting.
  • Vindicate — justify, exonerate, absolve; antonym: accuse, condemn.
  • Volatile — unstable, unpredictable, explosive; antonym: stable, steady.
  • Zealous — enthusiastic, fervent, passionate; antonym: apathetic, indifferent.

Near Misses the Examiner Exploits

Options are often related but not equivalent. Famous and notorious both mean well known, but notorious carries disapproval. Childish is negative; childlike is positive. Economical means saving money; economic means relating to the economy. Historic means important in history; historical means relating to history. Continual means repeated with breaks; continuous means without a break. Match the exact shade of meaning, not just the topic.

Also watch direction. If the stem asks for a synonym, an antonym option is the most common wrong answer. If the stem asks for an antonym, a synonym is the trap. Underline the instruction before reading the options.

Context-Based Elimination

When a word is unfamiliar, use the sentence around it. Contrast connectors such as but, although and whereas signal an opposite; addition connectors such as and, moreover and similarly signal a synonym. Punctuation matters too: a dash or colon often introduces a definition. Eliminate options that do not fit the grammar of the sentence even if their meaning is plausible.

Example 1 — Synonym in context
The committee's report was candid about the scheme's failures.

a) evasive b) frank c) hostile d) confused
Solution: b) Frank. Candid means honest and direct. Evasive is the antonym; hostile and confused do not fit the sense of honest disclosure.
Example 2 — Antonym
Choose the word opposite in meaning to transient.

a) fleeting b) temporary c) permanent d) passing
Solution: c) Permanent. Transient means short-lived; fleeting, temporary and passing are synonyms, so they are the trap.
Example 3 — Near miss
The scientist's meticulous records made the experiment easy to replicate.

a) careless b) detailed c) hasty d) vague
Solution: b) Detailed. Meticulous means showing great attention to detail. Careless, hasty and vague are antonyms.
Exam tip
Learn words in antonym pairs and in collocations (words that naturally go together). A word that is correct in meaning but wrong in collocation — for example make a decision, not do a decision — is still a wrong option in fillers and sentence improvement.

Revision Method

Keep a four-column notebook: word, meaning, synonym, antonym. Revise ten words a day and test yourself after three days. For SSC and banking, prioritise words that have appeared in previous-year papers; for CLAT and UPSC, prioritise words used in editorials. Read one editorial a day and mark every unfamiliar word, but learn only the words that change the meaning of the sentence. Depth beats a long list.
english/idioms-phrases:
How Idioms Are Asked

An idiom is a fixed expression whose meaning cannot be worked out from the individual words. Exams give the idiom in a sentence and ask for its meaning, or give a meaning and ask for the idiom. The common trap is the literal meaning: break the ice has nothing to do with ice, and pull someone's leg has nothing to do with legs. Learn the idiom as one unit, with one short example sentence.

Idioms About Effort and Work

  • Burn the midnight oil — study or work late into the night.
  • Bite the bullet — face a difficult situation bravely.
  • Pull up one's socks — prepare to work harder.
  • Put one's shoulder to the wheel — start working with determination.
  • Leave no stone unturned — try every possible method.
  • Go the extra mile — make more effort than expected.
  • Back to the drawing board — start again after a failure.
  • Burn one's fingers — suffer from one's own actions.
  • Make hay while the sun shines — use an opportunity while it lasts.
  • Strike while the iron is hot — act at the right moment.

Idioms About Speech and Secrets

  • Spill the beans — reveal a secret.
  • Let the cat out of the bag — disclose a secret accidentally.
  • Beat around the bush — avoid the main point.
  • Call a spade a spade — speak plainly and honestly.
  • Hit the nail on the head — say exactly the right thing.
  • Talk through one's hat — talk nonsense.
  • Bury the hatchet — end a quarrel and make peace.
  • Give someone the cold shoulder — ignore someone deliberately.
  • In hot water — in trouble.
  • Out of the frying pan into the fire — from one bad situation to a worse one.

Idioms About Money and Character

  • A blessing in disguise — something that seems bad but turns out good.
  • A drop in the ocean — a very small amount compared with what is needed.
  • Cost an arm and a leg — be very expensive.
  • Feel the pinch — suffer from a shortage of money.
  • Turn a deaf ear — refuse to listen.
  • Apple of one's eye — someone greatly loved.
  • At the drop of a hat — immediately, without hesitation.
  • Once in a blue moon — very rarely.
  • Teach someone a lesson — punish someone so they do not repeat a mistake.
  • Let sleeping dogs lie — avoid bringing up an old problem.

Phrases Often Confused

In the nick of time means just in time; at the eleventh hour means at the last possible moment. On the spur of the moment means without planning; at a snail's pace means very slowly. All in all means considering everything; all the same means nevertheless. In lieu of means instead of; in view of means considering. Learn the preposition with the phrase, because the examiner often changes it to create a wrong option.

Example 1
The new intern was asked to pull up his socks after a poor first week.

a) buy new socks b) work harder c) resign d) complain
Solution: b) Work harder. The idiom means to improve one's effort, not to buy clothing.
Example 2
Choose the meaning of to let sleeping dogs lie.

a) to wake animals b) to avoid an old controversy c) to sleep early d) to tell a secret
Solution: b) To avoid an old controversy. The idiom advises against reopening a settled problem.
Example 3
The donation was only a drop in the ocean for the flood victims.

a) a large help b) a very small help c) a dangerous gift d) a useless object
Solution: b) A very small help. The amount is tiny compared with the need, not worthless in itself.
Exam tip
Do not translate an idiom word by word. If an option repeats the literal words of the idiom, it is almost always the trap. Choose the option that states the figurative meaning in plain language.

How to Revise

Group idioms by theme (work, money, speech, conflict) rather than alphabetically. Write one sentence of your own for each idiom; an idiom you have used once is easier to recall than one you have only read. In the exam, if two options look similar, choose the one that matches the tone of the sentence and the grammar of the surrounding clause.

Idioms in Context

Idioms carry tone as well as meaning. To pass away is neutral and respectful; to kick the bucket is informal and can be flippant. To be in the family way is old-fashioned and gentle; to be pregnant is direct. In a formal letter or an essay, choose the neutral option even if both meanings are correct. Exams usually test the neutral meaning, but a tone question can turn on this difference.

Business and government idioms appear in banking and UPSC papers: red tape (excessive bureaucracy), to cut corners (do something cheaply or carelessly), to bail out (rescue financially), a level playing field (fair competition), to tighten the belt (reduce spending), to break the bank (cost too much), in the red (in debt), in the black (profitable).

Preposition changes the idiom. To look after is to care for; to look for is to search; to look into is to investigate; to look down on is to despise. When two options differ only in the particle, the particle is the question. Learn the phrase with its particle, never the verb alone.
english/one-word-substitutions:
What the Question Looks Like

A one-word substitution replaces a whole phrase with a single word. The stem gives a definition and the options are four words; the trap is a word that shares a root but has a different meaning. Learn the word with its exact definition, and group the words by category so that recall is faster in the exam hall.

People and Personal Qualities

  • Altruist — a person who lives for others.
  • Egoist — a person who thinks only of himself.
  • Egotist — a person who talks too much about himself.
  • Introvert — a person who is inward-looking.
  • Extrovert — a person who is outgoing and sociable.
  • Ambivert — a person with both introvert and extrovert traits.
  • Philanthropist — a person who loves mankind and donates to good causes.
  • Misanthrope — a person who hates mankind.
  • Misogynist — a person who hates women.
  • Optimist — a person who looks at the bright side.
  • Pessimist — a person who looks at the dark side.
  • Stoic — a person who remains calm in pain or trouble.
  • Gourmet — a person who enjoys fine food.
  • Gourmand — a person who eats too much.
  • Bibliophile — a person who loves books.
  • Philatelist — a person who collects stamps.
  • Numismatist — a person who collects coins.
  • Ornithologist — a person who studies birds.
  • Anthropologist — a person who studies human societies and culture.
  • Archaeologist — a person who studies ancient remains.

Places and Collections

  • Aquarium — a place where fish are kept.
  • Aviary — a place where birds are kept.
  • Apiary — a place where bees are kept.
  • Zoo — a place where wild animals are kept.
  • Museum — a place where historical objects are kept.
  • Arsenal — a place where weapons are stored.
  • Granary — a place where grain is stored.
  • Observatory — a place for studying stars and planets.
  • Dormitory — a place where students sleep.
  • Infirmary — a place for the sick.
  • Menagerie — a collection of wild animals.
  • Anthology — a collection of poems or essays.
  • Archipelago — a group of islands.
  • Constellation — a group of stars.
  • Grove — a small group of trees.

Sciences, Studies and Fears

  • Zoology — the study of animals.
  • Botany — the study of plants.
  • Geology — the study of the earth's crust.
  • Meteorology — the study of weather.
  • Astronomy — the study of celestial bodies.
  • Etymology — the study of word origins.
  • Entomology — the study of insects.
  • Pathology — the study of diseases.
  • Pedagogy — the art and science of teaching.
  • Claustrophobia — fear of closed spaces.
  • Acrophobia — fear of heights.
  • Hydrophobia — fear of water (also rabies).
  • Xenophobia — fear or dislike of foreigners.
  • Insomnia — inability to sleep.
  • Hypochondria — excessive worry about one's health.

More Exam Favourites

Extempore — a speech without preparation. Obituary — a notice of someone's death. Illegible — impossible to read. Invisible — impossible to see. Invincible — impossible to defeat. Inaudible — impossible to hear. Incorrigible — impossible to correct. Indispensable — impossible to do without. Inevitable — impossible to avoid. Omnipotent — all-powerful. Omnipresent — present everywhere. Omniscient — all-knowing. Anarchy — absence of government. Autocracy — government by one person. Bureaucracy — government by officials. Democracy — government by the people. Plutocracy — government by the wealthy. Theocracy — government by religious authority.

Example 1
One who is unable to pay his debts is called:

a) bankrupt b) miser c) creditor d) debtor
Solution: a) Bankrupt. A debtor owes money; a bankrupt is legally unable to pay debts. A creditor is owed money.
Example 2
A place where bees are kept is an:

a) aviary b) apiary c) aquarium d) arsenal
Solution: b) Apiary. An aviary keeps birds, an aquarium keeps fish and an arsenal stores weapons.
Example 3
A person who speaks without preparation gives an:

a) oration b) extempore c) elegy d) epilogue
Solution: b) Extempore. An oration is a formal speech, an elegy is a mournful poem and an epilogue is the closing part of a work.
Exam tip
Learn roots: bene good, male bad, omni all, phil love, phob fear, logy study. A root turns one memorised word into a family of words and makes elimination much faster.

Government, Law and Money

One-word questions in banking and civil-services papers draw on administration and law: amnesty (general pardon), armistice (agreement to stop fighting), referendum (direct vote on one issue), impeachment (charge of misconduct against a public official), quorum (minimum members needed for a meeting), mandate (authority given by voters), tariff (tax on imports), subsidy (government payment to lower a price), deficit (shortfall between income and spending), audit (official inspection of accounts).

Words about words and writing are also frequent: autobiography (life written by oneself), biography (life written by another), epitaph (words on a tomb), epilogue (closing section of a book), prologue (opening section), monologue (a long speech by one person), soliloquy (a speech to oneself on stage), manuscript (handwritten document), anecdote (a short amusing story), plagiarism (using another's work as one's own).

Build the answer by eliminating on the root. If the stem says "a person who studies insects", -ology words are the candidates and entomology is the answer; if it says "a place where bees are kept", the -ary place words are the candidates and apiary is the answer. Root families reduce four options to one much faster than memorising a list.
english/spelling-confusables:
Why Spelling Questions Are Easy Marks

Spelling questions ask you to pick the correctly spelt word or to spot the misspelt one. They are easy marks because the rules are finite and the tested words repeat. The harder part is confusable pairs: words that sound alike but differ in spelling and meaning, such as affect / effect and principal / principle. Learn the pair together with a sentence that fixes the difference.

Spelling Rules That Actually Help

  • i before e except after c — believe, achieve, receive, ceiling. Exceptions: seize, weird, leisure.
  • Drop the e before a vowel suffix — make + ing = making; love + able = lovable. Keep the e before a consonant suffix: hope + ful = hopeful.
  • Double the final consonant when a one-syllable word ends in a single vowel + consonant and the suffix begins with a vowel: run + ing = running; big + er = bigger.
  • Change y to i after a consonant before a suffix: happy + ness = happiness; carry + ed = carried. Keep y after a vowel: play + ed = played.
  • -able or -ible — -able is far more common (comfortable, dependable); -ible survives in older words (visible, possible, responsible).
  • -ance or -ence — learn the common words: attendance, maintenance, independence, existence.

Commonly Misspelt Words

Accommodation, achievement, acquaintance, apparent, argument, attendance, bureaucracy, calendar, cemetery, committee, consensus, definitely, discipline, embarrassment, environment, existence, February, foreign, government, grammar, guarantee, harassment, independent, indispensable, intelligence, liaison, maintenance, millennium, necessary, occasion, occurrence, parallel, parliament, perseverance, personnel, possession, prejudice, privilege, pronunciation, questionnaire, recommend, referred, rhythm, separate, successfully, supersede, tomorrow, unnecessary, vacuum, Wednesday.

Confusable Pairs

  • Accept / except — accept means receive; except means excluding.
  • Advice / advise — advice is the noun; advise is the verb.
  • Affect / effect — affect is usually the verb (to influence); effect is usually the noun (result).
  • Complement / compliment — complement completes something; a compliment praises.
  • Council / counsel — a council is a body; counsel means advice or to advise.
  • Principal / principle — principal means chief or the head of a school; principle means a rule or belief.
  • Stationary / stationery — stationary means not moving; stationery means writing materials.
  • Their / there / they're — possession, place, and they are.
  • Weather / whether — weather is climate; whether introduces a choice.
  • Lose / loose — lose is the verb; loose means not tight.
  • Quiet / quite — quiet means silent; quite means fairly or completely.
  • Desert / dessert — desert is dry land or to abandon; dessert is the sweet course.
Example 1
Choose the correctly spelt word:

a) accommodation b) accomodation c) acommodation d) accommodetion
Solution: a) Accommodation. The word has double c and double m.
Example 2
The manager's advice was to advise the client in writing.

Which pair is used correctly?

a) advice / advise b) advise / advice c) advice / advice d) advise / advise
Solution: a) Advice / advise. The noun is advice; the verb is advise.
Example 3
The principal explained the principle of the new policy.

Which pair is correct?

a) principle / principal b) principal / principle c) principal / principal d) principle / principle
Solution: b) Principal / principle. The head of the institution is the principal; a rule is a principle.
Exam tip
When two options differ by one letter, say the word aloud in syllables. Most misspellings add or drop a syllable (accom-odation, gov-ern-ment, Feb-ru-ary). Syllable counting catches more errors than visual memory alone.

British and American Spelling

Indian exams generally follow British spelling, but a question may test the difference. British keeps -our (colour, honour, labour), -re (centre, metre, theatre), -ise (organise, realise) and -ce for nouns (defence, licence). American uses -or, -er, -ize and -se. Choose the spelling used consistently in the rest of the paper; mixed spelling is marked wrong in a descriptive answer.

Doubling rules explain many misspellings. Double the final consonant when a one-syllable word ends in a single vowel + consonant and the suffix starts with a vowel: stop + ed = stopped, plan + ing = planning. Do not double when the word ends in two consonants (help + ed = helped) or when the stress is not on the final syllable (visit + ed = visited, but begin + ing = beginning).

Silent letters are the other trap: kn (know, knee), wr (write, wrong), mb at the end (comb, thumb), gh (light, though), ps at the start (psychology, pneumonia). Say the word in syllables and note the silent letter separately; visual memory alone fails under exam pressure.
english/tenses:
The Twelve Tense Forms

Tense questions test whether you can place an action in time and show whether it is complete, continuous or repeated. Learn the forms as a grid: three times (present, past, future) times four aspects (simple, continuous, perfect, perfect continuous). Once the grid is automatic, most error-spotting questions become a check of one cell.

  • Present simple — habits and general truths: She writes every day.
  • Present continuous — happening now or a fixed near-future plan: She is writing now.
  • Present perfect — past action with a present result or unfinished time: She has written three pages.
  • Present perfect continuous — started in the past and still continuing: She has been writing since morning.
  • Past simple — completed action at a definite past time: She wrote yesterday.
  • Past continuous — an action in progress in the past, often interrupted: She was writing when the phone rang.
  • Past perfect — the earlier of two past actions: She had written the letter before he arrived.
  • Past perfect continuous — an action continuing up to a past point: She had been writing for an hour when he came.
  • Future simple — a prediction or spontaneous decision: She will write tomorrow.
  • Future continuous — an action in progress at a future time: She will be writing at noon.
  • Future perfect — completed before a future point: She will have written the report by Friday.
  • Future perfect continuous — duration up to a future point: By June she will have been writing for a year.

Sequence of Tenses

If the main verb is past, the subordinate verb normally shifts to a past form: He said that he was busy. Exceptions are universal truths (He said that the earth revolves around the sun) and habitual facts that are still true. In conditional sentences, use the correct pair: If it rains, we will stay (first conditional); If it rained, we would stay (second); If it had rained, we would have stayed (third). Do not mix a past if clause with a future main clause.

Gerunds, Infinitives and Participles

A gerund is a verb + ing used as a noun: Swimming is good exercise. An infinitive is to + verb: She wants to swim. Some verbs take only a gerund (enjoy, avoid, suggest, mind), some take only an infinitive (want, decide, hope, refuse), and some take either with a change of meaning (remember, forget, stop). A participle is a verb form used as an adjective: a running tap, a broken window. A dangling participle occurs when the implied subject of the participle is not the subject of the main clause: Walking down the road, the tower came into view is wrong because the tower was not walking.

Example 1
She ________ in this office since 2019.

a) works b) worked c) has been working d) is working
Solution: c) Has been working. Since marks a point of origin and the action continues, so the present perfect continuous is required.
Example 2
By the time we reached the station, the train ________.

a) leaves b) left c) had left d) has left
Solution: c) Had left. The train left before another past action, so the past perfect is correct.
Example 3
He avoided ________ the question directly.

a) to answer b) answering c) answer d) answered
Solution: b) Answering. Avoid takes a gerund, not an infinitive.
Exam tip
Look for time markers first: since, for, ago, already, yet, by the time, when, while. Each marker narrows the tense before you read the options, which is faster than testing all four choices.

Common Tense Errors

Since vs for: since takes a point of time (since 2019, since Monday) and for takes a duration (for three years). Both usually need a perfect tense. Already vs yet: already appears in affirmative sentences, yet in negatives and questions. Ago vs before: ago counts back from now with the past simple; before counts back from a past point with the past perfect.

Stative verbs: verbs of thought, emotion, possession and perception (know, believe, like, own, seem) normally take the simple form, not the continuous. Say I know the answer, not I am knowing the answer. Some verbs change meaning between simple and continuous: I think it is true (opinion) versus I am thinking about it (mental activity).

Time clauses: after when, until, before, after, as soon as, use the present simple for a future meaning: I will call you when I reach home, never when I will reach. The same rule applies in first conditional if-clauses. This single rule accounts for a large share of tense questions in SSC and banking papers.
english/subject-verb-agreement:
The Core Rule

A verb must agree with its subject in number and person. The difficulty is not the rule but finding the real subject when words sit between the subject and the verb. Cross out prepositional phrases and relative clauses, then match the verb to the head noun: The box of chocolates is on the table (box, not chocolates).

Rules Examiners Test

  • Two subjects joined by and take a plural verb: Ram and Shyam are here. If the two nouns form one idea, use a singular verb: Bread and butter is my breakfast.
  • Either ... or / neither ... nor — the verb agrees with the nearer subject: Neither the manager nor the clerks were present.
  • With / along with / as well as / besides — the verb agrees with the first subject: The manager, along with the clerks, was present.
  • Collective nouns — singular when the group acts as one: The committee has decided. Plural when members act individually: The committee are divided.
  • Indefinite pronouns — each, either, neither, everyone, everybody, someone, nobody, anyone are singular: Everyone is ready.
  • None / some / all / most — agree with the noun they refer to: None of the boys was present or None of the boys were present depending on emphasis; follow the exam's singular preference for none.
  • A number of / the number of — A number of students are absent; The number of students is rising.
  • Each / every + singular noun — Each boy is ready.
  • Inversion — the verb agrees with the subject after it: There are three books on the table.
  • Units and amounts — a single quantity takes a singular verb: Ten kilometres is a long walk.

Pronoun Agreement

A pronoun must match its antecedent in number and gender. Every student must bring his or her book is grammatically safe; Every student must bring their book is now accepted in many style guides but may be marked wrong in a strict exam. With one of the + plural noun, the relative clause usually takes a plural verb: He is one of the students who work hard.

Example 1
The quality of the mangoes ________ not good.

a) are b) is c) were d) have been
Solution: b) Is. The subject is quality (singular); of the mangoes is a prepositional phrase.
Example 2
Neither the principal nor the teachers ________ available.

a) was b) were c) is d) has been
Solution: b) Were. With neither ... nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject, teachers.
Example 3
A number of applications ________ received.

a) was b) has been c) were d) is
Solution: c) Were. A number of means many and takes a plural verb; the number of would take a singular verb.
Exam tip
Underline the verb, then ask "who or what is doing this?" Cross out every phrase between the subject and the verb. The head noun that remains controls the verb.

Tricky Cases

Fractions and percentages agree with the noun after of: Two-thirds of the land is barren; Two-thirds of the students are present. Plural-looking singular nouns — news, mathematics, physics, economics, politics, measles — take singular verbs. Plural-only nouns — scissors, trousers, spectacles — take plural verbs, often with a pair of to make them singular.

Titles and names take a singular verb even when they look plural: The Arabian Nights is a famous collection. Money, distance and time take a singular verb when they express one amount: Five hundred rupees is a fair price; Ten years is a long time. There is / there are agree with the noun that follows, not with there.

Relative pronouns take the number of their antecedent: The boy who is standing there; The boys who are standing there. With one of the + plural noun + who, the verb in the relative clause is plural, as in one of the players who were selected. Check the antecedent before you check the verb.
english/articles-prepositions:
Articles: A, An and The

Use a before a consonant sound and an before a vowel sound, not before a vowel letter. A university (yu sound), an hour (silent h), a one-rupee coin (w sound), an MLA (em sound). Use the for something specific, already mentioned, unique, superlative, or defined by a phrase: the sun, the best answer, the book on the table.

Do not use an article before uncountable nouns used generally (Water is precious), before most proper nouns (India), or before plural nouns used generally (Books are useful). Use the with rivers, seas, mountain ranges, newspapers and famous buildings: the Ganga, the Himalayas, the Times of India, the Taj Mahal.

Fixed Prepositions

  • abide by, accused of, afraid of, agree with (a person), agree to (a proposal), angry with (a person), angry at (a thing).
  • apologise for, apply for (a job), apply to (an authority), ashamed of, aware of, believe in, belong to.
  • capable of, complain about, composed of, concentrate on, confident of, congratulate on, consist of, depend on.
  • differ from (a thing), differ with (a person), disappointed with, eligible for, envious of, expert in.
  • fond of, guilty of, insist on, interested in, jealous of, listen to, look after, married to, prefer to.
  • proficient in, proud of, rely on, responsible for, satisfied with, succeed in, superior to, think of, tired of.
  • wait for, warn against, wish for, worry about, yield to, acquit of, compare with (similar things), compare to (unlike things).

Conjunctions and Correlatives

Use although / though with a clause, despite / in spite of with a noun or gerund. Use because for a reason, so for a result. Do not pair although with but, or because with so. Correlative pairs must be parallel: not only ... but also, either ... or, neither ... nor, both ... and, no sooner ... than, hardly ... when, scarcely ... when, such ... as, so ... that.

Example 1
She is ________ honest officer.

a) a b) an c) the d) no article
Solution: b) An. Honest begins with a vowel sound because the h is silent.
Example 2
He is proficient ________ mathematics.

a) at b) in c) on d) with
Solution: b) In. The fixed collocation is proficient in a subject.
Example 3
No sooner had he arrived ________ the meeting began.

a) when b) then c) than d) that
Solution: c) Than. The fixed pair is no sooner ... than.
Exam tip
Prepositions are learned as collocations, not by translation. When you meet a new verb, note the preposition that follows it in the same line of your notebook: depend on, not depend of.

When to Omit the Article

Omit the article before plural countable nouns used generally (Dogs are loyal), before uncountable nouns used generally (Honesty is the best policy), before most proper nouns, and before names of languages and subjects (She studies economics). Keep the when the noun is made specific by a phrase or by shared knowledge: the water in this bottle, the government of India.

Fixed article patterns matter in error spotting: the Himalayas, the Ganga, the Sundarbans, the Times of India, the United Nations, but India, Delhi, Mount Everest, Lake Baikal. Use a with professions and frequencies: a doctor, twice a week. Use the with comparatives of degree: the more you practise, the better you get.

Common preposition traps: discuss takes no preposition, married to, senior/junior/superior/inferior to, prefer X to Y, comprise takes no of, consist of, deprive of, accuse of, charge with, congratulate on, apologise for. Learn these as whole phrases; the wrong preposition is the most common distractor in error-spotting questions.
english/sentence-improvement:
What the Question Asks

A sentence-improvement question gives a sentence with one underlined part and four replacements. You must choose the replacement that makes the sentence grammatically correct and idiomatic without changing its meaning. The original is sometimes already correct; an option that repeats it is then the answer. Read the whole sentence before looking at the options, because the error often depends on a word outside the underlined part.

What to Check, in Order

  • Subject-verb agreement — find the real subject and match the verb.
  • Tense and sequence — check time markers and the tense of the other clauses.
  • Pronoun reference — a pronoun must have one clear antecedent and match it in number.
  • Parallelism — items joined by and, or, not only ... but also must have the same grammatical form.
  • Modifiers — a modifier should sit next to the word it describes; avoid dangling participles.
  • Prepositions and articles — check fixed collocations.
  • Redundancy — remove repeated ideas such as return back, discuss about, more better.

Common Replacements

One of my friend becomes one of my friends. He is senior than me becomes he is senior to me. She prefers coffee than tea becomes she prefers coffee to tea. I am used to get up early becomes I am used to getting up early. Hardly had I reached when it started raining is correct; hardly ... than is wrong. Neither of the boys were present becomes neither of the boys was present in a strict exam. The scenery are beautiful becomes the scenery is beautiful.

Example 1
He is one of the best player in the team.

a) one of the best players b) one of best player c) one of the better player d) one best player
Solution: a) One of the best players. One of takes a plural noun.
Example 2
She prefers reading than watching television.

a) than to watch b) to watching c) than watch d) to watch
Solution: b) To watching. The pair is prefer X to Y, and both X and Y should be gerunds here.
Example 3
The teacher asked the students to discuss about the topic.

a) discuss about b) discuss on c) discuss d) discuss over
Solution: c) Discuss. Discuss is transitive and takes no preposition.
Exam tip
If two options are grammatically possible, choose the shorter one unless the sentence needs the extra word for meaning. Exam setters often include a wordy but correct option and a concise correct option; the concise one is usually the key.

Modifiers and Parallelism

A modifier must sit next to the word it describes. Walking down the road, I saw a tower is correct because I was walking; Walking down the road, the tower came into view is wrong because the tower was not walking. Fix a dangling participle by naming the doer in the main clause or by turning the participle into a full clause.

Parallelism means items joined by and, or, but, not only ... but also or either ... or must have the same grammatical form. She likes reading, writing and to paint should become She likes reading, writing and painting. When a comparison uses than or as, compare like with like: The population of Mumbai is larger than that of Pune, not larger than Pune.

Redundancy and idiom are the last checks. Cut return back, discuss about, more better, most unique, the reason is because, and each and every when one word is enough. Then confirm the fixed collocation: comply with, differ from, capable of, responsible for. If the underlined part is already correct, the option that repeats it is the answer.
english/para-jumbles:
The Method

A para jumble gives five or six sentences in random order and asks you to rebuild the paragraph. Do not read the sentences as isolated units. Look for the opening sentence first, then follow the chain of connectors, pronouns and chronology. The opening sentence usually introduces a topic without depending on any other sentence; it rarely begins with a pronoun or a conjunction.

Four Signals

  • Opening sentence — broad statement, definition or background; no pronoun referring backward, no this, therefore or however at the start.
  • Connectors — however, therefore, moreover, consequently, for example, in contrast. The sentence after a contrast connector must contrast with the previous one.
  • Pronoun chains — he, she, it, they, this, these must refer to a noun already introduced. A sentence beginning with This policy cannot come before the sentence that names the policy.
  • Chronology and cause — first, then, later, finally; a cause comes before its effect, and a problem before its solution.

Worked Example

Take these sentences: (A) The scheme was launched in 2015. (B) It initially covered only ten districts. (C) However, by 2020 it had expanded to all states. (D) The expansion required a new monitoring system. (E) That system is now being upgraded. The opening is A because it names the scheme and gives a date. B follows because it refers to the scheme. C contrasts with B and gives the later date. D follows from the expansion, and E follows because that system refers to the monitoring system. The order is A-B-C-D-E.

Example 1
Arrange: (A) It is therefore important to save water. (B) India receives most of its rain in four months. (C) The remaining months are dry. (D) Groundwater levels are falling in many cities.

a) B-C-D-A b) A-B-C-D c) D-B-C-A d) B-D-C-A
Solution: a) B-C-D-A. B introduces the rainfall pattern, C adds the dry months, D states the consequence and A draws the conclusion with therefore.
Example 2
Arrange: (A) The committee submitted its report. (B) The report recommended stricter safety checks. (C) The government accepted the recommendations. (D) New rules were notified last month.

a) A-B-C-D b) B-A-C-D c) C-A-B-D d) A-C-B-D
Solution: a) A-B-C-D. The report comes from the committee, the recommendation from the report, acceptance from the government and notification after acceptance.
Exam tip
Do not try every permutation. Find the opening sentence, then look for the one sentence that must follow it. Two fixed pairs usually reduce the choices to one option.

Elimination in the Exam

Most para-jumble questions can be solved without building the full order. Start by finding the opening sentence and the sentence that must follow it. Then check which options begin with that opening; usually only one or two do. If two options survive, use a fixed pair — a pronoun and its antecedent, or a cause and its effect — to break the tie.

Watch the demonstratives. This, these, that, those, such point backward and cannot open a paragraph unless the reference is obvious from the title. Watch the articles. A sentence that introduces a noun with a/an usually comes before a sentence that uses the for the same noun. Watch the time markers. In 1991 comes before by 2005, and initially before later.

Finally, read the reconstructed paragraph aloud in your head. If a sentence feels disconnected, the order is wrong even if every individual link looked plausible. Trust the chain of meaning over the chain of keywords; examiners insert a sentence that repeats a keyword precisely to mislead keyword-matchers.
english/phrasal-verbs:
What a Phrasal Verb Is

A phrasal verb is a verb plus a particle (preposition or adverb) that together carry a meaning different from the verb alone. Give means transfer; give up means quit. Look means direct the eyes; look after means take care of. Exams test the meaning in context, so learn the whole phrase with a short example.

Phrasal Verbs by Verb

  • Break — break down (stop working), break out (start suddenly), break up (end a relationship), break into (enter by force), break off (stop abruptly).
  • Bring — bring up (raise a child or mention), bring about (cause), bring out (publish or reveal), bring in (introduce), bring down (reduce or overthrow).
  • Call — call off (cancel), call on (visit), call for (demand), call up (telephone or summon), call out (shout).
  • Carry — carry on (continue), carry out (perform), carry away (lose control), carry off (win or manage).
  • Come — come across (find by chance), come up with (produce an idea), come down (decrease), come about (happen), come round (recover or agree).
  • Get — get over (recover), get away with (escape punishment), get along (be friendly), get rid of (remove), get through (finish or pass).
  • Give — give up (quit), give in (surrender), give away (donate or reveal), give out (distribute or fail), give back (return).
  • Go — go through (examine or experience), go over (review), go off (explode or stop working), go on (continue), go without (manage without).
  • Look — look after (take care of), look into (investigate), look for (search), look forward to (anticipate), look down on (despise).
  • Put — put off (postpone), put up with (tolerate), put on (wear), put out (extinguish), put down (suppress or write).
  • Run — run out of (exhaust), run into (meet unexpectedly), run over (hit with a vehicle), run away (flee), run through (review).
  • Set — set up (establish), set off (start a journey), set aside (reserve), set out (begin with an aim), set back (delay).
  • Take — take off (leave the ground or remove), take over (assume control), take after (resemble), take up (begin a hobby), take in (understand or deceive).
  • Turn — turn down (reject or reduce), turn up (arrive), turn out (prove to be), turn into (become), turn against (become hostile).

Separable and Inseparable

Some phrasal verbs allow the object between the verb and the particle: turn the offer down or turn down the offer. Others do not: look after the child, never look the child after. When the object is a pronoun, it must go between the verb and particle for separable verbs: turn it down, not turn down it. Learn the common separable verbs: turn on/off, put on/off, take off, give up, bring up, call off, carry out, set up.

Example 1
The meeting was ________ because of the storm.

a) called off b) called on c) called up d) called out
Solution: a) Called off. To call off is to cancel.
Example 2
She ________ her mother in appearance.

a) takes after b) takes off c) takes over d) takes up
Solution: a) Takes after. To take after someone is to resemble them.
Example 3
We have ________ sugar; please buy some.

a) run into b) run out of c) run over d) run through
Solution: b) Run out of. To run out of something is to exhaust the supply.
Exam tip
Group phrasal verbs by the particle as well as by the verb. Off often means separation or cancellation (call off, set off, take off); up often means completion or increase (give up, set up, turn up). The pattern helps when the exact phrase is unfamiliar.

Three-Part Phrasal Verbs

Some phrasal verbs take both a particle and a preposition and cannot be separated: put up with (tolerate), get along with (be friendly with), come up with (produce an idea), look forward to (anticipate), catch up with (reach the same level), run out of (exhaust), put down to (attribute to), make up for (compensate), stand up for (defend), get round to (finally do something).

Idiomatic meaning shifts: take off can mean remove clothing, leave the ground, or become successful suddenly. Turn up can mean arrive or increase the volume.
