  • Pakistan: Core issues — Kashmir (Article 370 abrogation, 2019), cross-border terrorism (26/11, Pathankot, Pulwama), Sir Creek, Siachen, water sharing (Indus Waters Treaty, 1960), and trade. No bilateral talks while terrorism continues, per India’s stated position. Kartarpur Corridor opened 2019 for Sikh pilgrims.
  • China: Border dispute — Line of Actual Control (LAC), Aksai Chin (claimed by China, administered by India as part of Ladakh), Arunachal Pradesh (claimed by China as “South Tibet”). Galwan clash (June 2020) killed 20 Indian soldiers; standoff continues at Depsang, Demchok, etc. Trade imbalance heavily favours China. India joined QUAD and advocates a free and open Indo-Pacific. Doklam (2017) standoff resolved diplomatically.
  • Nepal: Open border, 1950 Peace and Friendship Treaty, hydropower and connectivity projects. Irritants — Kalapani/Lipulekh border dispute, Nepal’s new map (2020), and perceived Chinese inroads.
  • Bhutan: Special relationship; India is Bhutan’s largest development partner. Hydropower cooperation. Doklam lies at the Bhutan-China-India tri-junction; Bhutan’s sovereignty is central to India’s security.
  • Bangladesh: Land Boundary Agreement (2015) resolved enclaves; Teesta water sharing remains pending; Rohingya issue; India provided vaccines and relief during COVID-19 and floods.
  • Sri Lanka: Ethnic Tamil issue and 13th Amendment to Sri Lankan Constitution (devolution to provinces); China’s Hambantota port lease; India’s economic assistance during Sri Lanka’s 2022 crisis; Katchatheevu island issue.
  • Myanmar: Strategic for India’s Act East and Northeast insurgency management (border fencing, Free Movement Regime review); Rohingya refugee issue; India-Myanmar-Thailand trilateral highway.
  • Afghanistan: India invested ~$3 billion (Salma Dam, Parliament building); evacuated citizens in 2021 after Taliban takeover; engages selectively on humanitarian grounds while concerned about Pakistan-backed terror groups.

Bilateral Relations — Major Powers

  • United States: Strategic partnership; Civil Nuclear Deal (2008); Logistics Exchange Memorandum of Agreement (LEMOA, 2016), Communications Compatibility and Security Agreement (COMCASA, 2018), Basic Exchange and Cooperation Agreement (BECA, 2020); iCET (Initiative on Critical and Emerging Technology); India is a Major Defense Partner. Issues — H-1B visa restrictions, trade tariffs, intellectual property, and Russia oil purchases.
  • Russia: Long-standing defence partner (S-400 Triumf missile deal despite US CAATSA concerns); BrahMos joint venture; nuclear energy (Kudankulam); India abstained on UN resolutions condemning Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, reflecting strategic autonomy.
  • European Union: India-EU Strategic Partnership; trade and investment negotiations resumed; connectivity through the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC).
  • United Kingdom: Comprehensive Strategic Partnership (2021); Roadmap 2030; migration and mobility pact; defence and technology cooperation.
  • Japan: Special Strategic and Global Partnership; bullet train (Mumbai-Ahmedabad); Act East anchor; supply chain resilience.
  • Australia: Economic Cooperation and Trade Agreement (ECTA, 2022); QUAD partner; Critical Minerals Investment Partnership.
  • Israel: Defence and agriculture cooperation; intelligence sharing; India balanced its West Asia policy (Israel-Palestine, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iran).

Global Groupings and Forums

  • United Nations: India is a founding member; contributes substantially to UN peacekeeping; seeks permanent membership of a reformed UN Security Council (G4 grouping with Brazil, Germany, Japan); supports expansion of both permanent and non-permanent categories.
  • G20: India held the presidency in 2023 (New Delhi Summit); adopted the African Union as a permanent member; focused on Global South, climate finance, digital public infrastructure, and women-led development.
  • BRICS: Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa; New Development Bank (NDB) headquartered in Shanghai; India pushed for BRICS expansion (2024 — Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, UAE joined).
  • Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO): Security and economic grouping; India and Pakistan joined in 2017; focuses on counter-terrorism, Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure (RATS), and connectivity.
  • QUAD: India, US, Japan, Australia — informal strategic forum for a free and open Indo-Pacific; maritime domain awareness, vaccine partnership, critical technology.
  • ASEAN: India is a sectoral dialogue partner (1992), summit-level partner (2002); Act East centrepiece; ASEAN-India Free Trade Agreement; Mekong-Ganga Cooperation.
  • BIMSTEC: Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation — Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Myanmar, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Thailand; alternative to SAARC given Pakistan’s obstructionism.
  • SAARC: South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation — largely moribund due to India-Pakistan tensions; last summit 2016 (Pakistan, cancelled after Uri attack).
  • I2U2: India, Israel, UAE, US — new minilateral for food security, clean energy, and water.
  • QUAD-plus / Indo-Pacific: India supports ASEAN centrality in the Indo-Pacific; opposes unilateral changes to the status quo (reference to China).

International Institutions

  • UN Security Council: India seeks permanent membership; argues the UNSC (P5: US, UK, France, Russia, China) does not reflect contemporary realities; India served as non-permanent member in 2021–22.
  • WTO: India is a founding member; key issues — agriculture subsidies (public stockholding for food security), special and differential treatment, e-commerce moratorium, and dispute settlement crisis (Appellate Body non-functional since 2019).
  • WHO: India is a major vaccine producer (“pharmacy of the world”); supplied vaccines under Vaccine Maitri during COVID-19; supports the TRIPS waiver proposal for COVID-19 vaccines.
  • IAEA: India’s civilian nuclear facilities under safeguards after the NSG waiver (2008); India seeks Nuclear Suppliers Group membership (blocked by China on NPT grounds).
  • ICJ: Kulbhushan Jadhav case (2019) — ICJ ruled Pakistan must consular access and review conviction; India’s victory.
  • ICC: India is not a party to the Rome Statute; concerns over sovereignty and the definition of crimes.
  • Financial Action Task Force (FATF): India is a member; works on anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing.

Diaspora

  • Overseas Indians: ~3.5 crore (NRIs, PIOs, OCIs); largest remittance-receiving country (~$100+ billion annually).
  • OCI (Overseas Citizen of India): Lifetime visa-free travel; introduced by Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2005; not dual citizenship (Constitution prohibits it, Article 9).
  • Pravasi Bharatiya Divas: Celebrated 9 January (commemorating Gandhi’s return from South Africa in 1915).
  • Evacuations: Operation Ganga (Ukraine, 2022), Operation Devi Shakti (Afghanistan, 2021), Operation Raahat (Yemen, 2015), Operation Sukoon (Lebanon, 2006).
Technique: Neighbourhood analysis
Question: “India’s Neighbourhood First policy faces a China challenge. Examine with reference to any two neighbours.”
Answer: In Nepal, China’s Belt and Road projects and Nepal’s 2020 map claiming Lipulekh reduce India’s traditional influence; India counters with hydropower and connectivity. In Sri Lanka, China’s Hambantota port (debt-for-equity swap) raises strategic concerns; India provided $4 billion emergency aid in 2022 and promotes the India-Middle East-Europe corridor. India’s response combines development assistance, security cooperation, and alternative multilateral forums (BIMSTEC, BBIN).
Technique: Multilateral forum choice
Question: Why did India prefer BIMSTEC over SAARC for regional cooperation?
Answer: SAARC summits require consensus; Pakistan blocked the 2016 summit after the Uri attack. BIMSTEC excludes Pakistan, allowing India to advance connectivity (BBIN motor vehicle agreement, coastal shipping) and security cooperation with Bay of Bengal littoral states without veto. SAARC is not dead but dormant; BIMSTEC is the practical vehicle now.

Common Traps

  • Confusing QUAD (security/Indo-Pacific) with BRICS (economic/global South) — different memberships and agendas.
  • Assuming India’s UNSC bid is supported by all P5 — China opposes it; others support conditionally.
  • Thinking non-alignment means neutrality on every issue — India now takes position-based stances (e.g., condemning terrorism, supporting territorial integrity).
  • Missing that the Indus Waters Treaty survives wars — it survived 1965, 1971, and 1999 conflicts.
  • Overlooking that IMEC is an economic corridor, not a military alliance.

Memory Tricks

  • Defence pacts with US: LEMOA, COMCASA, BECA — foundational agreements in order.
  • China border flashpoints: Aksai Chin (Ladakh), Arunachal Pradesh, Doklam (tri-junction).
  • Neighbourhood irritants: Pakistan–terror/Kashmir; China–LAC; Nepal–Kalapani; Sri Lanka–13th Amendment; Bangladesh–Teesta.
  • India’s global ambitions: UNSC permanent seat, NSG membership, G20 leadership, Quad leadership.
Mains exam-day strategy
For international relations, structure answers by bilateral, regional, and multilateral levels. Cite specific agreements (LEMOA, COMCASA, BECA, LBA, Indus Waters Treaty) and recent summits (G20 2023, QUAD, SCO). For China-Pakistan questions, balance security concerns with diplomatic channels. Use maps mentally — LAC, McMahon Line, Sir Creek, and Katchatheevu are commonly tested. End with India’s strategic autonomy as the unifying theme.
mains-gs2/answer-writing-gs2:
Directive Words in GS II

Directive words tell you what the examiner wants — describe, analyse, critically examine, discuss, evaluate, comment, or illustrate. Misreading the directive is the most common reason for lost marks in Mains GS II.

  • Discuss: Present arguments for and against, then conclude. A debate-style answer with multiple perspectives.
  • Analyse: Break the topic into components and explain how they relate. Example: “Analyse the federal features of the Indian Constitution” — list features (dual polity, Seventh Schedule, independent judiciary, written constitution) and show how each works.
  • Critically analyse / Critically examine: Analyse plus judge merits and demerits. Must include a balanced view — strengths, weaknesses, and a reasoned conclusion. Neutral tone; no unsupported ranting.
  • Evaluate / Assess: Weigh the value or impact. “Evaluate the effectiveness of MGNREGA” — coverage, wages, asset creation, leakages, and whether it reduced distress migration. Give a verdict with justification.
  • Comment: Give your informed opinion on a statement or issue. Shorter than “discuss”; take a position and support it.
  • Examine: Probe deeply into causes, effects, and implications. More analytical than descriptive.
  • Illustrate: Use examples, case studies, or data to clarify a point. “Illustrate with examples how judicial review works in India” — Kesavananda Bharati, Maneka Gandhi, Coelho, etc.
  • Enumerate / List: Simply list items without elaboration. Rare as a standalone directive in GS II.
  • Justify: Provide reasons in favour of a position or decision.
  • Compare and contrast: Show similarities and differences between two systems, schemes, or judgments (e.g., Indian vs US federalism).

Answer Structure

A high-scoring GS II answer follows a consistent architecture. The 250-word limit (15-mark question) or 150-word limit (10-mark question) demands discipline.

  • Introduction (15–20% of words): Define the core term, cite the constitutional article or recent context, and state your line of argument. Example: For “Article 356,” start with “Article 356 empowers the President to impose President’s Rule when constitutional machinery in a state has failed.”
  • Body (60–70% of words): Organise into 3–4 thematic paragraphs or bullet clusters. Use subheadings if the question is multi-part. Each paragraph: one idea, evidence (article number, scheme, judgment, data), and linkage back to the question.
  • Conclusion (10–15% of words): Forward-looking and balanced. Suggest reforms (2nd ARC, Punchhi Commission, Law Commission reports), cite the way forward, or restate the core finding. Never introduce a new fact here.

Multi-part questions: If a question has two parts (e.g., “What are the issues? Suggest measures”), divide the body accordingly and label them clearly. GS II questions often combine constitutional provisions with contemporary governance.

Content Enrichment for GS II

  • Constitutional anchoring: Cite Articles — 324 (Election Commission), 315–323 (UPSC/SPSC), 280 (Finance Commission), 148 (CAG), 352/356/360 (emergencies), 245–255 (legislative relations), 268–281 (financial relations), 368 (amendment), 74/75 (Council of Ministers), 53 (executive power of President), 123 (ordinances).
  • Schedules: Seventh Schedule (Union, State, Concurrent Lists), Tenth Schedule (anti-defection), Eleventh (Panchayats), Twelfth (Municipalities).
  • Judgments: Kesavananda Bharati (basic structure), Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (election dispute), S.R. Bommai (President’s Rule), Coelho (Ninth Schedule), Navtej Singh Johar (Section 377), Joseph Shine (adultery), Puttaswamy (privacy), Anuradha Bhasin (internet shutdowns).
  • Commissions: 2nd Administrative Reforms Commission, Punchhi Commission (Centre-state relations), Sarkaria Commission (Centre-state relations), L.M. Singhvi (local governance), N.N. Vohra (criminalisation of politics).
  • Schemes and institutions: MGNREGA, NFSA, PMJAY, Citizens Charter, Sevottam, e-Shram, MyGov, CIC, Lokpal, CVC, CAG, NCSC, NCST, NCBC.
  • Data: NITI Aayog MPI, NFHS-5, PLFS, NFSA coverage figures, election turnout, pendency in courts (National Judicial Data Grid).
  • Diagrams: Flowcharts for centre-state relations, separation of powers, or election process; tables for scheme comparisons. Draw neatly and label.

Word Limit and Time Management

  • 10-mark question: ~150 words, ~7 minutes.
  • 15-mark question: ~250 words, ~10 minutes.
  • Total GS II paper: 20 questions, 250 marks, 3 hours.

Stick to word limits — over-writing one question starves another. Use bullet points for readability but keep paragraphs for narrative directives (discuss, critically examine). Leave margins for additional points if you remember them mid-flow.

Common Traps

  • Writing a generic introduction (“In today’s globalised world…”) instead of addressing the specific question.
  • Ignoring the directive — describing when asked to critically evaluate.
  • No constitutional anchoring — opinions without article/scheme references score low in GS II.
  • One-sided answers — “critically examine” demands both sides; “evaluate” demands a verdict.
  • Exceeding word limits on early questions and rushing the last ones.
  • No conclusion — every answer must end with a forward-looking or balanced closing line.
  • Illegible handwriting or cluttered layout — the examiner scans hundreds of scripts; clarity wins.

Memory Tricks

  • Directive map: Discuss = for-and-against; Critically examine = merits-demerits + judgment; Evaluate = weigh + verdict; Comment = informed opinion.
  • Body rule: One idea per paragraph; one evidence per idea.
  • Conclusion: Reform + way forward + one line.
  • GS II toolkit: Article + Scheme + Judgment + Commission + Data — sprinkle 2–3 per answer.
Technique: Answering a 15-mark critically examine question
Question: “Critically examine the role of the Governor in state politics.”
Answer: Intro — Governor is the constitutional head (Article 153) and Centre’s representative (Article 154–163). Body — discretionary powers (Article 200, reserving bills), appointment of CM (hung Assembly), recommendation of President’s Rule (Article 356), and Chancellor role in universities. Criticism — partisan appointments, delay in assent, acting on Centre’s direction (S.R. Bommai limits discretion). Conclusion — Governor should act on aid and advice except in clearly discretionary areas; Punchhi Commission reforms (fixed tenure, removal by impeachment) should be implemented.
Technique: Diagram in GS II
Question: Explain the distribution of legislative powers between Centre and states.
Answer: Draw a three-box diagram — Union List (97 subjects: defence, foreign affairs, currency), State List (66 subjects: police, public health, agriculture), Concurrent List (47 subjects: education, marriage, adoption). Add residual powers with Parliament (Article 248). State that Parliament prevails on Concurrent List (Article 254), and during emergency Parliament can legislate on State List (Article 250).

Common Traps

  • Repeating the question in the introduction instead of defining terms.
  • Using first person (“I believe”) — maintain an objective, administrative tone.
  • Citing wrong article numbers — verify before writing.
  • No way forward — every GS II answer should end with reform suggestions.
  • Mixing up directives — “analyse” ≠ “comment” ≠ “evaluate.”

Memory Tricks

  • IBC: Introduction, Body, Conclusion — every answer.
  • ASJCD: Article, Scheme, Judgment, Commission, Data — enrich every body paragraph.
  • DIR: Define, Illustrate, Relate — structure for conceptual answers.
Mains exam-day strategy
Read the directive word twice before writing. Allocate time strictly (15-mark = 10 minutes). Use black ink for main text, blue only for subheadings if permitted. Draw one diagram per paper if relevant — it breaks monotony. Attempt all 20 questions; a partially answered question earns more than a blank one. In the last 10 minutes, complete any incomplete answers in point form rather than leaving blanks.
mains-gs1/heritage-culture:
Indian Art and Architecture

Indian art spans over 5,000 years, from the Indus Valley Civilisation to contemporary forms. It reflects religious, philosophical, and regional diversity, and is a recurring theme in UPSC Mains GS I.

  • Indus Valley: Dancing Girl (bronze), Priest King (steatite), seals (Pashupati, unicorn), pottery, bead-making, and urban planning (Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Lothal, Dholavira).
  • Mauryan art: Pillars of Ashoka (Sarnath lion capital — national emblem), rock-cut caves (Barabar), stupas (Sanchi, Bharhut), and yaksha/yakshi figures (Didarganj).
  • Post-Mauryan: Gandhara (Greco-Roman influence, Buddha in human form), Mathura (indigenous, red sandstone), Amravati (narrative panels, Jataka tales).
  • Gupta period (Golden Age): Ajanta and Ellora caves, Dashavatara temple (Deogarh), iron pillar (Delhi), coinage, and classical sculpture (Sarnath Buddha preaching).
  • Medieval temple architecture: Nagara (north India — Kandariya Mahadeva, Khajuraho), Dravida (south India — Brihadeeswara, Thanjavur), Vesara (Deccan — Hoysala temples at Belur, Halebidu).
  • Indo-Islamic architecture: Qutub Minar, Alai Darwaza, Taj Mahal, Fatehpur Sikri, Gol Gumbaz, Charminar — arches, domes, minarets, pietra dura, and charbagh gardens.
  • Modern art: Bengal School (Abanindranath Tagore, Nandalal Bose), Company style, Raja Ravi Varma, Progressive Artists' Group (M.F. Husain, S.H. Raza), and contemporary installations.

Indian Music, Dance, and Theatre

  • Classical music: Hindustani (north) and Carnatic (south) traditions; dhrupad, khayal, thumri, kriti; instruments — sitar, sarod, tabla, veena, mridangam, flute.
  • Classical dance (8 recognised): Bharatanatyam (Tamil Nadu), Kathak (Uttar Pradesh), Kathakali (Kerala), Kuchipudi (Andhra), Manipuri (Manipur), Mohiniyattam (Kerala), Odissi (Odisha), Sattriya (Assam).
  • Folk forms: Bihu (Assam), Garba (Gujarat), Bhangra (Punjab), Chhau (Jharkhand/Odisha/West Bengal), Lavani (Maharashtra), Yakshagana (Karnataka), Therukoothu (Tamil Nadu).
  • Puppetry: Kathputli (Rajasthan), Bommalattam (Tamil Nadu), Yampuri (Bihar), Gombeyatta (Karnataka).
  • Theatre: Sanskrit theatre (Kalidasa, Bhasa), folk theatre (Jatra, Tamasha, Nautanki, Bhavai), and modern Indian theatre (Prithviraj Kapoor, Habib Tanvir, Ebrahim Alkazi).

Literature and Languages

  • Ancient: Vedas, Upanishads, epics (Ramayana, Mahabharata), Puranas, Buddhist Jataka tales, Jain Agamas, Sangam Tamil literature (Tolkappiyam, Silappatikaram, Manimekalai).
  • Medieval: Bhakti and Sufi literature (Kabir, Tulsidas, Surdas, Mirabai, Guru Nanak, Amir Khusro, Raskhan); regional epics (Ramcharitmanas, Kamba Ramayanam).
  • Modern: Premchand, Rabindranath Tagore (Nobel 1913), Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay, Sarat Chandra, Iqbal, Faiz, Amrita Pritam, and post-independence writers in Indian languages.
  • Classical languages: Six languages granted classical status — Tamil (2004), Sanskrit (2005), Kannada (2008), Telugu (2008), Malayalam (2013), Odia (2014).

Festivals and Crafts

  • Major festivals: Diwali, Holi, Eid, Christmas, Pongal, Onam, Bihu, Navratri, Durga Puja, Baisakhi, Onam, Hornbill (Nagaland), Losar (Arunachal/Sikkim).
  • Crafts: Pashmina (Kashmir), Madhubani (Bihar), Warli (Maharashtra), Pattachitra (Odisha), Kalamkari (Andhra), Bandhani (Gujarat/Rajasthan), Chikankari (Lucknow), Phulkari (Punjab), blue pottery (Jaipur), and Bidri work (Karnataka).
Technique: Architecture identification
Question: “The Lingaraja Temple at Bhubaneswar is a specimen of which architectural style?”
Answer: Kalinga style (a regional variant of Nagara), characterised by a curvilinear spire (rekha deula), jagamohana (assembly hall), and use of laterite and sandstone. Built in the 11th century by the Somavamsi dynasty, dedicated to Shiva.
Technique: Classical vs folk distinction
Question: Distinguish between a classical dance and a folk dance with examples.
Answer: Classical dances are rooted in the Natya Shastra, have a formal grammar, require rigorous training, and are often temple/court-originated (e.g., Bharatanatyam, Kathak). Folk dances are community-based, seasonal, celebratory, and less codified (e.g., Bihu, Garba, Bhangra).

Common Traps

  • Confusing Gandhara (foreign-influenced) with Mathura (indigenous) art.
  • Assuming all classical dances are from south India — Kathak is north Indian, Sattriya is from Assam.
  • Missing that UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage listings include Chhau dance, Kumbh Mela, Navroz, and Yoga.
  • Overlooking that classical language status is given by the Ministry of Culture based on antiquity and original literature.

Memory Tricks

  • NAGADRA: Nagara (north), Dravida (south), Vesara (Deccan) — the three temple styles.
  • 8 classical dances: B-K-K-M-M-O-O-S (Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Kathakali, Kuchipudi, Manipuri, Mohiniyattam, Odissi, Sattriya).
  • Gupta = Golden Age: Ajanta, Ellora, Deogarh, Iron pillar, Sarnath Buddha.
Mains exam-day strategy
For art and culture questions, always name the period, dynasty, region, and distinguishing features. Use specific examples (Sanchi stupa, Khajuraho temples, Chola bronzes). If asked about a specific art form, mention its GI tag (Geographical Indication) status where relevant — this adds precision.
mains-gs1/modern-history:
Advent of Europeans and Consolidation of British Power

European arrival in India began with Vasco da Gama (1498, Portuguese). The Portuguese established Goa (1510), followed by the Dutch, French, Danes, and finally the British East India Company (EIC), which received a Royal Charter in 1600 and established its first factory at Surat (1608).

  • Battle of Plassey (1757): Robert Clive defeated Siraj-ud-Daulah with Mir Jafar's betrayal — marked the beginning of British political power.
  • Battle of Buxar (1764): Company defeated the combined forces of Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daulah, and Shah Alam II — granted Diwani rights of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa (1765).
  • Dual Government (1765–72): Company had Diwani (revenue) but Nawab had Nizamat (administration) — led to administrative paralysis and exploitation.
  • Wars: Three Anglo-Mysore Wars (Haider Ali, Tipu Sultan), three Anglo-Maratha Wars, Anglo-Sikh Wars, Anglo-Nepal War, Anglo-Burmese Wars, Anglo-Afghan Wars.
  • Doctrine of Lapse (Lord Dalhousie): Annexed Satara (1848), Sambalpur (1849), Udaipur (1852), Jhansi (1853), Nagpur (1854), Awadh (1856 on grounds of misrule).

Company Rule: Administration and Policies

  • Regulating Act 1773: First parliamentary control; Governor-General of Bengal (Warren Hastings); Supreme Court at Calcutta.
  • Pitt's India Act 1784: Dual control — Board of Control (political) and Court of Directors (commercial).
  • Charter Acts 1813, 1833, 1853: Ended trade monopoly (except tea), centralised legislation, introduced open competition for civil services, and began the Legislative Council.
  • Land revenue: Permanent Settlement (1793, Cornwallis — Bengal, Bihar, Orissa), Ryotwari (Madras, Bombay — direct with cultivators), Mahalwari (North-Western Provinces — village-based).
  • Commercial policies: De-industrialisation, drain of wealth (Dadabhai Naoroji's theory), forced commercialisation of crops (indigo, opium, cotton).

Socio-Religious Reform Movements

  • Brahmo Samaj (1828, Raja Ram Mohan Roy): Abolition of sati (1829), monotheism, opposition to idol worship and caste.
  • Arya Samaj (1875, Dayananda Saraswati): "Back to the Vedas," shuddhi (reconversion), opposition to cow slaughter and untouchability.
  • Prarthana Samaj (1867, Atmaram Pandurang): Western India, social reform (widow remarriage, women's education).
  • Ramakrishna Mission (1897, Swami Vivekananda): Service to humanity, Vedanta, Chicago Parliament of Religions (1893).
  • Theosophical Society (1875, H.P. Blavatsky and H.S. Olcott; Annie Besant later): Adyar headquarters, revival of ancient religions.
  • Aligarh Movement (Sir Syed Ahmad Khan): Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College (1875), modern education for Muslims, loyal to British initially.
  • Singh Sabha (1873, Amritsar): Sikh reform, Gurdwara reforms, Punjabi language.
  • Satya Shodhak Samaj (Jyotiba Phule): Anti-caste, education for lower castes and women, Satyashodhak marriage.
  • Self-Respect Movement (E.V. Ramasamy 'Periyar'): Anti-Brahminism, rationalism, women's rights, Tamil pride.

Revolt of 1857

  • Causes: Political (Doctrine of Lapse, annexation of Awadh), economic (land revenue, de-industrialisation), military (greased cartridges, disparity in pay/promotion), social (interference in customs, Christian missionary activity), and immediate (Enfield rifle cartridges, March 1857, Meerut outbreak May 10).
  • Centres and leaders: Delhi (Bahadur Shah II), Kanpur (Nana Sahib, Tantia Tope), Lucknow (Begum Hazrat Mahal), Jhansi (Rani Lakshmibai), Bihar (Kunwar Singh), Faizabad (Maulvi Ahmadullah).
  • Suppression: Delhi recaptured (September 1857), Lucknow (Campbell), Jhansi (Hughes), Kunwar Singh defeated.
  • Nature: Debated — sepoy mutiny (British view), first war of independence (Savarkar, nationalist view), or a combination of grievances without unified nationalism.
  • Consequences: End of Company rule (1858), Crown takeover, Queen's Proclamation (1858), end of Doctrine of Lapse, reorganisation of army, rise of racial antagonism.

Indian National Movement — Moderate Phase (1885–1905)

  • Indian National Congress (1885): Founded by A.O. Hume; first session Bombay (W.C. Bonnerjee, president). Early leaders — Dadabhai Naoroji, Gopal Krishna Gokhale, Pherozeshah Mehta, Surendranath Banerjee, Dinshaw Wacha.
  • Methods: Petitions, prayers, protests, constitutional agitation, educating public opinion.
  • Economic critique: Dadabhai Naoroji's "Poverty and Un-British Rule in India" (drain of wealth), R.C. Dutt's economic history.
  • Demands: Indianisation of services, separation of judiciary from executive, reduction of military expenditure, civil rights, legislative councils with elected members.

Extremist Phase and Swadeshi (1905–1918)

  • Partition of Bengal (1905, Lord Curzon): Divided Bengal into East Bengal and Assam (Muslim-majority) and West Bengal (Hindu-majority) — seen as "divide and rule."
  • Swadeshi and Boycott: Boycott of British goods, promotion of Indian industries (Bengal Chemical, Tata Steel), national education (Bengal National College), Swadeshi steamship company (V.O. Chidambaram Pillai).
  • Extremist leaders: Bal Gangadhar Tilak ("Swaraj is my birthright"), Lala Lajpat Rai, Bipin Chandra Pal (Lal-Bal-Pal), Aurobindo Ghosh.
  • Surat Split (1907): Congress split into Moderates and Extremists over methods and goal (self-government vs constitutional reforms).
  • Muslim League (1906, Dacca): Founded by Nawab Salimullah; supported Partition of Bengal; demanded separate electorates (Morley-Minto Reforms 1909).
  • Home Rule Movement (1916): Annie Besant and Tilak — demanded self-government within the British Empire on lines of Irish Home Rule.
  • Lucknow Pact (1916): Congress-Muslim League agreement on separate electorates and weightage; joint demand for self-government.

Gandhian Era (1919–1947)

  • Rowlatt Act (1919) and Jallianwala Bagh (April 13, 1919): General Dyer fired on unarmed crowd in Amritsar — turning point in Indian politics.
  • Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22): Launched after Khilafat issue and Jallianwala Bagh; boycott of schools, courts, councils, foreign goods; Chauri Chaura (February 1922) led Gandhi to withdraw it.
  • Swaraj Party (1923, Motilal Nehru, C.R. Das): Council entry to obstruct government from within.
  • Simon Commission (1927): All-British commission — boycotted ("Simon Go Back"); led to Nehru Report (1928) demanding dominion status.
  • Purna Swaraj (1929, Lahore session): Jawaharlal Nehru as president; January 26 declared Independence Day.
  • Civil Disobedience Movement (1930–34): Dandi March (March 12–April 6, 1930), salt law violation; Round Table Conferences (1930–32); Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931); Poona Pact (1932) — reserved seats for depressed classes within Hindu electorate.
  • Quit India Movement (1942): "Do or Die" (August 8, 1942); mass arrests, underground leadership, parallel governments (Ballia, Tamluk, Satara).
  • INA (Subhas Chandra Bose): Azad Hind Fauj, Provisional Government of Free India (Singapore, 1943), women's regiment (Rani of Jhansi Regiment, Lakshmi Sahgal).
  • Cabinet Mission (1946): Three-tier federal plan, interim government; rejected by League and Congress in parts; led to Direct Action Day (August 16, 1946) and communal violence.
  • Mountbatten Plan / Indian Independence Act 1947: Partition into India and Pakistan; August 15, 1947; princely states given option to join either.

Post-Independence Consolidation

  • Integration of princely states (Sardar Patel): Hyderabad (Operation Polo, 1948), Junagadh (plebiscite), Kashmir (accession, 1947, Article 370), Goa (Operation Vijay, 1961), Pondicherry (French, 1954).
  • States Reorganisation Act 1956: Linguistic states — Andhra (1953, first linguistic state), then reorganisation on language basis.
  • Constitution adopted (1950): Republic declared.
Technique: Movement chronology
Question: Arrange in chronological order: Swadeshi, Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience, Quit India.
Answer: Swadeshi (1905) → Non-Cooperation (1920) → Civil Disobedience (1930) → Quit India (1942). Each escalated in mass participation and British repression.
Technique: Assessing the Moderates
Question: “The Moderates failed because they lacked mass base.” Comment.
Answer: Moderates (1885–1905) relied on educated elite, petitions, and British goodwill. Their achievements — economic critique, Council Act 1892, Indianisation of services — were real but limited. Lack of mass mobilisation, faith in British justice, and no direct action made them vulnerable to the Extremist critique after Partition of Bengal (1905).

Common Traps

  • Confusing the Regulating Act (1773) with Pitt's India Act (1784).
  • Thinking the 1857 Revolt had a unified nationalist ideology — it was a collection of regional grievances.
  • Missing that Swadeshi was both economic (boycott British goods) and political (swaraj).
  • Assuming Gandhi withdrew Non-Cooperation only due to Chauri Chaura — also due to fear of losing control and British repression.
  • Confusing Poona Pact (1932, Gandhi-Ambedkar) with Communal Award (1932, Ramsay MacDonald).

Memory Tricks

  • 1857 → 1947: Revolt → Crown rule → INC (1885) → Swadeshi (1905) → Non-Cooperation (1920) → Civil Disobedience (1930) → Quit India (1942) → Independence (1947).
  • Lal-Bal-Pal: Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal — Extremist trio.
  • Three settlements: Gandhi-Irwin (1931), Poona Pact (1932), Cabinet Mission (1946).
Mains exam-day strategy
For modern history, always anchor events with dates, viceroys, and key leaders. Distinguish between causes, course, and consequences. For movement-based questions, discuss leadership, methods, participation, British response, and impact. Avoid hero-worship — critically assess limitations (e.g., Moderates' elite base, Gandhian withdrawals).
mains-gs1/world-history:
Enlightenment and Revolutions (18th–19th Century)

The Enlightenment (Age of Reason) emphasised reason, science, individual rights, and secularism, challenging monarchical and church authority. It shaped modern political revolutions.

  • Key thinkers: John Locke (natural rights, social contract), Montesquieu (separation of powers), Voltaire (freedom of speech, religious tolerance), Rousseau (general will, popular sovereignty), Adam Smith (capitalism, invisible hand), Immanuel Kant (reason, enlightenment).
  • American Revolution (1775–83): "No taxation without representation"; Declaration of Independence (1776); Articles of Confederation; US Constitution (1787) — federalism, checks and balances, Bill of Rights (1791). First anti-colonial revolution.
  • French Revolution (1789–99): Causes — financial crisis, inequality (Estates-General), bread shortages, Enlightenment ideas. Events — storming of Bastille (1789), Declaration of the Rights of Man (1789), Reign of Terror (Robespierre), rise of Napoleon. Ideals — Liberty, Equality, Fraternity. Spread nationalism and republicanism across Europe.
  • Industrial Revolution (late 18th–19th c.): Began in Britain; steam engine (James Watt), textile machinery, railways, coal, iron. Shift from agrarian to industrial economy; urbanisation; factory system; child labour; rise of capitalism and working class; colonial markets for raw materials and finished goods.

Ideologies and Unifications (19th Century)

  • Nationalism: Loyalty to nation over dynasty/religion; language, shared history, territory as unifying factors; led to unification and independence movements.
  • Liberalism: Constitutional government, individual rights, free markets, limited state.
  • Socialism: Utopian (Owen, Saint-Simon) and scientific (Marx, Engels); critique of capitalism; class struggle; Communist Manifesto (1848).
  • Italian unification (Risorgimento, 1861): Mazzini (Young Italy), Cavour (diplomacy), Garibaldi (Redshirts), Victor Emmanuel II (first king). Role of realpolitik.
  • German unification (1871): Otto von Bismarck's "blood and iron"; Danish War (1864), Austro-Prussian War (1866), Franco-Prussian War (1870–71); proclamation of German Empire at Versailles.
  • Russian emancipation (1861): Serfdom abolished by Alexander II; limited land for peasants; revolutionary ferment continued.

Imperialism and Colonialism (19th–Early 20th Century)

  • Old vs new imperialism: Old (trade, settlements) vs new (political control, economic exploitation, "civilising mission," social Darwinism).
  • Scramble for Africa (1880s–1900): Berlin Conference (1884–85) divided Africa among European powers without African consent; colonisation of Congo, South Africa, Egypt, etc.
  • Asia: British in India, Burma, Malaya; French in Indochina; Dutch in Indonesia; US in Philippines; Japan's Meiji Restoration (1868) — modernisation and imperial expansion (Korea, Taiwan, Manchuria).
  • Consequences: Economic drain, cultural imposition, plantation economies, famines, resistance movements, and seeds of 20th-century decolonisation.

World Wars and the Interwar Period

  • WWI (1914–18): Causes — militarism, alliances, imperialism, nationalism (M-A-I-N); assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand (Sarajevo, 1914); Central Powers vs Allies; trench warfare; Treaty of Versailles (1919) — war guilt clause, reparations, League of Nations (weakened by US non-membership).
  • Russian Revolution (1917): February Revolution (Tsar abdicated, Provisional Government); October Revolution (Bolsheviks, Lenin); Treaty of Brest-Litovsk; Russian Civil War; USSR formed (1922). First communist state.
  • Interwar (1919–39): Weimar Germany (hyperinflation, 1923); Great Depression (1929, US stock market crash, global impact); rise of fascism (Mussolini, Italy, 1922) and nazism (Hitler, Germany, 1933); appeasement; Spanish Civil War (1936–39).
  • WWII (1939–45): Invasion of Poland (1939); Axis (Germany, Italy, Japan) vs Allies (UK, USSR, US); Pearl Harbor (1941); Stalingrad (turning point, 1942–43); D-Day (1944); atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki (1945); Holocaust (6 million Jews); UN formed (1945); Nuremberg trials.

Cold War and Decolonisation (1945–1991)

  • Cold War: US-led capitalist bloc vs USSR-led communist bloc; Truman Doctrine (1947), Marshall Plan (1948), NATO (1949), Warsaw Pact (1955); Korean War (1950–53), Vietnam War, Cuban Missile Crisis (1962), Space Race; détente; fall of Berlin Wall (1989); USSR dissolved (1991).
  • Decolonisation: India (1947), Indonesia (1949), Algeria (1962), African nations (1950s–70s); Non-Aligned Movement (1961, Belgrade; Nehru, Nasser, Tito, Sukarno, Nkrumah); struggles against apartheid (South Africa, Nelson Mandela).
  • Middle East: Israel-Palestine conflict (1948 creation of Israel, wars 1956, 1967, 1973); oil politics; Iranian Revolution (1979); Gulf Wars.

Post-Cold War World

  • Unipolar moment: US as sole superpower; Gulf War (1991); intervention in Balkans.
  • Globalisation: WTO (1995), regional blocs (EU, NAFTA/USMCA, ASEAN, SAARC), information technology revolution, outsourcing, rise of China (economic reforms from 1978, WTO entry 2001), resurgence of Russia.
  • 21st century challenges: 9/11 and War on Terror (Afghanistan 2001, Iraq 2003), climate change, pandemics, rise of multipolarity, great-power competition (US-China), Brexit, regional conflicts.
Technique: Comparing revolutions
Question: Compare the American and French Revolutions.
Answer: Both challenged monarchy and drew on Enlightenment ideas. American Revolution was anti-colonial (independence from Britain), produced a stable federal republic, and preserved property relations. French Revolution was internal (against the ancien régime), more radical (regicide, Reign of Terror), abolished feudal privileges, and exported revolutionary ideals across Europe through Napoleonic wars. Both inspired later nationalist and democratic movements.
Technique: Cold War blocs
Question: What led to the end of the Cold War?
Answer: Economic stagnation in USSR, costly arms race, Afghanistan war (1979–89), Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms (glasnost — openness, perestroika — restructuring), rise of nationalist movements in Soviet republics, fall of Berlin Wall (1989), and dissolution of USSR (1991) into 15 independent states.

Common Traps

  • Confusing the February and October Revolutions of 1917.
  • Thinking the Treaty of Versailles punished Germany alone — Austria-Hungary and Ottoman Empire were also dismantled (Treaties of Saint-Germain, Sèvres/Lausanne).
  • Assuming decolonisation was peaceful everywhere — Algeria, Vietnam, Kenya (Mau Mau), and Congo saw violent struggles.
  • Missing that NAM was not neutrality but active independence from both blocs.

Memory Tricks

  • M-A-I-N: Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism, Nationalism — causes of WWI.
  • Three unifications: Italy (1861), Germany (1871) — both used realpolitik and wars.
  • Cold War acronyms: NATO (West), Warsaw Pact (East), NAM (independent).
  • UN = 1945: Successor to the failed League of Nations.
Mains exam-day strategy
For world history, connect events to ideas (Enlightenment → revolutions → ideologies). Use maps mentally — locate events geographically. For comparative questions, use a framework: causes, course, leadership, outcome, global impact. Mention treaties and their terms precisely (Versailles, Vienna, Berlin). Avoid Eurocentrism — include Asian, African, and Latin American perspectives where relevant.
mains-gs1/society:
Indian Society — Salient Features

Indian society is characterised by "unity in diversity" — immense regional, linguistic, religious, and cultural variation within a shared civilisational framework. Understanding its structure, dynamics, and challenges is central to GS I.

  • Diversity: 22 scheduled languages, hundreds of dialects, six major religions (Hinduism, Islam, Christianity, Sikhism, Buddhism, Jainism), numerous tribal communities, varied cuisines, attire, and customs across states.
  • Unity: Constitutional framework (single citizenship, federal structure), shared festivals, epics (Ramayana, Mahabharata), pilgrimage sites, and the idea of Bharatvarsha.
  • Caste system: Varna (four-fold classical division) and jati (thousands of birth-based groups); historically rigid, occupation-linked, with untouchability; constitutionally abolished (Article 17) but persists in social practice and politics.
  • Family and marriage: Joint family (traditional), nuclear family (growing, urban), arranged marriages, endogamy, changing gender roles, rising divorce and live-in relationships, LGBTQ+ recognition (Navtej Singh Johar, 2018).
  • Tribal societies: ~705 recognised STs (8.6% of population, 2011 Census); distinct languages, customs, autonomous councils (Sixth Schedule), forest-dependent livelihoods, vulnerable to displacement.

Role of Women and Women's Organisations

  • Constitutional provisions: Article 14 (equality), Article 15(3) (protective discrimination), Article 15(4), Article 16 (equal opportunity), Article 39(a),(d) (equal pay, livelihood), Article 42 (maternity relief), Article 243D/T (33% reservation in Panchayats and Municipalities).
  • Legislations: Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act 2005 (equal coparcenary rights), Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005, Sexual Harassment at Workplace Act 2013, Dowry Prohibition Act 1961, MTP Act 1971 (amended 2021), PCPNDT Act 1994 (sex selection ban), Prohibition of Child Marriage Act 2006.
  • Women's organisations: AIWC (All India Women's Conference, 1927), SEWA (Self-Employed Women's Association, Ela Bhatt), National Federation of Indian Women, Mahila Mandals, SHGs (Self-Help Groups), NGO-led movements (Narmada Bachao — Medha Patkar, Chipko — women's participation).
  • Issues: Declining child sex ratio, domestic violence, workplace harassment, low female labour force participation (~25–30%), political underrepresentation (Women's Reservation Bill 2023 — 33% in Lok Sabha and Assemblies, not yet implemented), trafficking, honour killings, witch-hunting.
  • Schemes: Beti Bachao Beti Padhao, Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana, Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana, Ujjwala (LPG for women), Stand-Up India (women entrepreneurs), Mission Shakti.

Population and Associated Issues

  • Demographic profile: ~1.4 billion (2023, India surpassed China), median age ~28 (young), fertility rate ~2.0 (below replacement), life expectancy ~70, urbanisation ~35% (rising).
  • Population explosion consequences: Pressure on resources (land, water, food), unemployment, urban slums, environmental degradation, strain on health and education infrastructure.
  • Demographic dividend: Large working-age population — opportunity if skilled and employed; risk if not (demographic burden).
  • Ageing: Rising elderly population (60+), erosion of joint family support, need for pension, healthcare, and elder-friendly infrastructure (National Policy for Older Persons, Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act 2007).
  • Migration: Rural-to-urban (distress and opportunity-driven), inter-state (linguistic and cultural friction), international (diaspora, remittances ~$100 billion), internal displacement (dams, disasters, conflict).
  • Census: Decennial exercise; Census 2021 delayed; SECC 2011 (socio-economic data); NFHS (health and nutrition).

Poverty and Developmental Issues

  • Poverty measurement: Tendulkar line, Rangarajan committee, NITI Aayog MPI (multidimensional — health, education, living standards); ~22% below poverty line (varies by estimate).
  • Vulnerable groups: SCs, STs, OBCs, minorities, landless labourers, informal workers (~90% of workforce), differently-abled, elderly.
  • Development vs growth: GDP growth without equitable distribution; HDI ranking (India ~134/193, 2022); inequality (Gini coefficient rising); regional disparities (south/west vs north/east).
  • Inclusive growth: Sabka Saath Sabka Vikas, Aspirational Districts Programme, Direct Benefit Transfer, financial inclusion (PMJDY), skill development.

Urbanisation and Its Problems

  • Trends: India urbanising fast (~35% now, projected ~50% by 2050); smart cities, AMRUT, PMAY-Urban.
  • Problems: Slums (Dharavi), housing shortage, traffic congestion, pollution (air, water, waste), inadequate water supply and sanitation, informal economy, urban heat islands, disaster vulnerability (floods — Chennai, Mumbai, Bengaluru).
  • Solutions: RERA (real estate), metro rail, waste-to-energy, rainwater harvesting, pedestrianisation, public transport, mixed-use development, participatory planning (74th Amendment — municipalities, ward committees).

Globalisation's Impact on Indian Society

  • Positive: IT and service sector growth, employment, consumer access, exposure to global ideas, women's workforce entry (BPOs, MNCs), remittances, medical tourism.
  • Negative: Consumerism, erosion of traditional values, nuclear families, loneliness, mental health issues, cultural homogenisation, job insecurity (gig economy), agricultural distress (WTO pressures, farmer suicides), digital divide.
  • Social movements: Anti-corruption (Anna Hazare, 2011), environmental (Chipko, Narmada, Save Aarey), gender (Nirbhaya protests, 2012; #MeToo India), caste (Rohith Vemula, 2016), farmers' protest (2020–21).
Technique: Social issue analysis
Question: “Declining child sex ratio reflects deeper societal issues.” Examine.
Answer: Child sex ratio (0–6 years) declined from 927 (2001) to 918 (2011 Census). Causes — son preference, dowry, patriarchy, sex-selective abortion (despite PCPNDT Act), small-family norm with gender bias. Consequences — bride trafficking, polyandry in some regions, skewed marriage markets. Solutions — Beti Bachao Beti Padhao, strict PCPNDT enforcement, women's education and employment, changing social norms through media and role models.
Technique: Demographic dividend
Question: Is India's young population a dividend or a burden?
Answer: It is a potential dividend — 65% of Indians are under 35. Realisation depends on education (NEP 2020), skill (PMKVY), health (Ayushman Bharat), and job creation (manufacturing, services, MSMEs). Without these, it becomes a burden — unemployment, social unrest, wasted potential. East Asia (South Korea, Taiwan) used this window in the 1970s–90s; India must replicate with Indian characteristics.

Common Traps

  • Assuming caste is only a Hindu phenomenon — it exists among Christians, Muslims, and Sikhs too.
  • Thinking urbanisation is only about cities — it includes peri-urban and rural-to-urban migration dynamics.
  • Missing that the Women's Reservation Bill (2023) is linked to delimitation and Census — not yet implemented.
  • Confusing demographic dividend with population explosion — both coexist (large population + young age structure).
  • Overlooking that tribal societies are not homogeneous — distinct languages, economies, and integration levels across regions.

Memory Tricks

  • Women's articles: 14, 15(3), 16, 39, 42, 243D/T.
  • Social evils → laws: Dowry → 1961; Sati → 1829 (Bentinck); Child marriage → 2006; Domestic violence → 2005.
  • Population: Young (median 28), fertility ~2.0, urban ~35%, elderly rising.
Mains exam-day strategy
For society questions, blend constitutional provisions, data (Census, NFHS, NITI Aayog MPI), schemes, and critical analysis. Avoid generalisations — regional, caste, and class differences matter. Use Supreme Court judgments (Navtej Johar, Joseph Shine, Puttaswamy) where relevant. Conclude with a way forward — behavioural change, law enforcement, education, and economic opportunity.
mains-gs1/world-geography:
Physical Geography of the World

World physical geography covers landforms, climate, oceans, and natural phenomena across continents — essential for understanding global resources, disasters, and human settlement patterns.

  • Geomorphic processes: Endogenic (folding, faulting, volcanism, earthquakes — plate tectonics, continental drift by Alfred Wegener, seafloor spreading) and exogenic (weathering, mass wasting, erosion, deposition by rivers, wind, glaciers, sea).
  • Major landforms: Mountains (fold — Himalayas, Alps, Andes; block — Vosges, Sierra Nevada; volcanic — Mt. Fuji, Mt. Kilimanjaro), plateaus (Tibetan — highest, Deccan, Brazilian), plains (alluvial — Indo-Gangetic, Mississippi; coastal), and plains formation.
  • Rocks: Igneous (granite, basalt), sedimentary (sandstone, limestone, shale), metamorphic (marble, slate, gneiss); rock cycle.
  • Earthquakes and volcanoes: Concentrated along plate boundaries — Circum-Pacific Ring of Fire (~75% of volcanoes), mid-ocean ridges, Alpine-Himalayan belt. Seismic zones (India — Zone V most vulnerable).
  • Drainage patterns: Dendritic, trellis, radial, rectangular, parallel — controlled by rock structure and slope.

Climatology

  • Atmosphere: Layers — troposphere (weather), stratosphere (ozone layer), mesosphere, thermosphere, exosphere. Composition — N2 (78%), O2 (21%), argon, CO2, trace gases.
  • Insolation and heat budget: Solar radiation, albedo, greenhouse effect, global warming. Factors affecting temperature — latitude, altitude, distance from sea, ocean currents, prevailing winds.
  • Pressure and winds: Pressure belts — equatorial low, subtropical highs (horse latitudes), subpolar lows, polar highs. Planetary winds — trade winds, westerlies, polar easterlies. Seasonal winds — monsoons. Local winds — land/sea breeze, monsoon, chinook, foehn, sirocco, harmattan, loo.
  • Cyclones: Tropical (hurricanes — Atlantic, typhoons — Pacific, cyclones — Indian Ocean) form over warm oceans (>26.5°C), Coriolis effect; temperate cyclones along fronts (mid-latitudes).
  • Climate classification (Köppen): A (tropical), B (dry), C (temperate), D (continental), E (polar). Major climate regions — equatorial, monsoon, Mediterranean, desert, temperate grassland, taiga, tundra.
  • El Niño and La Niña: Warming/cooling of central/eastern Pacific; affects Indian monsoon, global weather patterns (droughts, floods).

Oceanography

  • Ocean relief: Continental shelf, slope, rise, abyssal plain, mid-ocean ridges, trenches (Mariana — deepest), seamounts, guyots, atolls.
  • Ocean temperature and salinity: Varies with latitude, evaporation, precipitation, river inflow, ice melting. High salinity — Red Sea, Persian Gulf; low — Baltic, near river mouths.
  • Ocean currents: Warm (Gulf Stream, North Atlantic Drift, Kuroshio) and cold (Labrador, Oyashio, Humboldt, Benguela, Canary). Driven by winds, Coriolis, temperature/salinity differences. Affect climate (Western Europe warmth due to Gulf Stream), fishing grounds (where warm and cold currents meet — Grand Banks).
  • Tides: Spring (sun-moon alignment, higher range) and neap (right angle, lower range); tidal energy potential.
  • Ocean deposits: Terrigenous (land-derived), pelagic (marine organisms), volcanogenic; coral reefs — fringing, barrier, atoll (conditions: warm shallow water, salinity, sunlight).

Biogeography

  • Soils: Zonal (climate-controlled — laterite, chernozem, podzol, prairie), intrazonal, azonal. Soil formation factors — parent rock, climate, topography, organisms, time. Soil erosion (sheet, rill, gully) and conservation (contour bunding, terracing, afforestation).
  • Natural vegetation: Forests (tropical rainforest, deciduous, coniferous, tundra), grasslands (savanna, prairie, steppe, veldt, downs), deserts, tundra. Distribution linked to climate.
  • Biodiversity: Hotspots (36 globally — Western Ghats, Eastern Himalayas, Indo-Burma, Sundaland in India's neighborhood); endemism; threats — habitat loss, poaching, invasive species, climate change.
Technique: Ocean current-climate link
Question: “Western Europe has a milder climate than eastern Canada at the same latitude.” Explain.
Answer: The North Atlantic Drift (warm current, extension of Gulf Stream) flows past Western Europe, warming winds and keeping ports ice-free in winter. Eastern Canada is cooled by the cold Labrador Current. Prevailing westerlies carry these maritime influences to the respective landmasses.
Technique: Monsoon mechanism
Question: Why does the Indian subcontinent receive seasonal rainfall?
Answer: Differential heating of land (Tibetan plateau becomes intense low pressure in summer) and ocean; ITCZ shifts northward; moisture-laden southwest monsoon winds from Indian Ocean bring rain (June–September). Winter: high pressure over land, dry northeast monsoon from land to sea (Tamil Nadu coast gets rain).

Common Traps

  • Confusing weather (short-term) with climate (long-term average).
  • Assuming all deserts are hot — cold deserts exist (Ladakh, Gobi, Antarctica).
  • Missing that El Niño weakens the Indian monsoon, while La Niña often strengthens it.
  • Confusing tropical cyclones (warm-core, ocean-born) with temperate cyclones (front-based, mid-latitudes).
  • Thinking coral reefs grow in cold/deep water — they need warm (20–30°C), shallow, saline, clear water.

Memory Tricks

  • Pressure belts: Equator low, 30°N/S high, 60°N/S low, 90°N/S high.
  • Köppen letters: A-tropical, B-dry, C-temperate, D-continental, E-polar.
  • Ring of Fire: Pacific plate boundary — most earthquakes and volcanoes.
Mains exam-day strategy
For physical geography, always link process to pattern — e.g., plate tectonics → fold mountains → earthquakes. Draw diagrams (plate boundaries, monsoon winds, ocean current circulation, heat zones). Cite specific examples (Mariana Trench, Grand Banks fishing, El Niño 2015-16 impact on Indian monsoon). Conclude with human adaptation or disaster management where relevant.
mains-gs1/indian-geography-mains:
Physiographic Divisions of India

India's physical geography is divided into six major physiographic divisions, each with distinct geological history, relief, drainage, and resource base.

  • The Himalayas: Young fold mountains (formed by Indian-Eurasian plate collision, ~50 million years ago); three parallel ranges — Greater Himalaya (Himadri), Lesser Himalaya (Himachal), Shiwaliks; eastern and western syntaxes; important passes (Nathu La, Shipki La, Rohtang, Zoji La, Banihal, Bum La); rivers — Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra systems originate here.
  • The Northern Plains: Formed by alluvial deposition of Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra and tributaries; Punjab-Haryana-Delhi, Ganga plain, Brahmaputra plain; Bhabar, Terai, Bhangar, Khadar zones; fertile, densely populated.
  • The Peninsular Plateau: Oldest landmass (Gondwana land); triangular shape; bordered by Western and Eastern Ghats; subdivided into Central Highlands (Malwa, Bundelkhand, Baghelkhand, Chotanagpur) and Deccan Plateau; rich in minerals (coal, iron ore, manganese, mica); black cotton soil (regur) in Deccan.
  • The Indian Desert: Thar Desert (Rajasthan) — arid, sandy, sparse vegetation, Luni river, saline lakes (Sambhar), cold desert in Ladakh.
  • The Coastal Plains: Western (Konkan, Kanara, Malabar — narrow, rocky) and Eastern (Coromandel, Northern Circars — wider, deltaic, formed by Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri); lagoons (Chilika, Pulicat, Vembanad).
  • The Islands: Andaman and Nicobar (volcanic origin, Barren Island — only active volcano in India, Saddle Peak — highest), Lakshadweep (coral atolls, 36 islands, Minicoy).

Drainage System

  • Himalayan rivers (perennial): Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra — snow-fed, large basins, form deltas (Ganga-Brahmaputra — world's largest delta, Sundarbans), youthful topography (gorges, V-shaped valleys, waterfalls).
  • Peninsular rivers (seasonal): Narmada, Tapi (west-flowing, rift valleys), Godavari (Dakshin Ganga), Krishna, Kaveri, Mahanadi, Subarnarekha — older, graded, smaller basins, form estuaries (Narmada, Tapi) or deltas (others).
  • Drainage patterns: Dendritic (Indo-Gangetic), radial (Amarkantak — Narmada, Son), trellis (Himalayas), rectangular (Vindhyas).
  • River linking and disputes: Inter-state water disputes — Cauvery (Karnataka-Tamil Nadu), Krishna, Godavari, Mahanadi, Mahanadi, Ravi-Beas (Punjab-Haryana); River Boards Act 1956, Inter-State River Water Disputes Act 1956, tribunals.

Climate of India

  • Controls: Latitude (Tropic of Cancer passes through middle), altitude (Himalayas shield cold winds), pressure and wind systems (NE and SW monsoons), distance from sea, ocean currents, relief.
  • Seasons: Cold weather (Dec–Feb), hot weather (Mar–May), advancing monsoon (June–Sept), retreating monsoon (Oct–Nov).
  • Monsoon mechanism: Differential heating, ITCZ shift, Tibetan plateau heating, Somali jet (Findlater jet), easterly jet (Tropical Easterly Jet), El Niño effect.
  • Rainfall distribution: Very high (>200 cm) — Western Ghats, Northeast, Andaman; high (100–200) — Odisha, West Bengal, Bihar, eastern UP; moderate (50–100) — Gujarat, MP, AP, TN; low (<50) — Rajasthan, Ladakh, parts of Gujarat and Punjab.
  • Climate variability: Droughts, floods, cyclones (Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea), heat waves, western disturbances (winter rain in northwest).

Soils and Vegetation

  • Soil types (ICAR classification): Alluvial (Indo-Gangetic, most fertile), black/regur (Deccan, cotton), red (TN, Karnataka, Odisha, iron-rich), laterite (Kerala, Karnataka, NE hills, acidic), arid/desert (Rajasthan, saline), forest/mountain (Himalayas, acidic), peaty/marshy (Kerala, Sundarbans, Orissa).
  • Natural vegetation: Tropical evergreen (Western Ghats, Andaman, NE — rainforest), tropical deciduous (monsoon forests — most widespread, teak, sal, shisham), thorny/scrub (Rajasthan, Gujarat — acacia, babul), montane (Himalayas — pine, deodar, oak, rhododendron, alpine), mangroves (Sundarbans — sundari, Andaman, Pichavaram).
  • Conservation: National parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biosphere reserves (Nilgiri, Gulf of Mannar, Sundarbans, Nanda Devi, etc.), Project Tiger, Project Elephant, Project Rhino, Crocodile conservation.

Natural Resources and Agriculture

  • Mineral distribution: Iron ore (Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka, Goa, Jharkhand), coal (Jharia, Raniganj, Singrauli, Talcher — Gondwana and Tertiary), petroleum (Assam — Digboi, Mumbai High, KG basin, Rajasthan), natural gas, bauxite (Odisha, Gujarat), mica (Andhra, Rajasthan, Bihar), gold (Kolar, Hutti), copper (Khetri, Rajasthan), manganese (Odisha, Madhya Pradesh), limestone (cement).
  • Power resources: Conventional — coal (thermal), hydro (Bhakra, Hirakud, Tehri, Koyna), nuclear (Tarapur, Rawatbhata, Kudankulam, Kalpakkam, Kakrapar), natural gas; Non-conventional — solar (Rajasthan, Gujarat), wind (Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Maharashtra), biogas, tidal (Gulf of Kutch), geothermal (Ladakh, Himachal).
  • Agriculture: Types — subsistence, intensive, commercial, plantation, mixed; cropping seasons — kharif (rice, cotton, sugarcane), rabi (wheat, gram, mustard), zaid (vegetables, fodder); major crops distribution — rice (WB, UP, AP, TN), wheat (UP, Punjab, Haryana), cotton (Maharashtra, Gujarat, Punjab), tea (Assam, WB, Kerala), coffee (Karnataka, Kerala, TN), spices (Kerala), jute (WB, Assam).
  • Irrigation: Wells, tanks, canals (Indira Gandhi, Bhakra, Damodar), tube wells, drip and sprinkler (micro-irrigation); command areas and waterlogging/salinity issues.

Human Geography

  • Population distribution: Uneven — high density in Indo-Gangetic plains, coastal plains, deltas; low in mountains, deserts, NE hills; density ~464/km² (2011).
  • Migration: Rural-to-urban (employment), inter-state (Hindi belt to Maharashtra, Delhi, Gujarat), international (diaspora, Gulf, US, UK); internal displacement (dams, mining, disasters).
  • Settlements: Rural (compact, semi-compact, hamleted, dispersed) and urban (classified by size — census towns, statutory towns, urban agglomerations, million-plus cities, megacities).
  • Urban issues: Slums, traffic, pollution, waste management, water scarcity, urban floods, informal economy.
Technique: River dispute framing
Question: “Inter-state river water disputes are a recurring challenge in Indian federalism.” Examine with examples.
Answer: Water is a state subject (Entry 17, List II) but Centre can legislate for inter-state rivers (Entry 56, List I). Examples — Cauvery (Karnataka-TN, Supreme Court 2018 verdict), Krishna (AP-Telangana-Maharashtra), Mahanadi (Odisha-Chhattisgarh), Ravi-Beas (Punjab-Haryana-Rajasthan). Mechanisms — Inter-State River Water Disputes Act 1956, tribunals (Cauvery, Krishna, Godavari, Mahanadi, Vansadhara), but delays and non-compliance persist. Need — data sharing, basin-level planning, negotiation culture.
Technique: Monsoon variability
Question: How does El Niño affect Indian agriculture?
Answer: El Niño warms the eastern Pacific, often weakening the Indian summer monsoon (reduced rainfall, delayed onset, uneven distribution). Impact — kharif crop stress (rice, pulses), reservoir depletion, food inflation, rural distress. Not always deterministic — Indian Ocean Dipole (positive IOD can offset El Niño), and intra-seasonal variability matter more for local impacts.

Common Traps

  • Assuming all peninsular rivers form deltas — Narmada and Tapi form estuaries (flow west into rift valleys).
  • Missing that the Tropic of Cancer passes through 8 Indian states (Gujarat, Rajasthan, MP, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, WB, Tripura, Mizoram).
  • Confusing Western Ghats (continuous, higher, orographic rain) with Eastern Ghats (discontinuous, lower).
  • Thinking Andaman and Nicobar are coral islands — they are volcanic/tectonic; Lakshadweep are coral atolls.
  • Overlooking that soil erosion is worse in Shiwaliks, Chambal ravines, and NE hills (jhum cultivation).

Memory Tricks

  • Six physiographic divisions: Himalayas, Northern Plains, Peninsular Plateau, Indian Desert, Coastal Plains, Islands.
  • Perennial vs seasonal: Himalayan = snow-fed (perennial); Peninsular = rain-fed (seasonal).
  • Alluvial sub-divisions: Bhabar (pebble belt, streams disappear), Terai (marshy, stream re-emerges), Bhangar (older alluvium, kankar), Khadar (newer alluvium, fertile).
  • Black soil states: Maharashtra, MP, Gujarat, Andhra, Karnataka, TN — cotton belt.
Mains exam-day strategy
For Indian geography, always support descriptions with a locational map reference (state, river, mountain range). Use sketch maps where permitted. For resource questions, link distribution to geology (coal–Gondwana, iron–Odisha-Jharkhand, petroleum–Assam-Mumbai High). For climate questions, explain mechanism not just pattern. Conclude with sustainable management — conservation, micro-irrigation, disaster-resilient infrastructure.
mains-gs1/answer-writing-gs1:
GS I Answer Writing Framework

GS I covers History (Indian + World), Geography (Indian + World), Indian Society, and Culture. Questions range from factual (10 marks) to analytical (15 marks). The key is structured, dimension-rich answers with precise referencing.

Approach by Subject Area

  • Modern History: Chronology matters. For movement-based questions — background, causes, leadership, methods, participants, British response, outcome, limitations. For reformers — ideology, contributions, limitations, relevance. Cite Acts, sessions, dates, and viceroys.
  • World History: Connect events to ideas (Enlightenment → revolutions → ideologies → wars → Cold War → decolonisation). Use cause-effect-consequence framework. Mention treaties, leaders, and global impact.
  • Indian Culture: Name period, dynasty, region, distinguishing features. Specific examples (Sanchi, Khajuraho, Chola bronzes, Ajanta). GI tags add precision. Religion-philosophy-art linkages.
  • Physical Geography: Process → pattern linkage (plate tectonics → fold mountains → earthquakes). Draw diagrams (plate boundaries, monsoon, ocean currents, heat zones). Specific examples.
  • Indian Geography: Location + description + resources + issues. Sketch maps. Soil–crop–region links. River–dispute linkages. Monsoon mechanism.
  • Indian Society: Constitutional provisions + data (Census, NFHS, NITI Aayog MPI) + schemes + critical analysis. Avoid generalisations — regional, caste, class differences matter. SC judgments (Navtej Johar, Joseph Shine, Puttaswamy) where relevant.

Structure of a GS I Answer

  • Introduction (15–20%): Define the core term, cite constitutional/article reference or context, state the line of argument. Example: For "El Niño and Indian monsoon" — define El Niño, state its typical impact on Indian rainfall.
  • Body (60–70%): 3–4 thematic paragraphs or bullet clusters. Each paragraph: one idea, evidence (data, example, case study), linkage to question. Use subheadings for multi-part questions.
  • Conclusion (10–15%): Forward-looking, balanced, no new facts. Way forward, reforms, or restatement of core finding.

Dimension Enrichment Toolkit

  • History toolkit: Viceroy + Act + Year + Leader + Session + Outcome.
  • Geography toolkit: Location + Process + Distribution + Issue + Management.
  • Society toolkit: Constitutional article + Census/NFHS data + Scheme + SC judgment + Way forward.
  • Culture toolkit: Period + Dynasty + Region + Feature + Example + GI tag.

Diagrams and Maps

  • GS I rewards well-labelled diagrams — plate boundaries, monsoon winds, ocean currents, heat zones, river basins, physiographic divisions, crop distribution maps.
  • Draw neat, simple sketches — not works of art. Label clearly. Use one diagram per answer where relevant.
  • For map-based questions (e.g., "locate and mark"), be precise with locations.

Word Limit and Time

  • 10-mark: ~150 words, ~7 minutes.
  • 15-mark: ~250 words, ~10 minutes.
  • Total GS I: 20 questions, 250 marks, 3 hours.

Attempt all questions — partial answers score more than blanks. In the last 10 minutes, complete incomplete answers in point form.

Common Traps

  • Writing a generic introduction instead of addressing the specific question.
  • Ignoring directive words (analyse vs critically examine vs evaluate vs comment).
  • No factual anchoring — opinions without dates, Acts, articles, or data score low.
  • One-sided answers for "critically examine" (needs both sides + judgment).
  • Exceeding word limits early and rushing later questions.
  • No conclusion — every answer needs a closing line.
  • Illegible handwriting or cluttered layout.

Memory Tricks

  • IBC: Introduction, Body, Conclusion — every answer.
  • History chain: Viceroy → Act → Year → Leader → Outcome.
  • Geography chain: Process → Pattern → Example → Management.
  • Society chain: Article + Data + Scheme + Judgment + Way forward.
Technique: 15-mark critically examine answer
Question: “Critically examine the impact of British land revenue systems on Indian agriculture.”
Answer: Intro — Three systems (Permanent Settlement 1793, Ryotwari, Mahalwari) shaped agrarian relations. Body — Permanent Settlement created absentee landlordism in Bengal; Ryotwari over-assessed in Madras/Bombay; Mahalwari was village-based but inflexible. Common impact — commercialisation, indebtedness, famines, de-industrialisation. Critique — systems differed regionally; some irrigation and canal development occurred under British rule. Conclusion — extractive overall, but uneven impact; land revenue legacy shapes tenancy and land reform debates today.
Technique: Diagram-based geography answer
Question: Explain the mechanism of the Indian monsoon with a diagram.
Answer: Diagram — landmass heating (low pressure over NW India/Tibet), high pressure over southern Indian Ocean, ITCZ northward shift, SW monsoon winds (June–September), moisture from Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal branches, orographic rain on Western Ghats and NE. Body — El Niño weakens, positive IOD strengthens; western disturbances give winter rain. Conclusion — monsoon variability affects agriculture, water security, and economy; needs accurate forecasting and resilient crops.

Common Traps

  • Repeating the question in the introduction.
  • Using first person ("I believe") — maintain objective tone.
  • Citing wrong article/Act/year — verify before writing.
  • No way forward — every GS I answer should end with a forward path.
  • Mixing up directives — "analyse" ≠ "comment" ≠ "evaluate."

Memory Tricks

  • DIR: Define, Illustrate, Relate — structure for conceptual answers.
  • GS I toolkit: Date + Act/Article + Example + Data + Diagram — sprinkle 2–3 per answer.
  • Conclusion: Reform + way forward + one line.
Mains exam-day strategy
Read the directive word twice before writing. Allocate time strictly (15-mark = 10 minutes). Use black ink for main text; draw diagrams in pencil then label in ink. Attempt all 20 questions. If running out of time, write incomplete answers in bullet points — partial credit is better than zero.
mains-gs3/indian-economy-mains:
Economic Growth and Development

Indian economy is the world's fifth-largest by nominal GDP and third-largest by PPP. GS III economy covers growth, development, planning, mobilisation of resources, and inclusive growth challenges.

  • GDP vs GVA: GDP = gross value added + product taxes − subsidies. GVA = value of output − intermediate consumption. GVA by sector shows sectoral performance; GDP includes taxes.
  • Growth vs development: Growth = increase in output/income; development = growth + improvement in health, education, equity, freedom (HDI, multidimensional poverty).
  • HDI: Human Development Index (UNDP) — health (life expectancy), education (schooling), standard of living (GNI per capita). India ranks ~134/193 (2022).
  • Planning in India: Planning Commission (1950–2014) replaced by NITI Aayog (2015) — think tank, cooperative federalism, Aspirational Districts Programme, no five-year plans since 12th Plan (2012–17).
  • Mobilisation of resources: Tax revenue (direct — income, corporate; indirect — GST), non-tax (dividends, disinvestment, spectrum), borrowing (market stabilisation scheme, ways and means), external (World Bank, ADB, bilateral, sovereign bonds).

Fiscal Policy and Budgeting

  • Union Budget: Article 112 — Annual Financial Statement. Revenue account (current income/expenditure) and capital account (assets/liabilities). Presented Feb 1 (since 2017), merged Railway Budget (2017).
  • Fiscal deficit: Total expenditure − total receipts (excluding borrowings). FRBM Act 2003 targets — eliminate revenue deficit, reduce fiscal deficit to 3% of GDP (targets relaxed post-pandemic).
  • Revenue deficit: Revenue expenditure exceeds revenue receipts — indicates government is borrowing for consumption, not investment.
  • Primary deficit: Fiscal deficit minus interest payments — shows current-year borrowing excluding past debt burden.
  • Deficit financing: Borrowing from RBI (monetised deficit — now limited), market borrowing, external debt.
  • GST: 101st Amendment 2016, launched July 1, 2017 — one nation one tax, subsumed ~17 central/state taxes, dual GST (CGST/SGST/IGST), GST Council (constitutional body, Article 279A), compensation cess (ends 2026).

Monetary Policy and Banking

  • RBI: Established 1935, nationalised 1949; monetary authority, banker to banks/government, currency issuer, regulator, manager of forex.
  • Monetary Policy Committee (MPC): 2016 (Finance Act), 6 members (3 RBI + 3 external), inflation targeting — CPI inflation 4% ± 2% band; repo rate is policy rate.
  • Policy rates: Repo (RBI lends to banks), reverse repo (RBI borrows), MSF (marginal standing facility — emergency overnight), bank rate (same as MSF), CRR (cash reserve ratio), SLR (statutory liquidity ratio).
  • Inflation: CPI (retail, headline), WPI (wholesale), core inflation (excluding food and fuel). Causes — demand-pull, cost-push, imported (oil).
  • Banking: Public sector banks (PSBs), private banks, small finance banks, payment banks, regional rural banks (RRBs), local area banks. NPAs (bad loans), Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016, NCLT, SARFAESI Act, one-time settlement, bad bank (NARCL).
  • Financial inclusion: PMJDY (zero-balance accounts), MUDRA, Stand-Up India, SHG-bank linkage, BC (business correspondent) model, Jan Dhan-Aadhaar-Mobile (JAM) trinity, DBT.
  • Digital payments: UPI (NPCI), RTGS, NEFT, IMPS, BHIM, RuPay, AEPS, e-RUPI; RBI's regulatory sandbox.

External Sector

  • Balance of Payments (BoP): Current account (trade in goods/services, income, transfers) and capital account (FDI, FPI, ECB, NRI deposits, banking capital). BoP = current + capital + errors/omissions + reserve changes.
  • FDI vs FPI: FDI — long-term, controlling interest, brings technology/management (automatic route + government route sectors); FPI — portfolio investment, short-term, volatile (hot money).
  • Forex reserves: Foreign currency assets, gold, SDR, IMF reserve tranche; managed by RBI; import cover ~9–10 months.
  • Exchange rate: Managed float (RBI intervenes to curb volatility); real effective exchange rate (REER); rupee depreciation/appreciation effects on trade and inflation.
  • Trade agreements: FTAs (ASEAN, Japan, South Korea, UAE, Australia — ECTA/ECTA), bilateral investment treaties, RCEP (India opted out, 2019), WTO.

Inclusive Growth and Employment

  • Employment: PLFS (Periodic Labour Force Survey) — unemployment rate, labour force participation rate (LFPR), worker-population ratio; informal sector ~90%; gig/platform workers; Code on Wages 2019, occupational safety codes.
  • Poverty: NITI Aayog MPI, Tendulkar/Rangarajan lines; schemes — MGNREGA, NFSA, PMJAY, PMUY, PMAY, NSAP.
  • MSMEs: Definition (investment and turnover criteria, revised 2020), Udyam registration, Credit Guarantee Fund (CGTMSE), PMEGP, SFURTI, CHAMPIONS portal; contribution to GDP (~30%), exports (~45%), employment (~11 crore).
  • Startups: Startup India (2016), Fund of Funds (SIDBI), tax holidays, DPIIT recognition, unicorns; India is 3rd largest startup ecosystem.
  • Ease of Doing Business: India improved ranking (World Bank, discontinued 2021); reforms — single window, labour codes, GST, insolvency.

Investment Models

  • PPP (Public-Private Partnership): BOT (build-operate-transfer), BOOT, BOO, BLT, O&M; viability gap funding (VGF), Indian Infrastructure Finance Company (IIFCL), National Investment and Infrastructure Fund (NIIF).
  • Disinvestment/Privatisation: Strategic disinvestment (Air India, BPCL, Shipping Corporation), CPSE (central public sector enterprises), NIP (National Infrastructure Pipeline, ₹111 lakh crore).
Technique: Fiscal deficit framing
Question: “Fiscal deficit targets under FRBM are often breached — is the Act ineffective?”
Answer: FRBM Act 2003 mandates fiscal consolidation but escape clauses allow deviation (national security, calamity, structural reforms). Deviations occurred post-2008 crisis and during COVID (fiscal deficit ~9–10% in FY21). The Act institutionalised transparency (medium-term fiscal policy statement) but lacks enforcement teeth — targets are aspirational, and off-budget borrowings (FCI, NSSF) mask true deficit.
Technique: Monetary policy transmission
Question: “Repo rate cuts by RBI do not always reach borrowers.” Explain.
Answer: Transmission depends on banks' cost of funds, deposit rates, liquidity (surplus/deficit), NPA burden, and credit demand. If banks have excess liquidity or high NPAs, they may not pass on rate cuts. MPC's external benchmark linkage (since Oct 2019 — loans linked to repo/T-bill) improved transmission for new floating-rate loans.

Common Traps

  • Confusing fiscal deficit (total borrowing) with revenue deficit (borrowing for consumption).
  • Assuming FDI and FPI are similar — FDI is stable and long-term; FPI is volatile.
  • Missing that GST is a destination-based consumption tax, not origin-based.
  • Thinking RBI directly controls inflation — it influences via policy rates; supply-side inflation (food, oil) is harder to control.
  • Overlooking that NPA recognition and resolution (IBC) are different steps.

Memory Tricks

  • Deficits: Revenue < Fiscal < Primary (narrowest to widest concept).
  • RBI rates: Repo = RBI lends; Reverse repo = RBI borrows; MSF = emergency.
  • GST: One nation, one tax, one market.
  • External: Current account = trade + transfers; Capital account = investments + loans.
Mains exam-day strategy
For economy questions, always cite recent data (Budget, Economic Survey, RBI bulletin, PLFS, CPI/WPI). Use correct terminology (GVA, fiscal deficit, repo, CRR, FDI/FPI distinction). For policy questions, discuss objectives, achievements, gaps, and reforms. Conclude with a way forward — fiscal consolidation, financial inclusion, MSME support, infrastructure investment.
mains-gs3/agriculture-food:
Indian Agriculture — Overview

Agriculture employs ~45% of India's workforce and contributes ~18% to GDP. GS III covers cropping patterns, irrigation, storage, transport, marketing, e-technology, and farmer welfare.

  • Cropping seasons: Kharif (monsoon, June–October — rice, cotton, sugarcane, jowar, bajra), Rabi (winter, October–March — wheat, gram, mustard, barley), Zaid (summer — vegetables, fodder, watermelon).
  • Major crop regions: Rice — West Bengal, UP, Andhra Pradesh, Punjab, Tamil Nadu; Wheat — UP, Punjab, Haryana, MP; Cotton — Maharashtra, Gujarat, Punjab, Haryana; Sugarcane — UP, Maharashtra, Karnataka; Tea — Assam, WB, Kerala; Coffee — Karnataka, Kerala, TN; Spices — Kerala, Karnataka; Jute — WB, Assam.
  • Agricultural revolutions: Green (wheat/rice, 1960s, M.S. Swaminathan), White (milk, Verghese Kurien, Operation Flood), Blue (fish), Yellow (oilseeds), Golden (fibres/horticulture), Silver (wool/cotton).
  • Land holdings: 86% small and marginal (<2 hectares), average holding size declining (~1.08 ha), fragmentation a constraint to mechanisation.
  • Land reforms: Abolition of zamindari, tenancy reforms, ceiling on holdings, consolidation of holdings, Bhoodan movement (Vinoba Bhave), computerisation of land records (Digital India Land Records Modernisation Programme).

Irrigation and Water Management

  • Sources: Wells and tube wells (largest share), tanks (south/east), canals (Indira Gandhi, Bhakra, Damodar, Upper Ganga), micro-irrigation (drip, sprinkler — PMKSY-PDMC).
  • Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana (PMKSY): "Har Khet ko Pani" — end-to-end solutions in source creation, distribution, management, field application; per drop more crop.
  • Issues: Waterlogging and salinity (canal areas), groundwater over-exploitation (Punjab, Haryana, Tamil Nadu), inequitable distribution, evaporation losses.

Agricultural Marketing and Reforms

  • APMC Acts: State-regulated mandis; issues — commission agents (arhatiyas), market fees, restricted competition, farmer exploitation.
  • e-NAM (National Agriculture Market, 2016): Online trading platform connecting APMCs; transparent price discovery; quality assaying.
  • Model APLM Act 2017: Allows direct marketing, private markets, farmer-consumer markets, e-trading; adopted by many states.
  • Farm laws 2020 (repealed 2021): Farmers' Produce Trade and Commerce (Promotion and Facilitation) Act, Farmers (Empowerment and Protection) Agreement on Price Assurance and Farm Services Act, Essential Commodities (Amendment) Act — repealed after farmer protests (2020–21).
