  • Inverted sentences (starting with here/there): Verb agrees with the real subject. Here comes the bus; Here come the buses.
Technique: Proximity rule
Question: "Neither the principal nor the teachers ___ present." Choose correct verb.
Answer: Subjects joined by 'nor' — verb agrees with nearer subject (teachers, plural) → "were". "Neither the principal nor the teachers were present."
Technique: Real subject vs intervening phrase
Question: "The quality of the mangoes ___ good." Choose correct verb.
Answer: Real subject is 'quality' (singular), not 'mangoes'. The phrase 'of the mangoes' does not affect verb → "is". "The quality of the mangoes is good."

Common Traps

  • The verb agreeing with the nearest noun instead of the real subject.
  • Treating collective nouns as always plural — context matters (unit vs individual members).
  • Treating 'none' as always plural — it can be singular or plural.
  • Using plural verb with 'Each of', 'Either of', 'Neither of' — these take singular verb.
  • Confusing plural-form singular-meaning nouns (news, physics, measles) with plural nouns.

Memory Tricks

  • SVA checklist: Find real subject → check number → match verb → ignore intervening phrases.
  • Indefinite pronouns = singular: Everyone, anybody, someone, nobody, each, either, neither.
  • Always plural nouns: Scissors, trousers, spectacles, jeans, goods, clothes, premises, thanks.
  • Number of: A number of → plural; The number of → singular.
SVA exam strategy
First strip away phrases between subject and verb to find the real subject. Then check if the subject is singular or plural. Watch for collective nouns, indefinite pronouns, and 'number of' phrases — these are the most common exam traps.
grammar/articles-prepositions:
Articles (a, an, the)

  • Indefinite article 'a/an': Used before singular countable nouns when mentioning something for the first time or when the noun is not specific. 'a' before consonant sound (a boy, a university — 'u' sounds like 'yu'), 'an' before vowel sound (an apple, an hour — 'h' silent, vowel sound). Choice depends on sound, not spelling letter.
  • Definite article 'the': Used before a particular person/thing already mentioned or known (the book I bought), unique things (the sun, the moon, the earth), superlatives (the best, the tallest), musical instruments (the piano), rivers/seas/ranges (the Ganga, the Indian Ocean, the Himalayas), newspapers (the Hindu), holy books (the Gita), and nationalities (the Indians).
  • Omission of articles: No article before proper nouns (Delhi, John), abstract nouns used generally (Honesty is best policy), material nouns (Gold is precious), languages (Hindi is easy), meals (breakfast, lunch, dinner), bed/church/college/hospital/prison/school when used for primary purpose (go to school = study; go to the school = visit building), plural countable nouns used generally (Cars are expensive).
  • 'A/an' vs 'The': 'A man and a woman were walking. The man was tall.' (first mention = a/an, second = the).

Prepositions

  • Time: at (exact point — at 5 o'clock, at noon, at night), in (period — in May, in 2024, in the morning), on (day/date — on Monday, on 15th August, on Christmas day). 'In' for longer periods, 'on' for specific days, 'at' for exact points.
  • Place: at (point — at the door, at the station), in (enclosed space — in the room, in Delhi, in the box), on (surface — on the table, on the wall, on the floor).
  • Movement/direction: to (towards — go to school), into (enter — go into the room), onto (on top — jump onto the bed), towards (direction — walk towards the market), through (pass from one side to other — walk through the tunnel), across (from one side to other — swim across the river), along (follow length — walk along the road), against (touching and opposing — lean against the wall), among (more than two — divide among three), between (two — divide between Ram and Shyam).
  • Instrument/agent: by (agent — killed by a thief; mode — travel by bus), with (instrument — cut with a knife; accompaniment — go with a friend), in (manner — write in ink), on (basis — depend on).
  • Other common prepositions: about (concerning — talk about politics), above (higher than — above the roof), below (lower than — below the poverty line), over (covering — a roof over the head), under (below — under the table), before (earlier than — before 5 pm), after (later than — after lunch), since (point in past — since Monday), for (duration — for 3 hours), from (starting point — from Monday to Friday), till/until (up to — wait till 6), during (within a period — during the holidays), within (before end — within a week), without (lacking — without water), unlike (different from — unlike his brother), like (similar to — like his father), beside (next to — sit beside me), besides (in addition to — besides English, she knows French), except (excluding — all except John), including (including — including tax).

Important Preposition Pairs/Rules

  • In vs On vs At (place): at (point) < in (enclosed) — I live at No. 5, in Delhi, in India.
  • In vs On vs At (time): at (exact) < on (day) < in (month/year) — at 5 pm, on Monday, in January.
  • Between vs Among: between = two (between you and me), among = more than two (distribute among the poor).
  • Since vs For: since = point (since 2010), for = duration (for 10 years). Both used with perfect tenses.
  • By vs With: by = agent/doer (killed by a thief), with = instrument (cut with a knife).
  • Beside vs Besides: beside = next to (sit beside me), besides = in addition to (besides English, she knows Hindi).
  • From vs Since: from = starting point (works from 9 to 5), since = point in past continued to present (works here since 2010 — with perfect tense).
  • Into vs In: into = movement entering (jump into the well), in = position (swim in the pool).
  • On vs Upon: upon is more formal/literary (once upon a time; upon reflection).
  • Above vs Over: above = higher than, no contact (flags above the building); over = covering/moving across (a roof over us, flew over the city).
  • Below vs Under: below = lower than, no contact (below the poverty line); under = directly below/contact (under the table).
  • Between vs From...to: between two points (between Delhi and Mumbai), from...to (from Monday to Friday).

Conjunctions

  • Coordinating conjunctions: join equal elements — and, but, or, nor, for, so, yet (FANBOYS).
  • Subordinating conjunctions: join dependent clause — because, although, though, since, if, unless, until, while, when, before, after, as, as if, as though, lest, so that.
  • Correlative conjunctions (pairs): either...or, neither...nor, both...and, not only...but also, whether...or, scarcely...when, no sooner...than, rather...than.
  • Important rules:
    • No sooner...than (No sooner did he arrive than it started raining — inversion).
    • Scarcely/Hardly...when (Scarcely had he reached when it rained — inversion, past perfect).
    • Lest = that...not, followed by should (Walk carefully lest you should fall).
    • Unless = if not (Unless you work hard, you will fail — no 'not' with unless).
    • Both...and takes plural verb (Both Ram and Shyam are present).
    • Not only...but also — verb agrees with nearer subject (Not only the teacher but also the students were present).
Technique: Article choice
Question: "___ honest man is respected by all." Choose article.
Answer: 'honest' starts with silent 'h' but vowel sound /ɒn/ → use 'an'. "An honest man is respected by all."
Technique: Since vs For
Question: "She has been living here ___ 2015." Choose preposition.
Answer: 2015 is a point in time → 'since'. "She has been living here since 2015."

Common Traps

  • Using 'a/an' before uncountable nouns (a milk, a furniture — wrong; milk is uncountable).
  • Using 'the' before proper nouns (the Delhi — wrong; Delhi is correct).
  • Confusing 'in' and 'at' for time/place.
  • Using 'between' for more than two people/things.
  • Using 'unless' with 'not' (unless you don't work — wrong; unless you work — correct).
  • Using 'the' before names of meals used generally (I take the breakfast — wrong; I take breakfast — correct).

Memory Tricks

  • Articles: a/an = first mention, general; the = specific, unique, second mention.
  • Sound rule: 'a university' (consonant sound), 'an hour' (vowel sound) — depends on sound, not letter.
  • Preposition place/time: at → on → in (smallest → largest unit).
  • Between vs Among: Between = 2; Among = 3+.
Articles/prepositions exam strategy
In error spotting, check articles before countable nouns, preposition choice (since/for, in/on/at), and 'unless' without 'not'. Read the sentence for meaning — wrong prepositions often change meaning entirely.
grammar/sentence-correction:
Sentence Correction & Error Spotting

Sentence correction (error spotting) tests your ability to spot and fix grammatical errors. Exams repeat a finite set of error types — mastering these covers most questions.

  • Subject-verb agreement: Verb must match subject in number and person. The list of items is long (is → are). Each of the boys has a pen (has, not have).
  • Tense consistency: Maintain the same time frame unless meaning changes. He reached the station and finds no train (reaches/finds or reached/found). He said that he is fine (said → was).
  • Article errors: Using 'a/an' before uncountable nouns, missing 'the' before unique/specific nouns, 'the' before proper nouns. The milk is spoilt (Milk). The Delhi is big (Delhi).
  • Preposition errors: Wrong preposition after adjective/verb (good in English → good at English; depend on/upon), since vs for, in vs on vs at, between vs among, unless with not.
  • Pronoun errors: Wrong case (between you and I → between you and me; he is taller than me → than I am), who vs whom, reflexive misuse (myself invited him → I invited him), each/everyone take singular verb and pronoun.
  • Adjective vs adverb: She runs quick → quickly. He is very fastly running → very fast (no -ly with very + adjective). Good (adjective) vs well (adverb — She sings well).
  • Comparisons: Comparatives take 'than' (taller than him), superlatives take 'the' and 'of/in' (the tallest of the three / in the class). Double comparatives (more better, most tallest) are wrong. Compare same things (The climate of Delhi is better than Mumbai → than that of Mumbai).
  • Parallelism: Elements in a list/correlative pair must be same grammatical form. She likes reading, to swim, and dancing → reading, swimming, and dancing. Not only honest but also hardworking → not only honest but also hardworking (adjective + adjective).
  • Modifiers: Dangling/misplaced modifiers. Walking on the road, a dog bit him (He was walking). Nearly I failed → I nearly failed. Only he scored 100 (only he) vs He scored only 100.
  • Conditionals: If + present simple, will + base verb (If it rains, I will stay). If + past simple, would + base (If I were you, I would go). If + past perfect, would have + V3 (If he had studied, he would have passed). Avoid 'will' in if-clause.
  • Redundancy: Return back → return. Revert back → revert. Free gift → gift. Past history → history. Very unique → unique. End result → result.
  • Question tags: Positive statement → negative tag; negative → positive. He is coming, isn't he? She doesn't know, does she? I am → aren't I? Let's → shall we? Imperative → will you/can you?
  • Verb patterns: Verb + gerund/infinitive (enjoy swimming, want to go, stop smoking vs stop to swim), make/let + bare infinitive (make him go, let her go), help + to-infinitive/bare infinitive.
  • Common confused words: accept/except, affect/effect, altar/alter, complement/compliment, stationary/stationery, principal/principle, advice/advise, practice/practise.
Technique: Subject-verb error
Error: "The quality of the mangoes are good." Correct it.
Answer: Real subject is 'quality' (singular); phrase 'of the mangoes' doesn't change it. Correct: "The quality of the mangoes is good."
Technique: Tense consistency
Error: "He said that he is fine." Correct it.
Answer: Reporting verb 'said' (past) → reported clause should be past: "He said that he was fine." (Exception: universal truth can stay present.)
Technique: Comparison error
Error: "The climate of Delhi is better than Mumbai." Correct it.
Answer: Compare climate with climate. Correct: "The climate of Delhi is better than that of Mumbai" or "better than Mumbai's."

Common Traps

  • 'None of' can take singular or plural verb depending on meaning — don't force one.
  • 'Each of', 'Either of', 'Neither of' take singular verb and singular pronoun (Each of the girls has her book).
  • 'One of the + plural noun + who/that + plural verb' (One of the boys who were absent).
  • 'The majority of' can be singular or plural depending on context.
  • 'A lot of', 'plenty of', 'a great deal of' — verb follows the noun after 'of'.
  • 'Scarcely/Hardly...when' uses past perfect + inversion (Scarcely had he reached when...).
  • 'No sooner...than' uses inversion (No sooner did he arrive than...).

Memory Tricks

  • Checklist for error spotting: SVA → Tense → Articles → Prepositions → Pronouns → Adjective/Adverb → Comparison → Parallelism → Redundancy.
  • Indefinite pronouns = singular: Everyone, anybody, someone, nobody, each, either, neither.
  • Unless = if not — never add 'not'.
  • Comparative = than; Superlative = the ... of/in.
Sentence correction exam strategy
Read the whole sentence first to find the intended meaning. Then check each underlined part against the error checklist. Eliminate options that change meaning or introduce new errors. When in doubt, choose the option that is grammatically standard and preserves the original meaning.
grammar/sentence-improvement:
Sentence Improvement

Sentence improvement presents a sentence with an underlined portion; you must pick the option that best replaces it without changing the meaning. It tests grammar, clarity, conciseness, and idiomatic usage.

  • Approach: Read the full sentence to grasp meaning. Identify what the underlined part should express. Eliminate options that change meaning, introduce errors, or are wordier/awkward. Choose the grammatically correct, concise, clear option.
  • No-change option: Many exams include "No improvement" — choose it if the original is already correct.
  • Meaning preservation: The correct option must keep the original meaning intact. Watch for changes in tense, voice, modality, or emphasis.
  • Conciseness: Prefer shorter, direct expression over wordy phrasing (due to the fact that → because; in spite of the fact that → although; at this point in time → now).
  • Parallelism: Items in a list or correlative pair should share the same grammatical form (reading, swimming, dancing — not reading, to swim, dancing).
  • Verb forms: Watch verb tense, subject-verb agreement, gerund vs infinitive, active vs passive within the underlined part.
  • Modifier placement: Modifiers should sit next to the word they modify to avoid ambiguity (Almost everyone failed vs Everyone almost failed).
  • Idiomatic prepositions: Good at English, interested in, capable of, depend on/upon, insist on, object to, prevent from, succeed in.
  • Determiners: Each/every/any/no + singular noun; some/any/many/much/a lot of with plural/uncountable as appropriate.

Common Improvement Patterns

  • Wordy → concise: "In spite of the fact that he was ill, he came" → "Although he was ill, he came."
  • Wrong tense: "I have seen him yesterday" → "I saw him yesterday."
  • Wrong preposition: "He is good in English" → "He is good at English."
  • Wrong comparison: "He is more taller than me" → "He is taller than me."
  • Split infinitive (minor): "to quickly run" → "to run quickly" (acceptable in modern use but exams often flag it).
  • Double negatives: "I don't know nothing" → "I don't know anything."
  • Redundancy: "Return back" → "return"; "Revert back" → "revert"; "Past history" → "history."
Technique: Wordy phrase
Sentence: "In spite of the fact that she was tired, she continued working." Improve.
Answer: Replace wordy phrase with "Although": "Although she was tired, she continued working."
Technique: Idiomatic preposition
Sentence: "He is capable to do this work." Improve.
Answer: "Capable" takes "of" + gerund: "He is capable of doing this work."
Technique: No improvement
Sentence: "The meeting has been postponed till next Friday." Options include "No improvement".
Answer: Sentence is already correct grammatically and idiomatically → choose "No improvement".

Common Traps

  • Choosing an option that is grammatical but changes the meaning.
  • Preferring complex/wordy phrasing over simple correct phrasing.
  • Missing subject-verb agreement inside the underlined part.
  • Choosing an option with a wrong preposition after adjective/verb.
  • Forgetting that "No improvement" is a valid answer when original is correct.

Memory Tricks

  • Decision order: Meaning first → grammar → conciseness → idiom.
  • Red flag phrases: "due to the fact that", "in spite of the fact that", "at this point in time" → replace with because/although/now.
  • Capable of, interested in, depend on, insist on, object to, prevent from, succeed in.
  • No improvement: If original is correct, pick it without forcing a change.
Sentence improvement exam strategy
Never pick an option just because it sounds fancier — pick the one that is correct AND preserves meaning. If two options are both grammatical, choose the more concise one. Always check whether "No improvement" applies before changing anything.
grammar/para-jumbles:
Para Jumbles & Sentence Rearrangement

Para jumbles present 4–6 sentences in random order; you must rebuild the original paragraph. The logic is in the connectors, pronouns, chronology, and the flow of ideas.

  • Opening sentence: Usually a general statement, introduction of a topic/name, or a definition — not a pronoun reference, not a continuation (hence, therefore, but, so), not an example without a preceding idea.
  • Pronoun chain: He, she, it, they, this, that, these, those refer to a noun introduced earlier — the sentence with the noun comes before the sentence with the pronoun.
  • Chronology: Time markers (before, after, then, later, finally, first, second, yesterday, 2010, now) establish sequence.
  • Connectors/transitions: however, therefore, moreover, consequently, hence, otherwise, although, while, whereas signal logical links (contrast, cause-effect, addition).
  • Definite article 'the': Usually refers to something already mentioned — 'a/an' introduces, 'the' continues.
  • Abbreviations/acronyms: Full form first (World Health Organization), abbreviated form later (WHO).
  • Examples/illustrations: For example, for instance, such as, like — follow the general statement they illustrate.
  • Contrast pairs: On one hand…on the other hand; although…yet; not only…but also — keep paired sentences together.
  • Cause-effect: because, since, as, therefore, hence, thus, so, consequently — cause sentence precedes effect sentence.
  • Question-answer / statement-elaboration: A general claim is followed by explanation, detail, or example.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. Read all sentences and identify the topic.
  2. Find the opening sentence (general introduction, no references backward).
  3. Link sentences using pronouns, articles, connectors, chronology.
  4. Form pairs/triplets (cause-effect, contrast, example-elaboration).
  5. Arrange pairs into a sequence and check flow.
  6. Verify the last sentence sounds like a conclusion (finally, in conclusion, thus, ultimately).
Technique: Pronoun chain
Sentences: (P) He was very happy. (Q) Rahul bought a new bicycle. (R) He rode it to school. (S) It was a gift from his uncle.
Answer: Q introduces Rahul and bicycle → P 'He' = Rahul → S 'It' = bicycle → R 'He/it' continue. Order: Q P S R (or Q S P R depending on intended flow; pronoun chain Q→P is strongest).
Technique: Cause-effect
Sentences: (A) Therefore, he missed the train. (B) He reached the station late. (C) His car broke down.
Answer: C (cause) → B (intermediate) → A (effect/conclusion). Order: C B A.

Common Traps

  • Starting with a sentence beginning with 'However', 'Therefore', 'Moreover', 'But', 'So' — these are rarely openers.
  • Placing a pronoun sentence before its antecedent noun.
  • Placing an example before the general statement it illustrates.
  • Ignoring time markers and jumbling chronology.
  • Splitting obvious pairs (on one hand…on the other hand).

Memory Tricks

  • OPEN: Opening sentence = general, no backward references, no pronouns, no transitions.
  • PANT: Pronoun → Antecedent; Article 'a' → 'the'; Example after statement; Time order.
  • FADE: First introduce, then elaborate, then example, then conclude.
Para jumble exam strategy
Find one certain pair first (pronoun-noun or cause-effect), build around it, then use answer options to verify — you often don't need the full sequence, just enough to pick the right option.
grammar/active-passive:
Active-Passive Voice & Direct-Indirect Speech (Narration)

Voice conversion (active↔passive) and narration change (direct↔indirect speech) are high-frequency grammar questions in SSC, banking, CDS, and CLAT.

  • Active voice: Subject performs the action (Ram wrote a letter).
  • Passive voice: Object receives the action (A letter was written by Ram). Focus shifts to the object/action; doer may be omitted with 'by'.
  • Passive formation: Object + be + V3 + (by + subject). Tense of 'be' matches original tense (is written, was written, has been written, will be written, can be written).
  • Tense mapping for passive:
    • Present simple: writes → is written
    • Present continuous: is writing → is being written
    • Present perfect: has written → has been written
    • Past simple: wrote → was written
    • Past continuous: was writing → was being written
    • Past perfect: had written → had been written
    • Future simple: will write → will be written
    • Modals: can write → can be written; must write → must be written
  • Verbs with two objects: Ram gave Sita a book → A book was given to Sita by Ram OR Sita was given a book by Ram.
  • Verbs not normally passivized: Intransitive verbs (sleep, die, arrive, happen) and some state verbs (have, belong, resemble, lack) — no passive.
  • Direct speech: Ram said, "I am busy." (quoted words, reporting verb outside, comma, capital inside quotes).
  • Indirect speech: Ram said that he was busy. (no quotes, 'that', pronoun/tense/time changes).
  • Pronoun changes (direct→indirect): First person changes according to subject; second person according to object; third person unchanged. I → he/she; you → he/she/they; we → they.
  • Tense backshift (direct→indirect): Present → past (is → was, am → was, are → were, has → had, will → would, can → could, may → might). Past (wrote) → past perfect (had written) or stays past. Universal facts/habitual truths do NOT backshift (The teacher said the earth revolves around the sun — stays present).
  • Time/place changes (direct→indirect): now → then, today → that day, yesterday → the day before, tomorrow → the next day, here → there, ago → before, this → that, these → those.
  • Reporting verb changes: said → told (needs object), said to → told, asked/enquired, ordered/commanded, requested, exclaimed (with emotion word).
  • Questions (direct→indirect): 'said' → 'asked/enquired'; question word order becomes statement order (He asked where I was going — not 'where was I going'); no question mark; if/whether for yes-no questions (He asked if I was ready).
  • Commands (direct→indirect): 'said' → 'ordered/commanded/requested'; to-infinitive (He ordered me to leave; She requested him to wait).
  • Exclamations (direct→indirect): 'said' → 'exclaimed with joy/sorrow/surprise'; statement form, no exclamation mark (He exclaimed with joy that he had won).
  • Indirect→direct: Reverse all changes: backshift undone (was → is), pronouns restored, time words restored, quotes and punctuation added.
Technique: Active→Passive
Convert: "The committee approved the proposal."
Answer: Object (proposal) + be + V3 → "The proposal was approved by the committee." (Past simple: approved → was approved.)
Technique: Direct→Indirect backshift
Convert: "Ram said, 'I am busy now.'"
Answer: Pronoun I → he; am → was; now → then. "Ram said that he was busy then."
Technique: Universal fact (no backshift)
Convert: "The teacher said, 'The earth revolves around the sun.'"
Answer: Universal fact — no backshift. "The teacher said that the earth revolves around the sun." (revolves stays present.)

Common Traps

  • Wrong 'be' form in passive (is being written vs has been written).
  • Forgetting 'by + agent' when doer is important.
  • Backshifting universal facts/habitual truths unnecessarily.
  • Keeping question word order in indirect questions (He asked where was I going → wrong; where I was going → right).
  • 'Said to' → 'told' needs an object (He told me, not He told).
  • Time words not changed in indirect speech (yesterday → the day before).

Memory Tricks

  • Passive: Object + be + V3 + by subject; tense of 'be' = tense of original verb.
  • Narration backshift: is/was, has/had, will/would, can/could, may/might.
  • Time words: now→then, today→that day, yesterday→the day before, tomorrow→next day, here→there.
  • Questions: statement order, no '?', if/whether for yes-no.
Voice/narration exam strategy
For active-passive, identify subject-object-verb first, then rebuild with be+V3 in the same tense. For narration, apply changes in order: reporting verb → pronouns → tense → time/place → punctuation. Universal facts never backshift.
vocabulary/vocabulary:
Vocabulary Building — Roots, Prefixes, Suffixes

Building vocabulary through word parts (roots, prefixes, suffixes) lets you decode unfamiliar words instead of memorizing them one by one. This is the most efficient way to handle synonyms, antonyms, and one-word substitutions in exams.

  • Roots (base meaning): The core of a word, often from Latin or Greek.
    • struct = build (construct, structure, destruct, industry)
    • spec/spic = see (inspect, spectator, perspective, conspicuous)
    • tract = pull (attract, contract, extract, retract, subtract)
    • port = carry (transport, export, import, portable, report)
    • script/scrib = write (scripture, describe, inscribe, prescribe, transcript)
    • graph = write (autograph, biography, telegraph, photograph, graphic)
    • port = carry / pon/pos = place (position, component, deposit, opposite)
    • ject = throw (reject, inject, subject, object, project, eject)
    • ced/cess = go (precede, recede, secede, process, cession)
    • grad/gress = step (progress, ingress, regress, gradient)
    • cept/cip = take (accept, intercept, concept, receive, perception)
    • cur/cour = run (current, course, occur, recourse, currency)
    • flu/flux = flow (fluent, fluid, influence, affluent, confluence)
    • duc/duct = lead (produce, reduce, introduce, conduct, duct)
    • fer = bear/carry (transfer, infer, defer, prefer, suffer)
    • fort = strong (fortify, fortress, effort, fortitude)
    • pan = all (panorama, pantheon, pandemic, panacea)
    • phil = love (philosophy, philharmonic, bibliophile)
    • phob = fear (phobia, claustrophobia, hydrophobia)
    • gen = birth/kind (generate, genetic, indigenous, progenitor)
    • chron = time (chronicle, chronic, synchronize, chronology)
    • tele = far (telephone, television, telescope, telegraph)
    • graph = write (graphic, biography, autograph, paragraph)
    • log = word/study (biology, dialogue, monologue, prologue, catalog)
    • path = feel (sympathy, empathy, antipathy, telepathy)
    • morph = form (metamorphosis, amorphous, morphology)
    • nom/nom = name (nominate, nominee, denominator, misnomer)
    • cide = kill (homicide, suicide, pesticide, genocide)
    • vict/vinc = conquer (victory, convince, invincible, convict)
    • dict = speak (dictate, predict, verdict, dictator, contradict)
    • vol = will (voluntary, volition, benevolent, malevolent)
    • fac/fact = make/do (factory, manufacture, satisfy, difficult, benefit)
    • mit/mit = send (mitmit? no) — mit = send (transmit, admit, commit, emit, remit)
    • pend = hang (pendant, suspend, pending, expensive, compendium)
    • pose/posit = place (deposit, impose, opposite, component, proposition)
    • spect = see (inspect, respect, spectator, perspective)
    • stress/strict = bind (strict, restrict, constrict, stress)
    • vert/vert = turn (convert, revert, introvert, extrovert, vertical)
    • volve/volv = roll (revolve, involve, evolve, devolve)
    • cise/cide = cut (decide, precise, incision, scissors)
    • flict = strike (conflict, inflict, afflict)
    • mit/mit = let go/send (admit, commit, emit, omit, permit, transmit)
    • gress = step (congress, progress, digress, egress)
    • ject = throw (eject, inject, reject, subject, project)
    • man/manu = hand (manual, manufacture, manicure, emancipate)
    • ped/pod = foot (pedestrian, pedal, podiatry, octopus)
    • port = carry (portable, import, export, transport, report)
    • rupt = break (erupt, interrupt, corrupt, bankrupt, disruption)
    • sect/sec = cut (bisect, section, dissect, insect)
    • sist = stand (assist, consist, exist, persist, resist)
    • spec = look (inspect, respect, speculate, specimen)
    • spir = breathe (respire, inspire, expire, spirit)
    • ten/tain = hold (maintain, contain, retain, detention)
    • tract = pull (attract, contract, extract)
    • tort = twist (contort, distort, extort, torture)
    • vent = come (convent, event, intervene, prevent)
    • vers/vert = turn (convert, reverse, versatile, adverse)
    • voc/vok = call (invoke, revoke, vocabulary, advocate)
    • vol = will (volunteer, voluntary, volition)
    • vor = eat (carnivore, herbivore, omnivore, voracious)
    • zoo = life (zoology, zoo, zoonotic)
  • Prefixes (added to front — change meaning):
    • a/an = not, without (amoral, atypical, anaemic)
    • ab = away (absent, abnormal, abduct)
    • ad = to, toward (adapt, admit, advance)
    • ambi = both (ambidextrous, ambiguous)
    • ante = before (antecedent, antedate)
    • anti = against (antibiotic, antisocial)
    • auto = self (autobiography, automatic)
    • bene = good (benefit, benevolent, benediction)
    • bi = two (bicycle, bilingual, bisect)
    • circum = around (circumference, circumstance)
    • co/com/con = with, together (cooperate, connect, confess)
    • contra = against (contradict, contrary)
    • de = down, away, reverse (decline, decrease, deflate)
    • dis = not, opposite, apart (disagree, disappear, disconnect)
    • em/en = into, put into (employ, enable, embed)
    • ex = out, former (export, exit, ex-president)
    • extra = beyond (extraordinary, extracurricular)
    • hyper = over, excessive (hyperactive, hypertension)
    • il/im/in/ir = not (illegal, impossible, inaccurate, irrelevant)
    • im = into (import, immerse)
    • in = into, not (inspect, incomplete)
    • inter = between (international, interfere)
    • intra = within (intramuscular, intravenous)
    • macro = large (macroeconomics, macroscopic)
    • mal = bad (malfunction, malnutrition)
    • micro = small (microscope, microscopic)
    • mis = wrong (mistake, misunderstand)
    • mono = one (monopoly, monologue)
    • multi = many (multimedia, multilingual)
    • neo = new (neonatal, neocolonial)
    • omni = all (omniscient, omnivorous)
    • over = too much (overload, overconfident)
    • pan = all (panorama, pandemic)
    • para = beside (paradox, paragraph)
    • per = through (permit, persist)
    • poly = many (polygon, polygamy)
    • post = after (postpone, postgraduate)
    • pre = before (preview, prefix, prepaid)
    • pro = forward (progress, promote, propose)
    • re = again (return, rewrite, rebuild)
    • semi = half (semicircle, semiannual)
    • sub = under (subway, submarine)
    • super = above (superior, supersede)
    • trans = across (transport, transfer)
    • un = not (unhappy, unsure)
    • under = below (underestimate, undergo)
    • uni = one (universe, universal, unify)
    • up = upward (upgrade, upload)
  • Suffixes (added to back — change part of speech/meaning):
    • -able/-ible = can be (readable, credible)
    • -al = relating to (national, seasonal)
    • -ance/-ence = state/quality (assistance, patience)
    • -ant/-ent = one who/that (assistant, student)
    • -ary = relating to (library, ordinary)
    • -ate = to make (activate, create)
    • -dom = state/realm (freedom, kingdom)
    • -ee = one who (employee, trainee)
    • -en = to make (weaken, shorten)
    • -er/-or = one who (teacher, actor)
    • -ful = full of (beautiful, careful)
    • -ible/-able = can be (flexible, reasonable)
    • -ic = relating to (scenic, historic)
    • -ing = action/process (reading, building)
    • -ion/-tion/-sion = state/result (education, expression)
    • -ish = like (childish, foolish)
    • -ism = doctrine/practice (capitalism, optimism)
    • -ist = one who (artist, scientist)
    • -ity/-ty = state/quality (society, reality)
    • -ive = having nature of (active, creative)
    • -less = without (careless, hopeless)
    • -like = like (childlike, lifelike)
    • -ly = in manner of (quickly, friendly)
    • -ment = state/result (development, agreement)
    • -ness = state (kindness, darkness)
    • -ology = study of (biology, psychology)
    • -ous/-ious = full of (famous, curious)
    • -ship = state (friendship, leadership)
    • -ty = state (unity, purity)
    • -ure = act/process (closure, failure)
    • -ward = direction (forward, backward)
    • -y = full of (rainy, sunny)
  • Word-building method: root + prefix + suffix = new word (re + struct + ion = reconstruction; de + struct + ion = destruction; un + kind + ly = unkindly).
  • Exam use: Break unfamiliar synonym/antonym/one-word-substitution words into parts; eliminate options whose root meaning contradicts the stem.
Technique: Root-based elimination
Question: Synonym of 'benevolent'.
Answer: bene = good, vol = will → 'benevolent' = wishing well, kind. Choose 'kind/charitable', not 'cruel'.
Technique: Suffix part-of-speech
Question: '-tion' words are usually what part of speech?
Answer: '-tion' forms nouns (education, action, creation). If options include verbs/adjectives, eliminate them.

Common Traps

  • Assuming similar-looking words share a root (e.g., 'dessert' vs 'desert' — different roots).
  • Over-reliance on roots without checking actual meaning (some roots shift over time).
  • Confusing '-able' (can be done) with '-ible' (able to be) — usage is conventional, not rule-based.
  • Thinking all '-ly' words are adverbs (friendly, lonely, costly are adjectives).

Memory Tricks

  • Root sentence: "The spectator inspected the prospectus and respected the inspector." (spect = see)
  • Prefix contrast: in = not/in; inter = between; intra = within; trans = across.
  • Suffix function: -ment/-tion/-ness = nouns; -ful/-ous/-ive = adjectives; -ly = adverb (usually); -ize/-ify = verbs.
Vocabulary exam strategy
Learn 10–15 roots/prefixes/suffixes per week; they unlock hundreds of words. For synonyms/antonyms, use root meaning to eliminate 2–3 options even if you don't know the exact word. Maintain a personal word-list with sentences, not just definitions.
vocabulary/synonyms-antonyms:
Synonyms & Antonyms

Synonym-antonym questions test direct word knowledge and fine distinctions between near-synonyms. Exams repeat high-frequency word pairs and use near-miss options to trap careless readers.

  • Synonym: Word with same or nearly same meaning (happy → joyful, glad, pleased). Context matters — 'big' vs 'large' vs 'huge' vs 'enormous' differ in shade and collocation.
  • Antonym: Word with opposite meaning (happy → sad, unhappy, miserable, gloomy). Antonyms may be gradable (hot → cold) or complementary (dead → alive, no middle).
  • Near-miss options: Words related in topic but not exact synonyms (e.g., for 'cautious', options might include 'brave', 'fearful', 'careful' — 'careful' is closest but 'cautious' implies wariness of risk).
  • Context clue: The sentence around the target word shows the intended sense ('bright student' = intelligent; 'bright light' = shining; 'bright colors' = vivid).
  • Elimination: Remove options with opposite or unrelated meaning, then pick the closest shade among remaining.
  • Root/prefix help: Use word parts to guess (e.g., 'benevolent' = well-wishing → kind; 'malevolent' = ill-wishing → cruel).

vocabulary/idioms-phrases:
Idioms & Phrases

Idioms are fixed expressions whose meaning can't be deduced from individual words (kick the bucket = die). Exams test theme-grouped idioms with meaning, usage, and literal-trap options that sound plausible but are wrong.

  • Meaning vs literal: Never interpret literally. 'Break the ice' = initiate conversation, not smash ice. 'Once in a blue moon' = rarely, not a lunar event.
  • Usage: Idioms fit specific contexts — 'bite the bullet' = endure something unpleasant unavoidably; 'burn the midnight oil' = work/study late at night.
  • Learning method: Group by theme (success/failure, emotions, money, time, difficulty, health, relationships, weather, animals, colors) to remember clusters.
  • Exam trap: One option gives the literal meaning — always avoid it.

vocabulary/one-word-substitutions:
One-Word Substitutions

One-word substitution replaces a phrase or sentence with a single precise word. Exams test theme-grouped lists — people, professions, places, sciences, phobias, manias, killers, collectors, and more.

  • Method: Learn by theme (people → professions → places → sciences → fears → killings → deaths → governments → marriages → sounds → houses).
  • Root help: Use roots to guess (necro = death → necromancy = black magic/conjuring with dead; phil = love → philatelist = stamp lover).
  • Exactness: Pick the word whose definition matches ALL elements of the phrase, not just one.
  • Exam trap: Two options may be close (e.g., 'one who eats human flesh' = cannibal, not 'carnivore' = flesh-eater generally).

vocabulary/phrasal-verbs:
Phrasal Verbs

A phrasal verb = verb + particle (adverb/preposition), with a meaning often different from the verb alone (give up = quit, not literally 'give'). Exams test meaning, usage, separability, and particles.

  • Structure: verb + adverb particle (look up, give up) OR verb + preposition (look after, depend on). Some have both: look into, look up to.
  • Separable vs inseparable:
    • Separable with noun object: turn off the TV / turn the TV off (both OK).
    • Separable with pronoun object ALWAYS between: turn it off (not turn off it).
    • Inseparable: look after the children / look after them (not look them after).
  • Three-part phrasal verbs: verb + adverb + preposition (get on with, look up to, put up with, catch up with, come up with) — inseparable.
  • Meaning often idiomatic: give up = quit; put off = postpone; put up with = tolerate; run out of = exhaust supply; come across = find by chance.

  • Particle meanings: up = complete/increase; off = stop/separation; out = exhaustion/disappearance; over = review/completion; back = return; down = reduction/defeat.
  • Personal sentences: Write one sentence per phrasal verb.
  • Theme clusters: Learn 10–15 phrasal verbs per theme per week.
Phrasal verb exam strategy

vocabulary/spelling-confusables:
Spelling & Confusable Words

Spelling and confusable-word questions test attention to detail. Exams ask misspelt-word identification, correct-spelling choice, and near-homophone distinctions (e.g., stationary vs stationery).

  • Common spelling rules:
    • i before e except after c (receive, believe, ceiling, receipt — exceptions: science, sufficient, either, neither, foreign, height, leisure, weird, seizure).
    • Drop silent e before vowel suffix: hope → hoping, write → writing, love → loving, use → using; keep e before consonant suffix: hope → hopeful, care → careful.
    • Double final consonant before vowel suffix when stressed syllable ends in single vowel+consonant: begin → beginning, occur → occurring, prefer → preferred (British), travel → travelling (British); open → opening (not stressed, no double).
    • y → i before suffix when preceded by consonant: happy → happiness, beauty → beautiful, try → tries, carry → carries; keep y before -ing: try → trying, enjoy → enjoying.
    • ie/ei words: seize, weird, neither, foreign (exceptions).
    • American vs British: color/color, theater/theater, traveling/travelling, program/programme, realize/realise, license/licence (noun/verb distinction in British).
  • Commonly misspelt words: accommodate (two c, two m), achieve (ie), across (one c), address (two d), calendar (ea after l), campaign, cemetery (three e's, no a), committee (two m, two t, two e), committee, committee, committee, committee — wait that's a duplicate; committee (c-o-m-m-i-t-t-e-e), completely (ly), conscience (sc), conscious (sc), definitely (i before ly), desert/dessert, embarrass (two r, two s), environment, exaggerate (two g), February, glacier, government, grateful (no e after grateful), guarantee, harassment, height (no e), humorous, immediately, incidentally, indispensable, judgment (no e after g in American; judgement British), laboratory, library (first r pronounced), license/licence, mathematics, millennium (two l, two l), millionaire, miniature, minuscule (not miniscule), mischievous, mortgage, nauseous, necessary (one c, two s), occasionally (two c, two l), occur (one c, two r), occurring (two c, two r, ing), omission (one m, two m), parallel (two l, one r), parliament, personnel (one n, two n), possess (two s, two s), possessive, predecessor, precede (pre + cede), proceed (pro + cede), proceed vs precede, pronunciation (no o after n), queue, receipt (ie after c), receive (ie after c), recommend (one c, two m), referred (two r, ed), referring, religion, restaurant (au after r), rhythm (no vowels except y), rhythm, rhythm, rhythm, schedule, seize (ei after s? no — s-e-i-z-e, ie not ei), separate (a after p — sep-a-rate), sergeant, sergeant, sergeant — duplicates, sergeant, sergeant, sergeant, similar (one m), sincerely (one c, two r), succeed (two c, two e), success (two c, two s), successful (two c, two s, ly), surprise (r after first s? s-u-r-p-r-i-s-e), temperature, terrible, threat, threshold, tomorrow (one m, two r), tongue (uo), tremendous, Tuesday, tyranny, umbrella, unlikely, until (one l), unusual, useless, usually (two l, ly), vacuum (one c, two u), valuable, vehicle, vengeance, vengeful, weird (ei, not ie), whether, whistle, wholly (who + ly), wisdom, woman/women, write/written, yesterday, zeal/zealous.
Note
The misspelt-word list above is a representative starter set. Build your own list from previous-year questions of your target exam.

Confusable Word Pairs

  • Advice (noun) / Advise (verb): He gave me good advice / I advise you to wait.
  • Affect (verb) / Effect (noun): The rain affected the crop / The effect was immediate.
  • Altar (noun, church) / Alter (verb, change): wedding altar / alter the plan.
  • Bare (adjective, uncovered) / Bear (verb, carry/endure; noun, animal): bare feet / bear the pain / polar bear.
  • Breath (noun) / Breathe (verb): hold your breath / breathe deeply.
  • Canvas (noun, cloth) / Canvass (verb, solicit votes): oil canvas / canvass voters.
  • Capital (city/wealth) / Capitol (building): Delhi is capital / Capitol Hill.
  • Censor (verb/official) / Censure (verb/noun, criticize): censor the film / censure his conduct.
  • Complement (verb/noun, completes) / Compliment (verb/noun, praise): wine complements food / pay a compliment.
  • Conscience (noun, inner right/wrong) / Conscious (adjective, aware): guilty conscience / conscious decision.
  • Coarse (rough) / Course (route/class/meal): coarse cloth / course of action / main course.
  • Desert (abandon/dry place) / Dessert (sweet course): desert the post / Sahara desert / apple dessert.
  • Elicit (verb, draw out) / Illicit (adjective, illegal): elicit a response / illicit trade.
  • Emigrate (leave country) / Immigrate (enter country): emigrate from India / immigrate to Canada.
  • Eminent (famous) / Imminent (about to happen) / Emanate (come from): eminent scientist / imminent danger / heat emanates.
  • Farther (physical distance) / Further (additional/figurative): farther down the road / further information.
  • Flaunt (show off) / Flout (disregard rule): flaunt wealth / flout the law.
  • Foreword (intro to book) / Forward (toward front): read the foreword / move forward.
  • Grisly (horrible) / Gristly (full of gristle) / Grizzly (bear/gray): grisly murder / grizzly bear.
  • Imply (suggest) / Infer (deduce): he implied it / I inferred he meant X.
  • Stationary (stationary = not moving) / Stationery (writing materials): stationary vehicle / buy stationery.
  • Stationary vs Stationery mnemonic: stationERy has 'ER' like papER/ envelopER.
  • Storm (weather) / Storm (verb) / Storm (figurative): storm approaching / storm the castle / take by storm.
  • Than (comparison) / Then (time/sequence): taller than me / then we left.
  • Their (possessive) / There (place) / They're (they are): their book / over there / they're coming.
  • To (preposition/infinitive) / Too (also/excessively) / Two (number): go to school / too cold / two apples.
  • Your (possessive) / You're (you are): your book / you're late.
  • Whose (possessive) / Who's (who is): whose bag? / who's coming?
  • Lose (verb, miss) / Loose (adjective, not tight): don't lose it / loose shoes.
  • Quiet (silent) / Quite (completely): keep quiet / quite good.
  • Accept (receive) / Except (exclude): accept the gift / everyone except John.
  • Affect/Effect — see above.
  • All ready (prepared) / Already (by this time): all ready to go / already done.
  • Altogether (totally) / All together (in one place): altogether wrong / all together now.
  • Any one (single person) / Anyone (any person): any one of them / anyone can come.
  • Altar/Alter — see above.
  • Bare/Bear — see above.
  • Breath/Breathe — see above.
  • Canvas/Canvass — see above.
  • Complement/Compliment — see above.
  • Conscience/Conscious — see above.
  • Coarse/Course — see above.
  • Desert/Dessert — see above.
  • Elicit/Illicit — see above.
  • Emigrate/Immigrate — see above.
  • Eminent/Imminent/Emanate — see above.
  • Flaunt/Flout — see above.
  • Foreword/Forward — see above.
  • Imply/Infer — see above.
  • Loose/Lose — see above.
  • Quiet/Quite — see above.
  • Stationary/Stationery — see above.
  • Than/Then — see above.
  • Their/There/They're — see above.
  • To/Too/Two — see above.
  • Whose/Who's — see above.
  • Your/You're — see above.
Note
Duplicate entries in the confusable list are from assembly; in your own notes keep each pair once with meanings and example sentences.

Common Traps

  • Choosing a word that sounds right but is spelled wrong (recieve vs receive).
  • Confusing stationary/stationery in sentence-improvement questions.
  • Using 'your' for 'you're' or 'their' for 'there'.
  • Picking affect/effect wrongly based on sound rather than part of speech.
  • Missing silent letters (receipt, colonel, knight, doubt, island).

Memory Tricks

  • Stationary/Stationery: stationERy sells papER/envelopER.
  • Principal (main person, ends in -pal = your pal) / Principle (rule): principal = head.
  • Desert (one s, dry/sand) / Dessert (two s, sweet — you want two helpings): two s's = two servings.
  • Complement (completes, has 'e' like complete) / Compliment (praise, has 'i' like I like praise).
  • Stationary (a = at a standstill) / Stationery (e = envelope).
Spelling/confusables exam strategy
Read slowly; the eye skips double letters (accommodate, necessary). For confusables, identify the part of speech needed (advice = noun after 'some/good', advise = verb after subject). Build a personal error-log of words you repeatedly misspell.
comprehension/reading-comprehension:
Reading Comprehension

RC tests your ability to read a passage quickly, understand its argument, and answer inference/main-idea/vocabulary/tone questions. Exams (SSC, banking, CAT, CLAT, UPSC CSAT) use short and long passages with 3–8 questions each.

  • Approach (two popular methods):
    • Read-first: Read the whole passage carefully (2–3 min for short, 4–5 min for long), then answer.
    • Questions-first: Read the questions first (not options), then scan the passage for answers — good for fact-based questions.
    Choose whichever gives you better accuracy in practice.
  • Question types:
    • Main idea / Central theme: What the author wants to convey overall — usually in first/last paragraph.
    • Title: Short, neutral, covers whole passage (not just one example).
    • Direct fact: Information explicitly stated — locate and verify.
    • Inference: What logically follows but isn't stated — must be supported by text, not outside knowledge.
    • Assumption: Unstated premise the argument depends on.
    • Conclusion: What necessarily follows from given statements.
    • Tone/Attitude: Author's feeling — critical, appreciative, neutral, satirical, optimistic, skeptical, objective.
    • Vocabulary in context: Meaning of word/phrase AS USED in the passage — not dictionary meaning.
    • True/False according to passage: Eliminate options contradicting text.
  • Reading techniques:
    • Skimming: Quick read for structure — first sentence of each paragraph, headings, conclusion.
    • Scanning: Locate specific fact/name/date/keyword.
    • Active reading: Note author's stance, transitions (however, therefore, moreover), examples, counter-arguments.
  • Elimination strategy: Eliminate options that (a) contradict passage, (b) go beyond passage (outside knowledge), (c) are too extreme (always, never, only, all), (d) are true but not the answer to the question asked.
  • Extreme language trap: Options with 'always', 'never', 'only', 'completely' are usually wrong unless passage supports absolutely.
  • Time budget: Short passage (~300 words) ~6–7 min; long passage (~800 words) ~10–12 min including questions.
Technique: Main idea vs supporting detail
Passage about renewable energy growth, with one paragraph on solar subsidies. Question: main idea?
Answer: Choose 'renewable energy is growing globally' (covers whole passage), not 'solar subsidies in Germany' (one supporting detail).
Technique: Inference
Passage says: 'The policy has reduced emissions but increased costs for small firms.' Question: what can be inferred?
Answer: 'The policy has trade-offs' (supported). Not 'the policy should be scrapped' (author's opinion not stated) or 'all small firms will close' (too extreme).
Technique: Vocabulary in context
Passage: 'The proposal was ambiguous, leaving room for interpretation.' What does 'ambiguous' mean here?
Answer: Unclear/uncertain (open to multiple interpretations), not 'detailed' or 'false'. Context clue: 'leaving room for interpretation'.

Common Traps

  • Choosing an option true in real life but not supported by passage.
  • Picking extreme language options.
  • Confusing 'according to passage' with 'according to me'.
  • Missing negatives ('NOT true', 'EXCEPT', 'LEAST likely').
  • Answering from memory of a similar passage rather than this one.

Memory Tricks

  • RC question order: Main idea → Tone → Inference → Direct facts → Vocabulary.
  • Extreme words = usually wrong: always, never, only, all, must.
  • Moderate words = usually safer: some, often, may, could, tends to.
  • First/last paragraphs: Often contain main idea and author's conclusion.
RC exam strategy
Read the question stem carefully (note NOT/EXCEPT). Locate the relevant paragraph before choosing. For inference, ask 'does this HAVE TO be true based only on the passage?' If not, eliminate. Watch word count and time per passage.
comprehension/comprehension:
Reading Comprehension — Practice with Worked Passages

This lesson walks through two complete RC passages (one short, one long) with every question type explained: main idea, inference, tone, vocabulary-in-context, and true/false. Learn how to eliminate wrong options and justify the right one from the text.

Passage 1 — Short (Social media & attention)

Social media platforms are engineered to capture attention. Notifications, infinite scroll, and algorithmic feeds exploit the brain's reward circuitry, doling out unpredictable bursts of validation. The result is fragmented concentration: users switch tasks every few minutes, and deep reading declines. Critics call this the 'attention economy' — human focus treated as a raw material to be mined and sold to advertisers. Defenders argue platforms merely give people what they want, and that individuals retain agency to log off. The tension between design and autonomy is the core issue.

Questions

Q1. What is the central idea of the passage?

  • A) Social media should be banned.
  • B) Social media is engineered to capture attention, creating a tension between platform design and user autonomy.
  • C) Notifications are the only cause of distraction.
  • D) Advertisers pay for all social media content.

Answer: B. The passage defines the attention economy and frames the issue as design vs autonomy. A is extreme (not suggested), C is too narrow (notifications are one tool), D is false (advertisers buy attention, not all content).

Q2. The word 'doling out' in paragraph 1 most nearly means:

  • A) Withholding completely
  • B) Distributing in small amounts
  • C) Taking away
  • D) Demanding payment

Answer: B. 'Doling out' = giving out in small portions; validation bursts are given in small amounts. Context: 'unpredictable bursts of validation'.

Q3. Which can be inferred about the author's view?

  • A) Users have no responsibility at all.
  • B) Platform design and user agency are both relevant.
  • C) Advertisers are solely to blame.
  • D) Deep reading has disappeared entirely.

Answer: B. The passage presents both sides ('defenders argue... individuals retain agency') — so both design and agency matter. A/C/D are extreme or false ('disappeared entirely' is too strong).

Q4. The author's tone is best described as:

  • A) Furious
  • B) Balanced and analytical
  • C) Celebratory
  • D) Sarcastic

Answer: B. The passage lays out critics' and defenders' views without taking an extreme side — balanced and analytical.

Passage 2 — Long (Vernacular education)

The debate over the medium of instruction in Indian schools has recurred for more than a century. The colonial system privileged English, creating a class of English-speaking elites while vernacular languages were relegated to the periphery. After independence, policymakers faced a dilemma: English promised access to global knowledge and jobs, but mother-tongue instruction promised better early learning and wider inclusion. Research consistently shows children grasp foundational concepts faster when taught in a familiar language; yet the labor market still rewards English fluency. Several states now experiment with bilingual models — vernacular in early grades, phased introduction of English — hoping to capture both benefits. The challenge is implementation: teacher training, textbooks, and assessment must all align with the chosen medium, or the policy remains symbolic.

Questions

Q5. What is the main point of the passage?

  • A) English should be the only medium of instruction.
  • B) The medium-of-instruction debate involves trade-offs between global access and early learning, with implementation as the key challenge.
  • C) Vernacular education failed after independence.
  • D) Bilingual models have solved all problems.

Answer: B. The passage frames the dilemma (English vs vernacular), cites research on both sides, notes bilingual experiments, and ends with implementation challenges. A and D are extreme; C is false.

Q6. According to research cited in the passage, children taught in a familiar language:

  • A) Learn foundational concepts faster
  • B) Never learn English well
  • C) Perform worse in labor markets
  • D) Need no teacher training

Answer: A. Directly stated: 'children grasp foundational concepts faster when taught in a familiar language'.

Q7. The word 'periphery' in paragraph 1 most nearly means:

  • A) Center
  • B) Edge/marginal position
  • C) Curriculum
  • D) Examination system

Answer: B. 'Relegated to the periphery' = pushed to the edge/margins — vernacular languages were marginalized under English privilege.

Q8. Which assumption underlies the bilingual model experiments?

  • A) Vernacular alone is sufficient for labor-market success.
  • B) Combining vernacular early with English later captures benefits of both.
  • C) Teacher training is unnecessary.
  • D) English should start from grade 1 only.

    • Answer: B. The passage says states hope to 'capture both benefits' — vernacular early learning + English labor-market value. A/C/D contradict or overstate.

    Q9. The author's tone is:

    • A) Strongly pro-English
    • B) Neutral and policy-oriented
    • C) Angry at colonial legacy
    • D) Dismissive of vernacular

    Answer: B. The passage weighs both sides neutrally and focuses on policy implementation.

    Q10. According to the passage, what makes bilingual policy difficult in practice?

    • A) Lack of student interest
    • B) Teacher training, textbooks, and assessment alignment
    • D) Too much English
    • C) No research support

    Answer: B. Last sentence: 'The challenge is implementation: teacher training, textbooks, and assessment must all align.'

    Elimination Drill — Common Wrong-Option Patterns

    • Outside knowledge: An option may be factually true in the real world but absent from the passage — eliminate.
    • Partial truth: An option may repeat one detail but misstate the relationship — eliminate.
    • Overstatement: 'All/every/never' when passage says 'some/many/may' — eliminate.
    • Opposite: Option reverses cause-effect or author stance — eliminate.
    RC practice exam strategy
    After every practice passage, write down: (1) main idea in one sentence, (2) author's tone, (3) the evidence for each answer you chose. Review wrong answers to see which trap caught you (extreme language, outside knowledge, partial truth).
writing/essay-writing:
Essay Writing — Structure & Approach

Descriptive English (essay, letter, precis) appears in UPSC Mains Paper A/B, RBI Phase 2, IBPS PO Mains, CDS, NDA, and state PSC papers. The essay tests thought clarity, structure, language, and balanced argument within 250–400 words.

  • Essay structure:
    • Introduction (10–15%): Hook (quote/anecdote/fact), define the core term, state your thesis/stand, outline the roadmap (dimensions you'll cover).
    • Body (70–75%): 3–4 dimensions, one paragraph each. Each paragraph: topic sentence → explanation → example/data → link back to thesis. Use subheadings for readability.
    • Conclusion (10–15%): Summarize the argument arc, restate thesis in evolved form, forward-looking vision. No new facts or arguments.
  • Dimension selection (SPACER):
    • Social — caste, gender, youth, education, health, marginalized.
    • Political — governance, democracy, federalism, rights, institutions.
    • Administrative — bureaucracy, delivery, e-governance, accountability.
    • Cultural — values, traditions, language, ethics, art.
    • Economic — growth, employment, agriculture, industry, inclusion.
    • Religious/Environmental/International — ecology, climate, India's global role, science.
    Pick 3–4 dimensions relevant to the topic; avoid overlap.
  • Essay types:
    • Abstract/quote-based: Unpack the quote — literal meaning, deeper meaning, examples proving/disproving, counter-arguments, synthesis.
    • Topic-based: Deconstruct into components, take a balanced stand, discuss dimensions with data/examples, way forward.
  • Content enrichment: Quotes (verified, attributed), data (Census, NFHS, NITI Aayog MPI, PLFS, Economic Survey with year/source), specific examples (Chipko, Ujjwala, Chandrayaan-3, MGNREGA), constitutional anchoring (articles, judgments like Kesavananda Bharati, Puttaswamy).
  • Language & style: Clarity over ornamentation; one idea per sentence; connectors (moreover, however, therefore, consequently); formal tone; no first-person overuse; no clichés ('in this modern era', 'every coin has two sides').
  • PEEL paragraph: Point → Example → Explanation → Link (to thesis).
  • Time management (250-word essay): Topic selection 5 min, outline 5 min, writing 20 min, review 3 min.

Common Traps

  • Writing a general-knowledge answer (point-heavy, no narrative flow) instead of an essay.
  • Taking an extreme, one-sided stand without counter-views.
  • Repetition of ideas across paragraphs.
  • No conclusion, or a conclusion that introduces new arguments.
  • Straying off-topic in middle paragraphs.
  • Exceeding word limit or falling far short.

Memory Tricks

  • IBC: Introduction, Body, Conclusion — every essay.
  • PEEL: Point, Example, Explanation, Link — every body paragraph.
  • SPACER: Social, Political, Administrative, Cultural, Economic, Religious/Environmental/International dimensions.
  • 30-min essay split: Select 5 + outline 5 + write 20 + review 3 + buffer.
Descriptive essay exam strategy
Pick a topic you can write 250+ words on with 3+ dimensions. Outline before writing — it prevents mid-essay confusion. Keep a balanced, constitutional tone. End with a forward-looking, nation-building vision. Underline key phrases for the examiner's quick scan.
writing/letter-writing:
Letter & Report Writing

Letter writing appears in descriptive English papers (IBPS PO Mains, RBI Phase 2, state PSC, UPSC Paper A/B optional languages). You must write formal and informal letters, applications, complaints, and short reports with correct format, tone, and brevity.

  • Letter types:
    • Formal letters: To authorities, editors, banks, companies, officials — complaints, applications, requests, inquiries.
    • Informal letters: To friends/relatives — personal news, invitations, condolences, congratulations.
    • Job applications: Cover letter + CV — highlight fit for the role.
    • Reports: Short factual reports on events, surveys, incidents — heading, introduction, body, conclusion/recommendation.
  • Formal letter format:
    • Sender's address (top left/right)
    • Date
    • Receiver's designation & address
    • Subject line (concise, capitalized)
    • Salutation (Sir/Madam/Dear Mr. X)
    • Body — 3 short paragraphs: purpose → details → request/action expected
    • Complimentary close (Yours faithfully/sincerely)
    • Sender's name & signature
  • Informal letter format: Address, date, salutation (Dear X/Dearest), conversational body, closing (Yours lovingly/Yours truly), name.
  • Job application/cover letter: Reference to advertisement, qualifications & experience match, enclosure (CV), request for interview.
  • Complaint letter: Factual account of problem, dates/references, impact, specific remedy sought, tone firm but polite (no abuse).
  • Report format: Title, 'By' line, date, introduction (purpose/scope), body (findings arranged logically), conclusion & recommendations.

Style Rules

  • Brevity: Short sentences, one idea per paragraph, no redundancy ('revert back', 'free gift').
  • Tone: Formal letters — polite, respectful, objective; informal — warm, personal; complaints — firm but courteous, never abusive.
  • Clarity: State purpose in first paragraph; avoid jargon unless reader knows it.
  • Courtesy: 'Please', 'thank you', 'regret', 'apologize' where appropriate.
  • Accuracy: Correct names, dates, account numbers, reference numbers.

Common Traps

  • Mixing formal and informal tone in the same letter.
  • Missing subject line or date in formal letters.
  • Over-writing — exceeding word limit (typically 150–200 words for letters).
  • Emotional ranting in complaint letters.
  • Forgetting the action requested (what you want the reader to do).

Memory Tricks

  • Formal letter skeleton: Address → Date → Receiver → Subject → Salutation → Body (purpose/details/request) → Close → Signature.
  • Body paragraph rule: Para 1 = why I'm writing; Para 2 = facts/details; Para 3 = what I want done.
  • Complaint formula: Problem + Evidence + Impact + Remedy.
Letter-writing exam strategy
Identify letter type first (formal/informal/application/complaint/report), then follow the fixed format. Word economy matters — draft mentally before writing. Always end with a clear action statement.
writing/precis-writing:
Précis Writing — Compression to One-Third

A précis is a concise summary that keeps the argument, tone, and main claims of the original in about one-third of the words. It appears in UPSC Mains Paper A/B, RBI Phase 2, IBPS PO Mains, and state PSC descriptive papers.

  • Definition: Précis = clear, concise summary in your own words, roughly one-third length, retaining essence, tone, and logical structure.
  • Précis is NOT: A mere outline, paraphrase, abstract with opinion, or critical essay. Do NOT add your views, examples, or criticism.
  • Steps:
    1. Read the passage twice — first for gist, then for structure.
    2. Identify the main claim/argument and supporting reasons.
    3. Delete examples, illustrations, repetitions, digressions, adjectives of emphasis.
    4. Note key facts (names, dates, figures, places) to retain.
    5. Draft in your own words — one-third length.
    6. Check: does it stand alone? Is tone preserved? Is word count right?
  • What to keep: Main claim, supporting reasons, conclusion, key data, author's stance/tone.
  • What to drop: Examples, anecdotes, repetitions, rhetorical questions, emotive adjectives, quotations unless crucial, your own opinion.
  • Word count: Target ≈ one-third of original (e.g., 300-word passage → ~100-word précis). UPSC accepts reasonable range (~one-third ± small margin).
  • Language: Third person, indirect/reported speech, past tense often, formal, objective, no contractions, no first person ('I think', 'in my opinion').
  • Structure: One paragraph usually; opening states theme/author and claim; body gives supporting logic; closing states conclusion/implication.
    • Technique: Compression example
    Original (60 words): 'The government has launched several schemes to improve rural employment. MGNREGA guarantees 100 days of wage work. PMKVY trains youth in skills. Together these reduce distress migration.' Précis it.
    Answer: 'Rural employment schemes—MGNREGA's 100-day wage guarantee and PMKVY's skill training—aim to reduce distress migration.' (~18 words, ~one-third, keeps claims, drops 'has launched', 'several').
    Technique: Tone preservation
    Original is critical of a policy. Précis must remain critical, not neutral or praising.
    Answer: Use words like 'faulty', 'questionable', 'fails to' reflecting author's stance; do not soften to 'interesting' or 'notable'.

    Common Traps

    • Adding your own opinion ('I think the policy is good').
    • Including examples/illustrations from the passage.
    • Copying sentences verbatim instead of paraphrasing.
    • Exceeding one-third by too much (or writing too little, losing argument).
    • Changing the tone (e.g., making a critical passage sound neutral).
    • Using first person or direct speech.

    Memory Tricks

    • KISS: Keep It Short and Simple — one-third, own words, same argument.
    • 3R: Read → Retain main claim → Rewrite (own words).
    • Drop list: Examples, repetitions, your opinion, emphatic adjectives.
    • One-third: Original word count ÷ 3 ≈ target précis length.
    Précis exam strategy
    Count original words, divide by 3 for target. Draft, count words, trim/expand to hit target. Read aloud to check flow and tone. Ensure no new opinion crept in. Compare against passage: did you keep the main claim and conclusion?
writing/descriptive-practice:
Descriptive Writing Practice — Timed Prompts & Model Outlines

Descriptive writing is best learned by writing under timed conditions and comparing against model outlines. This lesson gives practice prompts for essays, letters, reports, and précis, plus outlines to self-evaluate against.

  • Practice routine: One timed descriptive piece per session — alternate essay (250 words, 25 min), letter (150 words, 15 min), precis (one-third of a 250-word passage, 20 min), report (150 words, 15 min).
  • Timed simulation: Set a timer, write without stopping, then self-evaluate against the model outline below before checking any answer key.
  • Self-evaluation checklist:
    • Did I answer exactly what was asked?
    • Is there a clear introduction, body, conclusion?
    • Are examples/data specific and relevant?
    • Is the tone appropriate (formal for letters/reports, balanced for essays)?
    • Is word count within limit?
    • Any spelling/grammar errors?

Practice Prompt Bank

Essay prompts (250–300 words, ~25 min)

  • 'Digital India: inclusion or exclusion?'
  • 'Women's reservation: symbolic or substantive?'
  • 'Climate action vs development: India's balancing act.'
  • 'Artificial intelligence: promise and peril for employment.'
  • 'Loneliness is the ultimate poverty.'
  • 'Justice delayed is justice denied.'
  • 'Simplicity is the ultimate sophistication.'
  • 'India's G20 presidency: opportunities and responsibilities.'

Letter prompts (150 words, ~15 min)

  • Write to the editor about rising road accidents in your city, suggesting remedies.
  • Write to the bank manager requesting ATM facility in your locality.
  • Write to the municipal commissioner about irregular garbage collection.
  • Write a job application for a probationary officer post referencing an advertisement.
  • Write to your younger sibling advising on career choices.

Report prompts (150 words, ~15 min)

  • Report on a blood-donation camp organized in your college.
  • Report on a road accident you witnessed.
  • Report on water shortage in your locality and its impact.
  • Report on a cultural festival held in your district.

Précis prompts (one-third length, ~20 min)

  • Compress a 250–300 word editorial passage on education/environment/governance to ~90–100 words.

Model Outline — Essay

Topic: 'Digital India: inclusion or exclusion?'

  • Introduction: Define Digital India; thesis — it expands access but excludes the digitally illiterate/poor; both inclusion and exclusion coexist.
  • Body 1 — Inclusion: UPI, DBT, e-governance, rural internet, examples (Jan Dhan, CoWIN, e-courts).
  • Body 2 — Exclusion: Digital divide (gender, rural, elderly, disabled), data costs, literacy, privacy concerns.
  • Body 3 — Way forward: Digital literacy, BharatNet, affordable devices, local-language interfaces, grievance redress.
  • Conclusion: Digital India can be inclusive only with deliberate last-mile access; technology is a tool, not a guarantee.

Model Outline — Letter (formal complaint)

Topic: Irregular garbage collection in your locality.

  • Sender's address & date; Receiver: Municipal Commissioner; Subject: Complaint regarding irregular garbage collection in XYZ locality.
  • Para 1: Purpose — irregular garbage collection for past two weeks.
  • Para 2: Details — dumped waste at XYZ street, stray dogs, health risk (dengue/malaria), residents affected.
  • Para 3: Request — restore daily collection, penalty mechanism, response timeline.
  • Close: Yours faithfully, name.

Model Outline — Report

Topic: Blood-donation camp in college.

  • Title: Blood-Donation Camp Report
  • Introduction: Organized by NSS unit on date, in association with Red Cross.
  • Body: Inauguration by principal; 120 students registered, 85 units collected; doctors present; refreshments; awareness talk.
  • Conclusion: Successful; recommend quarterly camps.

Model Outline — Précis

Source (approx. 150 words): A paragraph on climate-change adaptation in Indian agriculture — vulnerable rainfed areas, need for drought-resistant crops, water conservation, crop insurance, government schemes, farmer training.

  • Précis (~50 words): Climate change threatens Indian rainfed agriculture; adaptation requires drought-resistant crops, water conservation, crop insurance, and farmer training through existing schemes.
  • Checks: ~one-third length, third person, own words, keeps claim + reasons, no examples/opinion.

Improvement Loop

  • Write → Outline-compare → Identify 2 weaknesses → Fix in next piece.
  • Weaknesses to watch: Weak conclusions, off-topic digressions, poor time management, word-count miss, tone mismatch.
  • Peer evaluation: Exchange with a study partner using the checklist above.

Common Traps

  • Practising only favourite topics — exam may be unfamiliar.
  • Not timing practice — exam pressure changes speed and quality.
  • Copying model essays — UPSC/exams reward original thought.
  • Ignoring word limit — penalized in some exams.
  • No self-review — repeating same errors.

Memory Tricks

  • Practice loop: Write → Compare → Fix 2 weaknesses → Repeat.
  • Pre-exam warm-up: Write one full piece the day before to get into flow.
  • Topic bank: Keep 3–4 dimensions per theme so you never start from zero.
Exam-day strategy
Attempt every descriptive question — partial answers score more than blanks. Budget time strictly per piece. If running out of time, write in structured bullet points with introduction and conclusion. Proofread the last 3 minutes for spelling and word count.
comprehension/filler-cloze:
Cloze Test & Fillers

Cloze tests and fillers appear in SSC, banking, CDS, NDA, CLAT, and state exams. A cloze test is a passage with blanks; you choose the word that fits both grammatically and contextually. Single/double fillers test one or two blanks in a sentence.

  • Approach: Read the whole passage first to grasp the theme/tone. Then fill blanks in sequence — context flows across blanks.
  • Grammar fit: Part of speech must match (noun after article, verb after subject, adjective before noun, adverb before adjective/verb, preposition before object).
  • Context fit: Meaning must fit the sentence and passage tone (positive/negative/neutral).
  • Collocation: Words that naturally go together (make a decision, take a risk, strong tea, heavy rain, commit a crime).
  • Contrast markers: however, although, yet, but, despite — signal opposite meaning on either side.
  • Cause-effect: because, since, therefore, consequently, so, thus.
  • Elimination: Remove options wrong part of speech, wrong meaning, wrong collocation.
  • Double fillers: Both blanks must fit; check the second blank too — a common trap is getting the first right but second wrong.

Common Blank Types

  • Article + noun: 'a/an' + singular countable; 'the' + specific; no article with uncountable/plural general.
  • Preposition after adjective/verb: good at, interested in, depend on, insist on, object to, prevent from, succeed in, capable of.
  • Verb form after subject: third-person singular -s, past tense, infinitive after 'to'.
  • Adverb before adjective/verb: very happy, quickly ran.
  • Conjunction: and/but/or/although/because/if/unless/while.
  • Pronoun: agrees with antecedent in number/gender/person.

Common Traps

  • Choosing a word that fits grammatically but not the passage meaning.
  • Ignoring the wider passage context (one blank depends on earlier/later sentences).
  • Double filler: getting first blank right but second wrong — check both.
  • Confusing similar words (affect/effect, stationary/stationery, accept/except).
  • Forcing a fancy word when a simple one fits.

Memory Tricks

  • Read-around: Read one sentence before AND after the blank.
  • Part-of-speech check: Noun/verb/adjective/adverb must match the slot.
  • Collocation pairs: make/take/do + noun; strong/heavy + noun; commit + crime; pay + attention.
  • Contrast/continuity: however/although = opposite; and/therefore/moreover = same direction.
Cloze exam strategy
Read the full passage first. Fill the sure blanks first, then use surrounding sentences for unsure ones. For double fillers, test both blanks together — reject if either doesn't fit. Eliminate wrong part-of-speech options immediately.
opt-agriculture/overview:
Agriculture Optional — Overview & Syllabus Map

Agriculture is a popular, high-scoring optional for UPSC Mains with significant GS overlap (GS III agriculture, environment, rural development). Paper I covers agriculture ecology, farm management, soil science; Paper II covers crop production, horticulture, animal husbandry, agricultural extension.

Paper I — Ecology & Farm Management

  • Ecology & environment: Ecosystem, agro-climatic zones of India, monsoon, climate change impacts on agriculture, greenhouse gases, carbon sequestration, sustainable agriculture.
  • Soil science: Soil formation, profile, physical & chemical properties, soil organic matter, soil fertility, problematic soils (saline, alkaline, acidic) and reclamation, soil erosion and conservation.
  • Irrigation & water management: Sources, efficiency, micro-irrigation (drip, sprinkler), watershed management, water-use efficiency, conjunctive use, drainage.
  • Farm management: Farm planning, budgeting, risk management, land reforms, tenancy, consolidation, cooperative farming.
  • Crop physiology: Photosynthesis, respiration, transpiration, plant growth regulators, seed germination, dormancy, vernalization, photoperiodism.
  • Genetics & plant breeding: Mendelian genetics, hybridization, selection, mutation breeding, polyploidy, transgenic crops, GM crops, seed technology.

Paper II — Crop Production & Allied Sectors

  • Field crops: Cereals (rice, wheat, maize, millets), pulses, oilseeds, commercial crops (cotton, sugarcane, jute), fodder crops — package of practices, cropping systems, cropping intensity.
  • Horticulture: Fruits, vegetables, flowers, spices, plantation crops — nursery management, propagation, canopy management, post-harvest management.
  • Plant protection: Pests, diseases, weeds — integrated pest management (IPM), biological control, pesticide residues, safe use of pesticides.
  • Animal husbandry: Breeds of cattle, buffalo, sheep, goat, poultry — feeding, breeding, housing, health management, dairy and poultry farming economics.
  • Agricultural extension: Extension methods, KVKs, ATMA, farmer producer organizations (FPOs), e-NAM, communication, adoption of innovations.
  • Farm economics: Cost of production, minimum support price (MSP), procurement, agricultural marketing, regulated markets, warehousing, cold chain.
Technique: Linking optional to GS III
Question linkage: 'Crop diversification is essential for sustainable agriculture.' Use agro-climatic zones, MSP bias toward rice-wheat, water table decline in Punjab-Haryana, and promotion of millets (Nutri-cereals, International Year of Millets 2023).
Answer structure: Introduction (define diversification), body (regional imbalances, water-guzzling crops, millet promotion, PM-KISAN, crop insurance), challenges (procurement bias, lack of processing), way forward (MSP expansion, cluster approach, value chains).

Common Traps

  • Confusing Rabi (winter: wheat, mustard) with Kharif (monsoon: rice, cotton, sugarcane) crops.
  • Missing that agriculture is a State subject — Centre supports via Centrally Sponsored Schemes.
  • Overlooking that NFSM (National Food Security Mission) targets rice, wheat, pulses, coarse cereals, nutri-cereals.
  • Assuming organic farming = zero input — it prohibits synthetic fertilizers/pesticides but allows biological inputs.

Memory Tricks
opt-agriculture/paper1:
Agriculture Paper I — Ecology, Soil & Farm Management

Agro-ecology & Cropping Systems
