  • Agro-climatic zones of India: 15 zones (Planning Commission) — Western Himalayas, Eastern Himalayas, Northern Plain, Western Plain, Central Plateau, Eastern Plateau, Western Ghats, Eastern Ghats, Southern Plateau, Eastern Coastal, Western Coastal, Gujarat Plains, Islands — each with specific crops.
  • Cropping systems: Mono-cropping, multiple cropping, inter-cropping, mixed cropping, relay cropping — choice depends on rainfall, soil, market.
  • Cropping intensity: Gross cropped area / net sown area × 100 — indicates how intensively land is used.
  • Dryland agriculture: Rainfed areas (<750 mm rainfall) — drought-resistant crops, moisture conservation, contour bunding.
  • Watershed management: Ridge-to-valley approach, water harvesting structures, check dams, farm ponds, participatory watershed development (Neeranchal).

Soil Science & Fertility

  • Soil formation: Weathering of parent rock, organic matter accumulation, time, climate, topography.
  • Soil profile: Horizons — O (organic), A (topsoil), B (subsoil), C (parent material), R (bedrock).
  • Soil texture: Sand, silt, clay proportions — loam is ideal for most crops.
  • Soil fertility: Essential plant nutrients — N, P, K (primary), Ca, Mg, S (secondary), Zn, Fe, Mn, Cu, B, Mo, Cl (micronutrients).
  • Problem soils: Saline (high soluble salts), alkaline/sodic (high sodium, high pH), acidic (low pH, Al toxicity) — reclamation through gypsum, organic matter, drainage.
  • Soil erosion: Water erosion (sheet, rill, gully), wind erosion — control: contour bunding, terracing, contour ploughing, grassed waterways, afforestation.
  • Soil organic matter: Humus — improves structure, water holding, nutrient supply; green manuring, farmyard manure, compost.

Irrigation & Water Management

  • Sources: Wells, tube wells, tanks, canals, lift irrigation.
  • Irrigation efficiency: Conventional flood irrigation vs micro-irrigation (drip saves 30-50% water, sprinkler saves 25-30%).
  • Micro-irrigation: Drip irrigation (water near root zone), sprinkler (rain-like spraying), suitable for horticulture, water-scarce areas — PMKSI (Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana) — Per Drop More Crop.
  • Conjunctive use: Coordinated use of surface and groundwater.
  • Waterlogging & salinity: Causes: excessive irrigation, poor drainage — reclamation: surface/subsurface drainage, gypsum for sodic soils.
  • Watershed: Ridge-to-valley treatment, farm ponds, percolation tanks, community participation.

Farm Management & Land Reforms

  • Farm planning: Cropping pattern, input budget, risk management, diversification.
  • Land reforms: Abolition of zamindari, tenancy reforms (security of tenure, fair rent), ceiling on holdings, consolidation of holdings, cooperative farming.
  • Agricultural finance: Credit sources — institutional (PSBs, RRBs, cooperatives, NABARD refinance) vs non-institutional (moneylenders); Kisan Credit Card (KCC); interest subvention.
  • Crop insurance: PMFBY (Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana) — yield-based insurance, premium 2% kharif/1.5% rabi/5% commercial, rest Centre+State.
Technique: Soil reclamation answer
Question: 'Saline soils reduce crop productivity.' Explain causes and reclamation.
Answer: Causes — capillary rise, poor drainage, excessive irrigation. Reclamation: leaching (flushing salts below root zone), gypsum application for sodic soils, organic matter, salt-tolerant varieties, improved drainage.

Memory Tricks

  • NPK: N — leafy growth (nitrogen), P — roots/flowers (phosphorus), K — overall vigour/disease resistance (potassium).
  • Problem soils: Saline = white crust (salts); Alkaline/sodic = black crust (sodium); Acidic = sour, aluminium toxicity.
  • Irrigation efficiency: Drip > Sprinkler > Flood.
Mains strategy
For agriculture optional, link every topic to Indian context (states, crops, schemes). Draw diagrams: soil profile, irrigation methods, crop calendar. Quote latest data: agricultural GDP share (~18%), workforce (~45%), foodgrain production (~330 MT).
opt-agriculture/paper2:
Agriculture Paper II — Crop Production, Horticulture & Allied Sectors

Field Crops & Package of Practices

  • Rice: Kharif crop; puddled transplanted rice vs direct-seeded rice (DSR); SRI (System of Rice Intensification) — wider spacing, younger seedlings, less water; varieties: IRRI, Samba Mahsuri; pest: stem borer, brown planthopper.
  • Wheat: Rabi crop; varieties: HD-2967, HD-3086; diseases: rust, smut; critical stage: crown root initiation.
  • Maize: Kharif/rabi/summer; hybrid vs composite varieties; pest: fall armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda).
  • Pulses: Tur (arhar), moong, urad, gram — biological nitrogen fixation through Rhizobium; NFSM-pulses.
  • Oilseeds: Groundnut, mustard, soybean, sunflower, sesame — India imports edible oils; National Mission on Edible Oils (NMEO) — oil palm.
  • Commercial crops: Cotton (Bt cotton — only GM crop), sugarcane (ratooning), jute (retting).
  • Cropping intensity: Rice-wheat system (Indo-Gangetic plain) — issues: residue burning, water table decline, diversification needed.

Horticulture

  • Scope: Fruits (mango, banana, citrus, apple, grapes), vegetables (tomato, potato, onion), flowers (rose, marigold, gladiolus), spices (turmeric, pepper, cardamom), plantation crops (coconut, arecanut, cashew, tea, coffee, rubber).
  • Nursery management: Seed treatment, grafting, budding, layering, tissue culture (micro-propagation).
  • Canopy management: Training, pruning, high-density planting.
  • Post-harvest management: Maturity indices, harvesting, grading, packaging, cold chain, ripening (ethylene), value addition (juice, jam, pickles).
  • Post-harvest losses: 15-25% in fruits/vegetables — causes: poor storage, transport, handling; solutions: cold chain, processing, solar dryers.

Plant Protection

  • Pests: Sucking pests (aphid, jassid, whitefly), chewing (caterpillars), borers (stem borer, fruit borer).
  • Diseases: Fungal (blast, rust, blight), bacterial (blight), viral (mosaic, leaf curl — vector whitefly).
  • Weeds: Parasitic (Striga), noxious (Parthenium) — control: mechanical, chemical (herbicides: pre-emergence vs post-emergence), biological.
  • IPM (Integrated Pest Management): Ecological approach — cultural, mechanical, biological (biocontrol agents: Trichoderma, NPV, ladybird), chemical (last resort), action thresholds.
  • Pesticide residue: MRL (maximum residue limit), pre-harvest interval, safe use, PPE (personal protective equipment).

Animal Husbandry

  • Cattle & buffalo breeds: Cattle: Gir, Sahiwal, Red Sindhi (milch); Hallikar, Kangayam (draught); Buffalo: Murrah, Mehsana, Jaffarabadi (milch).
  • Poultry: Layers (eggs), broilers (meat); broiler management: brooding, litter, vaccination; layer management: lighting, cage/deep litter.
  • Feeding: Roughage (fodder, hay, silage), concentrates (grains, oil cakes), minerals, additives; green fodder: Napier, guinea, berseem, lucerne.
  • Breeding: Artificial insemination (AI), sex-sorted semen, embryo transfer (MOET), crossbreeding (Jersey/HF × indigenous for milk), indigenous conservation (Gir, Sahiwal).
  • Dairy economics: Milk production, procurement (dairy cooperatives — Amul model), value addition (cheese, ghee, powder), clean milk production.
  • Poultry diseases: Ranikhet (Newcastle), fowl pox, coccidiosis — vaccination schedule.

Agricultural Extension

  • Extension methods: Individual (farm visit, office call), group (method demonstration, result demonstration, farmer field school), mass (campaign, exhibition, kisan mela, radio, TV, ICT — Kisan Suvidha, mKisan).
  • Institutions: KVKs (Krishi Vigyan Kendras — technology assessment, refinement, demonstration), ATMA (Agricultural Technology Management Agency — district level), SAUs (State Agricultural Universities), ICAR (Indian Council of Agricultural Research — apex).
  • FPOs: Farmer Producer Organizations — collectivization, input procurement, output marketing, credit linkage.
  • e-NAM: Electronic National Agriculture Market — online trading platform connecting APMCs; quality assaying; transparent price discovery.
  • Adoption of innovations: Innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority, laggards (Rogers).
Technique: IPM answer
Question: 'Discuss Integrated Pest Management (IPM) as a sustainable plant protection strategy.'
Answer: IPM = ecological approach combining cultural (crop rotation, sanitation), mechanical (handpicking, traps), biological (biocontrol agents: ladybird, Trichoderma, NPV), chemical (pesticides as last resort, pre-harvest interval), monitoring (action thresholds, pheromone traps). Benefits: reduced pesticide residues, resistance management, biodiversity conservation, cost-effectiveness. Constraints: lack of awareness, non-availability of biocontrol agents, market preference for cosmetic perfection.

Memory Tricks

  • Crop seasons: Kharif = monsoon (rice, cotton); Rabi = winter (wheat, mustard); Zaid = summer (watermelon, cucumber).
  • PMFSI/PMFBY: Premium 2% kharif/1.5% rabi/5% commercial crops.
  • Biocontrol agents: Trichoderma (fungal diseases), NPV (caterpillars), ladybird (aphids).
  • GM crop in India: Bt cotton — only approved GM crop.
Mains strategy
For Paper II, structure answers: crop → agro-climatic zone → package of practices → pests/diseases → value addition → government scheme → challenges → way forward. Use flow charts for crop production cycles. Quote NFHS/NFSA/NABARD data where relevant.
opt-animal-husbandry/overview:
Animal Husbandry & Veterinary Science Optional — Overview

Animal Husbandry & Veterinary Science (AH&VS) is a popular optional for veterinary graduates and biology-background aspirants. Paper I covers animal genetics, breeding, nutrition, physiology; Paper II covers animal production (dairy, poultry, meat, wool), veterinary public health, epidemiology, zoo/wild animals.

Paper I — Animal Genetics, Breeding, Nutrition & Physiology

  • Animal genetics & breeding: Mendelian inheritance, qualitative vs quantitative traits, heritability, repeatability, selection methods (mass, progeny, family, within-family), crossbreeding, composite breeds, synthetic breeds, inbreeding & outbreeding, heterosis, breeding policies for cattle, buffalo, sheep, goat, pig, poultry, equine, canine, feline.
  • Animal nutrition: Nutrients — carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water; rumen fermentation (volatile fatty acids, microbial protein), bypass protein, bypass fat, feed additives (probiotics, prebiotics, enzymes, ionophores), feeding standards, ration formulation, feed additives, feed processing.
  • Animal physiology: Digestion in ruminants (rumen, reticulum, omasum, abomasum) vs monogastrics; circulation, respiration, excretion, thermoregulation, endocrinology (hormones: thyroid, adrenal, pituitary, gonadal), reproduction (estrous cycle, ovulation, gestation, parturition, lactation — milk synthesis & let-down: oxytocin, prolactin).
  • Environmental physiology: Heat stress, thermoregulation, shelter design, climate-resilient livestock production.
  • Population genetics: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, factors changing gene frequency (selection, mutation, migration, drift), effective population size, inbreeding depression.

Paper II — Animal Production & Veterinary Public Health

  • Dairy production: Cattle & buffalo breeds (Gir, Sahiwal, Red Sindhi, Tharparkar, Kankrej, Murrah, Jaffarabadi, Mehsana, Surti), clean milk production, mastitis (subclinical/clinical), mastitis control (teat dipping, dry cow therapy), milk composition, milk preservation & processing (pasteurization, homogenization), dairy plant equipment, clean milk production.
  • Poultry production: Broiler (meat) vs layer (egg) management — brooding (temperature, ventilation, litter), housing (deep litter, cage), lighting programs, feeding phases (starter, grower, finisher, layer), vaccination schedule (Marek's, RD/ND, IBD, IB, fowl pox), culling, economics.
  • Sheep, goat, pig, rabbit, rabbit, equine, camel, yak, mithun production: Breeds, feeding, housing, wool production (sheep breeds: Merino, Deccani, Magra, Chokla), meat (chevon, mutton, pork), fiber (wool, pashmina, angora).
  • Veterinary public health & epidemiology: Zoonoses (rabies, brucellosis, tuberculosis, anthrax, leptospirosis, avian influenza, COVID-19 origin debates), food-borne diseases, milk-borne diseases, anthrax, quarantine, disinfection, carcass disposal, rendering, abattoir hygiene, HACCP in meat/milk.
  • Veterinary epidemiology: Disease occurrence measures (incidence, prevalence, mortality, morbidity, case fatality rate), outbreak investigation, surveillance (passive/active), serosurveillance, vaccination programs (FMD, PPR, HS, BQ, anthrax, rabies), cold chain for vaccines.
  • Zoo & wild animal health: Zoo management, wildlife diseases, capture & immobilization, conservation breeding (Project Tiger, Project Elephant, vulture conservation), wildlife forensics.
  • Livestock products technology: Meat processing (slaughter, dressing, chilling, freezing), egg processing, wool grading, leather, by-products (blood meal, bone meal, hooves/horns), quality control (FPO, Agmark, BIS).
Technique: Mastitis answer
Question: 'Discuss mastitis in dairy animals: causes, detection, prevention.'
Answer: Mastitis = udder inflammation — causes: bacteria (Staph. aureus, Strep. agalactiae, E. coli), trauma, poor milking hygiene. Detection: clinical (clots, swelling, heat) vs subclinical (Somatic Cell Count, California Mastitis Test). Prevention: pre/post teat dipping, dry cow therapy, clean milking, culling chronic cases. Treatment: intramammary antibiotics, anti-inflammatories. Economic impact: reduced milk yield, discarded milk, treatment cost, culling.

Memory Tricks

  • Ruminant stomach: Rumen (fermentation), Reticulum (hardware), Omasum (water absorption), Abomasum (true stomach) — RROA.
  • Milk let-down hormones: Oxytocin (ejection), Prolactin (synthesis).
  • FMD vaccine: Foot-and-Mouth Disease vaccination under NADCP (National Animal Disease Control Programme).
  • Breeds: Milk — Gir, Sahiwal, Red Sindhi, Murrah buffalo; Meat — Boer goat, Hampshire pig; Wool — Merino, Deccani sheep.
Mains strategy
For AH&VS, combine production figures (India: largest milk producer ~230 MT, largest bovine population), schemes (Rashtriya Gokul Mission, NLM, NADCP, LIDCP), and disease facts. Draw diagrams: rumen compartments, milk secretion (alveolus → duct), reproductive cycle, dairy plant layout.
opt-animal-husbandry/paper1:
Animal Husbandry Paper I — Genetics, Breeding, Nutrition & Physiology

Animal Genetics & Breeding

  • Mendelian genetics: Law of segregation, law of independent assortment, dominance, incomplete dominance, codominance, epistasis, multiple alleles, sex-linked inheritance, sex-influenced traits, sex-limited traits.
  • Qualitative vs quantitative traits: Qualitative = simply inherited (few genes, little environmental effect — coat color, horned/polled); Quantitative = polygenic, environmental influence (milk yield, weight, growth rate) — measured by mean, variance, heritability.
  • Heritability (h²): Proportion of phenotypic variance due to additive genetic variance — high h² traits respond to selection (e.g., milk yield h² ~0.25-0.35, low-to-moderate; reproduction h² low ~0.05-0.15; conformation h² moderate-high).
  • Repeatability: Consistency of performance across records (e.g., milk yield across lactations).
  • Selection methods: Mass selection (phenotype), progeny testing (progeny performance — used for sires in dairy), family selection, within-family selection, index selection (multiple traits), genomic selection (genomic estimated breeding values - GEBV).
  • Crossbreeding: Crossbred cattle (Jersey/HF × indigenous) for milk; heterosis (hybrid vigor) in F1; rotational crossing, composite breeds (e.g., Friesian cross), synthetic breeds (e.g., Frieswal — HF × Sahiwal).
  • Inbreeding & outbreeding: Inbreeding = mating related animals — increases homozygosity, inbreeding depression (reduced fertility, vigor); Outbreeding = outcrossing, linebreeding, grading up (upgrading non-descript cattle using purebred sires).
  • Breeding policies: Crossbreeding for milk in plains (exotic × indigenous), pure breeding in breeding tracts, buffalo breeding (Murrah, Jaffarabadi, etc.), sheep breeding (merino crossing for wool), poultry breeding (layer/broiler lines).
  • Modern techniques: Artificial insemination (AI), sex-sorted semen, embryo transfer (MOET), MOET + IVF, cloning, genomic selection, gene editing (CRISPR — research stage).

Animal Nutrition

  • Nutrients: Water, energy (carbohydrates, fats), protein (amino acids), minerals (macro: Ca, P, Mg, Na, K, S; micro/trace: Cu, Zn, Se, Co, I, Fe, Mn, Mo), vitamins (A, D, E, K, B-complex).
  • Ruminant digestion: Ruminal fermentation by microbes — volatile fatty acids (acetate, propionate, butyrate), microbial protein synthesis (from NPN like urea), methane (CH₄) loss — enteric methane emission concern.
  • Bypass nutrients: Bypass protein (rumen undegradable protein - RUP), bypass fat — reach intestine directly for absorption.
  • Feed additives: Probiotics (live microbes), prebiotics (substrates for microbes), enzymes (phytase, xylanase), ionophores (monensin - improves propionate, reduces methane), buffers (sodium bicarbonate).
  • Feed processing: Chopping, grinding, pelleting, extrusion, silage (fermented fodder), hay (dried), ammoniation (urea treatment of straw), urea-molasses mineral blocks (UMMB).
  • Feeding standards: NRC (US), ICAR (India) — maintenance + production requirements (milk, growth, pregnancy, lactation).
  • Fodder crops: Green fodder: Napier, guinea, hybrid Napier, berseem, lucerne (alfalfa), oats, maize, sorghum (caution: prussic acid in young sorghum); tree fodder: subabul, sesbania, neem; silage: maize/sorghum silage; hay: dried legume/grass.

Animal Physiology

  • Ruminant vs monogastric digestion: Ruminants (cattle, buffalo, sheep, goat) — rumen fermentation, chew cud (rumination), can digest fibrous feeds; monogastrics (pig, poultry, horse) — simple stomach, limited fiber digestion.
  • Circulatory system: Heart (4 chambers), arteries/veins/capillaries, blood composition (plasma, RBC, WBC, platelets), lymph.
  • Respiratory system: Nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, lungs (alveoli — gas exchange), diaphragm.
  • Excretory system: Kidneys (nephrons — glomerulus, tubules), ureters, bladder, urethra; urine formation (filtration, reabsorption, secretion).
  • Endocrine system: Pituitary (master gland — GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, prolactin, oxytocin storage), thyroid (thyroxine - metabolism), parathyroid (calcitonin/PTH - calcium), adrenal (cortisol - stress, aldosterone - electrolytes), pancreas (insulin/glucagon - glucose), gonads (estrogen/progesterone/testosterone).
  • Reproduction: Estrous cycle (proestrus, estrus/heat, metestrus, diestrus), ovulation, fertilization, gestation (cattle ~283 days, buffalo ~310 days, sheep/goat ~150 days, pig ~114 days, horse ~340 days), parturition (oxytocin), lactation (mammary gland - alveoli, milk synthesis: glucose → lactose, acetate → fat, amino acids → casein/whey; milk ejection: oxytocin reflex; milk synthesis: prolactin).
  • Thermoregulation: Thermoneutral zone, heat stress (panting, sweating reduced in cattle), shelter design (shade, sprinklers, fans), breed adaptation (Bos indicus heat-tolerant vs Bos taurus cold-tolerant).
Technique: Breeding policy answer
Question: 'Discuss the crossbreeding policy for cattle in India.'
Answer: Crossbreeding exotic dairy breeds (Jersey, Holstein Friesian) with indigenous nondescript cows to increase milk yield — through AI with frozen semen; breeding policy: crossbreeding in plains, pure breeding in breeding tracts (Gir, Sahiwal, Red Sindhi, Tharparkar, Kankrej conservation); buffalo: Murrah, Nili-Ravi, Jaffarabadi, Surti, Mehsana, Pandharpuri breeding; challenges: heat stress tolerance of exotics, disease susceptibility, dilution of indigenous germplasm — hence breed conservation alongside crossbreeding; recent policy: Rashtriya Gokul Mission (indigenous breed conservation & development), sex-sorted semen for female calves.

Memory Tricks

  • Rumen compartments: RROA = Rumen (fermentation), Reticulum (hardware), Omasum (water), Abomasum (acid digestion).
  • Milk hormones: Oxytocin = ejection (let-down); Prolactin = synthesis (production).
  • Gestation: Cow 283 (~9 months), Buffalo 310 (~10 months), Sheep/Goat 150 (~5 months), Pig 114 (~3 months 3 weeks 3 days), Horse 340 (~11 months).
  • Dairy breeds: Cattle — Gir, Sahiwal, Red Sindhi, Tharparkar, Kankrej; Buffalo — Murrah, Nili-Ravi, Jaffarabadi, Surti, Mehsana.
Mains strategy
For AH&VS Paper I, draw diagrams: rumen compartments, mammary gland/alveolus, reproductive cycle (estrus), endocrine axes (HPG, HPT). Quote figures: India's milk production (~230 MT, world's largest), per capita milk availability (~450 g/day), livestock's contribution to agricultural GDP (~30%), share of livestock in farmer income (landless: ~50%). Link schemes: Rashtriya Gokul Mission, NLM, NADCP, LIDCP.
opt-animal-husbandry/paper2:
Animal Husbandry Paper II — Production, Veterinary Public Health & Allied Sectors

Dairy Production & Management

  • Cattle breeds: Milch: Gir, Sahiwal, Red Sindhi, Tharparkar, Kankrej, Deoni; Dual-purpose: Hariana, Ongole, Hallikar, Krishna Valley; Exotic dairy: Holstein Friesian, Jersey, Brown Swiss.
  • Buffalo breeds: Murrah (Haryana — highest milk), Nili-Ravi (Pakistan/Punjab), Jaffarabadi (Gujarat), Mehsana (Gujarat), Surti (Gujarat), Pandharpuri (Maharashtra), Bhadawari (UP).
  • Clean milk production: Clean udder, clean hands, clean utensils, clean environment, cooling (chilling to 4°C within 2 hours), testing (platform tests: clot-on-boiling, alcohol, acidity; laboratory: SNF, fat, microbial count).
  • Mastitis: Subclinical (no visible signs, detected by SCC/CMT) vs clinical (swollen, hot, painful udder, abnormal milk); pathogens: Staph. aureus, Strep. agalactiae, E. coli; prevention: teat dipping (pre/post), dry cow therapy, culling chronics, clean milking; treatment: intramammary antibiotics.
  • Milk composition: Water ~87%, fat 3-6% (buffalo higher), protein 3-3.5% (casein, whey), lactose 4.5-5%, minerals 0.7%; factors affecting: breed, stage of lactation, parity, season, nutrition, disease.
  • Milk processing: Chilling, filtration, clarification, pasteurization (HTST: 72°C/15s; LTLT: 63°C/30min; UHT: 135°C/1-2s), homogenization (prevents cream separation), packaging, cold chain.
  • Milk products: Butter, ghee, cheese (cheddar, paneer), skimmed milk powder (SMP), whole milk powder (WMP), condensed milk, ice cream, curd/yogurt, butter oil (ghee).
  • Dairy economics: Milk procurement by cooperatives (Amul model — Anand pattern: village society → district union → state federation → GCMMF), Operation Flood (White Revolution — Dr. Verghese Kurien), dairy plant economics, clean milk production incentives.

Poultry Production

  • Layers vs broilers: Layers = egg production (white leghorn, improved indigenous: Vanaraja, Gramapriya, Kalinga Brown); Broilers = meat (Cornish cross, Cobb, Ross).
  • Brooding (0-8 weeks): Temperature (95°F first week, reduce 5°F/week), ventilation, litter (wood shavings, rice husk), space (0.5 sq ft/chick), feed (starter crumbs), water.
  • Housing: Deep litter (floor litter system), cage system (battery cages for layers), free range; ventilation, temperature, humidity (50-65%), light.
  • Feeding phases: Starter (0-4 weeks), grower (5-8 weeks for broilers; up to 18 weeks for layers), finisher (broilers), layer mash (calcium for shell).
  • Vaccination: Day 1: Marek's; Day 7: RD/ND (Ranikhet/Newcastle); 2-3 weeks: IBD (Gumboro); 6-8 weeks: IB (Infectious Bronchitis); 8-10 weeks: RD booster; 12-14 weeks: fowl pox; layers: RD & IBD boosters, egg drop syndrome (EDS) at 14-16 weeks.
  • Economics: Feed cost ~65-70% of broiler cost; FCR (feed conversion ratio) ~1.6-1.8 for broilers (lower = better); egg production economics.

Sheep, Goat, Pig & Other Species

  • Sheep breeds: Wool: Merino, Deccani, Magra, Chokla, Jaisalmeri, Nellore; Meat: Muzaffarnagri, Avdehi, Bellary, Hassan, Mandya; Pashmina: Changthangi (Ladakh), Chegu.
  • Goat breeds: Meat: Boer, Beetal, Jamnapari, Barbari, Sirohi, Osmanabadi; Milk: Jamnapari, Beetal, Surti, Zalawadi; Fiber: Pashmina (Changthangi), Angora.
  • Pig breeds: Yorkshire, Landrace, Duroc, Hampshire (exotic); indigenous: Ghungroo, Niang Megha, Agonda Goan, T & W; pork production: fast growth, high FCR (~3:1), high prolificacy (litter size 8-12).
  • Rabbit, equine, camel, yak, mithun: Rabbit (meat/fur: Soviet Chinchilla, New Zealand White); Equine (horse: Marwari, Kathiawari, Marwari; mules/donkeys); Camel (Bikaneri, Jaisalmeri, Kutchi, Kalachiani); Yak (hilly); Mithun (NE India - mithun farming); Rabbit (meat & wool: Angora).

Veterinary Public Health & Epidemiology

  • Zoonoses: Rabies (dogs), brucellosis (abortion, undulant fever), tuberculosis (M. bovis), anthrax (Bacillus anthracis), leptospirosis, salmonellosis, campylobacteriosis, avian influenza (bird flu), COVID-19 (zoonotic origin discussions), Japanese encephalitis (pigs as amplifying host), nipah (bats/pigs).
  • Food-borne diseases: Salmonella, E. coli O157:H7, Listeria, Campylobacter, Staphylococcus aureus (enterotoxin), Clostridium botulinum (botulism) — from meat, milk, eggs.
  • Food safety systems: HACCP (Hazard Analysis Critical Control Points) in slaughterhouses & dairy plants; FSSAI standards; Agmark; BIS standards; milk & milk products order; meat food products order.
  • Abattoir & slaughter: Humane slaughter (stunning: captive bolt, electrical), halal/kosher considerations, dressing, chilling, inspection (ante-mortem & post-mortem), by-products (blood meal, meat meal, bone meal, hooves, horns, hides).
  • Epidemiology: Measures: incidence (new cases/population at risk), prevalence (existing cases), morbidity (illness), mortality (death), case fatality rate (deaths/cases), attack rate; outbreak investigation (descriptive: person, place, time; analytical: case-control, cohort); surveillance: passive (routine reporting) & active (active search); serosurveillance (antibodies in serum).
  • Vaccination programs (India): FMD (quadrivalent vaccine under NADCP), PPR (sheep/goat), HS (hemorrhagic septicemia - cattle/buffalo), BQ (black quarter - cattle), anthrax (cattle/sheep), rabies (dogs), ranikhet/Newcastle (poultry), fowl pox (poultry), IB (poultry).

Livestock Products Technology

  • Meat processing: Slaughter (stunning: captive bolt/electrical), bleeding (exsanguination), dressing (skinning, evisceration), chilling (0-4°C), aging/ripening (beef), cutting, packaging (vacuum, MAP), freezing (-18°C).
  • Egg processing: Collection, cleaning, grading (by weight & quality), candling (candling = examining egg interior by light), storage (cool), packaging.
  • Wool grading: Based on fiber diameter (micron), length, crimp, color, clean yield; breeds: Merino (fine), Deccani (coarse), Pashmina (ultra-fine, cashmere).
  • Leather: Curing (salting/drying), tanning (chrome/vegetable), finishing; from cattle, buffalo, sheep, goat skins/hides.
  • By-products: Blood meal, meat meal, bone meal, hoof/horn meal, gelatin, tallow, soap, pharmaceuticals (heparin, insulin - historical), albumin.
Technique: Mastitis economics
Question: 'Subclinical mastitis causes greater economic loss than clinical mastitis.' Comment.
Answer: Subclinical mastitis (no visible signs, detected by SCC/CMT) causes higher economic loss because: (1) undetected → continues lactation after lactation, (2) permanent udder damage, (3) milk discarded only when clinical, (4) spreads to herd via milkers, (5) reduces fat% & SNF. Clinical mastitis is detected early & treated. Losses: reduced yield (~15-30% in subclinical), discarded milk, treatment, culling, premature drying. Control: hygiene, teat dipping, dry cow therapy, regular SCC monitoring.

Memory Tricks

  • Milk hormones: Prolactin = makes milk; Oxytocin = lets milk out.
  • Ruminant stomach: Rumen (fermentation), Reticulum (hardware trap), Omasum (water absorption), Abomasum (acid digestion) = RROA.
  • Vaccines: FMD + Brucellosis under NADCP; HS/BQ for cattle; PPR for sheep/goat; RD/ND for poultry.
  • Broiler vs layer: Broiler = meat (fast growth, high FCR); Layer = eggs (longer life, layer mash with calcium).
Mains strategy
For AH&VS Paper II, link to schemes: Rashtriya Gokul Mission (indigenous cattle), National Livestock Mission (NLM), NADCP (FMD & Brucellosis), LIDCP (livestock health & disease control), Dairy processing & infrastructure development fund (DIDF). Quote figures: India largest milk producer (~230 MT), bovine population ~190-300 million, per capita milk availability ~450 g/day, livestock ~30% of agri-GDP, ~50% of income for landless households.
opt-anthropology/overview:
Anthropology Optional — Overview & Scope

Anthropology is the holistic study of humankind — biological, cultural, social, linguistic, and archaeological. It is a popular UPSC optional with a compact syllabus, good GS overlap (GS I society/culture, GS II social justice, GS IV ethics), and high scoring potential.

Paper I — Physical & Social Anthropology

  • Meaning, scope & development: Anthropology & its branches — physical, social-cultural, archaeological, linguistic; relation to other disciplines; holistic approach; history of anthropology (19th c. evolutionism, 20th c. functionalism, structuralism, postmodernism).
  • Human evolution: Primate characteristics, primate taxonomy & behavior; primate fossil record (Proconsul, Dryopithecus, Ramapithecus, Australopithecus, Homo habilis, H. erectus, H. sapiens); human variation & race concepts (critique of race); human genetics & adaptation.
  • Social anthropology: Culture & civilization; society & institution; marriage (monogamy, polygamy, polyandry, group marriage), family (nuclear, joint, extended), kinship (descent, residence, alliance, terminologies), religion (animism, animatism, totemism, naturism, magic, science & religion), economy (production, distribution, exchange — reciprocity, redistribution, market), political organization (band, tribe, chiefdom, state, acephalous vs stratified).
  • Fieldwork & methods: Participant observation, interview, case study, genealogy, life history, questionnaire, survey, PRA/RRA; ethics in anthropology; reflexivity.
  • Indian anthropology: Tribe & caste (jati & varna), dominant caste, Sanskritization, Westernization, modernization, globalization; tribal situation in India — problems & constitutional safeguards (5th & 6th Schedules, Article 342), tribal development programs, forest rights (FRA 2006).

Paper II — Archaeology & Applied Anthropology

  • Archaeological anthropology: Methods of excavation & dating (relative: stratigraphy, seriation; absolute: C-14, dendrochronology, thermoluminescence, potassium-argon); Paleolithic, Mesolithic, Neolithic, Chalcolithic, Iron Age cultures in India; megaliths; Harappan civilization; megalithic & post-megalithic cultures.
  • Applied anthropology: Development anthropology; displacement & rehabilitation (dams, mining, parks); tribal development & welfare; tribal-interface problems; forestry & environment; biodiversity & indigenous knowledge; medical anthropology (health, disease, healing systems); anthropology of development; NGOs & participatory development.
  • Tribal India: Tribal situation & problems (alienation, indebtedness, land alienation, displacement, migration, health, education, nutrition); constitutional safeguards (5th Schedule, 6th Schedule, Article 342, Article 275(1), Article 338A); tribal sub-plan, ITDPs/ITDAs, FRA 2006 (forest rights), PESA 1996; Naxalism & its links to tribal deprivation; tribal movements & identity politics.
  • Rural & urban communities: Village studies (M.N. Srinivas, André Beteille, D.N. Majumdar), rural-urban continuum, urban anthropology, slums, migration, informal sector.
  • Economic anthropology: Subsistence economies (hunting-gathering, pastoralism, shifting cultivation), peasantry, market economy, informal economy, globalization & livelihoods.
Technique: Sanskritization answer
Question: 'Sanskritization explains social mobility in India.' Examine.
Answer: M.N. Srinivas's concept — lower castes/tribes emulate upper-caste lifestyle (vegetarianism, Sanskrit names, rituals, endogamy) to claim higher status. Examples: Yadavs, Kurmis, Gonds sanskritic practices. Critique: doesn't alter structural hierarchy; reinforces sanskritic norms; ignores regional variations & dalit assertion (Ambedkarite politics). Use with power analysis (dominance, not just imitation).

Memory Tricks

  • Four fields: Physical, Social-cultural, Archaeological, Linguistic — PSAL.
  • Kin: Descent = lineage (patrilineal/matrilineal); Residence = where couple lives (patrilocal/matrilocal/neolocal); Marriage = who marries whom.
  • 5th vs 6th Schedule: 5th = scheduled areas in most states (tribal advisory councils); 6th = NE autonomous districts (Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram).
Mains strategy
Anthropology answers need concepts + Indian examples + thinkers (M.N. Srinivas, D.N. Majumdar, L.P. Vidyarthi, A.R. Radcliffe-Brown, Bronislaw Malinowski, E.E. Evans-Pritchard, Claude Lévi-Strauss, Lewis Morgan, Edward Tylor, Franz Boas, Margaret Mead, Ruth Benedict). Use maps for tribal areas. Diagram: kinship charts, caste pyramid, evolutionary sequence.
opt-anthropology/paper1:
Anthropology Paper I — Physical & Social-Cultural Anthropology

Human Evolution & Biological Anthropology

  • Primate characteristics: Forward-facing eyes (stereoscopic vision), grasping hands, opposable thumb, enlarged brain relative to body, prolonged infancy, social behavior, reduced snout, nails instead of claws.
  • Primate taxonomy: Prosimii (lemurs, lorises, tarsiers), Anthropoidea (monkeys, apes, humans); New World monkeys (platyrrhines, prehensile tails, flat noses), Old World monkeys & apes (catarrhines, non-prehensile tails, narrow noses), hominoids (apes & humans: gibbon, orangutan, gorilla, chimpanzee, human).
  • Fossil record: Dryopithecus (~12-9 Ma, Europe), Ramapithecus (~14-7 Ma, Siwaliks — once considered early hominid), Australopithecus (~4-2 Ma, Africa; A. africanus, A. afarensis "Lucy"), Homo habilis (~2.4-1.6 Ma, "handy man", Oldowan tools), Homo erectus (~1.8 Ma-0.1 Ma, Java man, Peking man, Acheulean tools, fire), Homo heidelbergensis, Homo neanderthalensis (Neanderthals, Mousterian tools, burial), Homo sapiens (~0.3 Ma-present, modern humans, Upper Paleolithic art, migration out of Africa ~70-50 kya).
  • Human variation: Skin color, blood groups, height, disease susceptibility — clines, adaptation (Bergmann's & Allen's rules), race concept critique (race is not a valid biological category — clinal variation, within-group > between-group variation).
  • Human genetics: Chromosomes (46), DNA structure, genes, alleles, genotype/phenotype, mutation, selection, genetic drift, gene flow, Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.

Social-Cultural Anthropology

  • Culture: Tylor's definition — "that complex whole which includes knowledge, belief, art, morals, law, custom, and any other capabilities and habits acquired by man as a member of society." Learned, shared, transmitted, symbolic, integrated, adaptive.
  • Culture traits, complexes, patterns: Trait = smallest unit; complex = cluster of related traits; pattern = configuration.
  • Marriage: Forms — monogamy (one spouse), polygamy (polygyny: one man multiple wives; polyandry: one woman multiple husbands — fraternal vs non-fraternal), group marriage, levirate & sororate, cross-cousin & parallel-cousin marriage. Functions: regulation of sex, reproduction, socialization, alliance, economic cooperation.
  • Family: Nuclear (parents + children), joint/extended (multiple generations), joint family (India — patrilineal, patrilocal, patriarchal). Functions: reproduction, socialization, economic cooperation, emotional support, status transmission.
  • Kinship: Descent — patrilineal (through father), matrilineal (through mother), bilateral (both), double descent. Residence — patrilocal (with husband's family), matrilocal (with wife's family), neolocal (new household), avunculocal (with husband's mother's brother). Kinship terminology — classificatory vs descriptive; kin groups — lineage, clan, kindred.
  • Religion: Animism (Tylor — spirits in nature), animatism (impersonal force — mana), totemism (clan-totem linkage), naturism (Max Müller — nature worship), magic (frazer: contagious, imitative), science vs religion vs magic (comparison), witchcraft & sorcery.
  • Economic anthropology: Modes of exchange — reciprocity (generalized, balanced, negative), redistribution (chiefdom/state), market exchange. Subsistence modes — hunting-gathering, pastoralism, horticulture, agriculture, industrialism.
  • Political organization: Band (small, egalitarian, kin-based), tribe (segmentary, big-man), chiefdom (ranked, redistribution, permanent leadership), state (stratified, bureaucracy, monopoly of force). Acephalous vs stratified societies.

Research Methods & Ethics

  • Fieldwork: Participant observation (Malinowski — Trobriand Islanders), long-term fieldwork, learning language, rapport building.
  • Methods: Interview (structured/unstructured), case study, genealogy, life history, questionnaire, survey, PRA (Participatory Rural Appraisal), RRA, photography, audio-video recording.
  • Ethics: Informed consent, confidentiality, anonymity, avoiding harm, reciprocity, reflexivity (researcher's positionality), decolonizing anthropology.
  • Key thinkers: E.B. Tylor (animism, culture definition), Lewis Morgan (kinship, evolution: savagery-barbarism-civilization), Émile Durkheim (totemism, collective consciousness), A.R. Radcliffe-Brown (structural-functionalism), Bronislaw Malinowski (functionalism, participant observation, needs theory), Claude Lévi-Strauss (structuralism, binary oppositions, myth), Lewis Henry Morgan (kinship systems, evolution), Franz Boas (cultural relativism, historical particularism), Margaret Mead (sex & temperament, Samoa), Ruth Benedict (patterns of culture), E.E. Evans-Pritchard (witchcraft, segmentary lineage), M.N. Srinivas (Sanskritization, dominant caste, dominant caste, fieldwork in India), D.N. Majumdar (tribal studies in India), L.P. Vidyarthi (sacred complex, nature-man-spirit complex), A.C. Mayer (village India), F.G. Bailey (stratagem, politics).
Technique: Structural-functionalism
Question: 'Explain Radcliffe-Brown's structural-functionalism.'
Answer: Society as an integrated system where parts (institutions — kinship, religion, economy, polity) function to maintain social equilibrium & social solidarity. Focus on observable social structure & functions (not individual psychology — Malinowski). Critique: conservative, ignores conflict/change, treats society as static. Applied: kinship & descent regulate marriage; religion reinforces social solidarity (Durkheim's influence).

Common Traps

  • Confusing race (biological, discredited) with ethnicity (cultural).
  • Treating all tribal societies as identical — enormous regional variation.
  • Missing that anthropology studies present-day societies too (not just "primitive" past).
  • Confusing matriarchy (rare/nonexistent) with matriliny/matrilocality (exist).
  • Assuming evolutionism = progress — modern anthropology rejects unilineal evolution.

Memory Tricks

  • Four fields: Physical, Social, Archaeological, Linguistic — PSAL.
  • Kinship: Descent = lineage; Residence = where couple lives; Marriage = partner rules.
  • Evolution sequence: Dryopithecus → Ramapithecus → Australopithecus → Homo habilis → H. erectus → H. sapiens.
Mains strategy
Anthropology answers need concept + thinker + Indian example + diagram (kinship chart, human evolution timeline, caste pyramid, tribal map). Quote names: Srinivas (dominant caste, Sanskritization), Vidyarthi (sacred complex), Evans-Pritchard (segmentary lineage), Malinowski (participant observation), Lévi-Strauss (structuralism).
opt-anthropology/paper2:
Anthropology Paper II — Archaeology & Applied Anthropology

Archaeological Anthropology

  • Methods: Survey (surface survey, aerial photography, remote sensing, GIS), excavation (stratigraphic excavation — Wheeler box grid, Wheeler-Kenyon method), dating methods.
  • Dating methods: Relative — stratigraphy (law of superposition), seriation, typology, fluorine dating. Absolute — radiocarbon (C-14, up to ~50,000 years), dendrochronology (tree rings), thermoluminescence (TL), potassium-argon (K-Ar, older sites), uranium-series, obsidian hydration.
  • Paleolithic (~2.5 Ma - 10,000 BP): Lower (Oldowan — Homo habilis; Acheulean — H. erectus hand axes), Middle (Mousterian — Neanderthals), Upper (blade tools, Homo sapiens, cave art — Lascaux, Chauvet, Bhimbetka in India).
  • Mesolithic (~10,000 - 8,000 BP): Microliths, bow-arrow, fishing, semi-sedentary, Mesolithic rock art (Bhimbetka, Bhimbetka shelters).
  • Neolithic (~8,000 - 4,000 BP): Agriculture & animal domestication (wheat, barley, rice, millets; sheep, goat, cattle, pig), pottery, polished stone axes, permanent villages (Jericho, Çatalhöyük, Mehrgarh in Pakistan), megaliths.
  • Chalcolithic (Copper-Stone, ~4,000-3,000 BP): Copper tools alongside stone, pottery, early urbanism (Mehrgarh phases, pre-Harappan).
  • Iron Age (~1,200 BP onwards): Iron technology, black-and-red ware, painted grey ware, megalithic burials (dolmens, cairns, menhirs, urn burials) in South India.
  • Harappan civilization (~2,600-1,900 BCE): Mature Harappan — Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Lothal, Dholavira, Kalibangan, Rakhigarhi; urban planning (grid, drainage, great bath, granary, citadel & lower town), seals, script (undeciphered), trade (Mesopotamia), weights & measures, decline theories (climate change, river shift, invasion/migration theories debated).
  • Megalithic & post-megalithic South India: Dolmens, cairn circles, menhirs, urn burials, rock-cut caves, black-and-red ware, early Tamil sangam associations.

Applied Anthropology

  • Definition: Application of anthropological knowledge & methods to practical problems — development, health, education, environment, business, forensics.
  • Development anthropology: Critique of top-down development; participatory approaches; cultural appropriateness; displacement & resettlement (dams, mines, national parks — oustees & rehabilitation).
  • Tribal development in India: Constitutional safeguards — Fifth Schedule (scheduled areas, TAC), Sixth Schedule (autonomous districts NE), Article 342 (scheduled tribes list), Article 275(1) (grants), Article 338A (NCST); Tribal Sub-Plan (TSP), Integrated Tribal Development Projects (ITDP/Agencies), Forest Rights Act 2006 (individual & community forest rights, habitat rights for PVTGs), PESA 1996 (gram sabha powers in scheduled areas), National Policy on Tribals, Vanbandhu Kalyan Yojana.
  • Tribal problems: Land alienation, indebtedness, displacement (dams, mines, parks), migration, health (malnutrition, sickle cell, malaria, TB), education (dropout, language), nutrition, livelihood loss, Naxalism/Maoist insurgency links to deprivation & alienation.
  • Medical anthropology: Health & disease as cultural constructs; ethnomedicine (traditional healers — ojha, baiga, vaidy), pluralistic health systems (biomedicine + traditional), nutrition, reproductive health, mental health, disability, pandemics & stigma, COVID-19 & indigenous communities.
  • Environmental anthropology: Indigenous ecological knowledge (IEK/TEK), sacred groves, community forestry, biodiversity conservation & displacement (protected areas & tribal rights), climate change & vulnerable communities.
  • Business/corporate anthropology: Organizational culture, consumer behavior, user-centered design.
  • Forensic anthropology: Identification from skeletal remains (age, sex, ancestry, stature, trauma), mass disaster identification.

Tribal India: Issues & Movements

  • Constitutional safeguards: Fifth Schedule (scheduled areas in 10 states — TAC, governor's role), Sixth Schedule (autonomous districts in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram — district councils), Article 342 (ST list), Article 275(1) (special grants), Article 338A (National Commission for STs), Article 164(1) (tribal ministers in MP, Bihar, Odisha, etc.), Article 350 (instruction in mother tongue).
  • PESA 1996: Gram sabha powers in scheduled areas — land, minor forest produce, local plans, institutions, money lending, intoxicants.
  • FRA 2006: Individual forest rights (cultivation & habitation), community forest rights (community use), habitat rights for PVTGs, right to protect & manage forests, gram sabha as decision authority.
  • Tribal movements: Santhal (1855-56), Munda (Birsa Munda, 1899-1900), Bhil, Koli, Naga, Mizoram, Jharkhand movement (Jharkhand Mukti Morcha), Bodoland, contemporary identity & autonomy movements; Naxalism/Maoism — roots in tribal deprivation, land alienation, lack of development, state response (security + development).
Technique: FRA 2006 answer
Question: 'FRA 2006 empowers forest-dwelling communities but implementation remains weak.' Discuss.
Answer: FRA recognizes individual & community forest rights, habitat rights for PVTGs, gram sabha as authority. Achievements: millions of claims filed, lakhs of titles issued (esp. Odisha, MP, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra). Weaknesses: forest department resistance, lack of awareness, diluted guidelines (2012), conservation vs rights tension (tiger core zones), delayed recognition, implementation gaps. Way forward: gram sabha empowerment, time-bound disposal, convergence with MGNREGA/NRLM, monitoring cells.

Memory Tricks

  • Archaeology sequence: Paleolithic (old stone) → Mesolithic (microliths) → Neolithic (agriculture, polished stone) → Chalcolithic (copper) → Iron Age.
  • Safeguards: 5th = scheduled areas (most states); 6th = autonomous districts (NE).
  • FRA 2006: Individual rights + community rights + habitat rights (PVTGs) + gram sabha decides.
Mains strategy
Paper II answers: concept → Indian tribal context → constitutional provision → scheme → problem → way forward. Draw maps (tribal concentration areas, fifth/sixth schedule areas), flow charts (displacement → rehabilitation). Quote census data (STs ~8.6% of population, concentrated in MP, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Jharkhand, Rajasthan, Gujarat, Maharashtra, NE states). Reference NFHS & NSSO data on tribal health, education, livelihoods.
opt-botany/overview:
Botany Optional — Overview & Syllabus Map

Botany is a popular optional for life-science graduates with a compact, factual syllabus and good overlap with GS III (environment, agriculture, biotechnology). Paper I covers microbiology, plant pathology, cryptogams, phanerogams, anatomy, embryology, palynology; Paper II covers plant physiology, biochemistry, genetics, plant breeding, biotechnology, ecology.

Paper I — Plant Diversity & Structure

  • Microbiology: Bacteria (structure, nutrition, reproduction, economic importance), viruses (structure, transmission, diseases), mycoplasma, lichens (structure, reproduction, ecological role), fungi (classification, reproduction, economic importance — edible, poisonous, medicinal, industrial), mycorrhiza.
  • Plant pathology: Symptoms, etiology, transmission, control of major plant diseases — rust, smut, blight, wilt, leaf spot, mosaic; integrated disease management.
  • Cryptogams: Algae (classification, thallus structure, reproduction, economic importance — food, fodder, biofuel, agar, carrageenan), fungi (as above), bryophytes (mosses, liverworts, hornworts — life cycle, alternation of generations, economic importance), pteridophytes (psilopsida, lycopsida, sphenopsida, pteropsida — life cycle, heterospory, seed habit origin).
  • Phanerogams: Gymnosperms (classification, Cycas, Pinus, Ephedra — morphology, reproduction, economic importance), Angiosperms (classification — Bentham & Hooker, Hutchinson, APG; flower structure, pollination, fertilization, double fertilization, endosperm, fruit types, seed structure & dormancy).
  • Anatomy: Tissues (meristematic, permanent — simple & complex), tissue systems (epidermal, ground, vascular), primary & secondary structure of dicot & monocot stem & root, leaf anatomy (C3/C4/Kranz), secondary growth, anomalous secondary growth (Bignonia, Dracaena, Boerhaavia), anomalous secondary growth.
  • Embryology: Microsporogenesis & megasporogenesis, fertilization, endosperm types, embryo development (dicot & monocot), polyembryony, apomixis, parthenocarpy.
  • Palynology: Pollen morphology, aperture types, exine ornamentation, pollen viability, pollen allergy, mellissopalynology, forensic palynology.

Paper II — Plant Physiology, Genetics & Ecology

  • Plant physiology: Water relations (osmosis, diffusion, imbibition, water potential), transpiration (mechanism, factors, antitranspirants), photosynthesis (C3, C4, CAM pathways, light & dark reactions, factors), respiration (glycolysis, Krebs cycle, ETS, fermentation), mineral nutrition (essential elements, functions, deficiency symptoms), nitrogen metabolism (nitrogen fixation, nitrification, denitrification), growth & development (phytohormones — auxin, gibberellin, cytokinin, ethylene, ABA, abscisic acid, flowering — photoperiodism, vernalization, florigen concept), senescence & abscission.
  • Biochemistry: Carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids — structure & function; enzymes (classification, mechanism, factors affecting enzyme activity), secondary metabolites (alkaloids, terpenoids, flavonoids, phenolics — functions & uses).
  • Genetics: Mendelian genetics, linkage & crossing over, gene interaction (epistasis, complementary, supplementary, duplicate genes), multiple alleles, polygenic inheritance, cytoplasmic inheritance, mutation (spontaneous & induced, mutagens), chromosomal aberrations (deletion, duplication, inversion, translocation), aneuploidy & euploidy (monosomy, trisomy, polyploidy — auto & allo), DNA structure & replication, transcription, translation, genetic code, gene regulation (lac operon).
  • Plant breeding: Objectives, centers of origin (Vavilov), germplasm collection & conservation, selection (mass, pure line, clonal, progeny), hybridization (emasculation, bagging, tagging, backcrossing), mutation breeding, polyploidy breeding, mutation breeding, tissue culture & micropropagation, somaclonal variation, protoplast fusion, transgenic plants (Bt cotton, Bt brinjal, golden rice), GMO regulations in India (GEAC).
  • Ecology: Ecosystem (structure, function, energy flow, food chains & webs, ecological pyramids), biogeochemical cycles (C, N, P, S), population ecology (growth forms, carrying capacity, r & K strategies), community ecology (succession — hydrosere, xerosere, climax), biomes of India, biodiversity (levels, hotspots — Western Ghats, Eastern Himalayas, Indo-Burma, Sundaland), biodiversity conservation (in-situ & ex-situ — national parks, sanctuaries, biosphere reserves, seed banks, gene banks, cryopreservation), IUCN categories, EIA.
  • Plant biotechnology: Tissue culture (micropropagation, organogenesis, embryogenesis, somaclonal variation), protoplast isolation & fusion (somatic hybridization), transgenic plants (methods — Agrobacterium, gene gun), marker-assisted selection (MAS), DNA fingerprinting (RAPD, RFLP, AFLP, SSR, ISSR, DNA barcoding), bioinformatics basics.
Technique: C4 photosynthesis answer
Question: 'Explain the C4 pathway and its advantages over C3.'
Answer: C4 pathway — CO2 initially fixed by PEP carboxylase in mesophyll cells into oxaloacetate (4C), converted to malate/aspartate, transported to bundle sheath cells, decarboxylated, CO2 refixed by RuBisCO in Calvin cycle. Advantages: no photorespiration, high temperature & light tolerance, high water & nitrogen use efficiency (maize, sugarcane, sorghum, amaranthus).

Memory Tricks

  • Alternation of generations: Gametophyte (n, produces gametes) alternates with sporophyte (2n, produces spores) — dominance shifts: bryophytes (gametophyte dominant) → pteridophytes → gymnosperms & angiosperms (sporophyte dominant).
  • C3 vs C4: C3 = Calvin cycle only, photorespiration losses (rice, wheat); C4 = PEP carboxylase first, Kranz anatomy (maize, sugarcane).
  • Double fertilization: One male gamete + egg → zygote (2n); second male gamete + two polar nuclei → endosperm (3n).
Mains strategy
Botany answers need labeled diagrams (flower LS, ovule, anther, root/stem/root anatomy, C4/Kranz anatomy, DNA structure, N-cycle). Quote schemes: National Horticulture Mission, NFSM, Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana (organic farming), Biotechnology policies, GEAC. Data: India's horticulture production (~330 MT), forest cover (~21.7% ISFR 2021), biodiversity hotspots in India (4).
opt-botany/paper1:
Botany Paper I — Plant Diversity, Anatomy & Embryology

Microbiology

  • Bacteria: Structure (cell wall — peptidoglycan, capsule, pili, flagella, plasmid), nutrition (autotrophs/heterotrophs, photo/chemo), reproduction (binary fission, conjugation, transformation, transduction), economic importance (industrial — curd, cheese, antibiotics; agriculture — nitrogen fixation, decomposition; pathogens — tuberculosis, cholera, typhoid, cholera, tetanus).
  • Viruses: Structure (nucleic acid core, protein capsid, envelope in some), characteristics (obligate intracellular parasites, crystallizable), transmission, diseases (TMV, influenza, HIV, COVID-19, rabies, polio), bacteriophages (lytic & lysogenic cycles).
  • Mycoplasma: Smallest free-living organisms, no cell wall, pleomorphic, cause plant diseases (little leaf, witches' broom) & animal diseases.
  • Lichens: Symbiosis of fungus (mycobiont) & alga/cyanobacterium (photobiont), reproduction (soredia, isidia, apothecia), economic importance (pollution indicators, dye, litmus, perfume, medicinal — Usnea), ecological role (pioneer species in primary succession).
  • Fungi: Classification (based on thallus, reproduction, spore formation) — Phycomycetes (algal fungi, e.g., Rhizopus, Mucor), Ascomycetes (sac fungi, e.g., Aspergillus, Penicillium, Claviceps, morels, truffles), Basidiomycetes (club fungi, e.g., Agaricus, Ustilago, Puccinia), Deuteromycetes (fungi imperfecti — no sexual stage known, e.g., Alternaria, Colletotrichum). Economic importance — edible (Agaricus), medicinal (Penicillin from Penicillium), industrial (citric acid, enzymes), pathogens (wheat rust — Puccinia, late blight of potato — Phytophthora infestans, apple scab — Venturia), mycorrhiza (symbiotic association of fungi with roots — ectomycorrhiza & endomycorrhiza/VAM, benefits: nutrient uptake, drought resistance).

Plant Pathology

  • Symptoms: Necrosis, chlorosis, wilting, dwarfing, malformation, galls, cankers, rust, smut, blight, mildew, mosaic, leaf curl, damping off.
  • Disease cycle: Inoculum, penetration, infection, colonization, symptom production, dissemination, survival.
  • Major diseases: Rust of wheat (Puccinia graminis), smut of wheat (Ustilago), late blight of potato (Phytophthora infestans — Irish famine), early blight of potato (Alternaria), blast of rice (Magnaporthe oryzae), bacterial blight of rice (Xanthomonas oryzae), wilt of cotton/pigeonpea (Fusarium), root-knot (Meloidogyne nematode), mosaic viruses (tobacco mosaic virus — TMV, first virus discovered), little leaf of brinjal (mycoplasma).
  • Disease management: Cultural (crop rotation, sanitation, resistant varieties), biological (biocontrol agents — Trichoderma, Pseudomonas fluorescens), chemical (fungicides — protectants vs systemic, Bordeaux mixture, copper oxychloride, carbendazim, mancozeb), integrated disease management (IDM).

Cryptogams

  • Algae: Classification (based on pigments, flagella, reserve food) — Chlorophyceae (green — Chlamydomonas, Volvox, Spirogyra, Ulothrix, Chara), Phaeophyceae (brown — Ectocarpus, Laminaria, Fucus, Sargassum), Rhodophyceae (red — Polysiphonia, Gracilaria, Porphyra, Corallina), Xanthophyceae (yellow-green — Vaucheria), Bacillariophyceae (diatoms — Navicula, Nitzschia), Euglenophyceae (Euglena). Economic importance — food (Porphyra, Laminaria), fodder, biofuel, agar-agar (Gelidium, Gracilaria), carrageenan (Chondrus), alginates (Macrocystis, Laminaria), diatomite (diatom skeletons), sewage treatment, bioindicators.
  • Fungi: As above — economic importance & plant pathogens.
  • Bryophytes: Mosses (Funaria, Polytrichum, Sphagnum — peat moss), liverworts (Marchantia, Riccia, Anthoceros), hornworts. Life cycle — gametophyte dominant (haploid), sporophyte dependent. Economic importance — Sphagnum as peat & packing material, pollution indicators, soil formation (pioneers), Reaumuria. Economic importance of bryophytes: Sphagnum peat as fuel & horticulture, soil binding, indicators of pollution.
  • Pteridophytes: Classes — Psilopsida (Psilotum), Lycopsida (Selaginella, Lycopodium), Sphenopsida (Equisetum), Pteropsida (ferns — Pteris, Dryopteris, Adiantum, Marsilea). Life cycle — sporophyte dominant, heterospory (Selaginella, Salvinia, Marsilea) & origin of seed habit, alternation of generations, economic importance (Equisetum — scouring, Selaginella — resurrection plant, fossil fuels from ancient pteridophytes).

Phanerogams

  • Gymnosperms: Classification — Cycadopsida (Cycas), Coniferopsida (Pinus, Cedrus, Abies, Pinus, Ginkgo), Gnetopsida (Ephedra, Welwitschia, Gnetum). Structure & reproduction of Cycas, Pinus, Ephedra. Economic importance — timber (Pinus, Deodar, Cedar), resin & turpentine, paper, ornamental (Cycas), Ephedra (ephedrine — medicinal), Ginkgo (living fossil, medicine).
  • Angiosperms: Classification systems — Bentham & Hooker (natural system, 3 cohorts: Dicotyledones — Polypetalae, Gamopetalae, Monochlamydeae; Monocotyledones), Hutchinson (phylogenetic), APG (Angiosperm Phylogeny Group — modern, APG IV). Flower — structure (calyx, corolla, androecium, gynoecium), aestivation, placentation (marginal, axile, parietal, free central, basal, superficial), pollination (agents: wind, water, insects, birds, bats), fertilization — double fertilization, endosperm (nuclear, cellular, helobial types), fruit types (simple — drupe, berry, pome, hesperidium, caryopsis, achene, samara, nut; aggregate — etaerio of berries, drupes, follicles; multiple — sorosis of pineapple, mulberry, syconus of fig), seed structure (dicot — castor, mustard; monocot — maize, wheat, orchid), seed dormancy & germination (epigeal, hypogeal), viability.
  • Anatomy: Tissues — meristematic (apical, lateral, intercalary), permanent (simple — parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma — fibres & sclereids; complex — xylem: tracheids, vessels, xylem fibres, xylem parenchyma; phloem: sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem fibres, phloem parenchyma). Tissue systems — epidermal (epidermis, stomata, trichomes, cuticle), ground (cortex, pericycle, pith, medullary rays), vascular (conjoint — collateral, bicollateral, concentric; open vs closed). Anatomy of dicot & monocot stem & root (differences), dorsiventral & isobilateral leaf anatomy, C4 leaf anatomy (Kranz anatomy — bundle sheath cells with large chloroplasts, centripetal arrangement), secondary growth (cambium activity, annual rings, heartwood & sapwood, heartwood formation), anomalous secondary growth (Bignonia stem — phloem wedges, Dracaena stem — anomalous cambium, Boerhaavia/Dioscorea — anomalous root), anomalous structures (Bougainvillea stem — phloem wedges).
Technique: C4 Kranz anatomy
Question: Draw & label Kranz anatomy & state its function.
Answer: Kranz anatomy = cluster of bundle sheath cells surrounding vascular bundles, with large chloroplasts, centripetal arrangement, thick walls, no intercellular spaces; mesophyll cells between bundle sheaths. Function: concentrates CO2 around RuBisCO via PEP carboxylase in mesophyll → decarboxylation in bundle sheath → minimizes photorespiration in C4 plants (maize, sugarcane, sugarcane, sorghum, amaranthus).

Embryology

  • Microsporogenesis: Microsporocyte → meiosis → microspore tetrad → microspore → pollen grain (vegetative cell + generative cell → 2 male gametes). Pollen wall — exine (sporopollenin) & intine; apertures (apertures — colpate, porate, colporate); pollen viability & storage.
  • Megasporogenesis: Megaspore mother cell → meiosis → linear tetrad → functional megaspore (chalazal) → embryo sac development (Polygonum type — 7-celled, 8-nucleate: egg apparatus — egg cell + 2 synergids with filiform apparatus, central cell with 2 polar nuclei, 3 antipodals).
  • Fertilization: Pollen germination on stigma, pollen tube growth (chemotropic), entry into ovule (porogamy/chalazogamy/mesogamy), double fertilization (syngamy → zygote 2n; triple fusion → primary endosperm nucleus 3n), post-fertilization changes (ovule → seed, ovary → fruit, petals/stamens/sepal wither).
  • Endosperm: Types — nuclear (coconut liquid endosperm), cellular (Petunia), helobial (between); function — nourishment of embryo.
  • Embryo development: Dicot (Capsella type) — zygote → proembryo → globular → heart → torpedo → mature dicotyledonous embryo (2 cotyledons, plumule, radicle, hypocotyl); monocot (grass embryo — scutellum, coleoptile, plumule, radicle, coleorhiza). Polyembryony (Citrus — cleavage polyembryony, adventitious embryony), apomixis (agamospermy — adventitious embryony, diplospory, apospory, parthenogenesis), parthenocarpy (seedless fruit — banana, grapes, seedless watermelon — natural & induced by auxins/gibberellins).
Technique: Apomixis answer
Question: 'What is apomixis? Give its significance.'
Answer: Apomixis = seed formation without fertilization (diplospory, apospory, adventitious embryony). Significance: maintains hybrid vigour, rapid multiplication of elite genotypes, disease-free seed production (citrus, mango, Citrus), used in hybrid seed production (apomictic hybrids don't segregate), reduction in hybrid seed cost.

Palynology

  • Pollen morphology: Size, shape, symmetry (radial, bilateral), apertures (colpi — colporate, colpate, inaperturate/porate, sulcate), exine ornamentation (reticulate, foveolate, striate, psilate, echinate), pollen units (monad, dyad, tetrad, pollinia in orchids & Asclepiads), pollen viability, pollen banks.
  • Applications: Melissopalynology (pollen in honey — floral source), forensic palynology (crime scene linkage), palaeopalynology (vegetation & climate reconstruction), allergy & aerobiology (pollen allergy — Parthenium, Prosopis, grass pollen), honey quality & authentication.
Mains strategy
Draw diagrams: flower LS, ovule LS, pollen grain, embryo sac, anther TS, root/stem/root anatomy (dicot vs monocot), Kranz anatomy, DNA structure, N-cycle. Quote schemes: National Horticulture Mission, NFSM, PKVY (organic farming), biotechnology policies, GEAC. Data: India's horticulture production (~330 MT), forest cover (~21.7% ISFR 2021), biodiversity hotspots in India (4: Western Ghats, Eastern Himalayas, Indo-Burma, Sundaland).
opt-botany/paper2:
Botany Paper II — Plant Physiology, Biochemistry, Genetics & Ecology

Plant Physiology

  • Water relations: Water potential (Ψw = Ψs + Ψp), osmosis, diffusion, imbibition, plasmolysis & deplasmolysis, aquaporins, water absorption (active & passive), transpiration (mechanism — cohesion-tension theory, stomatal opening/closing — K+ pump theory, anti-transpirants), guttation.
  • Photosynthesis: Light reaction (PSI & PSII, non-cyclic & cyclic photophosphorylation, Z-scheme), dark reaction (C3 cycle — Calvin cycle: carboxylation by RuBisCO, reduction, regeneration), photorespiration (C2 cycle — wasteful), C4 pathway (Kranz anatomy, PEP carboxylase, mesophyll & bundle sheath cells), CAM plants (stomata open at night, succulents), factors affecting photosynthesis (light, CO2, temperature, water, mineral nutrition), limiting factors (law of limiting factors — Blackman).
  • Respiration: Glycolysis (cytoplasm, glucose → 2 pyruvate + 2 ATP + 2 NADH), Krebs cycle (mitochondrial matrix, pyruvate → CO2 + NADH + FADH2 + ATP/GTP), oxidative phosphorylation (ETC — oxidative phosphorylation, chemiosmosis, ATP synthase), fermentation (alcoholic & lactic acid), RQ (respiratory quotient — carb 1.0, fat & protein < 1), pentose phosphate pathway.
  • Mineral nutrition: Essential elements (17 essential: C, H, O, N, P, K, Ca, Mg, S — macronutrients; Fe, Mn, Cu, Zn, Mo, B, Cl, Ni, Mo — micronutrients), functions & deficiency symptoms (chlorosis, necrosis), hydroponics, critical concentration, nitrogen cycle & biological nitrogen fixation (Rhizobium — symbiotic in legume root nodules, Azotobacter — free living, Azolla — cyanobacteria), nitrification (Nitrosomonas, Nitrobacter), denitrification.
  • Plant growth & development: Phytohormones — auxin (IAA — cell elongation, apical dominance, tropisms), gibberellin (stem elongation, seed germination, bolting), cytokinin (cell division, delay senescence), ethylene (fruit ripening, abscission, triple response), abscisic acid (ABA — stress hormone, stomatal closure, seed dormancy), florigen (flowering signal), photoperiodism (short-day, long-day, day-neutral plants, critical day length), vernalization (cold treatment induces flowering — wheat, vernalization genes), plant movements (tropic — phototropism, geotropism, hydrotropism, thigmotropism; nastic — nyctinasty, seismonasty), senescence & abscission (role of ABA & ethylene).

Biochemistry

  • Carbohydrates: Monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, galactose), disaccharides (sucrose, maltose, lactose), polysaccharides (starch — amylose & amylopectin, glycogen, cellulose, chitin), functions (energy, structure).
  • Proteins: Amino acids (20, essential & non-essential), peptide bond, levels of structure (primary, secondary — α-helix & β-pleated sheet, tertiary, quaternary), denaturation, functions (enzymes, transport, structural, contractile, storage, hormonal, protective).
  • Lipids: Fatty acids (saturated & unsaturated), triglycerides, phospholipids (lecithin, cephalin), glycolipids, sterols (cholesterol, phytosterols), functions (energy storage, membrane structure, insulation, hormones).
  • Nucleic acids: DNA (double helix, Watson-Crick model, base pairing A=T, G≡C, semiconservative replication — Meselson-Stahl experiment), RNA (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA), genetic code (triplet, degenerate, unambiguous, universal, non-overlapping), transcription, translation.
  • Enzymes: Classification (6 major classes — oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases, ligases), mechanism (lock & key, induced fit), factors affecting enzyme activity (temperature, pH, substrate concentration, enzyme concentration, inhibitors — competitive & non-competitive, activators), cofactors & coenzymes, allosteric regulation, feedback inhibition.
  • Secondary metabolites: Alkaloids (morphine, quinine, nicotine, caffeine — defense & medicinal), terpenoids (rubber, camphor, carotenoids — vision, pigment), flavonoids & phenolics (anthocyanins — color, tannins — astringency, UV protection), functions (defense against herbivores & pathogens, UV protection, signaling).

Genetics

  • Mendelian genetics: Monohybrid cross (3:1 F2), dihybrid cross (9:3:3:1 F2), law of segregation, law of independent assortment (exceptions — linkage). Test cross & back cross.
  • Linkage & crossing over: Linked genes (same chromosome), coupling & repulsion, crossing over during prophase I (chiasma formation), recombination frequency & genetic mapping (map units / morgan), Sturtevant's mapping.
  • Gene interaction: Epistasis (dominant — 12:3:1, recessive — 9:3:4, duplicate — 15:1, complementary — 9:7, supplementary — 9:3:4), polygenic inheritance (quantitative traits — skin color, height, yield — normal distribution, multiple genes + environment).
  • Multiple alleles: ABO blood groups (IA, IB, i), Rh factor.
  • Cytoplasmic inheritance: Mitochondrial & chloroplast DNA (maternal inheritance), rho (ρ) in Chlamydomonas, poky in Neurospora.
  • Mutation: Spontaneous & induced (mutagens — physical: X-rays, UV, gamma rays; chemical: EMS, mustard gas; chromosomal aberrations — deletion, duplication, inversion, translocation; aneuploidy — monosomy (2n-1), trisomy (2n+1, Down syndrome in humans), euploidy — haploidy, diploidy, polyploidy (autopolyploidy — colchicine induced, allopolyploidy — Triticale, Raphanobrassica).
  • Molecular genetics: DNA structure (Watson-Crick double helix, antiparallel, semiconservative replication — Meselson-Stahl), transcription (RNA polymerase, promoter, terminator), translation (ribosome, mRNA, tRNA, anticodon, initiation/elongation/termination), genetic code (triplet code, 64 codons, 3 stop codons, 1 start codon AUG, degenerate, unambiguous, universal, non-overlapping, commaless), gene regulation — lac operon (Jacob & Monod — structural genes lacZ, lacY, lacA, operator, promoter, repressor, inducer lactose), trp operon (repressible).
Technique: Lac operon answer
Question: 'Explain lac operon regulation in E. coli.'
Answer: lac operon = structural genes lacZ (β-galactosidase), lacY (permease), lacA (transacetylase), controlled by promoter (RNA polymerase binding), operator (repressor binding), regulator gene lacI (repressor protein). Without lactose: repressor binds operator → blocks transcription. With lactose (allolactose): inducer binds repressor → repressor released → transcription occurs. CAP-cAMP complex enhances transcription when glucose low (positive regulation).

Plant Breeding

  • Objectives: Higher yield, disease/pest resistance, drought/frost tolerance, quality (protein, oil, vitamin content), shorter duration, synchronous maturity, non-shattering, responsive to fertilizers.
  • Germplasm: Collection, evaluation, conservation (in-situ — national parks, sanctuaries, biosphere reserves; ex-situ — seed banks, gene banks, field gene banks, cryopreservation, DNA banks), centers of origin (Vavilov's centers — 8 centers: Chinese, Indian, Central Asiatic, Near Eastern, Mediterranean, Abyssinian, South American Mexican & Chilean, South American Brazilian-Paraguayan). India is secondary center for rice, mango, citrus, banana, pigeonpea, black pepper, ginger, turmeric, cardamom.
  • Breeding methods: Self-pollinated crops — mass selection, pure line selection (Johannsen), pedigree method, bulk method, backcross method (transfer of single gene), pedigree vs bulk. Cross-pollinated crops — mass selection, recurrent selection, synthetic varieties, composite varieties, hybrid varieties (inbred lines, combining ability — GCA & SCA, heterosis, CMS — cytoplasmic male sterility for hybrid seed production), mutation breeding (mutagens — physical: X-rays, gamma rays, UV; chemical: EMS, mustard gas, colchicine for polyploidy), somaclonal variation, tissue culture (micropropagation, organogenesis, embryogenesis, protoplast culture & fusion — somatic hybridization), genetic engineering (Agrobacterium tumefaciens as vector, gene gun, Bt cotton, Bt brinjal, golden rice — vitamin A enriched), marker-assisted selection (MAS), DNA fingerprinting (RAPD, RFLP, AFLP, SSR/ISSR, DNA barcoding).
  • Seed technology: Seed quality (genetic, physical, physiological, health), seed certification (breeder, foundation, certified seed), seed treatment, storage.

Ecology

  • Ecosystem: Structure (abiotic — climate, soil, water, light, temperature; biotic — producers, consumers, decomposers), function (productivity — primary & secondary, decomposition, energy flow — food chain & food web, ecological pyramids — number, biomass, energy — upright in most, inverted pyramid of biomass in aquatic), nutrient cycling (gaseous — C, N, O; sedimentary — P, S), residence time.
  • Biogeochemical cycles: Carbon cycle (photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, combustion, fossil fuels, oceanic exchange), Nitrogen cycle (nitrogen fixation — biological & industrial, nitrification — Nitrosomonas & Nitrobacter, denitrification — Pseudomonas, ammonification, assimilation), Phosphorus cycle (sedimentary, rock weathering), Sulphur cycle.
  • Population ecology: Population attributes (density, natality, mortality, age distribution, sex ratio, dispersal), population growth (J-shaped — exponential, S-shaped — logistic with carrying capacity K), r & K strategies (r — opportunistic, short-lived, high fecundity; K — competitive, long-lived, low fecundity, parental care), life tables & survivorship curves.
  • Community ecology: Community structure (stratification, dominance, keystone species, ecotone & edge effect), ecological succession (hydrosere — hydrarch, xerosere — xerarch, stages: pioneer → seral stages → climax, facilitation, tolerance & inhibition models), biomes (tundra, taiga/coniferous forest, temperate deciduous forest, tropical rainforest, savanna, desert, freshwater, marine).
  • Biodiversity: Levels — genetic, species, ecosystem; measurement (alpha, beta, gamma); hotspots (criteria — endemism & threat, 36 global, India has 4: Western Ghats, Eastern Himalayas, Indo-Burma, Sundaland), threats (habitat loss & fragmentation, overexploitation, alien invasive species — Lantana, Parthenium, Eichhornia, pollution, climate change), conservation — in-situ (national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biosphere reserves, sacred groves) & ex-situ (botanical gardens, seed banks, gene banks, cryopreservation, tissue culture), IUCN Red List categories (Extinct, Extinct in Wild, Critically Endangered, Endangered, Vulnerable, Near Threatened, Least Concern), India's biodiversity hotspots, Project Tiger, Project Elephant, CITES, CBD (Convention on Biological Diversity), Nagoya Protocol (access & benefit sharing), Ramsar Convention (wetlands), UNESCO MAB (Man & Biosphere Programme — biosphere reserves), National Biodiversity Authority (NBA), Biological Diversity Act 2002.
  • Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA): Process — screening, scoping, impact identification, prediction, mitigation, monitoring, public hearing, decision making; Environmental Management Plan (EMP).

Plant Biotechnology

  • Tissue culture: Totipotency, dedifferentiation & redifferentiation, explant types, callus culture, organogenesis (direct & indirect), embryogenesis (somatic embryogenesis), micropropagation (stages: establishment, multiplication, rooting, hardening), somaclonal variation, haploid production (anther & pollen culture), protoplast isolation & fusion (somatic hybridization — protoplast fusion, cybrids), embryo rescue.
  • Transgenic plants: Methods — Agrobacterium tumefaciens (Ti plasmid — T-DNA transfer), gene gun (biolistics), electroporation, microinjection; transgenic crops — Bt cotton (cry1Ac/cry2Ab against bollworm), Bt brinjal (approved but moratorium), Golden Rice (vitamin A enriched — β-carotene), Flavr Savr tomato, Bt brinjal (Bangladesh approved), regulatory framework in India — GEAC (Genetic Engineering Approval Committee), RCGM (Review Committee on Genetic Manipulation), IBSC (Institutional Biosafety Committee).
  • Molecular markers: RAPD (Random Amplified Polymorphic DNA), RFLP (Restriction Fragment Length Polymorphism), AFLP (Amplified Fragment Length Polymorphism), SSR (Simple Sequence Repeats / microsatellites), ISSR, DNA barcoding (rbcL, matK, trnH-psbA for plants), applications — germplasm characterization, diversity analysis, fingerprinting, marker-assisted selection (MAS).
  • Bioinformatics: Databases (GenBank, EMBL, DDBJ, PDB), BLAST, sequence alignment, phylogenetics.
Technique: GM crop answer
Question: 'Discuss the status of Bt crops in India.'
Answer: Bt cotton (Bollgard I & II — cry1Ac & cry2Ab against bollworm) approved 2002 & widely grown (~95% of cotton area). Bt brinjal approved by GEAC 2009 but moratorium imposed (2010) — not commercially released. Golden Rice (vitamin A enriched) in pipeline but not approved. Regulatory: GEAC is apex body; IBSC at institution level; RCGM under DBT. Concerns: biosafety, biodiversity impact, farmer dependence on MNC seeds, farmer suicides debate, farmer suicides debate. Way forward: case-by-case evaluation, stringent biosafety, farmer education, public sector GM research (public good traits — nutrition, stress tolerance).

Memory Tricks

  • C3 vs C4: C3 — photorespiration losses (rice, wheat); C4 — Kranz anatomy, PEP carboxylase, no photorespiration (maize, sugarcane).
  • Double fertilization: Male gamete 1 + egg → zygote (2n); male gamete 2 + 2 polar nuclei → primary endosperm nucleus (3n) → endosperm.
  • Gymnosperm vs angiosperm: Gymnosperm — naked seeds (cones), no flowers, wind pollination mostly; Angiosperm — seeds enclosed in ovary (fruit), flowers, double fertilization.
  • Mitosis vs meiosis: Mitosis — equational (2n → 2n), somatic; Meiosis — reductional (2n → n), reproductive, crossing over in prophase I.
Mains strategy
Botany answers need diagrams (flower LS, ovule LS, pollen grain, anther TS, root/stem/root anatomy, Kranz anatomy, DNA replication, N-cycle). Quote schemes: NFSM, PMKSY, PKVY (organic), DIDF, Biotechnology policies, GEAC. Data: horticulture production (~330 MT), foodgrain (~330 MT), forest cover (~21.7% ISFR 2021), India's 4 biodiversity hotspots (Western Ghats, Eastern Himalayas, Indo-Burma, Sundaland).
opt-civil-engineering/paper2:
Civil Engineering Paper II — Design of Steel Structures, Environmental Engineering & Geotechnical Engineering

Design of Steel Structures

  • Plastic Analysis: Plastic moment capacity, plastic hinge, plastic hinge mechanism, plastic collapse mechanism, plastic moment capacity M_p = f_y * Z_p where Z_p = plastic section modulus.
  • Plastic Design: Plastic hinge formation, collapse mechanism, load factor (load factor = collapse load / working load), plastic hinge formation sequence, plastic moment capacity M_p = f_y * Z_p.
  • Steel Structures: Limit state design (limit state of strength, limit state of serviceability), partial safety factors (γ_m for material, γ_f for loads), design strength in tension (T_d = min(f_y * A_g / γ_0, 0.9 * f_u * A_e / γ_1)), design strength in compression (design compressive strength f_d = χ * f_y / γ_0 where χ = elastic critical buckling stress / f_y = π² E / (f_y * (KL/r)²)), design of tension members, design of compression members (columns), design of tension members, design of compression members (columns), design of beams (flexural members), design of beam-columns (combined axial and bending).
  • Connections: Bolted connections (bearing type bolts, friction grip bolts, high strength friction grip bolts - HSFG, prying action, shear capacity of bolt P_sf = n * f_ub * A_n / (γ_b * γ_m0) where n = number of bolts, f_ub = ultimate tensile strength of bolt, A_n = net area of bolt at threads, γ_b = partial safety factor for bolts = 1.25, γ_m0 = 1.25), welds (fillet welds - throat thickness t = 0.7 * s where s = leg length, design strength of weld = f_u * t_e * l_eff / (√3 * γ_m0) where t_e = effective throat thickness = k * s where k depends on angle of bevel, maximum weld size = t - 1.5 mm for t ≤ 10 mm, t - 1.5 mm for t > 10 mm).
  • Columns: Axially loaded compression members (design compressive strength f_d = χ * f_y / γ_m0 where χ = elastic critical buckling stress / f_y = π² E / (f_y * (KL/r)²), λ = effective slenderness ratio = KL / r, φ = 0.5 * [1 + α(λ - 0.2) + λ²], χ = 1 / (φ + sqrt(φ² - λ²)), χ = 1 for λ ≤ 0.2).
  • Beams: Laterally supported beams (plastic moment capacity M_p = Z_p * f_y / γ_m0 where Z_p = plastic section modulus), laterally unsupported beams (lateral torsional buckling, moment capacity M_d = β_b * Z_p * f_y / γ_m0 where β_b = bend correction factor = 1.0 for I-section loaded on major axis), deflection limits (L/300 for simply supported, L/250 for cantilever).
