  • Columns: Slenderness ratio λ = kL / r where k = effective length factor, L = actual length, r = radius of gyration = √(I/A), slenderness ratio limits (180 for compression members carrying load from floors, 180 for compression members of buildings subject to wind, 180 for compression members of buildings supporting floors, 180 for industrial buildings subject to cranes, 180 for industrial buildings subject to cranes).
  • Plate Girders: Plate girder (built-up section), components (web plate, flange plates, stiffeners - transverse stiffeners, longitudinal stiffeners, bearing stiffeners, bearing stiffeners at supports and concentrated loads, intermediate stiffeners), tension field action, design of web panel (shear buckling), design of flange (flexural strength), design of stiffeners (transverse stiffeners at supports and at point loads, longitudinal stiffeners for deep girders), end bearing stiffeners (bearing stress, buckling of web).
  • Connections: Bolted connections (HSFG bolts - high strength friction grip bolts, slip resistance = μ * N * n where μ = friction coefficient = 0.5 for milled surface, N = clamp force = 0.7 * f_ub * A_b where A_b = shank area of bolt, f_ub = ultimate tensile strength of bolt, n = number of bolts), bearing type bolts (bearing stress = P / (d * t) where d = bolt diameter, t = thickness of thinner plate), weld fillet welds (throat thickness t = 0.7 * s where s = leg length, design strength of weld = f_u * t_e * l_eff / (√3 * γ_m0)), groove welds (complete joint penetration, partial joint penetration).

Steel Design Examples:

Technique: Tension Member Design
Question: Design a tension member to carry a factored load of 400 kN using double angle section. Use Fe 410 steel (f_y = 250 MPa, f_u = 410 MPa).
Answer: Design tension T_d = min(f_y * A_g / γ_0, 0.9 * f_u * A_n / γ_1). Assume A_g = 4000 mm², try ISA 100 x 100 x 10 (A_g = 1910 mm²). Check: T_d = min(250 * 4000 / 1.0, 0.9 * 410 * A_g / 1.25). For 4000 mm²: T_d = min(1000 kN, 0.9 * 410 * 4000 / 1.25) = min(1000 kN, 1168 kN) = 1000 kN > 400 kN OK. Design is adequate.

Memory Tricks

  • Limit State Design: Partial safety factors: γ_m (material) = 1.0 for shop fabrication, 1.25 for field fabrication; γ_f (loads) = 1.5 for DL, 1.5 for LL, 1.2 for wind/seismic.
  • Slenderness Ratio Limits: Compression member carrying load from floors: λ_max = 180; tension member: λ_max = 180; member carrying wind/seismic loads: λ_max = 250; tie member: λ_max = 350.
  • Slenderness Limits for Beams: λ_w / t_w ≤ 110 for web (Class 1), λ_f / t_f = 9.3 * ε for flange (Class 1), where ε = sqrt(250 / f_y).
  • Weld Size: Minimum fillet weld size = 3 mm for t ≤ 10 mm, 5 mm for 10 < t ≤ 20 mm, 6 mm for t > 20 mm.
Mains strategy
Design of steel structures: draw free body diagrams, show load paths, calculate effective lengths for columns based on end conditions, check slenderness limits, use IS 800:2007 clauses, quote codes (IS 800:2007 for steel design, IS 875 for loads), draw typical connection details (gusset plate, splice, column base). Data: IS 800:2007 partial safety factors: γ_m0 = 1.0 for shop fabrication, 1.25 for field fabrication; γ_f = 1.5 for DL, 1.5 for LL, 1.5 for wind/seismic; steel grades: Fe250 (250 MPa), Fe410 (410 MPa), Fe490 (490 MPa); common steel grades: Fe 250, Fe 410, Fe 490.
opt-commerce-accountancy/overview:
Commerce & Accountancy Optional — Overview

Commerce & Accountancy is a popular optional for commerce graduates with overlap in GS III (economy, inclusive growth) and GS IV (ethics). Paper I covers accounting, auditing, company law; Paper II covers cost accounting, financial management, business organisation, management accounting.

Paper I — Accounting & Company Law

  • Accounting principles: Accounting concepts & conventions (going concern, consistency, accrual, prudence, materiality, matching, separate entity, money measurement, dual aspect, periodicity), accounting standards (Ind AS — Indian Accounting Standards converged with IFRS: Ind AS 1-41, key standards — Ind AS 1 presentation, 2 inventories, 7 cash flows, 8 events after reporting, 10 events, 11 construction contracts, 12 income taxes, 16 property plant equipment, 17 leases, 18 revenue, 19 employee benefits, 21 related party, 23 borrowing costs, 24 related party disclosure, 27 separate FS, 28 investments in associates, 29 provisions, 32 financial instruments presentation, 33 financial instruments: presentation, 34 interim FS, 36 impairment, 37 provisions contingent liabilities/assets, 38 intangible assets, 39 financial instruments: recognition & measurement, 40 financial instruments: disclosures, 41 agriculture), Indian GAAP vs IFRS differences.
  • Final accounts: Trading account, profit & loss account, balance sheet (schedule III format), adjustments (closing stock, outstanding/prepaid expenses, accrued income, depreciation, bad debts & provision for bad debts, reserve for discount on debtors & creditors, interest on capital, drawings, depreciation methods — straight line, diminishing balance, annuity, sinking fund, machine hour, depletion, revaluation method), capital vs revenue expenditure, depreciation accounting (AS 6/Ind AS 16), inventory valuation (FIFO, LIFO not permitted under AS 2/Ind AS 2, weighted average, specific identification, retail price method, lower of cost or NRV), consignment & joint ventures, branch accounting (debtors system, debtors & stock control system, stock & debtors system, final accounts system), hire purchase & installment purchase, departmental accounting, royalty accounts, investment accounts, insolvency accounts (statement of affairs, deficiency account).
  • Company law: Companies Act 2013 — company definition, types (private, public, one person, small, associate, subsidiary, holding, foreign, government, listed/unlimited, producer, nidhi), incorporation (MoA, AoA, prospectus — shelf prospectus, abridged, red herring, misstatement liability), shares (issue at premium/discount/par, sweat equity, ESOP, buyback, redemption of preference shares, transfer & transmission, forfeiture & reissue, dematerialisation), debentures (types, issue, redemption), dividend (final vs interim, dividend distribution tax abolished, Dividend Distribution Rules), accounts (financial statements — balance sheet, P&L, cash flow statement, statement of changes in equity, notes, directors' report, auditor's report, audit of companies, appointment/removal/removal of auditor, audit report contents, CARO), corporate social responsibility (CSR — Section 135, 2% of average net profits), winding up (voluntary, tribunal), liquidation (official liquidator), insolvency (IBC 2016 — insolvency resolution process, NCLT/NCLAT, insolvency professional, moratorium, committee of creditors, liquidation), SEBI regulations (LODR, takeover code, insider trading regulations — prohibition), competition law (Competition Act 2002 — anti-competitive agreements, abuse of dominance, combinations, CCI).

Memory Tricks

  • Accounting equation: Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity (A = L + OE).
  • Double entry: Every debit has equal credit — for every transaction, at least two accounts affected.
  • Account types: Personal (natural, artificial, representative), Real (tangible/intangible), Nominal (revenue, expense, gain, loss) — Debit what comes in, credit what goes out (real); Debit receiver credit giver (personal); Debit all expenses/losses, credit all incomes/gains (nominal).
Mains strategy
For Commerce & Accountancy, numerical questions carry high weightage — show working notes clearly. Quote sections of Companies Act 2013, Ind AS numbers, SEBI regulations. Draw formats: balance sheet (Schedule III format), P&L, cash flow statement (direct & indirect method), fund flow statement. Data: India's GDP, FDI inflows, bank credit growth, stock market cap, IPO trends.
opt-commerce-accountancy/paper1:
Commerce Paper I — Accounting & Company Law (Detailed)

Company Accounts

  • Issue of shares: Issue at par, premium, discount (prohibited except sweat equity), forfeiture & reissue of shares, surrender of shares, calls in arrears & calls in advance, interest on calls in arrears & calls in advance (Table F — 10% & 12% respectively), issue of debentures (at par/premium/discount, for cash, for consideration other than cash, as collateral security), interest on debentures, redemption of debentures (out of profits, out of capital, DMDR — Debenture Redemption Reserve 25% for listed, 10% for unlisted unless exempt), redemption out of proceeds of fresh issue/sinking fund/investment method.
  • Final accounts of companies: Schedule III format — balance sheet (equity & liabilities: share capital, reserves & surplus, money received against share warrants, share application money pending allotment, non-current liabilities: long-term borrowings, deferred tax liabilities, other long-term liabilities, long-term provisions; current liabilities: short-term borrowings, trade payables, other current liabilities, short-term provisions; assets: non-current assets — tangible/intangible/Capital WIP/intangible assets under development, non-current investments, deferred tax assets (net), long-term loans & advances, other non-current assets; current assets — current investments, inventories, trade receivables, cash & cash equivalents, short-term loans & advances, other current assets), statement of profit & loss (revenue from operations, other income, total revenue, expenses — cost of materials consumed, purchase of stock-in-trade, changes in inventories, employee benefits expense, finance costs, depreciation & amortisation, other expenses, total expenses, profit before tax, tax expense — current tax & deferred tax, profit for the period, other comprehensive income, total comprehensive income, EPS), cash flow statement (operating, investing, financing — direct & indirect method), statement of changes in equity.
  • Branch accounting: Debtors system, debtors & stock control system, stock & debtors system, final accounts system (wholesale & retail price), independent branches (foreign branches — conversion of foreign currency, translation of foreign branches — monetary items at closing rate, non-monetary at historical, income items at average rate, exchange difference to P&L).
  • Departmental accounting: Departmental trading & P&L account, allocation of common expenses (sales value, floor area, number of employees, time, direct allocation), inter-departmental transfers (at cost or at market price), unrealised profit elimination (1/3rd or 1/(1+margin%) of unsold stock).
  • Consignment accounts: Consignor & consignee, commission (ordinary, del-credere, del-credere & over-riding), valuation of unsold stock (cost or market price whichever lower, less proportionate expenses), abnormal loss (normal loss estimated & spread over good units; abnormal loss valued at cost and transferred to P&L), goods sent on consignment at cost or invoice price (with loading & reserve for unsold stock).
  • Joint venture accounts: Joint venture vs partnership vs consignment, methods — (1) separate set of books, (2) no separate set of books (each venturer records own transactions), (3) memorandum joint venture account method, settlement of accounts.
  • Royalty accounts: Minimum rent (dead rent), short-workings, recoupment of short-workings, strike & lock-out clause, sub-lease, accounting treatment in books of lessee & lessor.

Company Law in Detail

  • Company formation: Promoters (duties, liabilities, pre-incorporation contracts), incorporation (application to ROC, MoA — clauses: name, situation, object, liability, capital, subscription; AoA — contents, alteration, entrenchment), certificate of incorporation, commencement of business (declaration under Section 10A for companies with share capital).
  • Share capital: Authorised, issued, subscribed, called-up, paid-up capital; issue at par/premium/discount; share premium account (uses per Section 52), sweat equity, employee stock option scheme (ESOS), buyback (Section 68 — conditions: 25% of paid-up capital & free reserves, debt-equity ratio not exceeding 2:1 after buyback, declaration of solvency), redemption of preference shares (Section 55 — out of profits or fresh issue, DRR, premium out of premium account/profits), transfer & transmission of shares, forfeiture & reissue, lien on shares, calls on shares, surrender of shares.
  • Debentures: Types (secured/unsecured, registered/bearer, convertible/non-convertible, redeemable/irredeemable, first/second mortgage), issue at discount/premium, issue for consideration other than cash, as collateral security, interest on debentures (payable periodically, income tax deduction), redemption (out of profits — DRM/DRR, out of proceeds of fresh issue, purchase in open market), redemption methods (lump sum, instalments, purchase in open market, conversion into shares/debentures), DRR (25% for listed companies, 10% for unlisted — exemptions: infrastructure companies, banks, housing finance companies, etc.).
  • Company management: Board of directors (appointment, retirement by rotation, removal, remuneration, duties — fiduciary duties, duty of care, duty to act within powers, disclosure of interest, restriction on related party transactions — Section 188), key managerial personnel (KMD — MD, CEO, CFO, CS, whole-time director), meetings (board meetings — notice, quorum, agenda, minutes, resolutions — ordinary & special; general meetings — AGM & EGM, notice period 21 days, quorum, proxy, poll, e-voting, postal ballot).
  • Company Secretary: Definition, appointment, duties (filing returns, maintaining registers & records, signing annual return, convening meetings), liabilities.
  • Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR): Section 135 — applicability (net worth ₹500 crore or turnover ₹1000 crore or net profit ₹5 crore), CSR committee, 2% of average net profits of preceding 3 years, activities (Schedule VII — eradicating hunger, education, gender equality, environmental sustainability, etc.), CSR report in board's report.
  • Winding up: Modes — voluntary (members' voluntary & creditors' voluntary), by tribunal (compulsory — grounds: inability to pay debts, just & equitable, default in filing RoC, acting against sovereignty/integrity/security of India), official liquidator, contributories, preferential payments (workmen's dues, government dues, secured creditors), declaration of solvency for voluntary winding up.
  • Insolvency & Bankruptcy Code 2016: Insolvency resolution process (corporate insolvency resolution process — CIRP, initiation by financial/operational creditor/corporate debtor, declaration of moratorium, appointment of interim resolution professional (IRP), constitution of committee of creditors (CoC), appointment of resolution professional (RP), invitation of resolution plans, approval by CoC (75% voting share), implementation, liquidation (liquidation order, liquidator, realisation of assets, distribution — waterfall: secured creditors, workmen & employees, central/state government debts, unsecured creditors, preference shareholders, equity shareholders), fast track insolvency resolution process (for small companies), cross-border insolvency (UNCITRAL Model Law adoption pending), personal insolvency (individuals & partnership firms), insolvency professionals & IPAs, information utilities (National e-Governance Services Ltd. — NeSL), adjudicating authority (NCLT for companies, NCLAT for appeals, DRT for individuals/Draft Appellate Tribunal for individuals).
  • SEBI regulations: SEBI (Listing Obligations & Disclosure Requirements) Regulations 2015 (LODR — listing agreement, continuous disclosure, related party transactions, corporate governance — composition of board, woman director requirement, independent directors — 50% for listed companies with non-executive chairman, 1/3 otherwise, audit committee, nomination & remuneration committee, stakeholders relationship committee), SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations 2015 (insider trading — definition, prohibited communications, trading window closure, code of conduct for designated persons, disclosures — initial disclosure, continual disclosure, annual disclosure), SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares & Takeovers) Regulations 2011 (open trigger 25%, creeping acquisition 5% per year, open offer 26% for listed companies, offer price — highest of negotiated price, volume weighted average price of last 26 weeks, highest price paid by acquirer in last 26 weeks, open offer timeline), SEBI (Prohibition of Fraudulent & Unfair Trade Practices) Regulations, SEBI (Issue of Capital & Disclosure Requirements) Regulations 2018 (ICDR — IPO & FPO eligibility, pricing, promoter contribution, lock-in, prospectus requirements), SEBI (Listing Obligations & Disclosure Requirements) — quarterly & annual disclosures, related party transactions policy, vigil mechanism/whistle blower, corporate social responsibility reporting.
  • Competition Law: Competition Act 2002 — anti-competitive agreements (horizontal — cartels: price fixing, market allocation, bid rigging, output restriction; vertical — tie-in arrangements, exclusive supply/distribution, refusal to deal, resale price maintenance), abuse of dominance (predatory pricing, barriers to entry, leverage in one market to another), combinations (mergers & acquisitions above thresholds — assets ₹1000 crore/turnover ₹3000 crore domestic, assets USD 1 billion with ₹500 crore in India / turnover USD 3 billion with ₹1500 crore in India cross-border), CCI powers, penalties.
Technique: Companies Act 2013 answer
Question: 'Discuss the provisions related to CSR under Companies Act 2013.'
Answer: Section 135 — applies to companies with net worth ₹500 crore or turnover ₹1000 crore or net profit ₹5 crore in any preceding financial year. Board must constitute CSR committee (3+ directors, at least 1 independent), formulate CSR policy, ensure spending 2% of average net profits of 3 preceding financial years on activities in Schedule VII (education, healthcare, rural development, environment, etc.), disclose in board report, disclose reasons if unspent (transfer to Unspent CSR Account & transfer to specified fund within 6 months), penalties for non-compliance (fine ₹50,000-₹25 lakh on company, imprisonment up to 3 years or fine ₹50,000-₹25 lakh or both for officer in default). Significance: India first country to mandate CSR; aligns business with social welfare.

Common Traps

  • Confusing provisional allotment with firm allotment in IPO.
  • Missing that buyback max 25% of paid-up capital & free reserves, debt-equity ≤ 2:1 post-buyback.
  • Assuming all companies need CSR — applies only to specified thresholds.
  • Confusing private company (max 200 members) with public company (no max).
  • Missing that LIFO is not permitted under Ind AS 2/AS 2 for inventory valuation.

Memory Tricks

  • Company types: Pvt Ltd (2-200 members), Public (7+ members, no max), OPC (1 member).
  • CSR: 2% rule.
  • Buyback: 25% cap, debt-equity 2:1 post-buyback.
  • Directors: rotation — 1/3rd retire every AGM.
Mains strategy
Company law answers: cite section numbers precisely, cite case laws (Salomon v. Salomon & Co — separate legal entity, Foss v. Harbottle — rule in Foss v Harbottle, majority rule & exceptions, Ashbury Railway Carriage & Iron Co v Riche — ultra vires, Guinness v Land Corporation of Ireland — prospectus misstatement), quote section numbers accurately, discuss recent amendments (Companies Amendment Act 2020 — decriminalisation of certain offences, CSR unspent account). Draw formats: balance sheet Schedule III format, cash flow statement direct & indirect methods, share capital structure, debenture redemption process flowchart.
opt-commerce-accountancy/paper2:
Commerce Paper II — Cost Accounting, Financial Management & Management Accounting

Cost Accounting

  • Cost accounting basics: Meaning, objectives, scope, difference between financial accounting & cost accounting, cost accounting vs management accounting, installation of costing system, essentials of a good costing system.
  • Elements of cost: Material, labour, overheads; prime cost, factory cost, cost of production, cost of sales; classification of costs (fixed, variable, semi-variable; direct & indirect; controllable & uncontrollable; relevant & irrelevant; sunk & opportunity cost; sunk & differential cost; avoidable & unavoidable cost; period cost & product cost).
  • Material costing: Material control (purchase procedure, storekeeping, bin card, bin register, stock levels — minimum level, maximum level, reorder level, average level, danger level; EOQ — Economic Order Quantity formula: Q = √(2DS/H) where D = annual demand, S = ordering cost per order, H = holding cost per unit per year; ABC analysis — A items high value low quantity, B medium, C low value high quantity; FIFO, LIFO (not under AS 2/Ind AS 2), weighted average, simple average, highest in first out (HIFO), base stock method), inventory valuation under AS 2/Ind AS 2 (lower of cost or NRV).
  • Labour costing: Time keeping & time booking, idle time (normal & abnormal), overtime, labour turnover (causes, measurement — separation method, replacement method, flux method, flux & replacement method), incentive schemes (Halsey — 50% bonus on time saved, Rowan — time saved / time allowed × time taken × rate, Bedeaux, Emerson, Gantt task & bonus plan, Merrick differential piece rate, Taylor differential piece rate), labour cost control.
  • Overheads: Classification (factory, office & administration, selling & distribution), collection & allocation of overheads (primary & secondary distribution — direct method, step-down/step-ladder method, repeated distribution method, simultaneous equation method), absorption of overheads (percentage of direct wages, direct labour hours, machine hour rate, unit rate), under-absorption & over-absorption (reasons, treatment — supplementary rate, transfer to costing P&L), capacity costs (idle capacity cost, actual capacity, normal capacity).
  • Costing methods: Job costing, batch costing, contract costing, process costing (process accounts, normal loss & abnormal loss/gain, equivalent units — FIFO & weighted average methods, inter-process profit), service costing (transport costing — tonne-km, power house costing, canteen costing, hospital costing), multiple costing (e.g., bicycle, bicycle tyre, television).
  • Cost volume profit analysis: Marginal costing — definition, features, assumptions, marginal cost equation (Sales − Variable Cost = Contribution = Fixed Cost + Profit), PV ratio = Contribution/Sales × 100, break-even point (units = Fixed Cost/Contribution per unit; sales value = Fixed Cost/PV ratio), margin of safety (sales − BEP sales; MOS% = MOS/Sales × 100), angle of incidence, profit-volume chart, applications (decision making — make or buy, accept or reject special order, retain or replace, product mix decisions under limiting factor — key factor analysis, shut down decisions), limitations of marginal costing.
  • Standard costing & variance analysis: Standard costing — meaning, advantages, limitations, setting standards (ideal vs practical standards), variance analysis — material cost variance (price & usage), material usage variance (mix & yield), labour cost variance (rate & efficiency), overhead variance (fixed overhead — expenditure, volume & efficiency/capacity/calendar; variable overhead — expenditure & efficiency), reconciliation of standard profit & actual profit.
  • Budgetary control: Budget & budgetary control — definition, objectives, essentials, types (fixed & flexible budgets, zero-based budgeting, performance budgeting, zero-based budgeting steps), cash budget, production budget, sales budget, materials purchase budget, labour budget, overhead budget, cash flow budget, master budget.

Financial Management

  • Financial management: Meaning, scope, objectives (profit maximisation vs wealth maximisation), role of finance manager, organisation of finance function, agency problem (agency theory), financial goals, time value of money (compounding & discounting, present value & future value of lump sum & annuity, annuity due & perpetuity), capital budgeting (techniques — payback period, accounting rate of return, net present value, internal rate of return, profitability index, discounted payback period, modified IRR), capital rationing, risk analysis in capital budgeting (risk adjusted discount rate, certainty equivalent, sensitivity analysis, scenario analysis, decision tree analysis).
  • Cost of capital: Cost of debt (before tax & after tax — Kd = I/NP × (1−T)), cost of preference capital (Kp = D/NP), cost of equity (dividend yield model — D/P0 + g; CAPM — Rf + β(Rm−Rf); Gordon's growth model — D1/P0 + g), cost of retained earnings (earnings yield approach — E/P0 − flotation cost; dividend growth model), cost of new issue of equity, weighted average cost of capital (WACC = ΣWiKi), marginal cost of capital.
  • Capital structure: Theories — net income approach (NI), net operating income approach (NOI), traditional approach, MM approach (with & without taxes — MM proposition I & II), operating leverage (DOL = % change in EBIT / % change in sales), financial leverage (DFL = % change in EPS / % change in EBIT), combined leverage (DOL × DFL), financial break-even point, capital structure theories & determinants of capital structure.
  • Dividend policy: Relevance theory (Walter's model — P = D + (r/k)(E−D)/k; Gordon's growth model — P = D1/(k−g)), irrelevance theory (MM approach — MM hypothesis on dividend irrelevance), factors affecting dividend policy, bonus shares & stock split, dividend policies (stable, stable rupee amount, constant payout ratio, residual policy), legal & procedural aspects of dividend declaration, bonus issue (capitalisation of profits), buyback of shares.
  • Working capital management: Meaning, types (gross & working, permanent & temporary/variable), factors affecting working capital, estimation of working capital requirements, operating cycle & cash cycle, financing of working capital (spontaneous liabilities — trade credit, accrued expenses; short-term bank finance — cash credit, overdraft, bills discounting/purchase, letter of credit; trade credit; commercial paper; inter-corporate deposits; public deposits), receivables management (objectives, credit policy variables — credit standards, credit terms, collection policy; ageing schedule, factoring, forfaiting, factoring vs discounting), inventory management (objectives, techniques — ABC analysis, EOQ, JIT, VED analysis, FSN analysis, HML analysis, SDE analysis), cash management (motives for holding cash — transaction, precautionary, speculative; optimum cash balance — Baumol model, Miller-Orr model, cash budgeting), inventory management (objectives, techniques — ABC analysis, EOQ, JIT, VED analysis, FSN analysis, HML analysis, SDE analysis), inventory valuation & control.
  • Dividend policy & dividend decisions: Dividend decisions — factors, Walter's model, Gordon's growth model, MM irrelevance hypothesis, bonus shares vs cash dividend, stock split vs bonus issue.
  • Lease financing: Operating lease & financial lease, advantages & limitations of leasing, evaluation of lease vs buy decision.
  • Venture capital: Meaning, features, stages of venture capital financing (seed, start-up, early stage, expansion, bridge/pre-IPO), process of venture capital financing, venture capital funds in India, SEBI (Venture Capital Funds) Regulations.
  • Mutual funds: Types (open-ended & close-ended, equity, debt, hybrid, gilt, liquid, index funds, sectoral, ELSS), NAV calculation, expenses (entry load, exit load, expense ratio), SEBI regulations for mutual funds.
Technique: WACC calculation
Company: Equity ₹400 crore @ 14%, Debt ₹100 crore @ 10% pre-tax, tax rate 30%. WACC?
Answer: Kd after tax = 10% × (1−0.30) = 7%. WACC = (400/500)×14% + (100/500)×7% = 0.8×14% + 0.2×7% = 11.2% + 1.4% = 12.6%.

Management Accounting

  • Management accounting: Meaning, scope, objectives, tools & techniques (financial statement analysis — comparative, common size, trend analysis; ratio analysis — liquidity, solvency, profitability, activity/turnover ratios; funds flow statement; cash flow statement; budgetary control; marginal costing; standard costing; CVP analysis; capital budgeting; management information system).
  • Ratio analysis: Liquidity ratios (current ratio, quick ratio/acid test, absolute liquid ratio), solvency ratios (debt equity ratio, proprietary ratio, capital gearing ratio, interest coverage ratio, debt service coverage ratio), activity ratios (stock turnover ratio, debtors turnover ratio, creditors turnover ratio, working capital turnover ratio, fixed assets turnover ratio, total assets turnover ratio), profitability ratios (gross profit ratio, net profit ratio, operating ratio, operating profit ratio, return on capital employed (ROCE) = PBIT/Capital Employed, return on equity (ROE) = PAT/Shareholders' Funds, return on total assets, earnings per share (EPS), price earnings ratio (P/E ratio), dividend per share (DPS), dividend payout ratio, earnings yield, market value per share).

Technique: Plate Tectonics
Question: 'Explain Plate Tectonics theory & its evidence.'
Answer: Plate tectonics - lithosphere broken into ~7 major & several minor plates floating on asthenosphere. Evidence: (1) Jigsaw fit of continents (South America & Africa), (2) Fossil evidence (Mesosaurus, Glossopteris, Lystrosaurus across continents), (3) Rock continuity across oceans, (4) Paleomagnetism & sea floor spreading (magnetic stripes symmetrical about mid-ocean ridges), (5) Earthquake & volcano distribution along plate boundaries, (6) GPS measurements of plate movement.   • Major river basins: Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra, Yamuna, Narmada, Tapti, Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Cauvery, Mahanadi, Subarnarekha, Damodar, Chambal, Betwa, Ken, Son, Gandak, Rapti, Gomti, Sharada, Alaknanda, Bhagirathi, Mandakini, Dhauliganga, Kali, Sarju, Ramganga, East Rapti, West Rapti, Gandak, Kosi, Gandak, Bagmati, Baghmati, Kamala, Bagmati, Tila, Tel, Indrawati, Seti, Karnali, Mahakali, Rapti, Babai, West Rapti, West Rapti, West Rapti, West Rapti, West Rapti, West Rapti, West Rapti, West Rapti, West Rapti, West Rapti.
Technique: River diversion & interlinking
Question: 'Explain the National River Linking Project (NRLP) & its challenges.'
Answer: NRLP aims to link Himalayan & peninsular rivers via canals to transfer water from surplus to deficit regions. Key links: Ken-Betwa, Damodar-Ganga, Parbati-Kalisindh-Chambal, etc. Benefits: irrigation, drinking water, hydropower, flood control. Challenges: ecological impact, displacement, cost, inter-state disputes, ecological impact on rivers & ecosystems.

Memory Tricks

  • Physiographic divisions: Himalayas, Northern Plains, Peninsular Plateau, Indian Desert, Coastal Plains, Islands.
  • River flow direction: Himalayan rivers flow east (Ganga, Brahmaputra) into Bay of Bengal; Peninsular rivers flow east (Godavari, Krishna) into Bay of Bengal OR west (Narmada, Tapi) into Arabian Sea.
  • Soil types: Alluvial (Indo-Gangetic - most fertile), Black/Regur (Deccan - cotton), Red (TN, Karnataka, Odisha - iron rich), Laterite (Kerala, Karnataka, NE hills - acidic), Arid/Desert (Rajasthan - saline), Forest/Mountain (Himalayas - acidic), Peaty/Marshy (Kerala, Sundarbans - Orissa).
  • Climate seasons: Cold weather (Dec-Feb), Hot weather (Mar-May), Advancing monsoon (Jun-Sept), Retreating monsoon (Oct-Nov).
Mains strategy
Geography answers: diagrams (physiographic divisions, river systems, monsoon winds, ocean currents, soil types, climate zones, population distribution, urban growth patterns). Quote facts: India's area (3.29 million sq km), coastline (7,517 km), land frontier (15,200 km), states (28) & UTs (8), forest cover (~21.7% ISFR 2021), biodiversity hotspots (4: Western Ghats, Eastern Himalayas, Indo-Burma, Sundaland), agricultural production (~330 MT foodgrains). Link physical geography to human geography (climate → agriculture → settlement patterns → urbanization → environmental issues).
opt-geography/overview:
Geography Optional — Overview & Syllabus Map

Geography is a popular optional with significant overlap with GS I (Indian & World Geography, Social Issues) and GS III (Agriculture, Environment, Disaster Management). Paper I covers Physical Geography & Human Geography; Paper II covers Geography of India (physical, economic, social, regional planning).

Paper I — Physical Geography & Human Geography

  • Physical Geography: Geomorphology (earth's interior, plate tectonics, earthquakes, volcanoes, weathering, fluvial, glacial, aeolian, coastal, karst landforms), Climatology (atmosphere, temperature, pressure belts, winds, cyclones, El Niño-La Niña, climate classification), Oceanography (ocean relief, temperature & salinity, ocean currents, tides, coral reefs, ocean deposits), Biogeography (soils, natural vegetation, biodiversity, soil erosion & conservation).
  • Human Geography: Population & settlement (population distribution, growth theories, migration patterns, rural & urban settlements, urbanization trends), Economic geography (primary activities - agriculture, mining; secondary activities - manufacturing industries; tertiary activities - services, tourism), Regional development & planning (regional disparities, watershed management, drought-prone area planning, river interlinking, environmental issues, climate change, disaster management).

Paper II — Geography of India

  • Physical Geography of India: Physiographic divisions (Himalayas, Northern Plains, Peninsular Plateau, Indian Desert, Coastal Plains, Islands), Drainage system (Himalayan & peninsular rivers, river disputes), Climate (controls, seasons, monsoon mechanism, rainfall distribution), Soils & natural vegetation (soil types, natural vegetation, conservation), Natural resources & agriculture (mineral distribution, power resources, agriculture types, cropping seasons, irrigation), Human geography (population distribution, migration, settlements, urban issues).
  • Regional development & planning: Regional disparities, watershed management, river interlinking, waterlogging & salinity, disaster management (floods, droughts, cyclones, earthquakes, landslides), environmental issues (pollution, climate change, biodiversity conservation), disaster management (NDMA, Sendai Framework).
Technique: Drainage pattern answer
Question: 'Explain the drainage pattern of Peninsular India.'
Answer: Peninsular rivers are mostly rain-fed (seasonal), flow through hard rock, have fewer tributaries, and flow eastward into Bay of Bengal (Godavari, Krishna, Mahanadi, Kaveri) or westward into Arabian Sea (Narmada, Tapi - forming estuaries not deltas). Drainage patterns: dendritic (Indo-Gangetic), radial (Amarkantak - Narmada, Son), trellis (folded mountains), rectangular (Vindhyas).

Memory Tricks

  • Physiographic divisions: Himalayas, Northern Plains, Peninsular Plateau, Indian Desert, Coastal Plains, Islands.
  • River flow direction: Himalayan rivers flow east (Ganga, Brahmaputra) into Bay of Bengal; Peninsular rivers flow east (Godavari, Krishna) into Bay of Bengal OR west (Narmada, Tapi) into Arabian Sea.
  • Soil types: Alluvial (Indo-Gangetic - most fertile), Black/Regur (Deccan - cotton), Red (TN, Karnataka, Odisha - iron rich), Laterite (Kerala, Karnataka, NE - acidic), Arid/Desert (Rajasthan - saline), Forest/Mountain (Himalayas), Peaty/Marshy (Kerala, Sundarbans).
  • Climate seasons: Cold weather (Dec-Feb), Hot weather (Mar-May), Advancing monsoon (Jun-Sep), Retreating monsoon (Oct-Nov).
Mains strategy
Geography answers need diagrams (physiographic divisions, river systems, monsoon mechanism, ocean currents, soil types, climate zones). Quote facts: India's area (3.29 million sq km), coastline (7,517 km), land frontier (15,200 km), states (28) & UTs (8), forest cover (~21.7% ISFR 2021), biodiversity hotspots (4: Western Ghats, Eastern Himalayas, Indo-Burma, Sundaland), agricultural production (~330 MT foodgrains). Link physical geography to human geography (climate → agriculture → settlement patterns).
opt-history/overview:
History Optional — Overview

History Optional covers ancient, medieval, modern India and world history. It has significant overlap with GS I (History, Art & Culture) and Essay. The subject is factual, chronological, and analytical — ideal for aspirants with a humanities background.

Paper I — Ancient & Medieval India

  • Prehistoric & Ancient India: Paleolithic, Mesolithic, Neolithic, Chalcolithic cultures; Indus Valley Civilization (Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Lothal, Dholavira — town planning, drainage, trade, decline); Vedic period (Early & Later Vedic — society, polity, religion, economy); Jainism & Buddhism (Buddha, Mahavira, teachings, councils, spread); Mauryan Empire (Chandragupta, Bindusara, Ashoka — edicts, dhamma, administration); Post-Mauryan (Indo-Greeks, Shakas, Parthians, Kushanas — Kanishka, Kanishka's council); Gupta Empire (Golden Age — Samudragupta, Chandragupta II, administration, art, literature, science); Post-Gupta (Vardhana dynasty — Harsha, Nalanda University).
  • Early Medieval India (750-1200 CE): Regional kingdoms (Palas, Pratiharas, Rashtrakutas, Cholas, Cheras, Pandyas); South Indian polities (Chola administration, local self-government); Arab conquest of Sindh (Muhammad bin Qasim 712 CE); Turko-Afghan invasions (Mahmud of Ghazni, Muhammad Ghori); Delhi Sultanate (Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid, Lodi dynasties); Vijayanagara & Bahmani kingdoms.
  • Bhakti & Sufi movements: Bhakti saints (Ramanuja, Kabir, Nanak, Chaitanya, Mirabai, Tulsidas, Eknath, Tukaram); Sufi saints (Moinduddin Chishti, Nizamuddin Auliya, Fariduddin Ganjshakar); impact on society & culture.

Paper II — Modern India & World History

  • Modern India (1750-1947): European advent (Portuguese, Dutch, French, British); East India Company rule (Battle of Plassey 1757, Battle of Buxar 1764, Diwani rights 1765); Company administration (Regulating Act 1773, Pitt's India Act 1784, Charter Acts); land revenue settlements (Permanent Settlement 1793, Ryotwari, Mahalwari); Revolt of 1857 (causes, course, consequences); Indian National Congress (1885) & early phase; Swadeshi & Boycott (1905); Extremist phase; Home Rule Movement; Lucknow Pact (1916); Gandhian era (Non-Cooperation 1920-22, Civil Disobedience 1930-34, Quit India 1942); Constitutional developments (Morley-Minto 1909, Montagu-Chelmsford 1919, Simon Commission, Nehru Report, Round Table Conferences, Government of India Act 1935); Provincial autonomy & provincial elections (1937); Cripps Mission (1942); Wavell Plan (1945); Cabinet Mission (1946); Mountbatten Plan (1947); Indian Independence Act 1947; Partition & Partition violence; Integration of princely states (Sardar Patel); Constitution making (Constituent Assembly, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, Constitution adopted 26 Nov 1949, enforced 26 Jan 1950).
  • World History: Renaissance & Reformation (15th-16th centuries); American Revolution (1776); French Revolution (1789) — causes, phases, impact; Napoleonic Wars; Industrial Revolution (18th-19th century — causes, impact, spread); American Civil War (1861-65); Unification of Italy (1861) & Germany (1871); Russian Revolution (1917); World War I (1914-18) — causes, course, consequences, Treaty of Versailles; League of Nations; Russian Revolution (1917) — Bolshevik Revolution, Lenin, Stalin; Great Depression (1929); Rise of Fascism (Mussolini, Italy 1922) & Nazism (Hitler, Germany 1933); World War II (1939-45) — causes, course, consequences, Holocaust, atomic bombing; UNO (1945); Cold War (1947-1991) — Cold War origins, Cold War blocs (NATO, Warsaw Pact), Cold War conflicts (Korean War 1950-53, Vietnam War, Cuban Missile Crisis 1962), decolonization (India 1947, Indonesia 1949, Algeria 1962, African countries 1960s), Non-Aligned Movement (1961), end of Cold War (1989-91), collapse of USSR (1991), globalization.
Technique: Revolt of 1857 answer
Question: 'Examine the causes & nature of the Revolt of 1857.'
Answer: Causes: Political (Doctrine of Lapse, annexation of Awadh, disrespect to Mughal emperor), Economic (land revenue policies, destruction of handicrafts, drain of wealth), Military (greased cartridges, disparity in pay & promotion, discrimination), Social (interference in customs & traditions, Christian missionaries), Immediate cause (greased cartridges of Enfield rifle). Nature of Revolt: Debated — Sepoy Mutiny (British view), First War of Independence (Savarkar & nationalist view), combination of grievances without unified leadership, localized revolts without coordinated leadership. Consequences: End of Company rule (1858), Crown rule (Queen's Proclamation 1858), end of Doctrine of Lapse, reorganization of army (proportion of British troops increased), racial antagonism increased.

Memory Tricks

  • Mughal emperors: Babur (1526), Humayun (1530), Akbar (1556), Jahangir (1605), Shah Jahan (1627), Aurangzeb (1658).
  • Delhi Sultanate dynasties: Mamluk (1206-1290), Khalji (1290-1320), Tughlaq (1320-1414), Sayyid (1414-1451), Lodi (1451-1526).
  • Maratha Empire: Shivaji (1674 coronation), Sambhaji, Rajaram, Tarabai, Shahu, Peshwas (Balaji Vishwanath 1713, Baji Rao I, Balaji Baji Rao), Third Battle of Panipat (1761).
  • Important dates: 1757 (Plassey), 1764 (Buxar), 1793 (Permanent Settlement), 1857 (Revolt), 1885 (INC founded), 1905 (Swadeshi), 1920-22 (Non-Cooperation), 1930-34 (Civil Disobedience), 1942 (Quit India), 1947 (Independence & Partition).
Mains strategy
History answers: chronology → causes → course → consequences → significance. Draw maps (extent of empires, battle sites, trade routes). Quote dates, rulers, battles, treaties, acts, commissions. Use source material (travelers' accounts — Megasthenes, Fa-Hien, Xuanzang, Al-Biruni, Ibn Battuta, Marco Polo; foreign travelers' accounts). Quote archaeological evidence (Harappan sites, Ashokan edicts, temple inscriptions, copper plates, coins). Quote literary sources (Vedas, Puranas, epics, Buddhist Jataka tales, Jain texts, court poet accounts — Banabhuta's Harshacharita, Kalhana's Rajatarangini).
opt-history/paper2:
Medieval India (750-1857 CE)

Early Medieval India (750-1200 CE)

  • Regional kingdoms: Palas (Bengal), Pratiharas (Kannauj), Rashtrakutas (Deccan), Cholas (Tamil Nadu), Cheras (Kerala), Pandyas (Tamil Nadu).
  • Chola administration: Local self-government (ur, sabha, nagaram), village administration, naval power, overseas trade (Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia), temple administration, land revenue system.
  • Arab conquest of Sindh (712 CE): Muhammad bin Qasim's conquest, impact on India-Islam contact.
  • Turko-Afghan invasions: Mahmud of Ghazni (17 invasions, 1001-1027 CE, Somnath temple 1026), Muhammad Ghori (1175-1206, Battles of Tarain 1191 & 1192), establishment of Turkish rule in India.

Delhi Sultanate (1206-1526 CE)

  • Mamluk/Slave Dynasty (1206-1290): Qutb-ud-din Aibak (founder, Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque, Qutb Minar), Iltutmish (consolidation, Iqta system, Silver tanka & copper jital coins), Razia (first woman ruler), Balban (blood & iron policy, espionage).
  • Khalji Dynasty (1290-1320): Jalaluddin Khalji (founder), Alauddin Khalji (market reforms, price control, market reforms, Mongol invasions repelled, South India expedition - Malik Kafur, Chittor conquest 1303), administrative reforms.
  • Tughlaq Dynasty (1320-1414): Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq (founder), Muhammad bin Tughlaq (capital shift to Daulatabad, token currency experiment, agricultural experiments, Doab famine), Firoz Shah Tughlaq (irrigation, public works, slavery, jaziya on non-Muslims, establishment of new towns).
  • Sayyid Dynasty (1414-1451): Khizr Khan (founder), weak rulers, decline of Delhi Sultanate.
  • Lodi Dynasty (1451-1526): Bahlul Lodi (founder), Sikandar Lodi (aggressive expansion, iconoclasm), Ibrahim Lodi (last Lodi ruler, defeated by Babur at First Battle of Panipat 1526).

Deccan & South India

  • Vijayanagara Empire (1336-1646): Harihara & Bukka (founders), Krishnadevaraya (greatest ruler, Amuktamalyada, foreign travelers - Abdur Razzak, Domingo Paes, Nicolo Conti), administration, art & architecture (Hampi, Hazara Rama Temple, Vitthala Temple), decline after Battle of Talikota (1565).
  • Bahmani Kingdom (1347-1527): Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah (founder), Muhammad Shah I, Muhammad Shah III, Mahmud Gawan (prime minister, Mahmud Gawan Madrasa), disintegration into five Deccan Sultanates (Ahmadnagar, Bijapur, Golconda, Berar, Bidar).
  • Bhakti & Sufi Movements: Bhakti saints (Ramanuja, Kabir, Kabir, Guru Nanak, Chaitanya, Mirabai, Tulsidas, Eknath, Tukaram, Namdev), Sufi saints (Moinduddin Chishti - Ajmer, Nizamuddin Auliya - Delhi, Fariduddin Ganjshakar - Pakpattan, Qutbuddin Bakhtiar Kaki - Delhi), Sufi orders (Chishti, Suhrawardi, Qadiri, Naqshbandi, Suhrawardi).

Common Traps

  • Confusing different dynasties with similar names (e.g., Khalji vs Tughlaq, Rashtrakuta vs Chalukya).
  • Mixing up dates of important battles (Tarain 1191 & 1192, Panipat 1526, Khanwa 1527, Ghaghra 1529, Haldighati 1576).
  • Confusing different Sufi orders and their saints.
  • Assuming all Delhi Sultans were equally powerful - many were weak figureheads controlled by nobles.
  • Missing the regional diversity of medieval India - not all regions were under Delhi Sultanate control.

Memory Tricks

  • Delhi Sultanate dynasties: Mamluk (1206-1290), Khalji (1290-1320), Tughlaq (1320-1414), Sayyid (1414-1451), Lodi (1451-1526) - MKTSL.
  • Vijayanagara founders: Harihara & Bukka (founded 1336).
  • Sufi saints: Moinuddin Chishti (Ajmer), Nizamuddin Auliya (Delhi), Fariduddin Ganjshakar (Pakpattan), Qutbuddin Bakhtiar Kaki (Delhi).
  • Bhakti saints: Kabir (Bhakti-Nirguna), Tulsidas (Ramcharitmanas), Kabir (Bijak), Guru Nanak (Guru Granth Sahib).
Mains strategy
Medieval India answers: dynasty → founder → important rulers → administration → art & architecture → decline. Draw maps (extent of Delhi Sultanate, Vijayanagara empire, Bahmani kingdom). Quote foreign travelers (Ibn Battuta, Marco Polo, Abdur Razzak, Domingo Paez, Nicolo Conti, Alberuni). Quote contemporary chronicles (Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi by Barani, Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi, Baburnama, Akbarnama).
opt-history/paper3:
Modern India (1750-1947 CE)

Advent of Europeans & Consolidation of British Power

  • European arrival: Vasco da Gama (1498, Portuguese), Dutch (1595), French (1667), British East India Company (1600, Royal Charter, first factory at Surat 1608).
  • Battle of Plassey (1757): Robert Clive defeated Siraj-ud-Daulah (with Mir Jafar's betrayal) - beginning of British political power.
  • Battle of Buxar (1764): Company defeated Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daulah, Shah Alam II - Diwani rights of Bengal, Bihar, Orissa (1765).
  • Dual Government (1765-1772): Company had Diwani (revenue), Nawab had Nizamat (administration) - administrative paralysis, exploitation.
  • Wars: Anglo-Mysore (Haider Ali, Tipu Sultan), Anglo-Maratha (three wars), Anglo-Sikh (two wars), Anglo-Nepal, Anglo-Burmese, Anglo-Afghan.
  • Doctrine of Lapse (Lord Dalhousie): Annexed Satara (1848), Sambalpur (1849), Udaipur (1852), Jhansi (1853), Nagpur (1854), Awadh (1856 - misrule).

Company Rule: Administration & Policies

  • Regulating Act 1773: First parliamentary control, Governor-General of Bengal (Warren Hastings), Supreme Court at Calcutta.
  • Pitt's India Act 1784: Dual control - Board of Control (political), Court of Directors (commercial).
  • Charter Acts (1813, 1833, 1853): Ended trade monopoly (except tea), centralised legislation, open competition for civil services.
  • Land revenue: Permanent Settlement (1793, Cornwallis - Bengal, Bihar, Orissa), Ryotwari (Madras, Bombay - direct with cultivators), Mahalwari (North-Western Provinces - village-based).
  • Commercial policies: De-industrialisation, drain of wealth (Dadabhai Naoroji's theory), forced commercialisation of crops (indigo, opium, cotton).

Socio-Religious Reform Movements

  • Brahmo Samaj (1828, Raja Ram Mohan Roy): Abolition of sati (1829), monotheism, opposition to idol worship and caste.
  • Arya Samaj (1875, Dayananda Saraswati): "Back to the Vedas", shuddhi (reconversion), opposition to cow slaughter and caste.
  • Prarthana Samaj (1867, Atmaram Pandurang): Western India, social reform (widow remarriage, women's education).
  • Ramakrishna Mission (1897, Swami Vivekananda): Service to humanity, Vedanta, Chicago Parliament of Religions (1893).
  • Theosophical Society (1875, H.P. Blavatsky & H.S. Olcott; Annie Besant later): Adyar headquarters, revival of ancient religions.
  • Aligarh Movement (Sir Syed Ahmad Khan): Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College (1875), modern education for Muslims, loyal to British initially.
  • Singh Sabha (1873, Amritsar): Sikh reform, Gurdwara reforms, Punjabi language.
  • Satya Shodhak Samaj (Jyotiba Phule): Anti-caste, education for lower castes and women, Satyashodhak marriage.
  • Self-Respect Movement (E.V. Ramasamy 'Periyar'): Anti-Brahminism, rationalism, women's rights, Tamil pride.

Revolt of 1857

  • Causes: Political (Doctrine of Lapse, annexation of Awadh), economic (land revenue, de-industrialisation), military (greased cartridges, disparity in pay & promotion), social (interference in customs, Christian missionary activity), immediate (Enfield rifle cartridges, March 1857, Meerut outbreak May 10).
  • Centres and leaders: Delhi (Bahadur Shah II), Kanpur (Nana Sahib, Tantia Tope), Lucknow (Begum Hazrat Mahal), Jhansi (Rani Lakshmibai), Bihar (Kunwar Singh), Faizabad (Maulvi Ahmadullah).
  • Suppression: Delhi recaptured (September 1857), Lucknow (Campbell), Jhansi (Hughes), Kunwar Singh (Hughes).
  • Nature: Debated - sepoy mutiny (British view), first war of independence (Savarkar, nationalist view), collection of grievances without unified leadership.
  • Consequences: End of Company rule (1858), Crown takeover, Queen's Proclamation (1858), end of Doctrine of Lapse, reorganisation of army (proportion of British troops increased), racial antagonism increased.

Indian National Movement - Moderate Phase (1885-1905)

  • Indian National Congress (1885): Founded by A.O. Hume; first session Bombay (W.C. Bonnerjee, president). Early leaders - Dadabhai Naoroji, Gopal Krishna Gokhale, Pherozeshah Mehta, Surendranath Banerjee, Dinshaw Wacha.
  • Methods: Petitions, prayers, protests, constitutional agitation, educating public opinion.
  • Economic critique: Dadabhai Naoroji's "Poverty and Un-British Rule in India" (drain of wealth), R.C. Dutt's economic history.
  • Demands: Indianisation of services, separation of judiciary from executive, reduction of military expenditure, civil rights, legislative councils with elected members.

Extremist Phase and Swadeshi (1905-1918)

  • Partition of Bengal (1905, Lord Curzon): Divided Bengal into East Bengal and Assam (Muslim-majority) and West Bengal (Hindu-majority) - seen as "divide and rule".
  • Swadeshi and Boycott: Boycott of British goods, promotion of Indian industries (Bengal Chemical, Tata Steel), national education (Bengal National College), Swadeshi steamship company (V.O. Chidambaram Pillai).
  • Extremist leaders: Bal Gangadhar Tilak ("Swaraj is my birthright"), Lala Lajpat Rai, Bipin Chandra Pal (Lal-Bal-Pal).
  • Muslim League (1906, Dacca): Founded by Nawab Salimullah; supported Partition of Bengal; demanded separate electorates (Morley-Minto Reforms 1909).
  • Home Rule Movement (1916): Annie Besant and Tilak - demanded self-government within the British Empire, on lines of Irish Home Rule.
  • Lucknow Pact (1916): Congress-Muslim League agreement on separate electorates, joint demand for self-government.

Gandhian Era (1919-1947)

  • Rowlatt Act (1919) and Jallianwala Bagh (April 13, 1919): General Dyer fired on unarmed crowd in Amritsar - turning point in Indian politics.
  • Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22): Launched after Khilafat issue and Jallianwala Bagh; boycott of schools, courts, councils, foreign goods; Chauri Chaura (February 1922) led Gandhi to withdraw it.
  • Swaraj Party (1923, Motilal Nehru, C.R. Das): Council entry to obstruct government from within.
  • Simon Commission (1927): All-British commission - boycotted ("Simon Go Back"); Nehru Report (1928) demanding dominion status.
  • Purna Swaraj (1929, Lahore session): Jawaharlal Nehru as president; January 26 declared Independence Day.
  • Civil Disobedience Movement (1930-34): Dandi March (March 12-April 6, 1930), salt law violation; Round Table Conferences (1930-32); Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931); Poona Pact (1932).
  • Quit India Movement (1942): "Do or Die" (August 8, 1942); mass arrests, underground leadership, parallel governments (Ballia, Tamluk, Satara).
  • INA (Subhas Chandra Bose): Azad Hind Fauj, Provisional Government of Free India (Singapore, 1943), women's regiment (Rani of Jhansi Regiment, Lakshmi Sahgal).
  • Cabinet Mission (1946): Three-tier federal plan, interim government; rejected by League and Congress in parts; led to Direct Action Day (August 16, 1946) and communal violence.
  • Mountbatten Plan / Indian Independence Act 1947: Partition into India and Pakistan; August 15, 1947; princely states given option to join either.

Post-Independence Consolidation

  • Integration of princely states (Sardar Patel): Hyderabad (Operation Polo, 1948), Junagadh (plebiscite), Kashmir (accession, 1947, Article 370), Goa (Operation Vijay, 1961), Pondicherry (French, 1954).
  • States Reorganisation Act 1956: Linguistic states - Andhra (1953, first linguistic state), then reorganisation on language basis.
  • Constitution adopted (1950): Republic declared.
Technique: Movement chronology
Question: Arrange in chronological order: Swadeshi, Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience, Quit India.
Answer: Swadeshi (1905) → Non-Cooperation (1920) → Civil Disobedience (1930) → Quit India (1942). Each escalated in mass participation and British repression.
Technique: Assessing the Moderates
Question: "The Moderates failed because they lacked mass base." Comment.
Answer: Moderates (1885-1905) relied on educated elite, petitions, and British goodwill. Their achievements - economic critique, Council Act 1892, Indianisation of services - were real but limited. Lack of mass mobilisation, faith in British justice, no direct action made them vulnerable to Extremist critique after Partition of Bengal (1905).

Common Traps

  • Confusing Regulating Act (1773) with Pitt's India Act (1784).
  • Thinking 1857 Revolt had unified nationalist ideology - it was collection of regional grievances.
  • Missing that Swadeshi was both economic (boycott British goods) and political (swaraj).
  • Assuming Gandhi withdrew Non-Cooperation only due to Chauri Chaura - also due to fear of losing control, British repression.
  • Confusing Poona Pact (1932, Gandhi-Ambedkar) with Communal Award (1932, Ramsay MacDonald).

Memory Tricks

  • 1857 → 1947: Revolt → Crown rule → INC (1885) → Swadeshi (1905) → Non-Cooperation (1920) → Civil Disobedience (1930) → Quit India (1942) → Independence (1947).
  • Lal-Bal-Pal: Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal - Extremist trio.
  • Three settlements: Gandhi-Irwin (1931), Poona Pact (1932), Cabinet Mission (1946).
Mains exam-day strategy
For modern history, always anchor events with dates, viceroys, and key leaders. Distinguish between causes, course, and consequences. For movement-based questions, discuss leadership, methods, participants, British response, and impact. Avoid hero-worship - critically assess limitations (Moderates' elite base, Gandhian withdrawals).
opt-law/paper1:
Constitutional Law of India

Constitutional Framework

  • Constitution of India: Adopted 26 Nov 1949, enforced 26 Jan 1950. Originally 395 Articles in 22 Parts and 8 Schedules; now over 450 Articles in 25 Parts and 12 Schedules.
  • Preamble: Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic; Justice (social, economic, political), Liberty (thought, expression, belief, faith, worship), Equality (status and opportunity), Fraternity (assuring dignity of individual and unity and integrity of Nation).
  • Citizenship: Articles 5-11; Citizenship Act 1955; acquisition by birth, descent, registration, naturalisation, incorporation of territory; termination by renunciation, termination, deprivation; CAA 2019 - accelerated citizenship for persecuted minorities from Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Pakistan.
  • Fundamental Rights (Part III, Articles 12-35): Right to Equality (14-18), Right to Freedom (19-22), Right against Exploitation (23-24), Right to Freedom of Religion (25-28), Cultural and Educational Rights (29-30), Right to Constitutional Remedies (32). Right to Property deleted (44th Amendment 1978, Art 300A - legal right).
  • Directive Principles (Part IV, Articles 36-51): Non-justiciable; social, economic, political welfare; Uniform Civil Code (44), separation of judiciary from executive (50), organisation of village panchayats (40), promotion of educational and economic interests of SC/ST/weaker sections (46).
  • Fundamental Duties (Part IVA, Article 51A): Added by 42nd Amendment 1976; 11 duties (originally 10, 11th added by 86th Amendment 2002 - parent/guardian to provide education to child 6-14 years).
  • Basic Structure Doctrine: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) - Parliament can amend any part of Constitution but cannot destroy/alter basic structure. Basic features: supremacy of Constitution, republican democratic republic, secularism, separation of powers, federalism, judicial review, freedom and dignity of individual, unity and integrity of nation.

Union Executive

  • President (Articles 52-62): Indirectly elected by electoral college (MPs + MLAs); 5-year term; re-election eligible; qualifications (citizen, 35+ years, qualified for Lok Sabha); qualifications, conditions (no office of profit), oath, impeachment (Article 61 - violation of Constitution).
  • Vice-President (Articles 63-71): Indirectly elected by electoral college (both Houses); ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha; 5-year term; impeachment (Rajya Sabha resolution passed by majority, agreed by Lok Sabha).
  • Prime Minister & Council of Ministers (Articles 74-75): PM appointed by President (leader of majority/coalition in Lok Sabha); other ministers appointed by President on advice of PM; collectively responsible to Lok Sabha (Art 75); individual responsibility; oath; salaries/allowances determined by Parliament.
  • Attorney General (Article 76): Appointed by President; must be qualified to be Supreme Court judge; holds office during pleasure of President; right to audience in all courts; right to speak in Parliament (but no voting); not a member of Cabinet.

Parliament

  • Parliament (Articles 79-122): Bicameral - President + Rajya Sabha (Council of States) + Lok Sabha (House of the People).
  • Rajya Sabha (245 members): 238 elected by State/UT Legislative Assemblies (proportional representation by single transferable vote), 12 nominated by President (special knowledge/practical experience in literature, science, art, social service). Permanent house - 1/3 retires every 2 years; 6-year term. Vice-President is ex-officio Chairman; Deputy Chairman elected from members.
  • Lok Sabha (545 members): 543 elected by direct election (single member constituencies), 2 nominated by President (Anglo-Indian - abolished by 104th Amendment 2019). 5-year term (can be dissolved earlier); Speaker (elected by Lok Sabha) presides; Deputy Speaker elected from members.
  • Qualifications for MP: Citizen of India; age 25 (LS) / 30 (RS); registered voter; not holding office of profit; not disqualified under 10th Schedule.
  • Disqualification (10th Schedule): Voluntarily giving up membership, voting against party whip, joining another party after election, independently elected member joining party, nominated member joining party after 6 months.
Technique: Article 32 - Right to Constitutional Remedies
Question: 'Article 32 is the heart and soul of the Constitution' - Dr. B.R. Ambedkar. Explain.
Answer: Article 32 provides right to approach Supreme Court directly for enforcement of Fundamental Rights. It makes Fundamental Rights justiciable/real. Supreme Court can issue writs: Habeas Corpus (produce person), Mandamus (command public official), Prohibition (stop lower court), Certiorari (transfer case), Quo Warranto (by what authority - challenge to public office). Without Art 32, Fundamental Rights would be mere declarations without enforcement mechanism.

Common Traps

  • Confusing Fundamental Rights (justiciable) with Directive Principles (non-justiciable).
  • Thinking President has executive power - President acts on aid & advice of Council of Ministers (Art 74).
  • Missing that Fundamental Duties are not legally enforceable (no penalty for violation).
  • Confusing Article 32 (Supreme Court) with Article 226 (High Court) - both issue writs, but SC jurisdiction is wider for FR enforcement while HC can enforce FR + other legal rights.
  • Overlooking that Emergency provisions (Articles 352, 356, 360) alter normal federal structure and can suspend Fundamental Rights (except Articles 20 & 21).

Memory Tricks

  • FR Articles: 12-35 (Part III); DPSP Articles: 36-51 (Part IV).
  • Fundamental Rights: Right to Equality (14-18), Freedom (19-22), Against Exploitation (23-24), Religion (25-28), Culture & Education (29-30), Constitutional Remedies (32).
  • Emergency Types: Article 352 (National Emergency), 356 (President's Rule), 360 (Financial Emergency).
  • Writs: Habeas Corpus (produce person), Mandamus (command), Prohibition (stop lower court), Certiorari (transfer case), Quo Warranto (challenge to public office).
Mains strategy
Constitutional law answers: constitutional provision (Article number) → judicial interpretation (Supreme Court judgments) → practical application → critical analysis (pros/cons, reforms). Raj Narain (judicial review of elections), Minerva Mills (balance between FR & DPSP), S.R. Technique: IPC Sections answer
Question: 'What is the difference between culpable homicide and murder?'
Answer: Culpable homicide (Section 299): causing death by doing an act with intention of causing death, or with intention of causing bodily injury likely to cause death, or with knowledge that act is likely to cause death. Murder (Section 300): culpable homicide is murder if (a) intention to cause death, (b) intention to cause bodily injury likely to cause death, (c) intention to cause bodily injury sufficient to cause death, (d) act imminently dangerous and likely to cause death, with knowledge. All murders are culpable homicide but all culpable homicides are not murder. Exceptions to murder: grave and sudden provocation, private defence, public servant acting in good faith, sudden fight, consent (death of person above 18 years who consents).

Common Traps

  • Confusing culpable homicide with murder - all murders are culpable homicide but not vice versa.
  • Confusing theft with robbery - robbery requires violence or threat of violence.
  • Confusing robbery with dacoity - dacoity requires 5 or more persons.
  • Confusing wrongful restraint with wrongful confinement - wrongful restraint prevents movement in one direction, wrongful confinement prevents movement in all directions.
  • Missing that Section 300 contains exceptions (grave and sudden provocation, private defence, etc.) that reduce murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.

Memory Tricks

  • Stages of crime: Intention → Preparation → Attempt → Commission.
  • Degrees of homicide: Culpable homicide → Murder (with intent/intention to cause death) → Death by negligence (Section 304A).
  • Offences against property: Theft → Extortion (threat) → Robbery (violence/fear) → Dacoity (5+ persons).
  • Writs: Habeas Corpus (body), Mandamus (command), Prohibition (stop), Certiorari (transfer), Quo Warranto (authority).
Mains strategy

Technique: Culpable Homicide vs Murder
Question: 'A strikes B with a stick on the head. B dies. Is A guilty of murder or culpable homicide not amounting to murder?'
Answer: Depends on intention/knowledge. If A intended to cause death → murder (s.300). If A intended to cause bodily injury likely to cause death → murder (s.300). If A intended bodily injury sufficient in ordinary course to cause death → murder (s.300). If act imminently dangerous and likely to cause death or bodily injury, with knowledge → murder (s.300). If none of these, but culpable homicide (s.299) → culpable homicide not amounting to murder (s.299). Key: intention/knowledge of death.

Common Traps

  • Confusing culpable homicide with murder - all murders are culpable homicide but not vice versa.
  • Confusing theft with robbery - robbery requires violence or threat of violence (putting in fear of instant death/hurt/wrongful restraint).
  • Confusing robbery with dacoity - dacoity requires 5 or more persons committing robbery.
  • Confusing wrongful restraint with wrongful confinement - wrongful restraint prevents movement in one direction, wrongful confinement prevents movement in all directions within circumscribing limits.
  • Missing that Section 300 contains exceptions (grave and sudden provocation, private defence, sudden fight, consent) that reduce murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
  • Confusing confession (admission of guilt) with admission (statement suggesting inference about fact in issue).
  • Missing that confession to police officer (s.25) is inadmissible, but confession while in custody (s.26) is admissible only if made in presence of Magistrate.

Memory Tricks

  • Stages of crime: Intention → Preparation → Attempt → Commission.
  • Offences against property: Theft → Extortion (threat) → Robbery (violence/fear of instant death/hurt/wrongful restraint) → Dacoity (5+ persons).
  • Offences against body: Hurt → Grievous Hurt → Culpable Homicide → Murder (with intent/intention to cause death) → Death by negligence (Section 304A).
  • Writs: Habeas Corpus (body), Mandamus (command), Prohibition (stop lower court), Certiorari (transfer case), Quo Warranto (challenge to public office).
