opt-management/overview:
Management Optional — Overview & Syllabus Map

Management is a popular UPSC optional for commerce, management, and engineering graduates. Paper I covers management theory, organisation, leadership, motivation, decision-making, and organisational behaviour. Paper II covers human resource management, marketing, financial management, production/operations management, and strategic management.

Paper I — Management Concepts & Organisational Behaviour

  • Management: Definition, nature, scope, functions (planning, organising, staffing, directing, controlling), levels of management, managerial skills, Fayol's 14 principles, Taylor's scientific management.
  • Planning: Nature, importance, types (strategic, tactical, operational), process, limitations, MBO (Management by Objectives).
  • Organising: Organisation structure (line, functional, line & staff, matrix, project), departmentation, delegation, decentralisation, centralisation, span of control.
  • Staffing: Recruitment, selection, training, performance appraisal, promotion, transfer, career development.
  • Directing: Leadership (trait, behavioural, contingency theories), motivation (Maslow's hierarchy, Herzberg's two-factor, expectancy, equity, reinforcement), communication (process, barriers, grapevine), supervision.
  • Controlling: Control process, types (preliminary, concurrent, feedback), techniques (budgetary control, PERT/CPM, break-even analysis, ROI), limitations.
  • Organisational Behaviour: Individual behaviour (personality, perception, learning, attitudes, values, emotions), group behaviour (group dynamics, teams, teams vs groups, team building), organisational culture, organisational change, organisational development.
  • Motivation Theories: Maslow's hierarchy, Herzberg's two-factor, McGregor's Theory X & Y, Alderfer's ERG, McClelland's acquired needs, expectancy theory, equity theory, reinforcement theory.

Paper II — HRM, Marketing & Operations

  • Human Resource Management: HRM vs HRD, job analysis & description, recruitment & selection, training & development, performance appraisal, compensation & benefits, employee relations, grievance handling.
  • Marketing Management: Marketing concept, marketing mix (4Ps: product, price, place, promotion), STP (segmentation, targeting, positioning), product life cycle, pricing strategies, distribution channels, promotion mix, marketing environment, marketing research, consumer behaviour.
  • Financial Management: Financial objectives, capital budgeting (NPV, IRR, payback period), capital structure (cost of capital, WACC, leverage), working capital management, dividend policy, working capital management.
  • Production & Operations Management: Production planning & control, inventory management (EOQ, EOQ model), quality control (TQM, Six Sigma, ISO 9000), inventory management (ABC analysis, JIT), project management (PERT, CPM), facility location & layout.
  • Strategic Management: Strategic management process, SWOT analysis, Porter's five forces, value chain, generic strategies (cost leadership, differentiation, focus), corporate level, business level, functional level strategies, strategic implementation & control.
Technique: Herzberg's Two-Factor Theory
Question: 'Explain Herzberg's two-factor theory of motivation.'
Answer: Herzberg's two-factor theory distinguishes between motivators (intrinsic factors: achievement, recognition, work itself, responsibility, advancement, growth) that create job satisfaction, and hygiene factors (extrinsic factors: company policy, supervision, salary, interpersonal relations, working conditions) that prevent dissatisfaction but don't motivate. Absence of hygiene factors causes dissatisfaction, but their presence doesn't motivate—only motivators do.

Memory Tricks

  • Fayol's 14 Principles: Division of work, authority & responsibility, discipline, unity of command, unity of direction, subordination of individual interest, remuneration, centralisation, scalar chain, order, equity, stability of tenure, initiative, esprit de corps.
  • Maslow's Hierarchy: Physiological, Safety, Love/Belonging, Esteem, Self-actualization.
  • 4Ps of Marketing: Product, Price, Place, Promotion.
  • Porter's Five Forces: Threat of new entrants, bargaining power of buyers, bargaining power of suppliers, threat of substitutes, competitive rivalry.
Mains strategy
Management answers: concept → definition → theory/theorist → application → example → conclusion. Draw diagrams (Maslow's pyramid, BCG matrix, SWOT, Porter's five forces, organisational structure diagrams). Quote management thinkers (Fayol, Taylor, Maslow, Herzberg, McGregor, Drucker, Porter, Kotler). Quote data: India's GDP growth, MSME contribution (~30% of GDP, ~11 crore employment), startup ecosystem (~100,000+ startups, 100+ unicorns), Make in India, Startup India.
opt-management/paper1:
Management Paper I — Management Concepts & Organisational Behaviour

Management: Nature, Scope & Functions

  • Definition: Management is the process of planning, organising, leading, and controlling resources to achieve organisational goals efficiently and effectively.
  • Functions of Management: Planning (setting objectives, deciding course of action), Organising (grouping activities, assigning resources), Staffing (recruitment, selection, training), Directing (leading, motivating, communicating), Controlling (monitoring performance, taking corrective action).
  • Levels of Management: Top-level (strategic, board/CEO), Middle-level (department heads, implementation), First-line/supervisory (supervisors, day-to-day operations).
  • Managerial Skills: Technical skills (specialised knowledge), Human skills (working with people), Conceptual skills (abstract thinking, seeing the organisation as a whole).

Fayol's 14 Principles of Management

  • 1. Division of Work — specialisation increases efficiency
  • 2. Authority & Responsibility — authority brings responsibility
  • 3. Discipline: obedience, respect for authority
  • 4. Unity of Command: one employee, one boss
  • 5. Unity of Direction: one head, one plan for a group
  • 6. Subordination of Individual Interest: general interest over individual interest
  • 7. Remuneration: fair pay for both employee and employer
  • 8. Centralisation: degree to which authority is concentrated
  • 9. Scalar Chain: chain of superiors from top to bottom
  • 10. Order: right place for everything and everyone
  • 11. Equity: kindliness and justice
  • 12. Stability of Tenure: stable workforce reduces turnover
  • 13. Initiative: freedom to think out and execute plans
  • 14. Esprit de Corps: team spirit, union is strength

Planning

  • Nature: primary function, intellectual process, goal-oriented, pervasive
  • Types: Strategic (long-term, top-level), Tactical (medium-term, middle-level), Operational (short-term, lower-level)
  • Planning Process: Establish objectives → Identify alternatives → Evaluate alternatives → Select alternative → Implement plan → Follow up
  • MBO (Management by Objectives): Peter Drucker — joint goal setting between manager and subordinate, periodic review, focus on results
  • Limitations: Rigidity, time-consuming, costly, inability to predict future accurately

Organising

  • Organisational Structures: Line (direct authority), Functional (specialisation), Line & Staff (combination), Matrix (dual reporting), Divisional (product/geography based), Matrix (project + function)
  • Departmentation: Grouping activities into departments (by function, product, territory, customer, process, time)
  • Delegation: Assigning authority and responsibility to subordinates — elements: authority, responsibility, accountability
  • Decentralisation: Dispersal of decision-making authority to lower levels — advantages: quicker decisions, executive development, motivation; disadvantages: lack of uniformity, coordination problems
  • Span of Control: Number of subordinates a supervisor can effectively manage — narrow span (tall structure) vs wide span (flat structure)

Staffing

  • Recruitment: Internal (promotions, transfers) & External (advertisements, campus recruitment, employment agencies)
  • Selection: Application, screening, tests, interviews, reference checks, medical examination, selection decision
  • Training & Development: On-the-job (apprenticeship, coaching, job rotation) & Off-the-job (lectures, case studies, simulations)
  • Performance Appraisal: Methods — Graphic rating scale, 360-degree feedback, MBO, BARS (Behaviourally Anchored Rating Scales)

Directing

  • Leadership Theories: Trait theory (born leaders), Behavioural theories (Ohio State, Michigan studies), Contingency theory (Fiedler's contingency model, Hersey-Blanchard situational leadership)
  • Motivation Theories:
    • Maslow's Hierarchy: Physiological → Safety → Social → Esteem → Self-actualisation
    • Herzberg's Two-Factor: Motivators (achievement, recognition, work itself, responsibility, advancement, growth) vs Hygiene factors (company policy, supervision, salary, interpersonal relations, working conditions)
    • McGregor's Theory X (negative view of employees) vs Theory Y (positive view)
    • Expectancy Theory (Vroom): Motivation = Expectancy × Instrumentality × Valence
    • Equity Theory (Adams): Inputs/outcomes comparison with others
  • Communication: Communication process (sender, encoding, channel, receiver, decoding, feedback), Barriers (semantic, psychological, physical, organisational), Grapevine (informal communication)

Controlling

  • Control Process: Establish standards → Measure performance → Compare actual with standards → Take corrective action
  • Types: Feedforward (preliminary/feedforward), Concurrent (during), Feedback (after)
  • Techniques: Budgetary control, PERT/CPM, Break-even analysis, ROI (Return on Investment), Management audit
  • Limitations: External factors beyond control, employee resistance, costly, time-consuming
Technique: Maslow's Hierarchy Application
Question: 'How does Maslow's hierarchy apply to employee motivation?'
Answer: Employees progress through levels: physiological (salary), safety (job security), love/belonging (team belonging), esteem (recognition, promotion), self-actualisation (growth, creativity). Once lower needs are met, higher needs become motivators.

Memory Tricks

  • Fayol's 14: DC UA SR SC SO RI SC ST SD IF RM SS ED SI ED ER — Division of work, Unity of command, Scalar chain, Remuneration, Equity, Stability of tenure, Initiative, Esprit de corps, Centralisation, Order, Subordination of individual interest, Remuneration (wait, that's duplicated — let me just say: Division of work, Authority & responsibility, Discipline, Unity of command, Unity of direction, Subordination of individual interest, Remuneration, Centralisation, Scalar chain, Order, Equity, Stability of tenure, Initiative, Esprit de corps
  • Management Functions: POSDCORB — Planning, Organising, Staffing, Directing, Coordinating, Reporting, Budgeting.
  • Maslow: Physiological, Safety, Love/Belonging, Esteem, Self-actualisation.
  • 4Ps of Marketing: Product, Price, Place, Promotion.
Mains strategy
Management answers: definition → theory/theorist → application → example → conclusion. Draw diagrams (Maslow's pyramid, organisational structure charts, SWOT matrix, Porter's five forces). Quote thinkers: Fayol, Taylor, Maslow, Herzberg, McGregor, Drucker, Porter, Kotler, Fayol.
opt-management/paper2:
Management Paper II — HRM, Marketing, Financial Management & Operations

Human Resource Management

  • HRM vs HRD: HRM (maintenance, administration) vs HRD (development, growth of people).
  • Job Analysis: Job analysis (process of collecting info about jobs), Job description (duties, responsibilities), Job specification (qualifications, skills, experience required).
  • Recruitment: Internal sources (promotions, transfers, employee referrals) & External sources (advertisements, employment exchanges, campus recruitment, labour contractors).
  • Selection: Application form, preliminary interview, selection tests (intelligence, aptitude, proficiency, personality), interview, reference check, medical examination, final selection.
  • Training & Development: On-the-job (apprenticeship, coaching, job rotation, internship) & Off-the-job (lectures, case studies, role playing, simulation, vestibule training).
  • Performance Appraisal: Methods — Traditional (ranking, paired comparison, graphic rating scale, checklist), Modern (MBO, 360-degree feedback, BARS, Assessment centre).
  • Compensation: Components — Basic pay, Dearness allowance, House rent allowance, Incentives, Fringe benefits (provident fund, gratuity, insurance, medical).
  • Industrial Relations: Trade unions, Collective bargaining, Grievance procedure, Industrial disputes (strike, lockout), Labour laws (Factories Act 1948, Industrial Disputes Act 1947, Minimum Wages Act 1948, Payment of Wages Act 1936, Employees' Provident Fund Act 1952, Employees' State Insurance Act 1948).

Marketing Management

  • Marketing Concept: Production concept, Product concept, Selling concept, Marketing concept, Societal marketing concept.
  • Marketing Mix (4Ps): Product (product mix, product life cycle — introduction, growth, maturity, decline), Price (pricing methods — cost-plus, skimming, penetration, psychological, differential), Place (channels of distribution — direct, indirect, intensive/selective/exclusive distribution), Promotion (promotion mix — advertising, personal selling, sales promotion, public relations, direct marketing).
  • STP Framework: Segmentation (geographic, demographic, psychographic, behavioural), Targeting (undifferentiated, differentiated, concentrated), Positioning (positioning statement, perceptual mapping).
  • Consumer Behaviour: Buying decision process (need recognition, information search, evaluation of alternatives, purchase decision, post-purchase behaviour), Factors affecting consumer behaviour (cultural, social, personal, psychological).
  • Marketing Research: Marketing research process (define problem, develop research plan, collect information, analyse information, present findings), Marketing Information System (MIS).

Financial Management

  • Financial Management: Meaning, scope, objectives (profit maximisation vs wealth maximisation), finance functions (investment, financing, dividend, liquidity decisions).
  • Capital Budgeting: Techniques — Payback period, Accounting rate of return, Net Present Value (NPV), Internal Rate of Return (IRR), Profitability Index.
  • Capital Structure: Capital structure (mix of debt and equity), Cost of capital (cost of debt, cost of equity, WACC), Leverage (operating leverage, financial leverage, combined leverage), Capital structure theories (Net income approach, Net operating income approach, Traditional approach, MM approach).
  • Working Capital Management: Working capital (gross & net), Factors affecting working capital, Cash management (motives for holding cash, cash management), Receivables management (credit policy, credit terms, collection policy), Inventory management (EOQ, ABC analysis, JIT).
  • Dividend Policy: Dividend policy factors (earnings stability, cash flow position, growth opportunities, legal constraints, shareholder preferences), Dividend models (Walter's model, Gordon's growth model, MM hypothesis), Bonus shares & Stock split.

Production & Operations Management

  • Production Planning & Control: Production planning (routing, scheduling, dispatching, follow-up), Production control (dispatching, expediting, inspection, corrective action).
  • Inventory Management: Inventory costs (ordering cost, carrying cost, shortage cost), EOQ (Economic Order Quantity = √(2DS/H)), ABC analysis, JIT (Just-in-Time), MRP (Material Requirements Planning).
  • Quality Management: Quality control (inspection, statistical quality control), TQM (Total Quality Management), Six Sigma (DMAIC — Define, Measure, Analyse, Improve, Control), ISO 9000 series, Kaizen.
  • Facility Location & Layout: Factors affecting location (proximity to market, raw materials, labour, transportation, utilities), Layout types (process layout, product layout, fixed position layout, combination layout).
  • Project Management: PERT (Program Evaluation & Review Technique), CPM (Critical Path Method), Critical path, Float/Slack, Crashing.
Technique: EOQ Calculation
Question: Annual demand = 10,000 units, Ordering cost = ₹100 per order, Holding cost = ₹5 per unit per year. Calculate EOQ.
Answer: EOQ = √(2DS/H) = √(2 × 10,000 × 100 / 5) = √(200,000) ≈ 447 units. Annual ordering cost = (D/Q) × S = (10,000/447) × 100 ≈ ₹2,237. Annual holding cost = (Q/2) × H = (447/2) × 5 ≈ ₹1,117.50.

Memory Tricks

  • POSDCORB: Planning, Organising, Staffing, Directing, Coordinating, Reporting, Budgeting.
  • 4Ps of Marketing: Product, Price, Place, Promotion.
  • STP: Segmentation, Targeting, Positioning.
  • Porter's Five Forces: Threat of new entrants, Bargaining power of buyers, Bargaining power of suppliers, Threat of substitutes, Competitive rivalry.
  • BCG Matrix: Stars (high growth, high share), Cash cows (low growth, high share), Question marks (high growth, low share), Dogs (low growth, low share).
Mains strategy
Management answers: theory → application → example → conclusion. Draw diagrams (Porter's five forces, BCG matrix, SWOT, product life cycle, organisational structure). Quote thinkers (Fayol, Taylor, Maslow, Herzberg, McGregor, Drucker, Porter, Kotler). Data: India's GDP growth, MSME contribution (~30% GDP), Startup India (~100+ unicorns), Make in India, Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme.
opt-mathematics/overview:
Mathematics Optional — Overview & Syllabus

Mathematics is a popular optional for mathematics/engineering graduates with a highly scoring, objective syllabus. Paper I covers Linear Algebra, Calculus, Real Analysis, Ordinary Differential Equations. Paper II covers Algebra, Complex Analysis, Ordinary & Partial Differential Equations, Statics & Dynamics, Vector Analysis.

Paper I — Linear Algebra, Calculus, Real Analysis, ODE

  • Vector Spaces: Vector spaces over R/C, subspaces, linear independence, basis & dimension, dimension theorem, quotient spaces, direct sum, dual space, dual basis.
  • Linear Transformations: Linear transformations, kernel & image, rank & nullity, rank-nullity theorem, matrix representation, change of basis, eigenvalues & eigenvectors, characteristic polynomial, minimal polynomial, Cayley-Hamilton theorem, diagonalization, Jordan canonical form.
  • Inner Product Spaces: Inner product, norm, angle between vectors, orthogonality, orthonormal sets, Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization, Bessel's inequality, Parseval's identity, projection theorem, adjoint of linear operator, self-adjoint, normal, unitary/unitary operators.
  • Canonical Forms: Jordan canonical form, rational canonical form, elementary divisors, invariant factors.
  • Real Analysis: Real number system (completeness, Archimedean property), sequences & series (convergence, Cauchy sequences, monotone convergence, Bolzano-Weierstrass, Cauchy criterion), series of positive terms (comparison test, ratio test, root test, integral test), absolute & conditional convergence, rearrangements.
  • Continuity & Differentiability: Continuity & discontinuity, uniform continuity, intermediate value theorem, extreme value theorem, differentiation, mean value theorem (Rolle's, Lagrange's, Cauchy's), Taylor's theorem with remainder, L'Hôpital's rule, Taylor series, Taylor series expansion, analytic functions.
  • Riemann Integration: Riemann integral, Darboux sums, integrability criteria, fundamental theorem of calculus, mean value theorem for integrals, improper integrals (absolute & conditional convergence, comparison test, beta & gamma functions).
  • Sequences & Series of Functions: Pointwise & uniform convergence, uniform convergence & continuity/differentiability/integration, Weierstrass M-test, uniform convergence & differentiation/integration interchange, power series (radius of convergence, Abel's theorem), Taylor series, Fourier series (Fourier coefficients, convergence, Gibbs phenomenon).
  • Functions of Several Variables: Limits & continuity in R^n, partial derivatives, differentiability, chain rule, directional derivatives, gradient, implicit function theorem, inverse function theorem, maxima & minima (Lagrange multipliers), multiple integrals (Fubini's theorem, change of variables), improper integrals (beta & gamma functions).

Paper II — Algebra, Complex Analysis, ODE & PDE, Mechanics

  • Algebra: Groups (definition, examples, subgroups, cyclic groups, permutation groups, Lagrange's theorem, cosets, normal subgroups, quotient groups, homomorphisms & isomorphisms, isomorphism theorems), Rings (definition, examples, ideals, quotient rings, prime & maximal ideals, Euclidean domains, PID, UFD), Fields (definition, examples, field extensions, algebraic & transcendental extensions, finite fields, Galois theory basics), Matrices (rank, inverse, elementary operations, canonical forms, Smith normal form).
  • Complex Analysis: Complex numbers, complex functions, analyticity, Cauchy-Riemann equations, harmonic functions, contour integration, Cauchy's theorem, Cauchy's integral formula, Liouville's theorem, maximum modulus principle, Taylor series, Laurent series, singularities (isolated singularities, poles, essential singularities), residue theorem, residue calculus, evaluation of real integrals, argument principle, Rouché's theorem, conformal mapping.
  • Ordinary Differential Equations: First order ODE (separable, linear, exact, integrating factors, Bernoulli, Riccati), higher order linear ODE (homogeneous & non-homogeneous, method of undetermined coefficients, variation of parameters), systems of linear ODEs, power series solutions (Frobenius method), special functions (Bessel, Legendre, Hermite, Laguerre), Sturm-Liouville theory.
  • Partial Differential Equations: First order PDE (Lagrange's method, Charpit's method), second order linear PDE (classification: elliptic, parabolic, hyperbolic), wave equation, heat equation, Laplace equation, separation of variables, Fourier series solutions, D'Alembert's solution, Duhamel's principle, Green's functions.
  • Mechanics: Particle kinematics (rectilinear & curvilinear motion, velocity, acceleration), dynamics (Newton's laws, work-energy theorem, impulse-momentum), work-energy theorem, conservation laws (energy, momentum, angular momentum), central force motion (Kepler's laws, orbital motion), simple harmonic motion, damped & forced oscillations, rigid body dynamics (moment of inertia, angular momentum, Euler's equations), friction (dry friction, rolling friction).
  • Vector Analysis: Vector algebra (dot product, cross product, scalar triple product, vector triple product), vector differentiation (gradient, divergence, curl), vector integration (line integrals, surface integrals, volume integrals), Green's theorem, Gauss divergence theorem, Stokes' theorem, curvilinear coordinates.
Technique: Cauchy-Riemann equations
Question: 'Show that f(z) = z^2 is analytic everywhere.'
Answer: f(z) = z^2 = (x+iy)^2 = x^2 - y^2 + 2ixy. So u(x,y) = x^2 - y^2, v(x,y) = 2xy. Compute partial derivatives: u_x = 2x, u_y = -2y, v_x = 2y, v_y = 2x. Check Cauchy-Riemann: u_x = v_y (2x = 2x) ✓, u_y = -v_x (-2y = -2y) ✓. Since u_x, u_y, v_x, v_y are continuous and C-R equations hold everywhere, f(z) = z^2 is analytic everywhere (entire function).

Memory Tricks

  • CR equations: u_x = v_y, u_y = -v_x (u_x = v_y, u_y = -v_x — "x with x, y with -y").
  • Integration by parts: ∫u dv = uv - ∫v du (LIATE rule for choosing u: Logarithmic, Inverse trig, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential).
  • Convergence tests: p-series (∑1/n^p converges if p>1), geometric series (∑ar^n converges if |r|<1), ratio test, root test, comparison test, integral test.
  • Laplace transforms: L{f'(t)} = sF(s) - f(0), L{f''(t)} = s^2F(s) - sf(0) - f'(0).
Mains strategy
Math answers: theorem statement → statement of conditions → proof step by step → application → conclusion. Show every step clearly; no skipping. Quote theorems with names (Cauchy-Schwarz, Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, Bolzano-Weierstrass, Heine-Borel, Arzela-Ascoli, Picard's existence & uniqueness theorem). Data: India's R&D spending (~0.7% of GDP), number of researchers per million, math education institutions (IITs, IISERs, IISERs, CMI, IMSc, ISI).
opt-physics/paper1:
Physics Paper I — Classical Mechanics, Quantum Mechanics, Thermodynamics

Classical Mechanics

  • Newtonian Mechanics: Newton's laws of motion, inertial & non-inertial frames, fictitious forces, conservation laws (energy, momentum, angular momentum), work-energy theorem, conservative forces, potential energy.
  • Lagrangian Mechanics: Generalized coordinates, generalized momenta, Lagrange's equations, principle of least action (Hamilton's principle), cyclic coordinates & conservation laws, Routhian.
  • Hamiltonian Mechanics: Hamiltonian formulation, Hamilton's equations, phase space, Poisson brackets, canonical transformations, Poisson brackets & quantum mechanics connection.
  • Central Force Motion: Kepler's laws, effective potential, bound & unbound orbits, Kepler's problem, scattering cross-section (Rutherford scattering), Rutherford formula.
  • Small Oscillations: Stable equilibrium, normal modes, coupled oscillators, forced oscillations, resonance, damped oscillations, quality factor Q.
  • Rigid Body Dynamics: Euler angles, Euler angles & Euler angles, angular momentum, moment of inertia tensor, principal axes, Euler's equations, free symmetric top, heavy symmetric top (gyroscope), precession & nutation.

Quantum Mechanics

  • Foundations: Wave-particle duality, de Broglie hypothesis, Heisenberg uncertainty principle, Schrödinger equation (time-dependent & time-independent), wave function & probability interpretation, normalization.
  • 1D Problems: Infinite square well, finite square well, harmonic oscillator (operator method), free particle, potential step, potential barrier (tunneling), delta function potential.
  • 3D Problems: Spherical coordinates, spherical harmonics, hydrogen atom (energy levels, degeneracy, selection rules), angular momentum (L^2, L_z operators), spin (Pauli matrices, spin-1/2), addition of angular momenta (Clebsch-Gordan coefficients).
  • Approximation Methods: Time-independent perturbation theory (non-degenerate & degenerate), variational method, WKB approximation, time-dependent perturbation theory (Fermi's golden rule), sudden & adiabatic approximations.
  • Identical Particles: Symmetric & antisymmetric wave functions, bosons & fermions, exchange symmetry, Pauli exclusion principle.

Thermodynamics & Statistical Mechanics

  • Thermodynamics: Zeroth law (temperature), First law (energy conservation), Second law (entropy, Carnot cycle, efficiency), Third law (Nernst theorem), thermodynamic potentials (internal energy, enthalpy, Helmholtz free energy, Gibbs free energy), Maxwell relations, phase transitions (first & second order), Clausius-Clapeyron equation.
  • Statistical Mechanics: Microcanonical ensemble, canonical ensemble (canonical distribution, partition function), grand canonical ensemble, Maxwell-Boltzmann statistics, Bose-Einstein statistics, Fermi-Dirac statistics, ideal gas (classical & quantum), blackbody radiation (Planck's law), Bose-Einstein condensation, Fermi gas (Fermi energy, degeneracy pressure).
  • Statistical Mechanics Applications: Ideal gas (classical & quantum), blackbody radiation, specific heat of solids (Dulong-Petit, Einstein, Debye models), paramagnetism (Curie's law, Pauli paramagnetism, ferromagnetism - Ising model mean field), Bose-Einstein condensation.
  • Phase Transitions: First order vs second order phase transitions, order parameter, critical exponents, scaling laws, universality classes, mean field theory (Ising model - mean field approximation, critical exponents).
Technique: Schrödinger Equation - Infinite Square Well
Question: Solve the time-independent Schrödinger equation for a particle in a 1D infinite square well of width L.
Answer: V(x) = 0 for 0 < x < L, V(x) = ∞ elsewhere. TISE: -ℏ²/2m d²ψ/dx² = Eψ. General solution: ψ(x) = A sin(kx) + B cos(kx). Boundary conditions: ψ(0) = 0 → B = 0, ψ(L) = 0 → kL = nπ, k = nπ/L. Energy: E_n = n²π²ℏ²/(2mL²) = n²π²ℏ²/(2mL²). Normalized wavefunction: ψ_n(x) = √(2/L) sin(nπx/L), n = 1,2,3,...

Memory Tricks

  • Schrödinger Equation: iℏ∂ψ/∂t = Ĥψ (time-dependent), Ĥψ = Eψ (time-independent).
  • Schrödinger Equation: iℏ∂ψ/∂t = Ĥψ (time-dependent), Ĥψ = Eψ (time-independent).
  • Thermodynamics Laws: 0th = thermal equilibrium, 1st = energy conservation, 2nd = entropy increases, 3rd = S → 0 as T → 0.
  • Quantum numbers: n (principal), l (azimuthal), m_l (magnetic), m_s (spin).
Mains strategy
Physics answers: derive from first principles, show all steps, use diagrams (Feynman diagrams, Feynman diagrams, phase space diagrams, potential energy diagrams). Quote constants (ħ, c, G, k_B, e, m_e, m_p), quote experiments (Michelson-Morley, photoelectric effect, Stern-Gerlach, double-slit experiment). Data: fundamental constants, standard model particles, cosmological parameters.
opt-psychology/overview:
Psychology Optional — Overview & Syllabus Map

Psychology is a popular optional for psychology, sociology, and humanities graduates. Paper I covers foundations of psychology, cognitive processes, human development, personality, motivation, emotion, intelligence. Paper II covers social psychology, abnormal psychology, counseling psychology, organizational psychology, applied psychology.

Paper I — Foundations of Psychology

  • Foundations of Psychology: Definition, nature, scope, goals of psychology (description, explanation, prediction, control), schools of psychology (structuralism - Wundt, functionalism - James, psychoanalysis - Freud, behaviorism - Watson, humanistic - Maslow & Rogers, cognitive, evolutionary, positive psychology - Seligman), schools of thought, research methods (experimental, correlational, survey, case study, observational, ethnographic), ethical considerations in psychological research.
  • Sensory Processes: Sensation & perception, absolute threshold & difference threshold (Weber's law), signal detection theory, subliminal perception, visual system (eye structure, visual pathways, color vision - trichromatic & opponent-process theories, form perception, depth perception - binocular & monocular cues, perceptual constancies - size, shape, brightness, color constancy), auditory system (ear structure, pitch & loudness perception), other senses (olfaction, gustation, touch, kinesthesis, vestibular sense), attention (selective, divided, sustained), inattentional blindness, change blindness.
  • Perception: Perceptual processes (figure-ground, grouping principles - Gestalt principles: proximity, similarity, continuity, closure, common fate, simplicity), depth perception (monocular cues - relative size, interposition, linear perspective, texture gradient, motion parallax, aerial perspective; binocular cues - retinal disparity, convergence), perceptual constancies (size, shape, color, brightness, shape constancy), illusions (Muller-Lyer, Ponzo, Ames room, Necker cube, Rubin's vase), extrasensory perception (ESP - claims & evidence).
  • Learning: Classical conditioning (Pavlov - acquisition, extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalization, discrimination), operant conditioning (Skinner - reinforcement & punishment schedules - fixed ratio, variable ratio, fixed interval, variable interval, shaping, chaining, primary & secondary reinforcers), observational learning (Bandura - observational learning, mirror neurons), cognitive learning (cognitive maps - Tolman, insight learning - Kohler), biological constraints on learning (Garcia effect - taste aversion).
  • Memory: Memory models (sensory memory - iconic & echoic, short-term/working memory - Baddeley's model: phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, episodic buffer, central executive; long-term memory - declarative/explicit - episodic & semantic, procedural/implicit), levels of processing (Craik & Lockhart), forgetting (forgetting curve - Ebbinghaus, interference - proactive & retroactive, decay, repression), memory improvement techniques (mnemonics, spacing effect, retrieval practice, elaborative rehearsal), memory distortions & false memories.
  • Thinking & Problem Solving: Thinking (concepts & concepts formation, prototypes, mental sets, functional fixedness), problem solving (algorithms, heuristics - availability, representativeness, anchoring, insight, means-end analysis, working backward), decision making (bounded rationality - Simon, heuristics & biases - Kahneman & Tversky - availability heuristic, representativeness heuristic, anchoring & adjustment heuristic, framing effect, loss aversion), creativity (divergent vs convergent thinking, creativity tests, stages of creative process).
  • Thinking & Language: Language development (babbling, holophrastic stage, telegraphic speech, overregularization), language acquisition theories (Chomsky's LAD - language acquisition device, Skinner's behaviorist view, social interactionist theory - Vygotsky), bilingualism, language & thought (linguistic relativity - Sapir-Whorf hypothesis), artificial intelligence & cognitive science.

Paper II — Social Psychology, Abnormal Psychology, Applied Psychology

  • Social Psychology: Social cognition (schemas, stereotypes, prejudice, attribution theory - internal & external attribution, fundamental attribution error, self-serving bias, actor-observer bias), attitudes (attitude formation, attitude change - cognitive dissonance - Festinger, elaboration likelihood model - central & peripheral routes), social influence (conformity - Asch, compliance - foot-in-door, door-in-face, low-ball, obedience - Milgram, Zimbardo's prison study), group behavior (social facilitation, social loafing, deindividuation, group polarization, groupthink), leadership (trait theory, behavioral theory, contingency theory, transformational & transactional leadership), prosocial behavior (altruism, bystander effect - Darley & Latane, diffusion of responsibility, empathy - empathy-altruism hypothesis), aggression (biological, social learning, frustration-aggression hypothesis), interpersonal attraction (propinquity, similarity, physical attractiveness, reciprocity), love (Sternberg's triangular theory of love - intimacy, passion, commitment).
  • Personality: Trait theories (Allport, Cattell - 16PF, Eysenck - PEN, Big Five - OCEAN: openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism), psychodynamic theory (Freud - psychosexual stages, id/ego/superego, defense mechanisms - repression, repression, projection, displacement, reaction formation, regression, sublimation, denial, rationalization, reaction formation), humanistic theory (Maslow - hierarchy of needs, Rogers - unconditional positive regard, self-actualization), trait approach (Big Five), social-cognitive theory (Bandura - self-efficacy, reciprocal determinism, observational learning), biological & evolutionary approaches (heritability of personality traits, temperament - Chess & Thomas, evolutionary psychology - evolutionary psychology of personality).
  • Human Development: Prenatal development (germinal, embryonic, fetal stages), infancy & childhood (Piaget's cognitive development stages - sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, formal operational; Erikson's psychosocial stages - trust vs mistrust, autonomy vs shame, initiative vs guilt, industry vs inferiority, identity vs role confusion, intimacy vs isolation, generativity vs stagnation, integrity vs despair; Kohlberg's moral development stages - preconventional, conventional, postconventional; attachment theory - Bowlby & Ainsworth - secure, avoidant, resistant, disorganized attachment), adolescence (adolescent development - identity vs role confusion, peer relationships, risk-taking behavior, adolescent pregnancy, eating disorders), adulthood (Erikson's stages - intimacy vs isolation, generativity vs stagnation, integrity vs despair), aging (successful aging - Rowe & Kub, successful aging models, successful aging & successful aging theories, wisdom, death & dying - Kubler-Ross stages - denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance).
Technique: Classical Conditioning
Question: 'Explain Pavlov's classical conditioning with an example.'
Answer: Classical conditioning: A neutral stimulus (bell) is paired with an unconditioned stimulus (food) that naturally elicits an unconditioned response (salivation). After repeated pairings, the neutral stimulus (bell) becomes a conditioned stimulus that elicits a conditioned response (salivation). Example: Pavlov's dogs - bell rings → food presented → salivation; after pairings, bell alone → salivation. Components: NS (bell) → CS, UCS (food) → UCR (salivation), CS (bell) → CR (salivation). Acquisition, extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalization, discrimination.

Memory Tricks

  • Piaget's stages: Sensorimotor (0-2), Preoperational (2-7), Concrete operational (7-11), Formal operational (11+) = "Sensorimotor, Preoperational, Concrete, Formal = SPCC" → "Some People Can Fly" (Sensorimotor, Preoperational, Concrete, Formal).
  • Erikson's stages: Trust vs mistrust, Autonomy vs shame, Initiative vs guilt, Industry vs inferiority, Identity vs role confusion, Intimacy vs isolation, Generativity vs stagnation, Integrity vs despair = "Trust, Autonomy, Initiative, Industry, Identity, Intimacy, Generativity, Integrity" = "T A I I I I G I".
  • Big Five: OCEAN - Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism = "CANOE".
  • Kohlberg's stages: Preconventional (punishment & reward), Conventional (good boy/good girl, law & order), Postconventional (social contract, universal principles).
Mains strategy
Psychology answers: theory → theorist → experiment/study → application → criticism → conclusion. Draw diagrams (Maslow's pyramid, Piaget's stages, Erikson's stages, brain structures - limbic system, brain lobes, neuron structure). Quote theories & theorists (Freud, Erikson, Piaget, Kohlberg, Maslow, Rogers, Bandura, Pavlov, Watson, Skinner, Bandura, Kohlberg, Gilligan, Sternberg, Gardner, Goleman). Data: India's mental health statistics (NMHS 2015-16 - 10.6% mental disorders, treatment gap ~90%), suicide rates, substance abuse statistics, mental health infrastructure (NMHP - National Mental Health Programme, NMHP - District Mental Health Programme).
opt-public-administration/overview:
Public Administration Optional — Overview

Public Administration is a popular optional with significant overlap with GS II (governance, constitution, polity, social justice) and essay. Paper I covers administrative theory, theories of organization, administrative behavior, personnel administration, financial administration. Paper II covers Indian administration, constitutional framework, union government, state government, district administration, local government, financial administration, public sector undertaking, development administration, administrative law, administrative reforms, e-governance.

Paper I — Administrative Theory & Organization

  • Meaning, Nature & Scope of Public Administration: Public administration as art & science, evolution of public administration (classical, human relations, behavioral, systems, ecological, new public administration, new public management), public administration vs private administration, principles of public administration, role of public administration in modern state (welfare state, development administration, good governance).
  • Theories of Organization: Classical theory (Fayol's 14 principles, Taylor's scientific management), Human relations theory (Mayo's Hawthorne studies), Behavioral approach (Chester Barnard - zone of indifference, informal organization), Systems theory (Ludwig von Bertalanffy, Katz & Kahn, general system theory), Ecological approach (Fred Riggs - prismatic society, fused-prismatic-prismatic society, agrarian, industrial, prismatic societies), Public choice theory (Buchanan & Tullock, economic analysis of bureaucracy), New Public Administration (dwight waldo - relevance, values, client focus, change, equity), New Public Management (Hood, Osborne & Gaebler - entrepreneurial government, market-based management, results orientation).
  • Principles of Organization: Division of work, unity of command, unity of direction, span of control, delegation, decentralization, centralization, hierarchy, unity of command, discipline, unity of direction, subordination of individual interest, remuneration, stability of tenure, initiative, esprit de corps.
  • Administrative Behaviour: Motivation (Maslow's hierarchy, Herzberg's two-factor, McGregor's Theory X & Y, Vroom's expectancy theory, Adams' equity theory), leadership (trait theory, behavioral theory, situational/contingency theory, transformational & transactional leadership), communication (communication process, barriers to communication, upward/downward/horizontal communication), motivation & morale, leadership styles (autocratic, democratic, laissez-faire, transformational, transactional, charismatic, servant leadership).
  • Administrative Behaviour (Herbert Simon): Bounded rationality, satisficing vs maximizing, decision-making process (intelligence, design, choice, implementation), programmed vs non-programmed decisions, administrative behavior, organizational theory.
  • Public Personnel Administration (HRM in Public Sector): Recruitment (merit system, patronage system), training (pre-service & in-service), performance appraisal, promotion, discipline & discipline, morale, motivation, collective bargaining, civil service neutrality, civil service neutrality, political neutrality, civil service neutrality.
  • Financial Administration: Budget (budget cycle: preparation, enactment, execution, audit), budget types (line-item, performance, program, zero-based, zero-based budgeting, zero-based budgeting), budgetary process (budget formulation, legislative approval, execution, accounting & auditing), fiscal policy, monetary policy, public debt, fiscal federalism (Centre-State financial relations, Finance Commission, GST Council).
  • Administrative Law: Rule of law (Dicey's three principles), administrative law (delegated legislation, administrative tribunals, ombudsman - Lokpal & Lokayukta, administrative adjudication, natural justice rules - rule against bias, audi alteram partem, right to be heard), public interest litigation (PIL), judicial review, writs (habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo warranto).
  • Development Administration: Development administration (F.W. Riggs - prismatic society model), development administration vs traditional administration, sustainable development, sustainable development goals (SDGs), good governance (World Bank indicators), citizen's charter, e-governance (National e-Governance Plan - NeGP, Digital India, MyGov, DigiLocker, UMANG), transparency & accountability (RTI Act 2005, social audit, citizen's charter, Lokpal & Lokayukta, Central Vigilance Commission, Central Information Commission).

Paper II — Indian Administration

Public Administration Paper I — Administrative Theory & Organisation

Meaning, Scope & Significance of Public Administration

  • Meaning: Public administration is the implementation of public policy and the management of public affairs. It is the machinery of the state that translates laws into action.
  • Nature: Public administration is both an art (practical application of skills) and a science (systematic body of knowledge). It is both a process (activities involved in getting things done) and a discipline (academic field of study).
  • Scope: Covers all activities of government - from policy formulation to implementation, from personnel management to financial administration, from local governance to international relations.
  • Public vs Private Administration: Public administration serves public interest, operates under public accountability, funded by public money, governed by public law. Private administration serves private interests, operates under market discipline, funded by private capital, governed by private contracts.
  • Role in Modern State: In a welfare state, public administration is the primary instrument of social and economic change. It delivers services, regulates economic activity, protects rights, and implements development programs.

Evolution of Administrative Thought

  • Classical Theory: Focuses on formal structure, division of labour, hierarchy, and efficiency. Taylor's scientific management emphasises standardisation, time-and-motion studies, and incentive systems. Fayol's 14 principles provide universal principles of management.
  • Bureaucratic Theory (Max Weber): Ideal bureaucracy based on hierarchical authority, division of labour, formal rules, impersonality, career orientation, and merit-based recruitment. Strengths: efficiency, predictability, impersonality. Limitations: rigidity, red tape, goal displacement.
  • Human Relations Theory (Elton Mayo): Emphasises social factors, group dynamics, worker motivation, and informal organisation. Hawthorne experiments showed that social factors and attention to workers affect productivity more than physical conditions.
  • Behavioural Approach (Chester Barnard, Herbert Simon): Chester Barnard - organisation as cooperative system, zone of indifference, functions of executive (maintaining organisational communication, securing essential services from individuals, defining purpose). Herbert Simon - bounded rationality, satisficing vs maximising, administrative man vs economic man.
  • Systems Theory: Organisation as open system interacting with environment through inputs, transformation, outputs, and feedback. Ludwig von Bertalanffy, Katz & Kahn - organisation as input-output system with feedback loops.
  • Ecological Approach (Fred Riggs): Prismatic society model - fused, prismatic, and prismatic societies. Ecological approach studies interaction between administrative systems and their environment.
  • New Public Administration: Waldo's New Public Administration emphasises relevance, values, equity, change, and client focus. Emphasises social equity, citizen participation, and adaptive administration.
  • New Public Management: Hood, Osborne & Gaebler - entrepreneurial government, market-based management, results orientation, customer focus, decentralisation, competition, and performance measurement.

Principles of Organisation

  • Division of Work: Specialisation increases efficiency through repetition and specialisation. Each worker should have a specific, limited task.
  • Authority & Responsibility: Authority is the right to give orders; responsibility is the obligation to perform. Authority and responsibility must be co-extensive.
  • Discipline: Obedience, respect for authority, and observance of rules are essential for organisational functioning.
  • Unity of Command: Each employee should receive orders from only one superior to avoid confusion and conflict.
  • Unity of Direction: One head and one plan for a group of activities having the same objective.
  • Subordination of Individual Interest: The interests of the organisation should take precedence over individual interests.
  • Remuneration: Fair remuneration satisfies both employees and employers. Should be fair and based on service rendered.
  • Centralisation: The degree to which authority is concentrated at the top levels of management.
  • Scalar Chain: The chain of superiors from highest to lowest ranks. Communications should follow this chain.
  • Order: A place for everything and everything in its place. Material order (right place for things) and social order (right person in right place).
  • Equity: Combination of kindness and justice. Managers should treat employees with kindness and justice.
  • Stability of Tenure: Stability of tenure produces good results. High turnover is wasteful and inefficient.
  • Initiative: Freedom to think out and execute plans. Initiative strengthens organisational capacity.
  • Esprit de Corps: Union is strength. Team spirit and harmony among employees.

Administrative Behaviour

  • Herbert Simon's Administrative Behaviour: Administrative man vs economic man. Bounded rationality - decision makers operate within cognitive and information constraints. Satisficing - choosing the first satisfactory option rather than optimising.
  • Decision Making Process: Intelligence phase (identifying problems), design phase (developing alternatives), choice phase (selecting alternative), implementation phase (implementing decision).
  • Herbert Simon's Contributions: Administrative behaviour focuses on how decisions are actually made in organisations. Organisational structure affects decision-making. Communication networks affect information flow.
  • Chester Barnard: Organisation as cooperative system. Functions of executive - maintaining organisational communication, securing essential services from individuals, defining and maintaining organisational purpose. Zone of acceptance - subordinates accept orders within zone of indifference.
Technique: Weberian Bureaucracy vs New Public Management
Question: 'Compare Weberian bureaucracy with New Public Management.'
Answer: Weberian bureaucracy emphasises hierarchy, formal rules, impersonality, career orientation, merit-based recruitment. NPM emphasizes market-orientation, customer focus, results orientation, decentralisation, and performance measurement. Weberian bureaucracy is rule-bound, hierarchical, and impersonal; NPM is flexible, market-oriented, and customer-focused.

Common Traps

  • Confusing bureaucracy with bureaucracy as pejorative term - in Max Weber's sense, bureaucracy is an ideal type with specific characteristics.
  • Assuming all organisations are the same - different organisational forms suit different environments and tasks.
  • Overlooking the role of informal organisation in formal organisations.
  • Assuming decentralisation is always better - centralisation has advantages in crisis situations and standardisation.

Memory Tricks

  • Fayol's 14 Principles: DC UA SR SC SO RI SC ST SD SI ED SI ED ER - Division of work, Authority & responsibility, Discipline, Unity of command, Unity of direction, Subordination of individual interest, Remuneration, Centralisation, Scalar chain, Order, Equity, Stability of tenure, Initiative, Esprit de corps.
  • Functions of Management: POSDCORB - Planning, Organising, Staffing, Directing, Coordinating, Reporting, Budgeting.
  • New Public Management: Entrepreneurial government, customer focus, results orientation, decentralisation, competition.
Mains strategy
Public Administration answers: concept → definition → theory/theorist → application → Indian context → way forward. Quote thinkers (Fayol, Taylor, Mayo, Weber, Simon, Barnard, Waldo, Hood, Riggs). Quote committees (ARC - 1st & 2nd Administrative Reforms Commission, Punchhi Commission, Sarkaria Commission). Quote data: India's civil servants (~4 million central + state employees), civil service reforms, e-governance initiatives.

opt-sociology/overview:
Sociology Optional — Syllabus Map & Strategy

Sociology is a two-paper optional of 250 marks each. Paper I covers the fundamentals of sociology; Paper II applies them to Indian society. The optional overlaps with GS I (Indian society, social justice) and GS II (governance, welfare schemes), so preparation does double duty.

Paper I — Fundamentals of Sociology

  • Introducing sociology: emergence, nature and scope; relationship with history, economics, political science, psychology and anthropology.
  • Research methods and analysis: qualitative and quantitative methods; ethnography, survey, case study, participant observation, interview, questionnaire and content analysis; objectivity and reflexivity.
  • Basic concepts: society, culture, social structure, social stratification, groups, institutions, social change, socialization, social control and social mobility.
  • Social institutions: family, marriage, kinship, religion, education, economy and polity — forms, functions and changing patterns.
  • Social stratification: caste, class, gender, race and ethnicity; functionalist, conflict and Weberian theories.
  • Social change: factors and processes; evolutionary, cyclical, conflict, modernization and globalization perspectives.
  • Socialization: agencies (family, school, peer group, media and religion), stages and gender socialization.

Paper II — Indian Society

  • Introducing Indian society: Indological, structural-functional, Marxist and subaltern perspectives; pluralism, hierarchy and holism.
  • Colonialism and its impact: changes in economy, polity, culture and education; emergence of nationalism.
  • Social structure: village community, jajmani system and caste ties; urbanization, slums and urban poverty; agrarian structure, land reforms and the Green Revolution.
  • Social change in India: Sanskritization, Westernization, modernization, globalization and liberalization; Dalit, women’s, environmental, farmers’ and tribal movements.
  • Social problems: poverty, unemployment, child labour, child marriage, domestic violence, communalism, regionalism and ethnic conflict.
  • Population: growth, policy, family planning, demographic transition, ageing and sex ratio.
  • Social policy and welfare: social justice, social security and schemes such as MGNREGA, NFSA, PMJAY, ICDS and Mid-Day Meal; implementation challenges.
Solved Example: Sanskritization
Question: Explain Sanskritization with examples.
Answer: M.N. Srinivas defined Sanskritization as the process by which a lower caste or tribe emulates the customs, rituals, diet and lifestyle of a higher caste to claim higher ritual status. Examples include Yadavs and Kurmis claiming Kshatriya status and tribal groups adopting vegetarianism and Sanskritic rituals. Critique: it changes ritual status more than structural hierarchy and can reinforce Sanskritic norms; Dalit assertion and regional variation qualify the model.

Key Thinkers

  • Auguste Comte: coined the term sociology in 1838; law of three stages.
  • Karl Marx: historical materialism, class conflict and alienation.
  • Emile Durkheim: social facts, division of labour, suicide and anomie.
  • Max Weber: interpretive sociology, ideal types, bureaucracy and the Protestant ethic.
  • Talcott Parsons and Robert Merton: structural functionalism; manifest and latent functions.
  • M.N. Srinivas, Andre Beteille and Yogendra Singh: Indian society, caste, village and social change.

Standard Sources

  • Haralambos & Holborn, Sociology: Themes and Perspectives
  • Anthony Giddens, Sociology
  • T.B. Bottomore, Sociology
  • Yogendra Singh, Modernization of Indian Tradition; Social Stratification in India
  • A.R. Desai, Social Background of Indian Nationalism
  • M.N. Srinivas, Caste in Modern India; The Remembered Village
  • Andre Beteille, Caste, Class and Power
  • NCERT Sociology, Classes XI–XII

Common Traps

  • Confusing sociology with individual psychology; sociology studies social relationships and structures.
  • Treating Sanskritization as a change in the material class structure rather than primarily ritual status.
  • Using caste and class interchangeably; they are distinct but related forms of stratification.
  • Presenting Indian society as static; emphasise change, contestation and regional variation.
  • Quoting outdated statistics without a date. Use Census 2011 (sex ratio 943; literacy 74.0%; SC 16.6%, ST 8.6%) and label later survey estimates separately.

Memory Tricks

  • Four pillars: society, culture, social structure, social institutions — SSCI.
  • Classical thinkers: Comte, Marx, Durkheim, Weber — CMDW.
  • Stratification: caste (ascribed, closed), class (achieved, open), gender, race and ethnicity.
  • Social change: Sanskritization, Westernization, modernization, globalization — SWMG.
Mains strategy
Answer structure: concept → definition → theory/theorist → application → Indian example → conclusion. Draw simple diagrams (stratification pyramid, family lineage, social-change model). Quote thinkers accurately. Keep a one-page data sheet from Census 2011 and the latest Economic Survey, and always date the figure you quote.

Sociology Paper I — Fundamentals of Sociology

Introducing Sociology

  • Emergence of sociology: Emerged in 19th century Europe due to industrial revolution, French Revolution, Enlightenment, scientific revolution. Key factors: industrialization, urbanization, secularization, rise of nation-states, colonialism.
  • Nature of sociology: Social science, empirical science, value-free (Weber), value-laden (Myrdal), interpretive vs positivist approaches.
  • Scope of sociology: Study of social relationships, social institutions, social groups, social institutions, social processes, social change, social problems.
  • Relationship with other social sciences: Anthropology (culture, primitive societies), Economics (production, distribution, consumption), Political Science (power, authority, state), Psychology (individual behavior), History (historical context), Geography (spatial distribution of population, resources).
  • Scope of sociology: Micro sociology (face-to-face interaction, small groups), Macro sociology (social institutions, social structure, social change), Micro-macro linkage.

Research Methods & Analysis

  • Scientific method: Observation, hypothesis formulation, data collection, data analysis, hypothesis testing, theory building, replication.
  • Research design: Experimental design, survey research, case study, ethnography, content analysis, historical-comparative research.
  • Data collection methods: Observation (participant, non-participant), interview (structured, semi-structured, unstructured), questionnaire, documents (primary, secondary sources), visual materials (photographs, films, videos).

Terms, Concepts & their Use in Sociological Analysis

  • Society: A group of people who share a common territory, interact with each other, and share a common culture.
  • Culture: Shared beliefs, values, norms, customs, practices, artifacts, symbols, language of a group or society.
  • Social structure: Patterned arrangement of institutions, groups, roles, statuses, and relationships that provide the framework for social interaction.
  • Social stratification: Hierarchical arrangement of individuals and groups based on wealth, power, prestige, prestige, education, occupation, race, ethnicity, gender.
  • Social groups: Primary groups (small, intimate, face-to-face interaction - family, peer group), Secondary groups (large, impersonal, task-oriented - organizations, bureaucracies, corporations).
  • Social institutions: Established patterns of behavior that satisfy basic human needs - family, education, religion, economy, polity, mass media.
  • Socialization: Process by which individuals learn the norms, values, beliefs, and behaviors of their society/culture - primary socialization (childhood, family), secondary socialization (adulthood, school, workplace, peer groups).
  • Social control: Mechanisms that encourage conformity to social norms - informal social control (gossip, ridicule, ostracism, social approval), formal social control (laws, police, courts, prisons).
  • Social mobility: Vertical mobility (upward or downward movement in social hierarchy), Horizontal mobility (movement within same social stratum), Intergenerational mobility (movement between generations), Intragenerational mobility (movement within one's lifetime).
  • Social change: Processes of change in social structure, social institutions, social relationships, social values, social norms - evolution, revolution, reform, diffusion, innovation, diffusion, cultural lag.

Statistics Optional — Overview

Statistics is a popular optional for mathematics/statistics graduates with good overlap with GS III (economy, data analysis) and essay. Paper I covers probability, probability distributions, sampling, statistical inference. Paper II covers linear models, design of experiments, sampling theory, quality control, operations research.

Paper I — Probability & Statistical Inference

  • Probability: Sample space, events, axioms of probability, conditional probability, Bayes' theorem, independence, random variables (discrete & continuous), probability mass function (pmf), probability density function (pdf), cumulative distribution function (cdf), expectation, variance, moments, moment generating function (mgf), characteristic function, probability generating function.
  • Distributions: Discrete: Bernoulli, binomial, Poisson, geometric, negative binomial, hypergeometric; Continuous: uniform, exponential, gamma, beta, normal (Gaussian), exponential, Cauchy, Laplace, Cauchy, logistic, Student's t, chi-square, F distribution.
  • Joint Distributions: Joint pmf/pdf, marginal distributions, conditional distributions, independence, covariance, correlation, conditional expectation, regression of Y on X, best linear predictor.
  • Convergence: Convergence in probability, almost sure convergence, convergence in distribution, law of large numbers (weak & strong), central limit theorem (CLT), Lindeberg-Lévy CLT, Lyapunov CLT.
  • Sampling Distributions: Sampling distribution of sample mean, sample variance, sample proportion, t-distribution, chi-square distribution, F-distribution, relationships between them.
  • Estimation: Point estimation (method of moments, maximum likelihood estimation - MLE, properties of MLE: consistency, efficiency, sufficiency, sufficiency via factorization theorem, completeness, completeness & sufficiency, UMVUE - uniformly minimum variance unbiased estimator, Rao-Blackwell theorem, Lehmann-Scheffe theorem), confidence intervals (for mean, proportion, difference of means, difference of proportions, ratio of variances).
  • Testing of Hypotheses: Null & alternative hypotheses, Type I & Type II errors, size & power of a test, most powerful test (MP), uniformly most powerful (UMP) test, Neyman-Pearson lemma, likelihood ratio test (LRT), likelihood ratio test (LRT) for various tests, p-value.
  • Non-parametric Tests: Sign test, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Wilcoxon rank-sum test (Mann-Whitney U test), Kruskal-Wallis test, runs test, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, chi-square test for goodness of fit, independence test (chi-square test of independence), Fisher's exact test.
  • Order Statistics: Distribution of order statistics, joint distribution of order statistics, distribution of sample range, sample median, sample quantiles, asymptotic distribution of sample quantiles.
Technique: MLE derivation
Question: 'Find the MLE of parameter θ for a random sample from Poisson(θ) distribution.'
Answer: Likelihood function: L(θ) = ∏(e^(-λ) λ^(x_i) / x_i!) = e^(-nλ) λ^(Σx_i) / ∏(x_i!). Log-likelihood: ℓ(λ) = -nλ + (Σx_i) log(λ) - Σ log(x_i!). Differentiate: ℓ'(λ) = -n + (Σx_i)/λ = 0 → λ̂ = (Σx_i)/n = x̄. Second derivative: ℓ''(λ) = -(Σx_i)/λ² < 0, so maximum. MLE of λ = x̄ (sample mean).

Memory Tricks

  • Distributions: Binomial (n, p) - fixed n trials, p success prob; Poisson (λ) - rare events, λ = mean; Geometric (p) - trials until first success; Negative binomial (r, p) - trials until r successes; Hypergeometric (N, K, n) - sampling without replacement.
  • Continuous: Uniform (a, b) - uniform density; Exponential (λ) - memoryless, memoryless property; Normal (μ, σ²) - bell curve, CLT; t (df) - small sample, unknown σ; Chi-square (df) - sum of squares of standard normals; F (df1, df2) - ratio of chi-squares.
  • Hypothesis Testing: H₀: null hypothesis (status quo), H₁: alternative (research hypothesis), Type I error (α = P(reject H₀ | H₀ true)), Type II error (β = P(fail to reject H₀ | H₁ false)), Power = 1 - β.
  • Estimators: Unbiased (E(θ̂) = θ), Consistent (θ̂ →p θ), Efficient (minimum variance), Sufficient (contains all info about θ), Complete (no non-zero function has expectation 0).
Mains strategy
Statistics answers: derive formulas step by step, show all assumptions, cite theorems (CLT, LLN, Rao-Blackwell, Lehmann-Scheffe, Neyman-Pearson), derive distributions step by step. Quote data: India's GDP growth, inflation rate, population growth, literacy rate, sex ratio, unemployment rate, poverty rate, industrial production index, wholesale price index (WPI), consumer price index (CPI), index of industrial production (IIP), foreign direct investment (FDI), foreign institutional investment (FII), balance of payments (BoP), balance of trade (BoT), fiscal deficit, revenue deficit, primary deficit, revenue deficit, effective revenue deficit, monetary policy (repo rate, reverse repo rate, CRR, SLR), inflation (headline inflation, core inflation, food inflation, fuel inflation), unemployment rate (UR), labor force participation rate (LFPR), worker population ratio (WPR), Gini coefficient, poverty headcount ratio (HCR), multidimensional poverty index (MPI), human development index (HDI), gender development index (GDI), gender inequality index (GII), environmental performance index (EPI), environmental performance index (EPI).

Statistics Paper I — Probability, Distributions & Inference

Probability Theory

  • Sample Space & Events: Sample space S (set of all possible outcomes), events (subsets of S), elementary events, compound events, mutually exclusive events, exhaustive events, mutually exclusive and exhaustive events.
  • Axioms of Probability (Kolmogorov): P(A) ≥ 0, P(S) = 1, P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) if A ∩ B = ∅, P(∅) = 0.
  • Conditional Probability: P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B), P(B) > 0.
  • Independence: P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B), P(A|B) = P(A) if independent.
  • Bayes' Theorem: P(Aᵢ|B) = P(B|Aᵢ)P(Aᵢ) / Σ P(B|Aⱼ)P(Aⱼ), prior probability, posterior probability, likelihood.
  • Random Variables: Discrete random variable (pmf), continuous random variable (pdf), mixed random variable, cumulative distribution function (cdf) F(x) = P(X ≤ x), properties of cdf.
  • Expectation & Moments: E[X] = Σ x·p(x) (discrete), E[X] = ∫ x·f(x)dx (continuous), properties: E[aX + b] = aE[X] + b, E[c] = c, variance Var(X) = E[(X - E[X])²] = E[X²] - (E[X])², standard deviation σ = √Var(X), moment generating function M_X(t) = E[e^(tX)], characteristic function φ_X(t) = E[e^(itX)], cumulant generating function K(t) = log M(t).
  • Higher Moments: Skewness (third standardized moment), kurtosis (fourth standardized moment), moment generating function properties, cumulant generating function, cumulants.

Standard Distributions

  • Discrete Distributions:
    • Bernoulli(p): P(X = 1) = p, P(X = 0) = 1-p, E = p, Var = p(1-p)
    • Binomial(n, p): P(X = k) = C(n,k) p^k (1-p)^(n-k), E = np, Var = np(1-p)
    • Poisson(λ): P(X = k) = e^(-λ) λ^k / k!, E = λ, Var = λ, rare events, large n small p approximation to binomial
    • Geometric(p): P(X = k) = (1-p)^(k-1) p, k = 1,2,..., E = 1/p, Var = (1-p)/p²
    • Negative Binomial (r, p): number of trials until r-th success, E = r/p
    • Hypergeometric(N, K, n): sampling without replacement, P(X = k) = C(K,k) C(N-K, n-k) / C(N,n)
  • Continuous Distributions:
    • Uniform(a, b): f(x) = 1/(b-a), a ≤ x ≤ b, E = (a+b)/2, Var = (b-a)²/12
    • Exponential(λ): f(x) = λe^(-λx), x ≥ 0, E = 1/λ, Var = 1/λ², memoryless property
    • Gamma(α, β): f(x) = (β^α / Γ(α)) x^(α-1) e^(-βx), x ≥ 0, E = α/β, Var = α/β²
    • Beta(α, β): f(x) = x^(α-1)(1-x)^(β-1) / B(α,β), 0 < x < 1
    • Normal(μ, σ²): f(x) = (1/√(2πσ²)) e^(-(x-μ)²/(2σ²)), E = μ, Var = σ², standard normal Z ~ N(0,1)
    • Chi-square (k df): sum of k independent standard normal squares, E = k, Var = 2k, used in goodness-of-fit, independence test
    • t-distribution (ν df): ratio of standard normal to sqrt(chi-square/df), heavier tails than normal
    • F-distribution (d1, d2 df): ratio of two independent chi-squares divided by degrees of freedom, used in ANOVA
  • Joint Distributions: Joint pmf/pdf, marginal distributions, conditional distributions, independence (f(x,y) = f_X(x) f_Y(y)), covariance Cov(X,Y) = E[(X-μ_X)(Y-μ_Y)], correlation ρ = Cov(X,Y)/(σ_X σ_Y), -1 ≤ ρ ≤ 1, conditional expectation E[Y|X=x], regression of Y on X, best linear predictor.
  • Convergence of Random Variables: Convergence in probability (X_n →p X), almost sure convergence (X_n → X a.s.), convergence in distribution (X_n →d X), relationships: a.s. convergence ⇒ convergence in probability ⇒ convergence in distribution, weak law of large numbers (WLLN), strong law of large numbers (SLLN), central limit theorem (CLT): (X̄_n - μ)/(σ/√n) →d N(0,1).
Technique: MLE for Poisson
Question: Find MLE of λ for X₁,...,X_n ~ Poisson(λ) i.i.d.
Answer: L(λ) = ∏ e^(-λ) λ^(x_i) / x_i! = e^(-nλ) λ^(Σx_i) / ∏x_i!, ℓ(λ) = -nλ + (Σx_i)log λ - Σlog(x_i!), ℓ'(λ) = -n + (Σx_i)/λ = 0, λ̂ = (Σx_i)/n = x̄, ℓ''(λ) = -(Σx_i)/λ² < 0, maximum at λ̂ = x̄.

Memory Tricks

  • Distribution relationships: Binomial(n, p) → Poisson(λ) as n→∞, p→0, np→λ; Binomial(n, p) → Normal(np, np(1-p)) as n→∞; Poisson(λ) → Normal(λ, λ) as λ→∞; Chi-square(k) → Normal(k, 2k) as k→∞.
  • Properties: Normal is closed under linear transformation, sum of independent normals is normal, sum of independent Poissons is Poisson, sum of independent binomials with same p is binomial, sum of independent exponentials is Gamma.
  • Moments: Mean = 1st moment, Variance = 2nd central moment, Skewness = 3rd standardized moment, Kurtosis = 4th standardized moment - 3 (excess kurtosis).
Mains strategy
Statistics answers: state assumptions clearly, write down the pdf/pmf, show derivation step by step, state theorems by name (CLT, LLN, Neyman-Pearson, Rao-Blackwell, Lehmann-Scheffe), verify assumptions before applying tests, show all steps in derivations. Data: India's population growth rate, literacy rate, sex ratio, infant mortality rate, life expectancy, GDP growth rate, inflation rate, unemployment rate, poverty headcount ratio.
opt-statistics/paper2:
Statistics Paper II — Statistical Inference & Sampling

Sampling Distributions

  • Sampling Distributions: Sample mean distribution (μx̄ = μ, σ_x̄ = σ/√n), sample proportion (p̂ ~ N(p, p(1-p)/n)), difference of means (X̄1 - X̄2 ~ N(μ1-μ2, σ₁²/n₁ + σ₂²/n₂)), difference of proportions.
  • Central Limit Theorem: For large n (n ≥ 30), X̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n) regardless of population distribution; applies to sample means and proportions.
  • Confidence Intervals: CI = point estimate ± margin of error; margin of error = critical value × standard error; z-interval vs t-interval; confidence level interpretation.
  • Sample Size Determination: n = (z_α/2 × σ / E)² for mean; n = (z_α/2)² p̂(1-p̂)/E² for proportion; finite population correction factor.

Hypothesis Testing

  • Hypothesis Testing: Null hypothesis (H₀) vs alternative hypothesis (H₁), null hypothesis contains equality (=, ≤, ≥), alternative contains ≠, <, or >.
  • Type I & Type II Errors: Type I error (reject true H₀, probability α), Type II error (fail to reject false H₀, probability β), power of test = 1 - β.
  • Test Statistics: z-test (σ known, n large), t-test (σ unknown, n small), chi-square test (variance/independence), F-test (ratio of variances).
  • p-value Approach: p-value = P(test statistic ≥ observed | H₀ true); reject H₀ if p-value ≤ α.
  • Two-Sample Tests: Difference of means (independent samples: pooled vs unpooled variance), paired samples (paired t-test), difference of proportions.
  • Chi-Square Tests: Goodness-of-fit test (observed vs expected frequencies), test of independence (contingency table), test of homogeneity.
  • F-Distribution: F-distribution (ratio of two chi-square variables divided by dfs), F-test for equality of variances (F = s₁²/s₂²), ANOVA (one-way & two-way).

Linear Regression & Correlation

  • Correlation: Pearson correlation coefficient (r = Σ(x-x̄)(y-ȳ)/√(Σ(x-x̄)²Σ(y-ȳ)²)), range [-1, 1], interpretation (strength & direction), coefficient of determination (R² = proportion of variance explained).

Technique: Confidence Interval for Mean
Question: n=36, x̄=50, s=12, find 95% CI for μ.
Answer: Since n ≥ 30, use z-distribution: z_0.025 = 1.96. SE = s/√n = 12/√36 = 2. Margin of error = 1.96 × 2 = 3.92. CI: 50 ± 3.92 = (46.08, 53.92). Interpretation: We are 95% confident the true population mean lies between 46.08 and 53.92.

Memory Tricks

  • Confidence Level: 90% → z=1.645, 95% → z=1.96, 99% → z=2.576 (memorize these three!).
  • t-distribution vs z-distribution: Use t when σ unknown AND n < 30; use z when σ known OR n ≥ 30.
  • p-value rule: If p-value ≤ α, reject H₀; if p-value > α, fail to reject H₀ (small p-value = strong evidence against H₀).
  • Confidence Interval width: Increases with confidence level, decreases with sample size, increases with population variability.

opt-statistics/paper3:
Statistics Paper III — Sampling Theory & Official Statistics

Sampling Theory

  • Simple Random Sampling: SRSWR and SRSWOR, unbiased estimator of population mean ȳ = (1/n)Σy_i, Var(ȳ) = (1-f)S²/n where f = n/N is sampling fraction, S² = (1/(N-1))Σ(y_i - ȳ_N)², estimated variance: ŝ² = (1/n)(1 - n/N)S² where S² = (1/(n-1))Σ(y_i - ȳ)², confidence interval: ȳ ± t_(α/2, n-1) × SE(ȳ).
  • Stratified Random Sampling: Population divided into H strata, N_h units in stratum h, sample n_h from stratum h, sample mean ȳ_st = Σ(W_h ȳ_h) where W_h = N_h/N, Var(ȳ_st) = Σ(W_h²(1-f_h)S_h²/n_h) where f_h = n_h/N_h, proportional allocation n_h = n(N_h/N), optimal allocation (Neyman): n_h ∝ N_hS_h (minimize variance for fixed cost), cost-optimal allocation (minimize cost for fixed variance), gain from stratification: Var(ȳ_ran) - Var(ȳ_st) = ΣW_h(μ_h - ȳ)² - ΣW_hS_h²/n_h + (1/n)ΣW_hS_h² - (1/n)ΣW_h²S_h²/n_h ... actually Var(ȳ_st) = ΣW_h²S_h²/n_h(1-f_h), gain = S_b² - ΣW_hS_h²/n_h where S_b² = ΣW_h(μ_h - ȳ)² is between-stratum variance.
  • Systematic Sampling: Select every k-th unit where k = N/n (sampling interval), start randomly between 1 and k, Var(ȳ_sys) = (1-f)S²/n when population randomly ordered, Var(ȳ_sys) < Var(ȳ_SRS) when population ordered monotonically (periodic variation aligned with k increases variance), systematic sampling is more efficient than SRS when population is ordered (periodic or monotonic), less efficient when population has periodic variation matching sampling interval.
  • Cluster Sampling: Two-stage sampling: select n₁ PSUs (primary sampling units), then n₂ SSUs (secondary sampling units) from each selected PSU, Var(ȳ_2stage) = (1-f₁)S₁²/n₁ + (1-f₂)S₂²/(n₁n₂) where S₁² = between-PSU variance, S₂² = within-PSU variance, intraclass correlation ρ = S_b²/(S_b² + S_w²), design effect DEFF = 1 + (m-1)ρ where m = n₂ (number of SSUs per PSU), DEFF > 1 means cluster sampling less efficient than SRS of same size, DEFF < 1 means more efficient.
  • Multistage Sampling: Three-stage sampling: select n₁ PSUs, then n₂ SSUs from each, then n₃ tertiary units from each SSU, Var increases with more stages, cost considerations: C = C₀ + n₁c₁ + n₁n₂c₂ + n₁n₂n₃c₃, optimal allocation minimizes variance for fixed cost or minimizes cost for fixed variance.
  • Ratio & Regression Estimators: Ratio estimator: ȳ_R = (ȳ/x̄)X̄, bias ≈ (1/n)(θ̄_x/μ_x)(S_y²/σ_y² - ρσ_y/σ_x), MSE ≈ (1-f)(1/n)(S_y² + R²S_x² - 2ρS_yS_x), regression estimator: ȳ_reg = ȳ + β(x̄ - x̄_0), β = S_xy/S_x², Var(ȳ_reg) = (1-f)(1/n)(S_y² - ρ²S_y²) = (1-f)(S_y²/n)(1-ρ²), regression estimator more efficient when ρ² > 0 (correlation between auxiliary variable x and study variable y), ratio estimator more efficient when ρ > 0 and relationship passes through origin.
  • Double Sampling: Two-phase sampling: Phase 1: measure auxiliary variable x on large sample n₁, Phase 2: measure study variable y on subsample n₂ ⊂ n₁, ratio estimator with estimated population mean: ȳ_R = (ȳ₂/x̄₂)X̄ where x̄₂ is mean of x in phase 2 sample, or use x̄₁ from phase 1: ȳ_R = (ȳ₂/x̄₂)x̄₁, variance: Var(ȳ_R) ≈ (1-f₁)(S_y²/n₁) + (1-f₂)(S_y²/n₂) - 2ρS_y²/n₂ approximately, optimal allocation: n₁/n₂ = S_y√(1-ρ²)/(S_y√(ρ²) + C₂/C₁ something like that... actually optimal: n₂/n₁ = S_y√(1-ρ²)/(c₂(S_y√(1-ρ²) + c₁S_y)) ... complex formula, approximately n₂/n₁ = S_y√(1-ρ²)/(S_y√(ρ²)) ... approximately n₂/n₁ = √((1-ρ²)/ρ²) ... let me just say optimal allocation balances cost and variance.

Sampling Theory - Advanced Topics

  • Ratio Estimator Properties: Ratio estimator is biased but consistent, bias ≈ (1/n)(θ̄_x/μ_x)(S_y²/σ_y² - ρσ_y/σ_x), bias is O(1/n), MSE = Var + Bias² ≈ (1-f)(1/n)(S_y² + R²S_x² - 2ρS_yS_x), ratio estimator more efficient than ȳ when ρ > S_x/(2S_y) approximately, i.e., when correlation is high and x is not too variable relative to y.
  • Regression Estimator: ȳ_reg = ȳ + β̂(x̄ - x̄_0), β̂ = S_xy/S_x², Var(ȳ_reg) = (1-f)(1/n)(S_y²(1-ρ²)), regression estimator more efficient than ratio estimator when ρ² > 0 (always better than SRS when ρ ≠ 0), more efficient than ratio estimator when relationship doesn't pass through origin.
  • Ratio vs Regression Estimator: Ratio estimator assumes linear relationship through origin, regression estimator allows intercept, regression estimator more efficient when relationship doesn't pass through origin, ratio estimator simpler but more restrictive.

Sampling Theory - Advanced Topics II

  • Ratio Estimator Properties: Ratio estimator is biased but consistent, bias ≈ (1/n)(θ̄_x/μ_x)(S_y²/σ_y² - ρσ_y/σ_x), bias is O(1/n), MSE = Var + Bias² ≈ (1-f)(1/n)(S_y² + R²S_x² - 2ρS_yS_x), ratio estimator more efficient than ȳ when ρ > S_x/(2S_y) approximately, i.e., when correlation is high and x is not too variable relative to y.
  • Regression Estimator: ȳ_reg = ȳ + β̂(x̄ - x̄_0), β̂ = S_xy/S_x², Var(ȳ_reg) = (1-f)(1/n)(S_y² - ρ²S_y²) = (1-f)(S_y²/n)(1-ρ²), regression estimator more efficient than ȳ when ρ² > 0 (always better than SRS when ρ ≠ 0), more efficient than ratio estimator when relationship doesn't pass through origin.
  • Ratio vs Regression Estimator: Ratio estimator: linear relationship through origin, regression estimator: linear relationship with intercept, regression estimator more efficient when relationship doesn't pass through origin, ratio estimator simpler but more restrictive.
  • Ratio vs Regression Estimator: Ratio estimator: linear relationship through origin, regression estimator allows intercept, regression estimator more efficient when relationship doesn't pass through origin, ratio estimator simpler but more restrictive.
Technique: Ratio Estimator
Question: Estimate total yield Y from sample: n=50 farms, sample mean yield ȳ=2.5 tons/ha, sample mean area x̄=5 ha, total area X̄=10,000 ha.
Answer: Ratio estimator ȳ_R = (ȳ/x̄)X̄ = (2.5/5)×10,000 = 5,000 tons. Variance: Var(ȳ_R) ≈ (1-f)(1/n)(S_y² + R²S_x² - 2ρS_yS_x), assuming ρ=0.8, S_y=1.5, S_x=2: Var ≈ (1-50/1000)(1/50)(1.5² - 2(0.8)(1.5)(2) + 0.5²×2²) = 0.95(0.02)(2.25 - 4.8 + 4) = 0.95(0.02)(1.25) = 0.02375. SE(ȳ_R) ≈ √0.02375 = 0.154 tons/ha. Total estimate: 5,000 ± 1.96×0.154×100 = 5,000 ± 154 tons.

Memory Tricks

  • SRS Variance: Var(ȳ) = (1-f)S²/n, where f = n/N is sampling fraction, S² = population variance.
  • Stratified Sampling: Var(ȳ_st) = ΣW_h²S_h²/n_h(1-f_h), optimal allocation n_h ∝ N_hS_h (Neyman allocation), proportional allocation n_h = n(N_h/N).
  • Cluster Sampling: Var(ȳ_c) = (1-f₁)S₁²/n₁ + (1-f₂)S₂²/(n₁n₂), DEFF = 1 + (m-1)ρ, DEFF > 1 means cluster sampling less efficient than SRS.
  • Ratio Estimator: ȳ_R = (ȳ/x̄)X̄, more efficient when ρ > S_x/(2S_y) approximately.
  • Regression Estimator: ȳ_reg = ȳ + β̂(x̄ - x̄_0), Var(ȳ_reg) = (1-f)(1/n)(S_y² - ρ²S_y²) = (1-f)(S_y²/n)(1-ρ²), more efficient than ratio estimator when relationship doesn't pass through origin.
Mains strategy
